A 47-year-old man comes to the office because he has coughed up blood five times during the past 2 weeks. During this time, he also has had shortness of breath, temperatures to 38.1°C (100.6°F), and progressive fatigue. He has had a 4.5-kg (10-lb) weight loss during the past 4 months despite no change in appetite. During the past 6 years, he has had chronic nasal congestion and 10 episodes of sinusitis. He does not smoke cigarettes or drink alcohol. He is sexually active and monogamous with his wife. He works as a chemical engineer. His temperature is 37.7°C (99.9°F), pulse is 84/min, respirations are 22/min, and blood pressure is 130/80 mm Hg. Scattered crackles are heard bilaterally. The remainder of the examination shows no abnormalities. Laboratory studies show:
Hematocrit33%
Leukocyte count12,000/mm³
Serum
Urea nitrogen30 mg/dL
Creatinine2 mg/dL
Urine RBC casts2/lpf

Results of a sputum culture are negative. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.stemHtml:
A 47-year-old man comes to the office because he has coughed up blood five times during the past 2 weeks. During this time, he also has had shortness of breath, temperatures to 38.1°C (100.6°F), and progressive fatigue. He has had a 4.5-kg (10-lb) weight loss during the past 4 months despite no change in appetite. During the past 6 years, he has had chronic nasal congestion and 10 episodes of sinusitis. He does not smoke cigarettes or drink alcohol. He is sexually active and monogamous with his wife. He works as a chemical engineer. His temperature is 37.7°C (99.9°F), pulse is 84/min, respirations are 22/min, and blood pressure is 130/80 mm Hg. Scattered crackles are heard bilaterally. The remainder of the examination shows no abnormalities. Laboratory studies show:

Hematocrit33%
Leukocyte count12,000/mm³
Serum
Urea nitrogen30 mg/dL
Creatinine2 mg/dL
Urine RBC casts2/lpf

Results of a sputum culture are negative. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.subject: Rheumatology

explanationPanel.whyCorrect:
Educational Objective: This patient most likely has granulomatosis with

polyangiitis (GPA). GPA is a necrotizing small-and medium-vessel vasculitis that primarily affects the lungs, sinuses, kidneys, and skin. Manifestations include recurrent sinusitis, epistaxis, hemoptysis, and renal dysfunction including nephritic syndrome.

Evaluation: Patients typically present with constitutional symptoms such as fever, weight

loss, and fatigue, with additional symptoms based on specific organ involvement. Sinopulmonary manifestations include chronic nasal congestion, recurrent sinusitis, otitis media, mastoiditis, nasal ulcerations with epistaxis, hemoptysis, cough, and dyspnea. The

kidneys are typically involved, and patients often present with hematuria with an increased risk for developing rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis and renal failure. Skin lesions are common, especially lower extremity purpura.

Definition: GPA is a systemic necrotizing granulomatous vasculitis that affects small and

medium vessels. It is associated with antineutrophil cytoplasmic autoantibody and primarily affects the sinopulmonary tract, kidneys, and skin.

Prevention: There are no known ways to prevent GPA. Prompt diagnosis and treatment

are necessary to prevent progression and more severe sequelae of the disease.

Treatment: Treatment to induce remission typically involves corticosteroids in combination

with rituximab or methotrexate, or with cyclophosphamide for severe, life-threatening disease.

Differential: Of the inflammatory conditions listed, GPA classically affects the sinuses,

which narrows the differential.

wrongAnswers.A: Goodpasture syndrome is incorrect. Goodpasture syndrome is caused by antibodies against collagen, type IV, which is found predominantly in pulmonary capillaries and glomerular basement membranes. Features include hemoptysis and hematuria, which can progress to diffuse alveolar hemorrhage and glomerulonephritis, respectively. Sinonasal manifestations are uncommon.
wrongAnswers.C: Polyarteritis nodosa is incorrect. This medium-vessel necrotizing vasculitis predominantly affects the renal and gastrointestinal organ systems, sparing the lungs. Polyarteritis nodosa typically presents with systemic inflammatory symptoms, hypertension, renal damage, renal microaneurysms, abdominal pain, and melena. Skin lesions may include nodules, purpura, ulcers, vesicles, or bullae.
wrongAnswers.D: Sarcoidosis is incorrect. This idiopathic inflammatory disease results in the formation of noncaseating granulomas in a variety of involved organs, often involving the lungs. Pulmonary manifestations include dry cough and shortness of breath; hemoptysis and sinus involvement are uncommon.
wrongAnswers.E:
Tuberculosis is incorrect. While tuberculosis does present with fevers, night sweats, and hemoptysis, it is unlikely given this patient’s lack of risk factors such as

immigration from, or frequent travel to, an endemic country, and living or working in a crowded environment where tuberculosis is most likely to spread.

explanationPanel.rule: Chronic sinus disease plus hemoptysis and nephritic urine findings is granulomatosis with polyangiitis.
explanationPanel.trap: Goodpasture causes lung-kidney disease but does not cause chronic sinusitis or upper-airway granulomatous disease.

layer4.rule: Chronic sinus disease plus hemoptysis and nephritic urine findings is granulomatosis with polyangiitis.
layer4.trap: Goodpasture causes lung-kidney disease but does not cause chronic sinusitis or upper-airway granulomatous disease.

questions.stem: A 7-year-old girl is brought to the clinic by her mother because of increasing concerns about the child's impulsive behavior. The patient was adopted at the age of 6 years after having lived with her parents for 18 months in foster care. The mother says that the patient "has no fear" when interacting with adult strangers and does not seem to understand social boundaries. The patient will walk up to strangers at the store to start talking to them, hug them, or ask them to pick her up and hold her. The mother says she hates taking the patient to the store because the child will wander off "without a care in the world." The mother is distressed and adds that the patient "could be separated from us for hours and it wouldn't faze her!" The principal at her school recently reported that at dismissal the patient approached the car of a parent she did not know and asked the driver to give her a ride home. The mother says that the patient's appetite and sleep have been normal. The patient has no history of serious illness and receives no medications. Prior to foster care placement with her parents, the patient had lived with four different foster families since the age of 2 years. She was removed from her biological mother's care at the age of 9 months when the biological mother was sent to prison. Initial attempts to place the patient with family members failed because of neglect and abuse allegations. Vital signs are within normal limits. Physical examination discloses no abnormalities. Mental status examination shows a happy mood and full range of affect. There is no evidence of psychosis or suicidal or homicidal ideation. Which of the following is the most likely explanation for this patient's behavior?
questions.stemHtml: A 7-year-old girl is brought to the clinic by her mother because of increasing concerns about the child's impulsive behavior. The patient was adopted at the age of 6 years after having lived with her parents for 18 months in foster care. The mother says that the patient "has no fear" when interacting with adult strangers and does not seem to understand social boundaries. The patient will walk up to strangers at the store to start talking to them, hug them, or ask them to pick her up and hold her. The mother says she hates taking the patient to the store because the child will wander off "without a care in the world." The mother is distressed and adds that the patient "could be separated from us for hours and it wouldn't faze her!" The principal at her school recently reported that at dismissal the patient approached the car of a parent she did not know and asked the driver to give her a ride home. The mother says that the patient's appetite and sleep have been normal. The patient has no history of serious illness and receives no medications. Prior to foster care placement with her parents, the patient had lived with four different foster families since the age of 2 years. She was removed from her biological mother's care at the age of 9 months when the biological mother was sent to prison. Initial attempts to place the patient with family members failed because of neglect and abuse allegations. Vital signs are within normal limits. Physical examination discloses no abnormalities. Mental status examination shows a happy mood and full range of affect. There is no evidence of psychosis or suicidal or homicidal ideation. Which of the following is the most likely explanation for this patient's behavior?
questions.subject: Psychiatry

explanationPanel.whyCorrect:
Educational Objective: The most likely explanation for this patient's behavior is

disinhibited social engagement disorder (DSED). Thought to result from childhood neglect, DSED presents with disinhibited and overfamiliar social behavior.

Evaluation: DSED is a psychiatric condition in children that presents with disinhibited and

overfamiliar social behavior. Patients commonly approach unfamiliar adults and avoid checking with their primary caregivers.

Definition: Patients have typically experienced severe neglect by caregivers, leading to a

lack of selective attachment to caregivers. DSED is especially common in children in foster care. Diagnosis typically requires a comprehensive assessment with structured interviews and measures.

Prevention: DSED can be prevented by minimizing institutional care and cultivating

nurturing relationships with primary caregivers.

Treatment: Attachment-based psychotherapy and increasing environmental stability (eg,

minimizing frequent moves or changes in caregivers) can treat DSED.

Differential: Reactive attachment disorder also results from caregiver neglect or abuse but

presents with inhibited or withdrawn social behavior rather than overly familiar social behavior.

wrongAnswers.A: Attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder is incorrect. Attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder presents with chronic symptoms of hyperactivity/impulsivity and/or inattention that occur in more than one setting and impair academic, social, and/or emotional function. This patient’s hyperactivity occurs in the setting of attachment disruption and does not involve inattentive symptoms, making DSED more likely.
wrongAnswers.B: Autism spectrum disorder (ASD) is incorrect. ASD is also characterized by difficulty in social relationships, though patients with ASD are typically inhibited rather than overfamiliar. Patients with ASD also demonstrate repetitive language and restricted interests.
wrongAnswers.D: Impulse control disorder is incorrect. Impulse control disorders are a group of psychiatric conditions involving the inability to resist an impulse or drive to do a harmful action (eg, gambling, kleptomania, trichotillomania). This patient’s overfamiliarity occurs in the context of attachment difficulties rather than impulse dyscontrol.
wrongAnswers.E: Reactive attachment disorder is incorrect. Reactive attachment disorder also results from caregiver neglect or abuse but presents with inhibited or withdrawn social behavior rather than overly familiar social behavior, making DSED more likely.

explanationPanel.rule: Severe early neglect with indiscriminate overfamiliarity toward strangers is disinhibited social engagement disorder.
explanationPanel.trap: Reactive attachment disorder is the inhibited/withdrawn attachment disorder, not the overly familiar one.

layer4.rule: Severe early neglect with indiscriminate overfamiliarity toward strangers is disinhibited social engagement disorder.
layer4.trap: Reactive attachment disorder is the inhibited/withdrawn attachment disorder, not the overly familiar one.

questions.stem: A 4-year-old boy is admitted to the hospital because of a 6-month history of difficulty passing stool. He has no history of serious illness. He receives no medications. Height, weight, and BMI are at the 50th percentile. Vital signs are within normal limits. Physical examination shows a distended, nontender abdomen. Contrast enema imaging is shown. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
questions.stemHtml: A 4-year-old boy is admitted to the hospital because of a 6-month history of difficulty passing stool. He has no history of serious illness. He receives no medications. Height, weight, and BMI are at the 50th percentile. Vital signs are within normal limits. Physical examination shows a distended, nontender abdomen. Contrast enema imaging is shown. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
choices: Resection of the normal caliber bowel
questions.subject: Pediatrics/Neonatology

explanationPanel.whyCorrect:
Educational Objective: This young patient presents with difficulty passing stool and

a contrast enema notable for a transition zone between the lower and upper colon, which is suggestive of congenital megacolon (Hirschsprung disease). The most appropriate next step in management is a suction rectal biopsy to confirm the diagnosis.

Evaluation: Hirschsprung disease is a congenital disorder thought to result from defective

migration of neural crest cells, resulting in the absence of ganglion cells in the myenteric and submucosal plexuses of the intestine. This leads to a functional bowel obstruction. Classically, Hirschsprung disease presents in the neonatal period; however, patients with less severe disease can remain undiagnosed until childhood.

Definition: The gold standard for diagnosis of Hirschsprung disease is a suction rectal

biopsy notable for the absence of ganglion cells.

Prevention: There are no known strategies to prevent Hirschsprung disease.

Treatment: Treatment involves surgical resection of the aganglionic segment of colon.

Differential: The differential diagnosis in a child with concern for Hirschsprung disease

includes functional constipation, bowel obstruction, hypothyroidism, and internal anal sphincter achalasia. However, the results of this patient’s contrast enema make those less likely than Hirschsprung disease.

wrongAnswers.A: Abdominal ultrasonography is incorrect. It has a variety of uses but would be unable to provide information regarding innervation of the bowel.
wrongAnswers.B: Air-contrast enema is incorrect. Air-contrast enema is commonly used for the diagnosis and treatment of intussusception. This patient does not have symptoms consistent with intussusception.
wrongAnswers.D: Resection of the dilated bowel is incorrect. The dilated bowel indicates normal bowel that is not aganglionic, but rather is dilated due to distal stricture at the level of the aganglionic bowel, resulting, in this case, in a partial obstruction pattern.
wrongAnswers.E: Resection of the normal caliber bowel is incorrect. This can be a therapeutic option after confirmation of a diagnosis of Hirschsprung disease; however, the most appropriate next step in management is rectal biopsy to first confirm the diagnosis.
wrongAnswers.F: Sigmoid biopsy is incorrect. In this case, the sigmoid colon is not the section of colon that is aganglionic.

explanationPanel.rule: Contrast enema transition zone suggests Hirschsprung disease, which is confirmed with suction rectal biopsy.
explanationPanel.trap: Do not resect bowel before biopsy confirmation; the dilated segment is normally innervated upstream bowel.

questions.stem: A 33-year-old woman, gravida 3, para 1, aborta 1, at 27 weeks' gestation comes to the office for a routine prenatal visit. She feels well and pregnancy has been uncomplicated. She reports good fetal movement. She has no history of serious illness. Medications are an oral prenatal vitamin and oral iron supplementation. The patient has been following a vegan diet since the start of pregnancy. Fundal height is 26 cm. Fetal heart tones are 143/min. Hemoglobin concentration is 11.2 g/dL. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
questions.stemHtml: A 33-year-old woman, gravida 3, para 1, aborta 1, at 27 weeks' gestation comes to the office for a routine prenatal visit. She feels well and pregnancy has been uncomplicated. She reports good fetal movement. She has no history of serious illness. Medications are an oral prenatal vitamin and oral iron supplementation. The patient has been following a vegan diet since the start of pregnancy. Fundal height is 26 cm. Fetal heart tones are 143/min. Hemoglobin concentration is 11.2 g/dL. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
choices: Addition of intravenous iron supplementation to the regimen
Recommendation to add more soy to the patient's diet
No further management is indicated at this time
questions.subject: Obstetrics

explanationPanel.correct: E. No further management is indicated at this time
explanationPanel.whyCorrect:
Educational Objective: This pregnant patient presents with mild anemia during a

routine prenatal visit. Despite her vegan diet, mild anemia is expected during pregnancy, and no further management is indicated currently.

Key Concept: Normal hemoglobin concentrations in pregnant patients are greater than

11.0 g/dL in the first and third trimesters and greater than 10.5 g/dL in the second trimester. Explanation: Mild anemia is common during pregnancy because of an increase in circulating plasma volume that is out of proportion to the increase in hemoglobin needed to supply oxygen to the developing fetus. However, other causes of anemia, such as folic acid, iron, and vitamin B12 (cobalamin) deficiencies should be excluded when anemia is more significant than expected. Vitamin B12 concentrations may be decreased in vegan diets, and a deficiency can result in megaloblastic anemia. Symptoms include pallor, fatigue, and light-headedness. Neurologic symptoms, such as dementia, ataxia, muscle weakness, paresthesia, loss of proprioception and vibration sensation, and abnormal deep tendon reflexes, can occur in severe cases.

Differential: This patient’s hemoglobin is at an expected concentration for 27 weeks'

gestation. Additionally, she is taking a multivitamin, which decreases the risk for significant

nutritional deficiencies associated with her vegan diet.

wrongAnswers.A: Addition of intravenous iron supplementation to the regimen is incorrect. Intravenous iron is used in the treatment of iron deficiency anemia, which is a common cause of anemia in pregnant patients. Intravenous iron is classically reserved for severe cases of anemia or in those patients who cannot tolerate oral supplementation of iron. This patient has mild anemia that would be expected at her gestational age.
wrongAnswers.B: Nonstress testing is incorrect. Nonstress tests are used to evaluate fetal health by examining the fetal heart rate over a period of 20 to 30 minutes. This patient’s mild anemia does not place her child at risk for adverse outcomes that would warrant a nonstress test.
wrongAnswers.C: Pelvic ultrasonography is incorrect. Significant anemia can lead to fetal growth restriction. However, this patient’s anemia is mild, and her fundal height is consistent with her gestational age. As such, pelvic ultrasonography is not warranted.
wrongAnswers.D: Recommendation to add more soy to the patient’s diet is incorrect. While soy is an important source of protein for a patient with a vegan diet, additional soy is not indicated based on the information provided. Adding more soy may be warranted if the patient was failing to gain weight or if her fetus was small for gestational age due to suspected nutritional deficiency.

explanationPanel.rule: Hemoglobin above the trimester threshold in pregnancy is physiologic; no additional management is needed.
explanationPanel.trap: A vegan diet alone does not mandate IV iron or imaging when hemoglobin and fundal height are acceptable.

layer4.rule: Hemoglobin above the trimester threshold in pregnancy is physiologic; no additional management is needed.
layer4.trap: A vegan diet alone does not mandate IV iron or imaging when hemoglobin and fundal height are acceptable.

questions.stem: A 33-year-old resident is undergoing his last year of training. Recently, some of his co-residents have become concerned about the frequency of the resident's partying and drinking excessive amounts of alcohol outside of work. These residents have never noticed him impaired at work. When questioned by one of the co-residents, the resident states he is having stressful life issues. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step by the co-residents?
questions.stemHtml: A 33-year-old resident is undergoing his last year of training. Recently, some of his co-residents have become concerned about the frequency of the resident's partying and drinking excessive amounts of alcohol outside of work. These residents have never noticed him impaired at work. When questioned by one of the co-residents, the resident states he is having stressful life issues. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step by the co-residents?
choices: Discuss the concerns with the program director
Encourage the resident to take a physician substance abuse course
Offer to cover a work shift of the resident so he can rest
Report the resident to the state medical board
questions.subject: Ethics/Social Sciences

explanationPanel.correct: A. Discuss the concerns with the program director
explanationPanel.whyCorrect:
Educational Objective: If a co-resident notices a resident struggling with their

mental health or with substance misuse, they should discuss the concerns with their program director. The program director can provide supportive interventions that may prevent work impairment and patient safety issues.

Key Concept: Substance misuse, especially of alcohol and benzodiazepines, is relatively

common among medical trainees. For residents struggling with substance misuse or mental health concerns, residency program leadership can provide supportive interventions, which can be especially beneficial if the problem is caught early. Thus, resident colleagues who observe a resident excessively using a substance should notify the residency program director. Explanation: Detecting and addressing substance use in medical trainees is important given trainees’ access to controlled substances and, in severe cases, patient safety concerns. It is recommended that residency programs drug test residents and, if substances are detected, provide supportive rather than punitive interventions to prevent exacerbation of the problem.

Differential: In the absence of concern about work impairment, there is no need for

colleagues to report physicians to physician impairment programs.

wrongAnswers.B: Encourage the resident to take a physician substance abuse course is inappropriate. This intervention may be appropriate for a residency program director to recommend, but not a peer.
wrongAnswers.C: Offer to cover a work shift of the resident so he can rest is incorrect. This option neglects an opportunity for early intervention on this resident’s mental health and substance misuse.
wrongAnswers.D: Report the resident to the state medical board is unnecessary. If a physician is suspected of being impaired at work, a colleague can report the physician to a physician impairment program, which can determine whether to report the physician to the state medical board. In the absence of concern about work impairment, there is no need for colleagues to report physicians to physician impairment programs.
wrongAnswers.E: No further intervention is indicated is incorrect. This option neglects an opportunity for early intervention on this resident’s mental health and substance misuse.

explanationPanel.rule: Concerns about a resident’s substance misuse without work impairment should be discussed with the program director for supportive intervention.
explanationPanel.trap: State board reporting is for impairment/patient-safety risk, not early peer concern outside work.

layer4.rule: Concerns about a resident’s substance misuse without work impairment should be discussed with the program director for supportive intervention.
layer4.trap: State board reporting is for impairment/patient-safety risk, not early peer concern outside work.

questions.stem: A 62-year-old man comes to the office because of a 4-month history of generalized, dull morning headaches. The pain gradually improves within 1 hour of awakening. He also has a 5-year history of fatigue and daytime sleepiness that causes him embarrassment. He lives alone and says he sleeps 9 hours nightly and only awakens once to urinate. He adds that he began exercising less and gaining weight after retiring from his job 2 years ago. He has major depressive disorder treated with sertraline. He is 173 cm (5 ft 8 in) tall and weighs 102 kg (225 lb); BMI is 34 kg/m². Temperature is 37.0°C (98.6°F), pulse is 76/min, respirations are 16/min, and blood pressure is 126/72 mm Hg. Physical examination shows no papilledema or scalp tenderness. Cardiopulmonary examination discloses no abnormalities. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
questions.stemHtml: A 62-year-old man comes to the office because of a 4-month history of generalized, dull morning headaches. The pain gradually improves within 1 hour of awakening. He also has a 5-year history of fatigue and daytime sleepiness that causes him embarrassment. He lives alone and says he sleeps 9 hours nightly and only awakens once to urinate. He adds that he began exercising less and gaining weight after retiring from his job 2 years ago. He has major depressive disorder treated with sertraline. He is 173 cm (5 ft 8 in) tall and weighs 102 kg (225 lb); BMI is 34 kg/m². Temperature is 37.0°C (98.6°F), pulse is 76/min, respirations are 16/min, and blood pressure is 126/72 mm Hg. Physical examination shows no papilledema or scalp tenderness. Cardiopulmonary examination discloses no abnormalities. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
questions.subject: Pulmonology

explanationPanel.whyCorrect:
Educational Objective: This patient with obesity, fatigue, daytime sleepiness, and

morning headaches most likely has obstructive sleep apnea hypopnea syndrome (OSAHS). The most appropriate next step in management is a sleep study.

Evaluation: OSAHS classically presents with loud snoring, daytime sleepiness, fatigue,

poor concentration, and morning headaches. Hypertension, especially during the mornings, is common.

Definition: OSAHS features repetitive obstruction of the pharyngeal airway during sleep

and typically occurs in patients with obesity due to a combination of structural, vascular, and neuromuscular factors. Though older male patients are most affected, younger and female patients may also have the disorder. Patients commonly experience hypoxemia several times nightly with fragmented sleep. Untreated OSAHS patients are at increased risk for adverse cardiovascular outcomes, including stroke, as well as polycythemia, pulmonary hypertension, and right ventricular dysfunction, if severe.

Prevention: The most important preventative measure is maintenance of a healthy body

weight.

Treatment: Treatment includes the use of continuous positive airway pressure during

sleep.

Differential: This patient has headaches that are isolated to the morning, which makes an

underlying intracranial pathology, such as a mass or infection, unlikely. While his symptoms may be due to a psychiatric disorder or a benign cause, OSAHS should first be ruled out with polysomnography during a sleep study.

wrongAnswers.A: CT scan of the head is incorrect. A CT scan of the head can be used to identify intracranial abnormalities that could present with headache, such as a subarachnoid hemorrhage or tumor. This patient has had morning headaches for 4 months in the absence of any other symptoms, such as nausea, seizures, or muscle weakness, that would suggest increased intracranial pressure or a mass lesion.
wrongAnswers.B: Psychiatric evaluation is incorrect. Many psychiatric disorders can present with vague somatic symptoms, such as headache, fatigue, and abdominal discomfort. However, this patient’s symptoms are more consistent with OSAHS, especially in the absence of any mood changes. As such, a sleep study is a more appropriate next step than a psychiatric evaluation.
wrongAnswers.D: Syphilis serology is incorrect. Tertiary syphilis results in neurosyphilis, with ataxia, pupils that accommodate but do not react to light, and intermittent, stabbing pains. Tertiary syphilis would not be expected to present with morning headaches, daytime sleepiness, and fatigue.
wrongAnswers.E: Reassurance and observation is incorrect. This patient has signs and symptoms of OSAHS. Failure to diagnose and treat his condition increases the likelihood of complications, such as worsening symptoms, hypertension, pulmonary hypertension, and right ventricular dysfunction.

explanationPanel.rule: Obesity with daytime sleepiness and morning headaches warrants polysomnography for obstructive sleep apnea.
explanationPanel.trap: Head CT is not the next step without focal neurologic signs, papilledema, seizures, or mass-effect features.

layer4.rule: Obesity with daytime sleepiness and morning headaches warrants polysomnography for obstructive sleep apnea.
layer4.trap: Head CT is not the next step without focal neurologic signs, papilledema, seizures, or mass-effect features.

questions.stem: A 59-year-old man comes to the office 3 months after undergoing placement of a stent following a myocardial infarction. During this time, the patient has been asymptomatic. Medical history also is remarkable for type 2 diabetes mellitus diagnosed 10 years ago. Medications are clopidogrel, metformin, metoprolol, empagliflozin, atorvastatin, and daily aspirin. His most recent hemoglobin A1c obtained 1 week ago was 8.5%. The patient has been adherent to his medication regimen. He has been following a low-fat diet and walks for 45 minutes, three to four times weekly. He is 165 cm (5 ft 5 in) tall and weighs 100 kg (220 lb); BMI is 37 kg/m². Vital signs are within normal limits. Physical examination discloses no abnormalities. Which of the following is the most appropriate pharmacotherapy to add to this patient's medication regimen?
questions.stemHtml: A 59-year-old man comes to the office 3 months after undergoing placement of a stent following a myocardial infarction. During this time, the patient has been asymptomatic. Medical history also is remarkable for type 2 diabetes mellitus diagnosed 10 years ago. Medications are clopidogrel, metformin, metoprolol, empagliflozin, atorvastatin, and daily aspirin. His most recent hemoglobin A1c obtained 1 week ago was 8.5%. The patient has been adherent to his medication regimen. He has been following a low-fat diet and walks for 45 minutes, three to four times weekly. He is 165 cm (5 ft 5 in) tall and weighs 100 kg (220 lb); BMI is 37 kg/m². Vital signs are within normal limits. Physical examination discloses no abnormalities. Which of the following is the most appropriate pharmacotherapy to add to this patient's medication regimen?
questions.subject: Endocrinology

explanationPanel.whyCorrect:
Educational Objective: This patient with a history of myocardial infarction and type

2 diabetes mellitus on metformin and empagliflozin is found to have increased hemoglobin A1c. The most appropriate medication to add to his regimen, given his history of myocardial infarction, is a glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonist (GLP-1 RA), such as semaglutide.

Evaluation: Dual-agent failure in type 2 diabetes mellitus occurs when glycemic control is

unable to be obtained despite the use of two oral antihyperglycemic agents. In this patient’s case, a GLP-1 RA should be added as the next agent.

Definition: Type 2 diabetes mellitus can be diagnosed with either a measurement of

hemoglobin A1c greater than 6.5%, a fasting serum glucose concentration greater than 126 mg/dL, a 2-hour serum glucose concentration greater than 200 mg/dL during an oral glucose tolerance test, or a nonfasting serum glucose concentration greater than 200 mg/dL in a patient with symptoms of hyperglycemia.

Prevention: Prevention of type 2 diabetes mellitus includes lifestyle modifications, such as

maintaining healthy weight and regular exercise.

Treatment: First-line treatment for diabetes mellitus includes metformin. Patients with

known cardiovascular or kidney comorbidities should be treated with medications that confer benefit, such as sodium-glucose cotransporter-2 inhibitors or GLP-1 RAs.

Differential: This patient presents with diabetes mellitus and a hemoglobin A1c that is not

at goal, despite lifestyle modifications and two oral agents. The next best step, especially given his cardiovascular risk profile, is to start a third oral medication, such as semaglutide.

wrongAnswers.A: Glipizide and linagliptin are incorrect. Glipizide, a sulfonylurea, and linagliptin, a dipeptidyl-peptidase-4 inhibitor, are oral agents but do not provide the same cardiovascular benefit as semaglutide, making them less appropriate for this patient.
wrongAnswers.B: Insulin glargine and insulin lispro are incorrect. This patient should be trialed on a third oral agent before starting insulin. Furthermore, semaglutide has a higher level of cardiovascular benefit than insulin.
wrongAnswers.C: Insulin glargine and insulin lispro are incorrect. This patient should be trialed on a third oral agent before starting insulin. Furthermore, semaglutide has a higher level of cardiovascular benefit than insulin.
wrongAnswers.D: Glipizide and linagliptin are incorrect. Glipizide, a sulfonylurea, and linagliptin, a dipeptidyl-peptidase-4 inhibitor, are oral agents but do not provide the same cardiovascular benefit as semaglutide, making them less appropriate for this patient.

explanationPanel.rule: T2DM with established ASCVD and elevated A1c despite metformin/SGLT2 inhibitor should add a GLP-1 receptor agonist.
explanationPanel.trap: Sulfonylureas, DPP-4 inhibitors, and insulin lack the same ASCVD benefit in this stable patient.

layer4.rule: T2DM with established ASCVD and elevated A1c despite metformin/SGLT2 inhibitor should add a GLP-1 receptor agonist.
layer4.trap: Sulfonylureas, DPP-4 inhibitors, and insulin lack the same ASCVD benefit in this stable patient.

questions.subject: Otolaryngology

explanationPanel.correct: B. Aspiration of the right ear
explanationPanel.whyCorrect:
Educational Objective: Aspiration of the right ear is the most appropriate next step

in management. This patient’s clinical findings (swelling, erythema, and bruising of the right pinna) are consistent with auricular hematoma.

Evaluation: Auricular hematomas may present with swelling, erythema, and bruising of the

pinna of the ear.

Definition: Cauliflower ear, also known as wrestler’s ear, is associated with prior auricular

hematoma of the ear following blunt trauma. Auricular hematoma triggers inflammation and cartilaginous necrosis, which may trigger fibrocartilaginous overgrowth and later a cauliflower-like appearance.

Prevention: Patients may avoid auricular hematoma and cauliflower ear by avoiding blunt

trauma to the ear or wearing protective headgear.

Treatment: In patients who develop auricular hematoma, aspiration of the hematoma is

recommended. Aspiration may prevent cartilaginous necrosis and subsequent inflammation, which may trigger fibrocartilaginous overgrowth of the ear.

Differential: In a patient with trauma and subsequent development of swelling, redness,

and erythema of the ear, auricular hematoma is the most likely diagnosis. In patients who develop an auricular hematoma, the first step in management is aspiration of the hematoma to prevent worsening of the condition.

wrongAnswers.A:
Application of ice is incorrect. While ice may decrease the size of the

hematoma and alleviate pain of the ear, persistence of the hematoma will compromise blood supply to the cartilage. In these cases, application of ice may be considered following aspiration of a hematoma; however, it is not the most appropriate first step in management.
wrongAnswers.C: CT scan of the head is incorrect. Auricular hematoma may be diagnosed based on clinical history of trauma and physical examination findings showing bruising and swelling of the ear. When there is concern for additional trauma or concern for intracranial bleed, CT scan of the head may be considered.
wrongAnswers.D: Oral cephalexin therapy is incorrect. Cephalexin is a cephalosporin antibiotic used to treat skin infections, including cellulitis. While cellulitis is associated with redness, pain, and swelling, this patient’s presentation is consistent with auricular hematoma.
wrongAnswers.E: No management is indicated at this time is incorrect. In cases of auricular hematoma, aspiration is recommended. Long-term complications of untreated auricular hematoma include cauliflower ear, related to fibrocartilaginous overgrowth following necrosis and inflammation to the cartilage.

explanationPanel.rule: Traumatic pinna swelling after wrestling is an auricular hematoma that requires aspiration to prevent cauliflower ear.
explanationPanel.trap: Ice or observation leaves blood separating cartilage from perichondrium and risks cartilage necrosis.

layer4.rule: Traumatic pinna swelling after wrestling is an auricular hematoma that requires aspiration to prevent cauliflower ear.
layer4.trap: Ice or observation leaves blood separating cartilage from perichondrium and risks cartilage necrosis.

questions.stem: A 25-year-old woman comes to the office because of a 2-day history of increased urinary frequency and a burning sensation with urination. She just returned from the Cayman Islands. She has not had fever, nausea, vomiting, or back pain. She has been avoiding drinking fluids, but this has not decreased her urinary frequency. The patient has recently been married and has only had two sexual partners in her lifetime. She is otherwise healthy and her only medication is ibuprofen. She appears uncomfortable. Vital signs are within normal limits. Physical examination shows no abnormalities. Urine culture grows a citrate-negative, indole-positive, gram-negative rod. Analysis of a clean catch urine sample is most likely to show a decrease of which of the following in this patient?
questions.stemHtml: A 25-year-old woman comes to the office because of a 2-day history of increased urinary frequency and a burning sensation with urination. She just returned from the Cayman Islands. She has not had fever, nausea, vomiting, or back pain. She has been avoiding drinking fluids, but this has not decreased her urinary frequency. The patient has recently been married and has only had two sexual partners in her lifetime. She is otherwise healthy and her only medication is ibuprofen. She appears uncomfortable. Vital signs are within normal limits. Physical examination shows no abnormalities. Urine culture grows a citrate-negative, indole-positive, gram-negative rod. Analysis of a clean catch urine sample is most likely to show a decrease of which of the following in this patient?
questions.subject: Nephrology/Urology

explanationPanel.whyCorrect:
Educational Objective: This patient’s presentation is consistent with a urinary tract

infection. Urinary tract infections classically present in female patients with dysuria, urinary frequency, urgency, and suprapubic discomfort, and are often caused by Escherichia coli. E. coli urinary tract infections have been found to be associated with a decreased urine pH.

Evaluation: Lower urinary tract infections, including cystitis, may present with hematuria

and frequently lack symptoms of fever or costovertebral angle tenderness. Urinalysis shows the presence of leukocytes as well as positive leukocyte esterase and nitrites. The patient in this case has a citrate-negative, indole-positive, gram-negative rod identified on urine culture, which is consistent with E. coli infection.

Definition: Urinary tract infections are often caused by E. coli and gram-negative enteric

flora.

Prevention: Urinary tract infections may be prevented with increased fluid intake, proper

hygienic practices, and postcoital voiding.

Treatment: Antibiotics are recommended for the treatment of urinary tract infections. First-

line antibiotics include trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole, nitrofurantoin, cephalexin, ceftriaxone, and fosfomycin.

Differential: The patient in this case is presenting with urinary frequency and dysuria as

well as urine culture results consistent with urinary tract infection. The findings of a citrate-negative, indole-positive, gram-negative rod on urine culture is consistent with E. coli infection, which has been found to be associated with a decreased urine pH.

wrongAnswers.A: Erythrocytes is incorrect. Urinary tract infections may present with hematuria or increased erythrocytes on analysis of a urine sample. Hematuria is a common finding in urinary tract infection due to inflammation of the bladder.
wrongAnswers.B: Glucose is not the most likely decreased finding on analysis of the urine sample. Patients with a history of poorly controlled diabetes mellitus may have increased urine glucose concentrations, which may predispose to development of a urinary tract infection. A finding of decreased urine pH is more likely in the probable case of an E. coli urinary tract infection.
wrongAnswers.C: Leukocyte esterase is incorrect. Leukocyte esterase is classically increased in cases of urinary tract infections. Urine pH is more likely to be decreased in this patient.
wrongAnswers.E: Specific gravity is not the most likely decreased finding on analysis of the urine sample. Urine specific gravity can be variable in cases of urinary tract infections. Urine pH is the most likely to be decreased in this patient.

explanationPanel.rule: Citrate-negative indole-positive gram-negative rod cystitis is E coli, which is associated with decreased urine pH.
explanationPanel.trap: Leukocyte esterase, RBCs, and sometimes specific gravity increase in UTI; pH is the decreased finding asked for.

layer4.rule: Citrate-negative indole-positive gram-negative rod cystitis is E coli, which is associated with decreased urine pH.
layer4.trap: Leukocyte esterase, RBCs, and sometimes specific gravity increase in UTI; pH is the decreased finding asked for.

questions.stem: The electronic health record (EHR) system at a primary care practice was recently upgraded so that physicians can update patient charts from their mobile devices. Prior to the EHR upgrade, a physician would receive after-hour calls from clinic patients and make notes on paper by hand. The notes would then be transcribed the next day by an administrative assistant and added to the patient's chart. Following the EHR upgrade, physicians can search for the patient in the EHR on their mobile device and add notes directly to the EHR. Typically, a clinic physician receives approximately 40 phone calls nightly between 5:00 PM and 7:30 AM. A patient named John Doe (date of birth, 7/28/1982) calls multiple times one evening to refill his albuterol prescription. The physician on call orders the medication and documents it in the EHR from her mobile device. The next day, it is discovered that the order has been placed in the EHR of another patient, who has a similar name, as shown. Which of the following interventions is most likely to prevent this type of error from recurring?
questions.stemHtml: The electronic health record (EHR) system at a primary care practice was recently upgraded so that physicians can update patient charts from their mobile devices. Prior to the EHR upgrade, a physician would receive after-hour calls from clinic patients and make notes on paper by hand. The notes would then be transcribed the next day by an administrative assistant and added to the patient's chart. Following the EHR upgrade, physicians can search for the patient in the EHR on their mobile device and add notes directly to the EHR. Typically, a clinic physician receives approximately 40 phone calls nightly between 5:00 PM and 7:30 AM. A patient named John Doe (date of birth, 7/28/1982) calls multiple times one evening to refill his albuterol prescription. The physician on call orders the medication and documents it in the EHR from her mobile device. The next day, it is discovered that the order has been placed in the EHR of another patient, who has a similar name, as shown. Which of the following interventions is most likely to prevent this type of error from recurring?
choices: Design the EHR so patients with identical names are displayed in different colors
Increase the font size in the mobile device-based EHR
Instruct physicians to search the EHR by a patient's social security number
Mandate physicians to acknowledge patient identity when entering medication orders in the EHR
Require use of two patient identifiers to access a patient chart
questions.subject: Ethics/Social Sciences

explanationPanel.correct: E. Require use of two patient identifiers to access a patient chart
explanationPanel.whyCorrect: This is a wrong-patient order caused by selecting a chart from a list of patients with the same name. The most effective prevention is a systems-level hard stop requiring two identifiers, such as name plus date of birth, before opening or ordering in the chart.

wrongAnswers.A: Color-coding identical names may help visually, but it does not reliably verify the patient identity or prevent look-alike chart selection.
wrongAnswers.B: Increasing font size may improve readability but does not address the root cause: selecting a chart without verifying identity.
wrongAnswers.C: Social security numbers are sensitive identifiers and are not the preferred routine patient-safety check.
wrongAnswers.D: A simple acknowledgement depends on memory and attention; a forced two-identifier access step is a stronger systems intervention.

explanationPanel.rule: Wrong-patient chart selection is best prevented by requiring two patient identifiers before chart access/orders.
explanationPanel.trap: Education, font size, color-coding, or an acknowledgement prompt is weaker than a forced identification safeguard.

layer4.rule: Wrong-patient chart selection is best prevented by requiring two patient identifiers before chart access/orders.

Question: In addition to surgical consultation, which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
questions.subject: Hematology/Oncology

explanationPanel.whyCorrect:
Educational Objective: This patient, who presents with persistent bleeding after a

tonsillectomy, has increased partial thromboplastin time (PTT) and decreased factor VIII (antihemophilic factor) activity, von Willebrand factor (vWF) antigen, and vWF:ristocetin cofactor (RCo) assay. She most likely has von Willebrand disease. The most appropriate next step in management is desmopressin therapy.

Evaluation: Von Willebrand disease is one of the most common hereditary bleeding

disorders and is caused by quantitative or qualitative abnormalities of vWF, which binds

platelets and subendothelial collagen in primary hemostasis.

Definition: Patients with von Willebrand disease present with signs and symptoms of

decreased platelet function. Deficiencies in vWF cause dysfunction with platelet adhesion. Factor VIII is a critical component of the intrinsic coagulation pathway, and decreased concentrations can lead to a prolonged PTT, although PTT can be normal.

Prevention: Von Willebrand disease is inherited in an autosomal dominant pattern. Risk

for this disease may be mitigated by genetic counseling.

Treatment: Treatment depends on the site and severity of bleeding and may include

desmopressin therapy, such as in this patient. Desmopressin functions by promoting release of additional vWF from endothelial cells.

Differential: This patient with persistent bleeding has symptoms suggestive of a bleeding

disorder. Her laboratory studies confirm the diagnosis of von Willebrand disease.

wrongAnswers.A: Cryoprecipitate therapy is incorrect. While cryoprecipitate would increase the coagulation factors, including vWF, desmopressin is preferred as treatment to normalize vWF concentrations and control bleeding.
wrongAnswers.C: Platelet transfusion is incorrect. While platelet transfusion would increase the number of platelets, without vWF, platelet adhesion is unable to occur. Platelet transfusion may be used as an adjunctive treatment, but the mainstay of treatment for this patient is desmopressin.
wrongAnswers.D: Red blood cell (RBC) transfusion is incorrect. RBC transfusion would not improve this patient’s hemostasis, as it would not improve the coagulation cascade. However, if this patient develops severe anemia from ongoing bleeding, RBC transfusion may be used as an adjunctive therapy to maintain hemodynamics while hemostasis is achieved.
wrongAnswers.E: Tranexamic acid therapy is incorrect. While tranexamic acid can be used as an adjunctive therapy to control bleeding, the mainstay of treatment is desmopressin or, if severe, administration of vWF concentrate.

explanationPanel.rule: Mucosal/procedural bleeding with low vWF antigen/activity and low factor VIII is treated with desmopressin.
explanationPanel.trap: Platelets or RBCs do not correct the vWF-mediated platelet adhesion defect; tranexamic acid is adjunctive.

questions.subject: Hematology/Oncology

explanationPanel.whyCorrect:
Educational Objective: Mediastinal masses, when malignant, may represent

lymphoma, thymoma, teratoma, or thyroid tissue, among other differentials. This patient’s pancytopenia and lymphadenopathy are consistent with lymphoma, and as treatment commences, there will be rapid turnover of cells with increased electrolyte, uric acid, and purine/pyrimidine release, a constellation called tumor lysis syndrome. Oral allopurinol therapy is indicated to prevent renal failure in tumor lysis syndrome.

Evaluation: Tumor lysis syndrome should be anticipated following treatment for

malignancies with high cell turnover. The condition is diagnosed clinically, and severity is gauged by laboratory studies and the presence or absence of associated organ failure.

Definition: Tumor lysis syndrome most commonly occurs following initiation of

chemotherapy for leukemia or lymphoma. The abrupt destruction of many tumor cells results in interstitial and serum release of their contents, manifesting as hyperphosphatemia, hypocalcemia, hyperkalemia, and hyperuricemia. Patients with tumor lysis syndrome can present with fever, nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, lethargy, cardiac dysrhythmias, seizures, tetany, muscle cramps, and syncope, and are at risk of sudden death secondary to the electrolyte and metabolic abnormalities. Purine nucleic acids are metabolized to hypoxanthine and xanthine, which are converted to uric acid by xanthine oxidase, resulting in hyperuricemia. Uric acid can crystallize in the renal tubules, leading to nephropathy and acute kidney injury. Uric acid can also be deposited in the joints, leading to arthralgias (gout).

Prevention: Hydration and allopurinol therapy can help minimize the consequences of

tumor lysis syndrome.

Treatment: Treatment of tumor lysis syndrome involves supportive care and correction of

electrolyte and metabolic abnormalities. Allopurinol is a xanthine oxidase inhibitor that prevents formation of uric acid and therefore decreases risk for gout and acute kidney injury. Rasburicase is used to promote the degradation of uric acid and is used in both prevention and treatment of tumor lysis syndrome. In patients with severe kidney injury and refractory electrolyte derangements, renal replacement therapy with dialysis may be indicated.

Differential: The presence of a mediastinal mass with lymphadenopathy and pancytopenia

is consistent with lymphoma. Tumor lysis syndrome is a known consequence of lymphoma and leukemia after initiation of chemotherapy.

wrongAnswers.A:
Emergency mediastinal radiation therapy is incorrect. Emergency mediastinal radiation therapy could be appropriate in cases of compressive mediastinal masses compromising respiratory or cardiovascular function, or those that are rapidly expanding. In this case, emergency mediastinal radiation therapy would not decrease the risk for tumor lysis syndrome, and it may worsen the possibility of tumor lysis syndrome by

increasing cell lysis.
wrongAnswers.B: Intravenous methylprednisolone therapy is incorrect. Intravenous methylprednisolone therapy may decrease edema and inflammation associated with malignancy, may promote tumor cell lysis or apoptosis, and may enhance the effect of chemotherapy and radiation used in the management of malignancy. Intravenous methylprednisolone therapy may also decrease nausea, vomiting, and neuropathy associated with malignancy. However, methylprednisolone therapy does not prevent uric acid formation or promote metabolism of urates and therefore does not decrease the risk for kidney injury.
wrongAnswers.C: Leukapheresis is not the most appropriate next step. Leukapheresis can be appropriate in the management of leukemia and lymphoma in cases of hyperviscosity from hyperleukocytosis. Leukapheresis would remove malignant cells from circulation; however, it is invasive and carries risks for bleeding, pain, and infection, among other things. Allopurinol is a more appropriate choice.
wrongAnswers.E: Transfusion of packed red blood cells is not the most appropriate next step. Transfusion of packed red blood cells is appropriate in this patient’s case given pancytopenia and hemoglobin less than 7.0 g/dL; however, transfusion of packed red blood cells would not decrease cell turnover from tumor lysis syndrome or prevent acute kidney injury from urate formation.

explanationPanel.rule: High-turnover lymphoma before treatment requires tumor lysis prevention with hydration and allopurinol/urate-lowering therapy.
explanationPanel.trap: Radiation or steroids may increase cell lysis and do not prevent uric acid nephropathy.

questions.stem: A 17-year-old boy comes to the surgery clinic with his mother for tonsillectomy evaluation. Medical history is remarkable for recurrent tonsillitis. He does not smoke cigarettes, drink alcoholic beverages, or use other substances. He has no other history of serious illness and takes no medications. The patient is a US Marine. History and physical examination are performed by a surgeon. After a discussion about the benefits and risks of the procedure, the patient agrees to sign the informed consent form. The mother says that under no circumstances would she allow the surgeon to remove her son's tonsils. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
questions.stemHtml: A 17-year-old boy comes to the surgery clinic with his mother for tonsillectomy evaluation. Medical history is remarkable for recurrent tonsillitis. He does not smoke cigarettes, drink alcoholic beverages, or use other substances. He has no other history of serious illness and takes no medications. The patient is a US Marine. History and physical examination are performed by a surgeon. After a discussion about the benefits and risks of the procedure, the patient agrees to sign the informed consent form. The mother says that under no circumstances would she allow the surgeon to remove her son's tonsils. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
choices: Advise the patient that he cannot go against his mother’s wishes
Attempt to persuade the mother of the positive benefits the procedure will provide her son
Explain to the mother that surgery will be scheduled because the patient has provided informed consent
Recommend that the patient discuss the procedure with his mother and reschedule the visit
questions.subject: Ethics/Social Sciences

explanationPanel.correct: C. Explain to the mother that surgery will be scheduled because the patient has provided informed consent
explanationPanel.whyCorrect:
Educational Objective: Patients younger than 18 years may legally provide

informed consent to medical care in several states. The surgery will be scheduled because the patient has provided informed consent. Consent is not required from this patient’s mother.

Key Concept: Informed consent involves a discussion between the physician and patient

about the risks, benefits, and alternatives to a procedure. Obtaining informed consent is a legal requirement. Typically, an informed consent discussion is documented (in an informed consent form) to provide evidence that the informed consent discussion has occurred. Explanation: State laws vary concerning the legal age of consent to medical care. Many states allow patients older than 16 years to provide informed consent. Given that the surgeon is offering the informed consent form to this patient, the scenario likely occurs in a state that allows 17-year-olds to provide consent.

Differential: Parents may sign the informed consent form for minors or minors below a

certain age in certain states.

wrongAnswers.A: Advise the patient that he cannot go against his mother’s wishes is incorrect. Patients older than 16 years may provide informed consent in several states.
wrongAnswers.B: Attempt to persuade the mother of the positive benefits the procedure will provide her son is incorrect. This patient’s mother appears adamantly opposed to the procedure despite the physician’s prior explanation about the procedure’s benefits.
wrongAnswers.D: Recommend that the patient discuss the procedure with his mother and reschedule the visit is incorrect. This option would lead to unnecessary delays in this patient undergoing the procedure.

explanationPanel.rule: A legally authorized mature minor/adolescent who provides informed consent can proceed despite parental objection.
explanationPanel.trap: Do not assume a parent can veto when the stem shows the patient is being offered and signing consent.

layer4.rule: A legally authorized mature minor/adolescent who provides informed consent can proceed despite parental objection.
layer4.trap: Do not assume a parent can veto when the stem shows the patient is being offered and signing consent.

questions.stem: A 59-year-old man comes to the office because of a 3-day history of progressive fever, shortness of breath, nausea, diarrhea, and cough productive of minimal sputum. His symptoms began 4 days after he returned home from a 7-day vacation at a spa resort. He has a history of chronic bronchitis and currently takes no medications. He has smoked one pack of cigarettes daily for 40 years. Temperature is 39.4°C (102.9°F), pulse is 90/min and regular, respirations are 22/min, and blood pressure is 155/85 mm Hg. Pulse oximetry on room air shows an oxygen saturation of 94%. Cardiopulmonary examination discloses diffuse crackles best heard at the lung bases and no murmurs, rubs, or gallops. The abdomen is soft and nontender. Gram stain of sputum shows multiple neutrophils but no bacteria. Result of a rapid polymerase chain reaction test for coronavirus is negative. Which of the following is the most appropriate pharmacotherapy for this patient at this time?
questions.stemHtml: A 59-year-old man comes to the office because of a 3-day history of progressive fever, shortness of breath, nausea, diarrhea, and cough productive of minimal sputum. His symptoms began 4 days after he returned home from a 7-day vacation at a spa resort. He has a history of chronic bronchitis and currently takes no medications. He has smoked one pack of cigarettes daily for 40 years. Temperature is 39.4°C (102.9°F), pulse is 90/min and regular, respirations are 22/min, and blood pressure is 155/85 mm Hg. Pulse oximetry on room air shows an oxygen saturation of 94%. Cardiopulmonary examination discloses diffuse crackles best heard at the lung bases and no murmurs, rubs, or gallops. The abdomen is soft and nontender. Gram stain of sputum shows multiple neutrophils but no bacteria. Result of a rapid polymerase chain reaction test for coronavirus is negative. Which of the following is the most appropriate pharmacotherapy for this patient at this time?
questions.subject: Infectious Disease

explanationPanel.whyCorrect:
Educational Objective: Community-acquired pneumonia (CAP) is the most likely

diagnosis of this patient with fever, dyspnea, and productive cough. Specifically, Legionella pneumophila may be the causative agent, given his recent travel to a spa resort, his underlying lung disease, the presence of nausea and diarrhea, and the absence of bacteria on Gram stain. Levofloxacin is an appropriate empiric antibiotic choice for CAP in patients with underlying lung disease, such as this one, and is the treatment of choice for mild to moderate cases of Legionella pneumonia.

Key Concept: For patients without major medical comorbidities, such as chronic

obstructive pulmonary disease, diabetes mellitus, liver, cardiac, or kidney disease, first-line oral antibiotics for CAP include doxycycline and/or amoxicillin. Patients with comorbidities or acute distress are given alternative antibiotics, such as amoxicillin and clavulanic acid or levofloxacin. Explanation: CAP can be diagnosed in an ambulatory patient who presents with fever, productive cough, and identifiably pulmonary infiltrate or infiltrates on chest x-ray. CAP is

frequently caused by bacteria including Streptococcus pneumoniae, Haemophilus influenzae, Moraxella (Branhamella) catarrhalis, Mycoplasma pneumoniae, Staphylococcus aureus, L. pneumophila, and Chlamydophila pneumoniae among others. Antibiotics are selected to cover these organisms.

Differential: For patients who present with pneumonia in the setting of underlying lung

disease, outpatient therapy consists of amoxicillin and clavulanic acid or levofloxacin. This patient also has relatively reassuring vital signs, making intravenous antibiotics unnecessary.

wrongAnswers.A: Amoxicillin is incorrect. Amoxicillin provides coverage against many gram-positive and some gram-negative bacteria. It is most used in ear, nose, and throat infections. It is less effective than amoxicillin and clavulanic acid against common causes of CAP, including H. influenzae and M. catarrhalis, making it not the most appropriate choice for this patient.
wrongAnswers.B: Ceftriaxone is incorrect. Ceftriaxone is a third-generation cephalosporin with coverage of both gram-positive and gram-negative bacteria. Ceftriaxone is an intravenous antibiotic that may be used in the treatment of CAP in hospitalized patients. This patient has relatively stable vital signs, making admission for intravenous antibiotics unnecessary.
wrongAnswers.C: Fluconazole is incorrect. Fluconazole is an antifungal, commonly used in the treatment of oral thrush and vulvovaginal candidiasis. Fluconazole is not used in the treatment of CAP.
wrongAnswers.E: Rifampin is incorrect. Rifampin is a drug primarily used in the treatment of tuberculosis. Tuberculosis most commonly presents with subacute or chronic cough, weight loss, and night sweats. It would be less likely to present acutely with fever, dyspnea, and productive cough, making levofloxacin the most appropriate pharmacotherapy.

explanationPanel.rule: Pneumonia after spa exposure with GI symptoms and negative Gram stain in COPD is treated with a respiratory fluoroquinolone.
explanationPanel.trap: Plain amoxicillin does not cover atypical Legionella and is not preferred in CAP with comorbidity.

layer4.trap: Plain amoxicillin does not cover atypical Legionella and is not preferred in CAP with comorbidity.

questions.stem: A 16-year-old girl is brought to the office by her mother because of a 6-month history of increasingly severe lower abdominal cramps that begin 2 days before the start of her menstrual period and last for 4 days. She has missed a total of 10 days of school because of the pain. She otherwise is asymptomatic. Menarche was at the age of 15 years. Menses occur at regular 28-day intervals, last 5 days, and initially occurred without pain. She is not sexually active. She has no history of serious illness and takes no medications. Examination of the abdomen and external genitalia shows no abnormalities. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
questions.stemHtml: A 16-year-old girl is brought to the office by her mother because of a 6-month history of increasingly severe lower abdominal cramps that begin 2 days before the start of her menstrual period and last for 4 days. She has missed a total of 10 days of school because of the pain. She otherwise is asymptomatic. Menarche was at the age of 15 years. Menses occur at regular 28-day intervals, last 5 days, and initially occurred without pain. She is not sexually active. She has no history of serious illness and takes no medications. Examination of the abdomen and external genitalia shows no abnormalities. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
questions.subject: Gynecology

explanationPanel.whyCorrect:
Educational Objective: This patient, with chronic perimenstrual pain and an

otherwise normal examination, is likely experiencing primary dysmenorrhea, which reflects pain around the time of menses with no evident examination, laboratory, or radiographic explanation. Nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) are the treatment of choice.

Key Concept: Primary dysmenorrhea, or painful menstruation, is a common cause of

cyclic pelvic pain in healthy female patients, and is believed to arise via a prostaglandin-mediated mechanism. Explanation: Primary dysmenorrhea occurs in the absence of secondary causes, such as endometriosis, adenomyosis, cervical stenosis, or uterine fibroids. Symptoms often begin during adolescence and commonly interfere with quality of life and with essential activities such as school or work. Patients describe cramping lower abdominal or pelvic pain that begins several days prior to the onset of menses, which persists for several days, and may be accompanied by fatigue, nausea, vomiting, presyncopal symptoms, and headache. Endometrial sloughing is accompanied by the production of prostaglandins, which stimulate painful uterine contractions. Patients are typically treated with NSAIDs that inhibit cyclooxygenase enzymes, thereby limiting prostaglandin synthesis, or with oral hormonal contraceptives.

Differential: This patient’s characteristic chronic pelvic and abdominal pain around the

time of menstrual periods with otherwise normal historical features and examination narrows the differential to primary dysmenorrhea. Imaging and cytology are normal in cases of primary dysmenorrhea, and patients should be treated with NSAIDs.

wrongAnswers.A: Abdominal and pelvic ultrasonography is incorrect. Abdominal and pelvic ultrasonography is appropriate in the assessment of multiple inflammatory, infectious, and structural types of pathology, along with routine surveillance of pregnancy. In primary dysmenorrhea, ultrasonography findings are normal. No further imaging is necessary to diagnose primary dysmenorrhea.
wrongAnswers.B: Laparoscopy is incorrect. Laparoscopy is used in the diagnosis and treatment of multiple abdominal and pelvic pathologies, including endometriosis. Endometriosis may cause cyclic pelvic pain; however, there may be abnormal findings on examination such as limited mobility of the uterus, or visible endometrial implants. This patient lacks these features, and laparoscopy is unnecessarily invasive at this time.
wrongAnswers.D: Cervical cytology is incorrect. Cervical cytology is used to assess malignant and/or infectious cervical pathology. Cervical cytology is not indicated in this 16-year-old patient, and she has not yet been sexually active.
wrongAnswers.E: Reassurance only is not the most appropriate next step. This patient is experiencing debilitating menstrual period-related pain and has missed several school days. Treatment is more appropriate.

explanationPanel.rule: Adolescent cyclic menstrual cramping with normal exam is primary dysmenorrhea treated first with NSAIDs.
explanationPanel.trap: Ultrasound/laparoscopy are for secondary features or refractory symptoms, not a classic normal-exam presentation.

layer4.rule: Adolescent cyclic menstrual cramping with normal exam is primary dysmenorrhea treated first with NSAIDs.
layer4.trap: Ultrasound/laparoscopy are for secondary features or refractory symptoms, not a classic normal-exam presentation.

questions.stem: A 28-year-old African American woman comes to the Veterans Affairs urgent treatment center because of a history of migraines that began after she sustained a blast injury from an improvised explosive device in Afghanistan 7 years ago. Until 1 month ago, her migraines had been well controlled for 2 years with nightly prophylactic amitriptyline, and they had occurred no more than twice monthly. When they occurred, they resolved quickly with sumatriptan. Today, the patient reports a 1-month history of daily moderate headaches on awakening that are not relieved by sumatriptan or naproxen. She says these new types of headaches have not been accompanied by sensitivity to light or sound or by the unilateral "pounding" sensation typical of her previous migraines. During the past week, she has had several episodes of momentary blindness and has heard a "whooshing" sound occurring in synchrony with her pulse. During the past 2 days, she has had constant double vision that resolves when she covers one eye. She also reports occasional nausea and vertigo that occur only after she has taken minocycline, which her dermatologist prescribed 2 months ago for acne. She does not smoke cigarettes, drink alcohol, or use other substances. She appears to be in moderate distress. She is 165 cm (5 ft 5 in) tall and weighs 72 kg (158 lb); BMI is 26 kg/m². Vital signs are within normal limits. Ocular and funduscopic examinations show the findings depicted in the photographs. The remainder of the examination discloses no abnormalities. CT scan of the head was performed prior to performing the lumbar puncture; the findings confirmed no contraindication for lumbar puncture. Cerebrospinal fluid analysis is most likely to show which of the following sets of findings?

questions.subject: Neurology

explanationPanel.whyCorrect:
Educational Objective: This patient who is prescribed minocycline and presents

with signs of increased intracranial pressure (ICP) (eg, headache, vision changes, extraocular muscle dysfunction, papilledema) is likely experiencing minocycline-induced intracranial hypertension. Analysis of cerebrospinal fluid typically shows an increased opening pressure and normal WBC count.

Evaluation: The tetracycline class of antibiotics is thought to disrupt cerebrospinal fluid

dynamics and lead to increased ICP. Increased ICP typically presents with headache, blurred vision, vision loss, and diplopia. Increased ICP can lead to cranial nerve palsies, especially in the abducens nerve due to its long length, leading to horizontal diplopia and impaired lateral eye movement.

Definition: Funduscopic examination shows signs of papilledema (swollen optic disc,

engorged and tortuous retinal veins, retinal hemorrhages). Cerebrospinal fluid analysis typically shows increased open pressure without significant increases in WBCs or protein.

Prevention: The risk for minocycline-induced intracranial hypertension can be mitigated by

using the lowest effective dose, considering alternative therapies in patients with risk factors (eg, obesity, young age, female sex), and avoiding concomitant use of isotretinoin (a medication also associated with intracranial hypertension).

Treatment: Minocycline should be immediately discontinued, an urgent ophthalmologic

evaluation should be pursued, and increased ICP should be addressed with medications such as acetazolamide.

Differential: An alternative cause of increased ICP in female patients of childbearing age is

idiopathic intracranial hypertension.

questions.stem: Thirty minutes after undergoing CT scan of the abdomen with intravenous contrast, a 57-year-old woman has the onset of generalized pruritus. She was admitted to the hospital for diverticulitis 2 days ago and has been receiving intravenous ampicillin-sulbactam therapy since then. Her temperature is 37.2°C (99.0°F), pulse is 100/min, respirations are 24/min, and blood pressure is 80/50 mm Hg while supine. Examination shows multiple, 2-cm, erythematous, raised lesions over the trunk and all extremities. Expiratory wheezes are heard bilaterally. Which of the following is the most appropriate initial pharmacotherapy?
questions.stemHtml: Thirty minutes after undergoing CT scan of the abdomen with intravenous contrast, a 57-year-old woman has the onset of generalized pruritus. She was admitted to the hospital for diverticulitis 2 days ago and has been receiving intravenous ampicillin-sulbactam therapy since then. Her temperature is 37.2°C (99.0°F), pulse is 100/min, respirations are 24/min, and blood pressure is 80/50 mm Hg while supine. Examination shows multiple, 2-cm, erythematous, raised lesions over the trunk and all extremities. Expiratory wheezes are heard bilaterally. Which of the following is the most appropriate initial pharmacotherapy?
questions.subject: Emergency/Critical Care

explanationPanel.whyCorrect:
Educational Objective: This patient, with acute, pruritic urticaria, wheezing,

tachycardia, and hypotension occurring after exposure to intravenous contrast dye, is experiencing anaphylaxis. First-line management of anaphylaxis is administration of epinephrine.

Evaluation: Anaphylaxis, a severe type I (immediate) hypersensitivity reaction, presents

following exposure to an allergen. Anaphylaxis is caused by widespread IgE-mediated mast cell degranulation and is characterized by histaminergic responses within multiple organ systems leading to flushing, angioedema, bronchospasm, nausea, vomiting, abdominal discomfort, and vasodilation, which can lead to airway obstruction and circulatory collapse. The diagnosis is clinical and should be suspected after a patient presents with some or all of these features after exposure to a known or potential allergen.

Definition: Anaphylaxis is a form of distributive shock, which is characterized by a primary

decrease in systemic vascular resistance (SVR). This decrease in SVR is secondary to IgE-mediated histamine and cytokine release. Cardiac output increases to compensate for low SVR in the early stages of distributive shock. If anaphylaxis is not appropriately treated with epinephrine, further decompensation can occur, resulting in progressive hypotension and insufficient perfusion with associated end-organ damage.

Prevention: Avoidance of known allergens is the only prevention for anaphylaxis as

unknown allergens can also trigger the condition.

Treatment: First-line treatment of anaphylaxis is epinephrine. Epinephrine is generally

administered intramuscularly, though subcutaneous and intravenous are also potential routes of administration. Antihistamines, corticosteroids, and intravenous fluids are also cornerstones of care, though they are adjunct therapies.

Differential: Corticosteroids are generally given to prevent delayed or biphasic

presentations of anaphylaxis, though they have less of a role in the immediate management of anaphylaxis than epinephrine. There is no recognized role for heparin or gentamicin in the management of anaphylaxis.

wrongAnswers.A: Inhaled fluticasone and intravenous hydrocortisone are incorrect. These are corticosteroid medications that have an adjunct role in preventing biphasic anaphylactic reactions and decreasing the overall inflammatory burden; however, the standard management includes oral dexamethasone or prednisone. Intravenous corticosteroids would be acceptable, but the chosen corticosteroids should be those with primarily glucocorticoid activity.
wrongAnswers.B: Intravenous gentamicin is incorrect. Antibiotics are indicated in the management of bacterial infection, not anaphylaxis. This patient’s presentation relates to the recent administration of intravenous contrast, not her underlying reason for hospitalization, diverticulitis. Additionally, gentamicin has a narrow therapeutic window and is used infrequently in adult medicine when more suitable alternatives exist.
wrongAnswers.C: Intravenous heparin is incorrect. Heparin is used in the management of acute coronary syndrome and venous or arterial thromboembolic disease. This patient’s presentation is related to anaphylaxis, not thrombosis.
wrongAnswers.D: Inhaled fluticasone and intravenous hydrocortisone are incorrect. These are corticosteroid medications that have an adjunct role in preventing biphasic anaphylactic reactions and decreasing the overall inflammatory burden; however, the standard management includes oral dexamethasone or prednisone. Intravenous corticosteroids would be acceptable, but the chosen corticosteroids should be those with primarily glucocorticoid activity.

explanationPanel.rule: Acute urticaria, wheezing, and hypotension after contrast exposure is anaphylaxis; epinephrine is first-line.
explanationPanel.trap: Corticosteroids and inhaled medications are adjuncts and do not reverse immediate shock/bronchospasm.
