questions.stem: A 47-year-old woman comes to the office for a follow-up evaluation of blood pressure control. At two previous visits during the past 3 months, her blood pressure was 154/94 mm Hg and 160/96 mm Hg, respectively. During the past 3 months, she has been following a low-sodium diet and a regimen of exercise and has limited her alcohol intake. She is 165 cm (5 ft 5 in) tall and weighs 60 kg (132 lb); BMI is 22 kg/m². Today, her blood pressure is 152/96 mm Hg. Physical examination shows no other abnormalities. ECG and laboratory studies show no abnormalities. In addition to advising the patient to continue her diet and exercise program and monitor her blood pressure at home, which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
questions.stemHtml: A 47-year-old woman comes to the office for a follow-up evaluation of blood pressure control. At two previous visits during the past 3 months, her blood pressure was 154/94 mm Hg and 160/96 mm Hg, respectively. During the past 3 months, she has been following a low-sodium diet and a regimen of exercise and has limited her alcohol intake. She is 165 cm (5 ft 5 in) tall and weighs 60 kg (132 lb); BMI is 22 kg/m². Today, her blood pressure is 152/96 mm Hg. Physical examination shows no other abnormalities. ECG and laboratory studies show no abnormalities. In addition to advising the patient to continue her diet and exercise program and monitor her blood pressure at home, which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
choices: No additional monitoring or treatment now; reevaluate in 2 months
questions.subject: Cardiology

explanationPanel.whyCorrect:
Educational Objective: Blood pressure that has not reasonably improved with

lifestyle modification should be treated medically. First-line therapies include thiazide diuretics, ACE inhibitors, and calcium channel blockers.

Key Concept: Hypertension increases patient risk for stroke, retinopathy, cardiovascular

disease, renal failure, and peripheral artery disease among other conditions. Patients who do not respond to lifestyle modification should be treated with medication. Explanation: While guidelines vary slightly based on recommending body and patient comorbidities, generally appropriate blood pressure goals for a 47-year-old female patient without other known comorbidities include systolic and diastolic pressures less than 140/90 mm Hg. Lifestyle interventions including but not limited to dietary improvement (decreasing sodium, alcohol, refined carbohydrates, and fats), exercise (increasing cardiovascular fitness), sleep (treating sleep apnea, sleeping at least 7 to 8 hours nightly), smoking cessation, and reducing stress may be suitable to decrease blood pressure to safe ranges in many patients. If after an appropriate period of time, generally 3 to 6 months, these interventions are not successful, or if the initial presenting blood pressure range is severe or suggestive of a secondary cause, treatment should occur. First-line therapies include thiazide diuretics (eg, hydrochlorothiazide), calcium channel blockers (eg, amlodipine), and ACE inhibitors (eg, lisinopril).

Differential: First-line therapies for managing essential hypertension do not include α- or

β-adrenergic blockers; these classes of medications may be used in specific cases or for treatment of co-presenting disease (eg, heart failure).

wrongAnswers.A: Prescribe an α-adrenergic blocking agent is incorrect. α-Adrenergic blockers are used in the management of benign prostatic hyperplasia, post-traumatic stress disorder, and nephrolithiasis, among other conditions. They are not the first-line choices for managing essential hypertension.
wrongAnswers.B: Prescribe a β-adrenergic blocking agent is incorrect. β-Adrenergic blockers were previously a first-line choice in the management of hypertension; however, evidence shows that they are less effective than thiazide diuretics, calcium channel blockers, and ACE inhibitors in essential hypertension. They may be used for competing or co- presenting conditions, such as heart failure, but should not be used to control blood pressure in essential hypertension without other indications if first-line medications have not yet been used.
wrongAnswers.D: No additional monitoring or treatment now; reevaluate in 2 months is not the best choice. While this patient’s blood pressure may continue to improve with lifestyle modification, she has already performed a reasonable trial of lifestyle therapy. It is appropriate at this time to prescribe antihypertensives to prevent consequences of untreated hypertension.

explanationPanel.rule: Persistent stage 2-range hypertension after lifestyle trial should start first-line therapy such as a thiazide diuretic.
explanationPanel.trap: Beta blockers and alpha blockers are not first-line for uncomplicated essential hypertension.

layer4.rule: Persistent stage 2-range hypertension after lifestyle trial should start first-line therapy such as a thiazide diuretic.
layer4.trap: Beta blockers and alpha blockers are not first-line for uncomplicated essential hypertension.

questions.stem: A 24-year-old woman comes to the clinic because of a 2-day history of right lower abdominal pain that was sudden in onset. She has not had fever, nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, or constipation. Medical history is remarkable for asthma and occasional headaches. Medications are an oral contraceptive, inhaled albuterol as needed, and ibuprofen as needed for headaches. She lives with her boyfriend of 2 years and works as a research analyst. Menses occur regularly at 28-day intervals; her last menstrual period was 1 week ago. Temperature is 36.7°C (98.0°F), pulse is 80/min, respirations are 20/min, and blood pressure is 120/66 mm Hg. The patient appears anxious. There is a fading ecchymosis over the right cheek. Cardiopulmonary examination discloses no abnormalities. Abdominal examination shows an ecchymosis over the right lower quadrant. Bowel sounds are normoactive. Abdomen is soft with tenderness to palpation in the right lower quadrant; a hematoma is palpated in the area of tenderness. There is bruising of the patient's inner thighs. Pelvic examination discloses cervical motion tenderness. The patient reluctantly confirms that her injuries were inflicted by her boyfriend and that nonconsensual intercourse occurred. In addition to discussing reporting requirements and safety with the patient and ordering a urine pregnancy test and forensic rape examination, which of the following is most appropriate to offer this patient at this time?

Abdomen is soft with tenderness to palpation in the right lower quadrant; a hematoma is palpated in the area of tenderness. There is bruising of the patient's inner thighs. Pelvic examination discloses cervical motion tenderness. The patient reluctantly confirms that her injuries were inflicted by her boyfriend and that nonconsensual intercourse occurred. In addition to discussing reporting requirements and safety with the patient and ordering a urine pregnancy test and forensic rape examination, which of the following is most appropriate to offer this patient at this time?
questions.subject: Ethics/Social Sciences

explanationPanel.whyCorrect:
Educational Objective: Intimate partner violence can include physical,

psychological, and/or sexual abuse. Patients, such as this one, presenting after sexual assault should undergo a standard evaluation including pregnancy test, forensic rape examination, and screening for sexually transmitted infections (STIs), including HIV testing.

Key Concept: Intimate partner violence, which is often undiagnosed, can include physical,

psychological, and/or sexual abuse. Explanation: Common signs of intimate partner violence are injuries to the abdomen, breast, and genitals, injuries in various stages of healing, depression, anxiety, eating disorders, substance use, and dissociative disorders. Initiating a supportive and open-

ended conversation is important to identify intimate partner violence and to allow for counseling and referral for services.

Differential: Patients presenting after sexual assault should undergo a standard evaluation

including urine pregnancy test, forensic rape examination, and screening for STIs including HIV, Chlamydia trachomatis, Neisseria gonorrhoeae, Trichomonas vaginalis, hepatitis B, and syphilis.

wrongAnswers.A: CT scan of the abdomen is incorrect. This modality is useful in the evaluation of hemodynamically stable patients after blunt abdominal trauma; however, this patient’s abdominal symptoms are mild and directly correlate to her known abdominal wall trauma.
wrongAnswers.B: Hepatitis C testing is incorrect. Like hepatitis B, hepatitis C can be sexually transmitted; however, acute viral hepatitis is far more commonly caused by hepatitis B. Hepatitis C testing is more appropriate in high-risk populations such as those who use intravenous drugs.
wrongAnswers.D: Pelvic ultrasonography is incorrect. This modality is indicated for evaluation of disorders of the reproductive tract including retained products of conception, gestational trophoblastic tumors, and structural abnormalities such as polyps or fibroids. This patient’s abdominal and cervical motion tenderness are most likely secondary to the sexual assault and/or an acute STI, and screening for STIs is more appropriate.

explanationPanel.rule: After sexual assault, offer STI screening including HIV testing along with pregnancy testing and forensic examination.
explanationPanel.trap: Hepatitis C testing is not the highest-yield routine next offer compared with HIV and standard STI evaluation.

layer4.rule: After sexual assault, offer STI screening including HIV testing along with pregnancy testing and forensic examination.
layer4.trap: Hepatitis C testing is not the highest-yield routine next offer compared with HIV and standard STI evaluation.

A 35-year-old woman, gravida 2, para 2, is brought to the emergency department because of a 1-day history of severe headache and photosensitivity, low-grade fever, and neck stiffness. She has not had sore throat, rash, chest or joint pain, shortness of breath, or diarrhea. She has not had any sick contacts. She has no history of serious illness or known allergies. Her only medication is ibuprofen as needed. She does not smoke cigarettes, drink alcoholic beverages, or use tobacco. She lives in a rural area of North Carolina. Two weeks ago, she spent the weekend camping and received multiple tick bites. She does not believe that any of the ticks were attached for more than 24 hours. Temperature is 38.4°C (101.1°F), pulse is 104/min and regular, respirations are 18/min, and blood pressure is 104/74 mm Hg. She appears well nourished and in moderate distress. She is shielding her eyes from light. Examination of the skin shows no rash. There is evidence of tick bites over the right shoulder. Examination of the head shows no evidence of trauma. There is no papilledema. There is mild nuchal rigidity. The remainder of neurologic examination discloses no abnormalities. Cardiopulmonary examination discloses no abnormalities. questions.subject: Infectious Disease

explanationPanel.whyCorrect:
Educational Objective: Headache, fever, photophobia, and neck stiffness in this

patient with a recent history of tick bites suggests meningitis from a tick-borne source, such as Rickettsia species. Rickettsial meningitis is diagnosed by lumbar puncture and treated with intravenous antibiotics.

Evaluation: Meningitis classically presents with acute fever, headache, mental status

changes, photophobia, phonophobia, neck stiffness, and/or rash, with variation depending on the causative pathogen. The clinical history should guide evaluation, and in this case, a tick-borne pathogen should be suspected given the patient’s recent exposure. Lumbar puncture is indicated in the evaluation of meningitis to diagnose the condition and guide treatment with pathogen identification and antibiotic susceptibility analysis.

Definition: Rickettsia are a group of intracellular bacteria that cause diseases including but

not limited to spotted fevers, typhus, pox, meningitis, and encephalitis. The bacteria are vectored to humans via tick bite. On infection, the bacteria can spread to various organs, with resultant infection and inflammation causing the clinical presentation. In cases of rickettsial meningitis, which may occur as a primary manifestation of rickettsial infection or as a component of spotted fever or typhus, headache, fever, photo-and phonophobia, altered mental status, and neck stiffness are common presenting features. The diagnosis is made via lumbar puncture, with spinal fluid studies typically showing lymphocytic pleocytosis, normal or increased protein, and normal or increased glucose. Rickettsial species are intracellular pathogens; thus, organisms are not usually seen on Gram stain.

Prevention: Rickettsial species are vectored to humans via tick bites; thus, preventing tick

bites by frequently checking for and removing any attached ticks, using insect repellant, and avoiding travel to or outdoor activities in endemic areas are methods of prevention.

Treatment: Doxycycline and chloramphenicol are the antibiotics of choice in the

management of rickettsial meningitis.

Differential: The key step in diagnosing meningitis is performing a lumbar puncture. In

cases of meningitis, treatment should be empirically initiated promptly; however, correct antibiotic choices should be made based on the likely pathogens. Studies that take days or weeks to result, such as serologies, should not be relied on in the evaluation of potential meningitis.

wrongAnswers.A: Acyclovir therapy is incorrect. Acyclovir is an antiviral medication used to treat herpetic and/or varicella meningitis. Acyclovir has no known activity against Rickettsia.
wrongAnswers.B: Ampicillin therapy is incorrect. Ampicillin is a β-lactam antibiotic that is used to treat Listeria meningitis. Ampicillin is not the drug of choice in treating rickettsial meningitis.
wrongAnswers.D: Serum antibodies to Rickettsia is not the best answer. Antibodies require days (IgM) to weeks (IgG, IgA, IgD, and IgE) to be detectable in serum. Delaying diagnosis or treatment for any amount of time in cases of meningitis is inappropriate, as the consequences for untreated disease may include permanent disability or death.
wrongAnswers.E: Serum cryptococcal antigen is incorrect. Cryptococcal meningitis characteristically presents in patients with immunocompromise. This patient is otherwise healthy and her risk factors for rickettsial infection are greater.

explanationPanel.rule: Suspected meningitis after CT excludes contraindication requires lumbar puncture to diagnose and guide therapy.
explanationPanel.trap: Rickettsial serology takes days to weeks; do not delay meningitis evaluation for send-out antibodies.

layer4.rule: Suspected meningitis after CT excludes contraindication requires lumbar puncture to diagnose and guide therapy.
layer4.trap: Rickettsial serology takes days to weeks; do not delay meningitis evaluation for send-out antibodies.

questions.stem: A 63-year-old woman comes to the physician for a follow-up examination. Five years ago, she underwent a left mastectomy with adjunctive radiation therapy and chemotherapy for carcinoma of the breast. She is currently asymptomatic. Physical examination shows a well-healed mastectomy scar on the left. The most likely site of metastasis in this patient would be shown by a radionuclide scan of which of the following?
questions.stemHtml: A 63-year-old woman comes to the physician for a follow-up examination. Five years ago, she underwent a left mastectomy with adjunctive radiation therapy and chemotherapy for carcinoma of the breast. She is currently asymptomatic. Physical examination shows a well-healed mastectomy scar on the left. The most likely site of metastasis in this patient would be shown by a radionuclide scan of which of the following?
questions.subject: Hematology/Oncology

explanationPanel.whyCorrect:
Educational Objective: The bone is the most common site of breast cancer

metastasis, and it is the most likely site to show metastatic disease in this patient on radionuclide scan.

Evaluation: Metastatic breast cancer may present with symptoms such as bone pain,

headache, nausea, and vomiting.

Definition: Metastatic breast cancer may develop in about 30% of patients who are

originally diagnosed with early-stage disease. The most common site of metastasis in cases of breast cancer is the bone, with other common sites including the brain, lung, and liver.

Prevention: Risk factors for the development of breast cancer include exogenous

estrogen administration, a family history of breast cancer, genetic mutations (eg, BRCA1, BRCA2), early menarche, late menopause, nulliparity, and obesity.

Treatment: Treatment of metastatic breast cancer includes endocrine therapy or

chemotherapy depending on the biology of the metastatic disease. Emphasis is also placed on alleviation of metastatic symptoms and improvement of quality of life.

Differential: This patient has a history of breast cancer treated with radiation,

chemotherapy, and mastectomy. The bone is the most likely site to identify metastatic disease on radionuclide scan.

wrongAnswers.B: The kidneys is incorrect. Cancers most likely to spread to the kidney include cancer of the lung, stomach, intestine, pancreas, and melanoma. Breast cancer is most likely to metastasize to the bone.
wrongAnswers.C: The liver is not the most likely site of metastasis. While the liver is a common site of metastasis in cases of metastatic breast cancer, metastasis to the bone is more likely.
wrongAnswers.D: The parotid gland is incorrect. Metastasis to the parotid gland is uncommon. Cancers that may spread to the parotid gland include squamous cell carcinoma or melanoma of the overlying skin.
wrongAnswers.E: The thyroid gland is not the most likely site of metastasis. Metastatic disease of the thyroid may occur in cases of colorectal cancer, lung cancer, breast cancer, and renal cell carcinoma. Bone metastasis is most likely in cases of breast cancer.

explanationPanel.rule: Breast cancer most commonly metastasizes to bone, often detected by radionuclide bone scan.
explanationPanel.trap: Liver and lung are common metastatic sites but bone is the most likely single answer.

layer4.rule: Breast cancer most commonly metastasizes to bone, often detected by radionuclide bone scan.
layer4.trap: Liver and lung are common metastatic sites but bone is the most likely single answer.

questions.stem: A 4-year-old boy is brought to the office by his mother for a well-child examination. She is concerned that he is a picky eater because he refuses to eat any green vegetables. He has been toilet-trained during the day for 14 months but continues to wet the bed nightly; his mother uses behavior charts to reward nighttime dryness. The patient awakens from nightmares once or twice weekly. He is able to count to five and use four-word sentences. He has no history of serious illness and receives no medications. Vaccinations are up-to-date. He is at the 50th percentile for height and 40th percentile for weight. Examination discloses no abnormalities. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.stemHtml: A 4-year-old boy is brought to the office by his mother for a well-child examination. She is concerned that he is a picky eater because he refuses to eat any green vegetables. He has been toilet-trained during the day for 14 months but continues to wet the bed nightly; his mother uses behavior charts to reward nighttime dryness. The patient awakens from nightmares once or twice weekly. He is able to count to five and use four-word sentences. He has no history of serious illness and receives no medications. Vaccinations are up-to-date. He is at the 50th percentile for height and 40th percentile for weight. Examination discloses no abnormalities. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.subject: Pediatrics/Neonatology

explanationPanel.whyCorrect:
Educational Objective: This patient presents with behaviors appropriate for his age.

The most likely diagnosis in this case is normal development.

Evaluation: The well-child examination is important in screening for developmental

abnormalities in motor, social, verbal, and cognitive domains.

Definition: Normal developmental milestones for a 4-year-old child include the ability to

hop on one foot, participate in cooperative play, and use complete sentences with prepositions. Toilet training often begins between ages 22 and 30 months, with daytime continence often achieved months to years before nocturnal continence.

Prevention: Well-child examinations may identify developmental delays, which allows for

early intervention as needed.

Treatment: No treatment is indicated for this patient. If an abnormality was identified on

well-child examination, treatment would include addressing the underlying issue.

Differential: This patient presents with age-appropriate behaviors as well as average

height and weight. The most likely diagnosis in this case is normal development.

wrongAnswers.A: Enuresis is not the most likely diagnosis. Enuresis is defined as urinary incontinence while sleeping in children aged 5 years or older. This patient is 4 years old.
wrongAnswers.B: Obsessive-compulsive disorder is incorrect. Obsessive-compulsive disorder is an anxiety disorder typically characterized by obsessions (unwanted, intrusive thoughts that produce anxiety) that the patient attempts to neutralize with compulsions (repetitive behaviors). This patient has been refusing green vegetables, which may be a normal finding at this age.
wrongAnswers.C: Oppositional defiant disorder is not the most likely diagnosis. Oppositional defiant disorder manifests as a persistent pattern of angry mood, defiant behavior, and vindictiveness that causes distress and impaired functioning in the child or their caretakers. This patient is not demonstrating these behaviors.
wrongAnswers.D: Sleep terror disorder is not the most likely diagnosis. Sleep terror disorder is a common sleep disorder characterized by recurrent episodes of sympathetic hyperactivity (eg, tachycardia, diaphoresis) and vocalizations (eg, screams) during non-REM sleep within the first 2 hours of falling asleep. Patients are typically unaware and unarousable during the episode and amnestic to the episode afterward.

explanationPanel.rule: Nighttime wetting before age 5, nightmares, and picky eating can be normal development.
explanationPanel.trap: Enuresis is diagnosed at age 5 or older; sleep terrors involve non-REM arousal with amnesia.

layer4.rule: Nighttime wetting before age 5, nightmares, and picky eating can be normal development.
layer4.trap: Enuresis is diagnosed at age 5 or older; sleep terrors involve non-REM arousal with amnesia.

questions.stem: An 18-year-old primigravid woman comes to the emergency department (ED) because of a 1-day history of heavy vaginal bleeding. Her last menstrual period was 15 weeks ago. Menses previously occurred at regular 28-day intervals. Urine pregnancy test result in the ED is positive. She has no history of serious illness and takes no medications. Her father has a history of colon cancer. The patient's vital signs are within normal limits. Cardiopulmonary examination discloses no abnormalities. Pelvic examination shows normal external female genitalia and a closed cervix; there is no blood in the vaginal vault. Bimanual examination discloses a uterus consistent in size with a 20-week gestation. Pelvic ultrasonography shows a heterogeneous-appearing mass within the cavity with cystic spaces and no fetal parts. Quantitative serum β-hCG concentration is 320,000 mIU/mL. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

Menses previously occurred at regular 28-day intervals. Urine pregnancy test result in the ED is positive. She has no history of serious illness and takes no medications. Her father has a history of colon cancer. The patient's vital signs are within normal limits. Cardiopulmonary examination discloses no abnormalities. Pelvic examination shows normal external female genitalia and a closed cervix; there is no blood in the vaginal vault. Bimanual examination discloses a uterus consistent in size with a 20-week gestation. Pelvic ultrasonography shows a heterogeneous-appearing mass within the cavity with cystic spaces and no fetal parts. Quantitative serum β-hCG concentration is 320,000 mIU/mL. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
questions.subject: Obstetrics

explanationPanel.whyCorrect:
Educational Objective: Hydatidiform moles may present with vaginal bleeding and a

uterus larger than the expected gestational age with β-hCG concentration markedly increased on laboratory studies. Treatment of a molar pregnancy includes dilatation and curettage, which is the most appropriate next step for this patient.

Evaluation: Hydatidiform moles commonly present with persistent nausea and vomiting,

first trimester vaginal bleeding, early preeclampsia, and uterine size out of proportion to the expected gestational age.

Definition: Hydatidiform moles are either caused by the fertilization of an empty egg by a

single sperm followed by duplication of the paternal DNA resulting in 46 chromosomes (complete) or the dual fertilization of a normal ovum resulting in 69 chromosomes (incomplete). Complete moles contain no fetal tissue, while incomplete moles contain some fetal tissue. Neither are viable pregnancies, and no fetal heartbeat will be found on Doppler ultrasonography. Ultrasonography of the pelvis will show bilateral multilocular ovarian cysts (theca-lutein cysts) and echogenic structures in the uterus with no fetal parts.

Prevention: There is no known way to prevent a molar pregnancy.

Treatment: Molar pregnancies are treated with dilatation and curettage, followed by

appropriate contraception and sequential measurement of serum β-hCG to monitor for the development of malignant gestational trophoblastic diseases such as invasive moles or choriocarcinoma. These malignant diseases are treated with chemotherapy.

Differential: This patient presents with heavy vaginal bleeding in the first trimester of her

pregnancy with a uterus larger than expected gestational age, markedly increased quantitative serum β-hCG concentration, and pelvic ultrasonography showing a heterogeneous-appearing mass with no fetal parts. The most likely diagnosis in this case is a hydatidiform mole, which is treated with dilatation and curettage.

wrongAnswers.A: Administration of methotrexate is incorrect. Methotrexate may be used as prophylactic chemotherapy after a molar pregnancy has been evacuated if there is a high concern for the development of gestational trophoblastic neoplasia. Dilatation and curettage is more appropriate for this patient.
wrongAnswers.B: Administration of misoprostol is not the most appropriate next step in management. It is generally not recommended to use medication-only methods for molar pregnancy evacuation with medication such as misoprostol or mifepristone. The most appropriate next step in management for this patient is dilatation and curettage.
wrongAnswers.D: Expectant management is incorrect. A hydatidiform mole is not a viable pregnancy. Treatment with dilatation and curettage is more appropriate.
wrongAnswers.E: Hysterotomy is not the most appropriate next step in management. Hysterotomy describes the making of a surgical incision into the uterus and is the method for accessing the intrauterine environment during cesarean section, myotomy, and other uterine surgical procedures. While hysterotomy could be performed to manage a hydatidiform mole, hysterotomy is invasive, and dilatation and curettage will achieve the same result with a less morbid approach.

explanationPanel.rule: Molar pregnancy with very high beta-hCG, large uterus, cystic intrauterine mass, and no fetal parts requires dilation and curettage.
explanationPanel.trap: Methotrexate is for gestational trophoblastic neoplasia risk/treatment after evacuation, not first-line evacuation.

layer4.rule: Molar pregnancy with very high beta-hCG, large uterus, cystic intrauterine mass, and no fetal parts requires dilation and curettage.
layer4.trap: Methotrexate is for gestational trophoblastic neoplasia risk/treatment after evacuation, not first-line evacuation.

questions.stem: A 30-year-old man comes to the office because of a 6-month history of chronic thirst and urinary frequency. He has bipolar disorder. Current medications are lithium carbonate and a daily multivitamin. Vital signs are within normal limits. Physical and neurologic examinations show no abnormalities. Laboratory studies are most likely to show which of the following sets of findings in this patient?
questions.stemHtml: A 30-year-old man comes to the office because of a 6-month history of chronic thirst and urinary frequency. He has bipolar disorder. Current medications are lithium carbonate and a daily multivitamin. Vital signs are within normal limits. Physical and neurologic examinations show no abnormalities. Laboratory studies are most likely to show which of the following sets of findings in this patient?
questions.subject: Nephrology/Urology

explanationPanel.whyCorrect:
Educational Objective: This patient receiving lithium treatment presents with

urinary frequency and chronic thirst, most suggestive of nephrogenic diabetes insipidus in the setting of lithium use. This patient’s laboratory studies are most likely to show increased serum sodium and decreased urine osmolality.

Evaluation: Nephrogenic diabetes insipidus is the inability of the renal system to respond

to ADH (vasopressin), which leads to excessively diluted urine. It typically presents with polyuria and polydipsia, with laboratory studies notable for hypernatremia and decreased urine osmolality. Lithium use is a common cause of acquired nephrogenic diabetes insipidus, as lithium downregulates aquaporin-2 channels, which impairs water reabsorption in the collecting ducts.

Definition: Nephrogenic diabetes insipidus secondary to lithium use is confirmed with a

water-restriction test.

Prevention: Routine monitoring of renal function panels and lithium concentrations is

crucial in mitigating side effects from lithium use.

Treatment: Lithium should be discontinued in this patient, if possible from a psychiatric

perspective. Furthermore, his acute electrolyte derangement can be treated with amiloride.

Differential: This patient presents with chronic thirst and urinary frequency consistent with

polyuria, which has a differential diagnosis that includes disease states such as new-onset diabetes mellitus (osmotic diuresis) and diabetes insipidus (water diuresis). Further history is notable for lithium use, which raises the concern for a lithium-related side effect, such

as nephrogenic diabetes insipidus. A water restriction test would be helpful in confirming the diagnosis.

wrongAnswers.A: Increased sodium and increased urine osmolality is incorrect. This would be seen in patients with primary dehydration from decreased oral intake.
wrongAnswers.C: Decreased sodium and increased urine osmolality is incorrect. This would be seen in patients with syndrome of inappropriate antidiuretic hormone secretion.
wrongAnswers.D: Decreased sodium and decreased urine osmolality is incorrect. This would be seen in primary polydipsia.

explanationPanel.rule: Lithium nephrogenic DI causes polyuria/polydipsia with increased serum sodium and decreased urine osmolality.
explanationPanel.trap: Primary polydipsia has low sodium with dilute urine; dehydration has concentrated urine.

layer4.rule: Lithium nephrogenic DI causes polyuria/polydipsia with increased serum sodium and decreased urine osmolality.
layer4.trap: Primary polydipsia has low sodium with dilute urine; dehydration has concentrated urine.

questions.stem: A 34-year-old man comes to the physician because of a 3-week history of abdominal pain. He is a diesel mechanic. He has smoked 1½ packs of cigarettes daily for 15 years, drinks two cases of beer weekly, and drinks a large pot of coffee daily. Physical examination shows no abnormalities. He says that he is concerned that he might have pancreatic cancer, as one of his coworkers was recently diagnosed with this condition. Which of the following is this patient's most significant risk factor for pancreatic cancer?
questions.stemHtml: A 34-year-old man comes to the physician because of a 3-week history of abdominal pain. He is a diesel mechanic. He has smoked 1½ packs of cigarettes daily for 15 years, drinks two cases of beer weekly, and drinks a large pot of coffee daily. Physical examination shows no abnormalities. He says that he is concerned that he might have pancreatic cancer, as one of his coworkers was recently diagnosed with this condition. Which of the following is this patient's most significant risk factor for pancreatic cancer?
questions.subject: Hematology/Oncology

explanationPanel.whyCorrect:
Educational Objective: This patient presents with abdominal pain and worries about

developing pancreatic cancer. Cigarette smoke is a carcinogen, and cigarette smoking is a well-established risk factor for pancreatic cancer.

Evaluation: Cigarette smoking promotes chronic inflammation and has been shown to

induce genetic mutations that increase the pathways for pancreatic cancer development.

Definition: Pancreatic cancer typically presents with nonspecific symptoms such as

abdominal pain, jaundice, and weight loss. The diagnosis involves abdominal imaging, such as a CT scan with intravenous contrast, often followed by endoscopic ultrasonography with fine-needle aspiration for diagnostic confirmation.

Prevention: While there are many risk factors for the development of pancreatic cancer,

such as alcohol consumption and increased weight, cigarette smoking is the most significant.

Treatment: Treatment for pancreatic cancer depends on the location and stage of the

disease. Patients often undergo chemotherapy and, if the malignancy is amenable, surgical resection.

Differential: The cause of this patient’s abdominal pain is unclear, and it would be rare for

this patient to develop pancreatic cancer. However, he does have a few risk factors.

wrongAnswers.A: Age and alcohol intake are incorrect. While risk for pancreatic cancer increases with age and alcohol intake, cigarette smoking is a more significant risk factor.
wrongAnswers.B: Age and alcohol intake are incorrect. While risk for pancreatic cancer increases with age and alcohol intake, cigarette smoking is a more significant risk factor.
wrongAnswers.D: Coffee consumption and exposure to diesel fumes are incorrect. These are not known risk factors for pancreatic cancer.
wrongAnswers.E: Coffee consumption and exposure to diesel fumes are incorrect. These are not known risk factors for pancreatic cancer.

explanationPanel.rule: Cigarette smoking is the strongest established listed risk factor for pancreatic cancer.
explanationPanel.trap: Coffee and diesel fumes are not established major risks, and alcohol is less significant than smoking.

layer4.rule: Cigarette smoking is the strongest established listed risk factor for pancreatic cancer.
layer4.trap: Coffee and diesel fumes are not established major risks, and alcohol is less significant than smoking.

questions.stem: An 18-month-old boy is brought to the clinic because of a 1-day history of fever and foul-smelling urine. He had a febrile urinary tract infection 6 months ago. He does not receive any medications. Length is at the 75th percentile, weight is at the 90th percentile, and head circumference is at the 90th percentile. Temperature is 38.7°C (101.7°F), pulse is 98/min, respirations are 20/min, and blood pressure is 96/52 mm Hg. He appears mildly fussy. Physical examination shows no other abnormalities. Urinalysis shows 1+ blood and 3+ leukocyte esterase. Urine culture grows greater than 100,000 CFU/mL Escherichia coli. Kidney ultrasonography shows normal-size kidneys for age with no hydronephrosis, masses, or calculi. Voiding cystourethrography shows contrast in the ureter and renal pelvis without dilation on the right side, the bladder without filling defects, and urethra without dilation. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.stemHtml: An 18-month-old boy is brought to the clinic because of a 1-day history of fever and foul-smelling urine. He had a febrile urinary tract infection 6 months ago. He does not receive any medications. Length is at the 75th percentile, weight is at the 90th percentile, and head circumference is at the 90th percentile. Temperature is 38.7°C (101.7°F), pulse is 98/min, respirations are 20/min, and blood pressure is 96/52 mm Hg. He appears mildly fussy. Physical examination shows no other abnormalities. Urinalysis shows 1+ blood and 3+ leukocyte esterase. Urine culture grows greater than 100,000 CFU/mL Escherichia coli. Kidney ultrasonography shows normal-size kidneys for age with no hydronephrosis, masses, or calculi. Voiding cystourethrography shows contrast in the ureter and renal pelvis without dilation on the right side, the bladder without filling defects, and urethra without dilation. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.subject: Nephrology/Urology

explanationPanel.whyCorrect:
Educational Objective: This patient most likely has primary vesicoureteral reflux

(VUR). VUR is characterized by incomplete closure of the vesicoureteral junction during voiding causing retrograde flow of urine from the bladder to the ureters. Patients with VUR are at an increased risk for recurrent urinary tract infections, including pyelonephritis.

Evaluation: Primary VUR often begins during childhood and may occur because of

anatomical abnormalities resulting in the incomplete closure of the ureterovesical junction. VUR may present with postrenal azotemia and hydroureteronephrosis with the possibility of developing chronic renal failure if not corrected.

Definition: Patients may present with varying degrees of dilated ureters, renal pelves,

blunted renal calyces, and/or compressed, atrophic renal parenchyma. The extent and distribution of upper urinary tract dilation and renal parenchymal atrophy depends on the severity and chronicity of VUR. The diagnosis is established by voiding cystourethrography (VCUG), which involves injection of contrast dye into the bladder via catheterization and allows for visualization of reflux during voiding.

Prevention: There is no known way to prevent primary VUR.

Treatment: Primary VUR often resolves spontaneously as the bladder grows. Surgical

management may be indicated in patients with persistent VUR or recurrent infections despite treatment with prophylactic antibiotics.

Differential: The patient in this case is presenting with two urinary tract infections within

the past 6 months with VCUG showing contrast reflux into the ureter and renal pelvis on the right side during voiding. These findings are consistent with a diagnosis of primary VUR.

wrongAnswers.A: Neurogenic bladder is not the most likely diagnosis. Neurogenic bladder may lead to secondary VUR due to increased bladder pressures during voiding. Primary VUR is the most likely diagnosis in this case.
wrongAnswers.B: Posterior urethral valves is incorrect. Posterior urethral valves are a common cause of urinary tract obstruction, which is typically identified by prenatal ultrasonography with findings of bilateral hydronephrosis and dilated bladder. Infants with posterior urethral valves often present with failure to thrive.
wrongAnswers.D: Ureterocele is not the most likely diagnosis. A ureterocele is a dilation of the terminal ureter into the bladder or urethra. Patients often initially present due to urinary tract infection; however, the condition may also be identified during the antenatal stage with ultrasonography.
wrongAnswers.E: Urethral stricture is incorrect. A urethral stricture may be identified in patients presenting with dysuria or urinary retention. The patient in this case has findings of VUR identified on VCUG making primary VUR the most likely diagnosis.

explanationPanel.rule: Recurrent febrile UTIs with VCUG reflux into ureter/renal pelvis and no obstruction is primary vesicoureteral reflux.
explanationPanel.trap: Posterior urethral valves cause obstructive findings such as bilateral hydronephrosis and dilated bladder/urethra.

layer4.rule: Recurrent febrile UTIs with VCUG reflux into ureter/renal pelvis and no obstruction is primary vesicoureteral reflux.
layer4.trap: Posterior urethral valves cause obstructive findings such as bilateral hydronephrosis and dilated bladder/urethra.

questions.stem: A previously healthy 47-year-old man is brought to the emergency department 45 minutes after the sudden onset of generalized weakness and "fluttering" in his chest. His symptoms began as he was working in a coffee shop. On arrival, he is pale, anxious, and diaphoretic. His pulse is 150/min and irregular, respirations are 22/min, and blood pressure is 100/60 mm Hg. The lungs are clear to auscultation. Cardiac examination discloses irregular tachycardia. The remainder of the examination shows no abnormalities. ECG is shown. Which of the following is the most likely cause of these findings?
questions.stemHtml: A previously healthy 47-year-old man is brought to the emergency department 45 minutes after the sudden onset of generalized weakness and "fluttering" in his chest. His symptoms began as he was working in a coffee shop. On arrival, he is pale, anxious, and diaphoretic. His pulse is 150/min and irregular, respirations are 22/min, and blood pressure is 100/60 mm Hg. The lungs are clear to auscultation. Cardiac examination discloses irregular tachycardia. The remainder of the examination shows no abnormalities. ECG is shown. Which of the following is the most likely cause of these findings?
questions.subject: Cardiology

explanationPanel.whyCorrect:
Educational Objective: Atrial fibrillation may present with fatigue, palpitations,

irregular heart rhythm, light-headedness, and near-syncope/syncope. ECG will show an irregular RR interval, without discernable P waves, as in this patient.

Evaluation: Atrial fibrillation is a common cardiac dysrhythmia. While atrial fibrillation can

be asymptomatic, symptoms, especially if rapid ventricular response (tachycardia) is present, include palpitations, fatigue, shortness of breath, light-headedness, angina, and presyncope or syncope.

Definition: Atrial fibrillation is caused by disorganized action potential generation in the

atria, escaping control of the sinus node and native His-Purkinje system. Random and irregular action potentials are conducted to the ventricles via the atrioventricular node, resulting in irregular ventricular conduction. Physical examination will disclose an irregularly irregular pulse and may disclose signs of heart failure or a heart murmur. An

ECG with an irregular RR interval and absent P wave confirms the diagnosis. Risk factors for the development of atrial fibrillation include hypertension, coronary artery disease, structural heart or valvular disease, pulmonary embolism, lung disorders such as obstructive sleep apnea or chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, stimulant overuse, and hyperthyroidism. Complications of atrial fibrillation include tachycardia-induced heart failure, hemodynamic instability, and left atrial appendage thrombus formation.

Prevention: Reduction of modifiable risk factors can limit progression of any underlying or

developing cardiac conduction disease. Patients with a new diagnosis of atrial fibrillation should receive evaluation for reversible causes. In this patient’s case, stimulant overuse (caffeine) should be considered.

Treatment: Treatment includes heart rate control with β-adrenergic blockers or

nondihydropyridine calcium channel blockers, such as metoprolol or diltiazem, and anticoagulation for patients at an increased risk for stroke, which can be assessed using a validated tool such as the CHA2DS2-VASc score.

Differential: The presence of an irregular RR interval and absence of discernable P wave

activity narrows the electrocardiographic differential to atrial fibrillation.

wrongAnswers.B: Atrioventricular block is incorrect. Atrioventricular block is shown on ECG as prolonged PR interval (first degree), progressively longer PR interval with an eventual dropped beat (second degree type one), a fixed ratio of P waves to QRS complexes followed by a nonconducted beat (second degree type two), or atrioventricular dissociation (third degree). This patient’s ECG shows disorganized atrial activity with frequent and rapid, irregular QRS complexes.
wrongAnswers.C: Junctional tachycardia and sinus tachycardia are incorrect. Junctional tachycardia is shown on ECG as a regular, narrow QRS complex with rate greater than 100 beats per minute, without associated P wave activity. Sinus tachycardia is shown on ECG as a regular, narrow QRS complex with rate greater than 100 beats per minute, and with associated P wave activity before each QRS complex indicating sinus nodal control of action potentials. This patient’s ECG shows disorganized atrial activity with frequent and rapid, irregular QRS complexes.
wrongAnswers.D: Junctional tachycardia and sinus tachycardia are incorrect. Junctional tachycardia is shown on ECG as a regular, narrow QRS complex with rate greater than 100 beats per minute, without associated P wave activity. Sinus tachycardia is shown on ECG as a regular, narrow QRS complex with rate greater than 100 beats per minute, and with associated P wave activity before each QRS complex indicating sinus nodal control of action potentials. This patient’s ECG shows disorganized atrial activity with frequent and rapid, irregular QRS complexes.
wrongAnswers.E:
Ventricular tachycardia is incorrect. Ventricular tachycardia is shown on ECG by a regular, wide QRS complex tachycardia without discernable P wave activity, often with a rate of approximately 180 beats per minute. Retrograde P waves may be visible. This

patient’s QRS complex is narrow and irregular.

explanationPanel.rule: Irregularly irregular narrow-complex tachycardia without discrete P waves is atrial fibrillation.
explanationPanel.trap: Sinus, junctional, and AV nodal rhythms are regular; ventricular tachycardia is wide-complex.

layer4.rule: Irregularly irregular narrow-complex tachycardia without discrete P waves is atrial fibrillation.
layer4.trap: Sinus, junctional, and AV nodal rhythms are regular; ventricular tachycardia is wide-complex.

questions.stem: A 45-year-old man has a video telemedicine visit with a physician for a routine examination. He has hypercholesterolemia and says he often feels anxious about work and his family's finances. He is employed as a business executive and has been working at home since the outbreak of a novel viral illness 9 months ago that resulted in an emergency declaration and stay-at-home orders. When asked how he is coping with the changes in his life, he says, "My wife thinks something is wrong, but I think I'm OK. I can relax when I need to, and I never enjoyed socializing much anyway." He says he has always worked hard but works "even more now," which he attributes to the ease of working from home and concerns about the economic future of the company. He adds, "I don't trust some of my employees to do things the way they should be done." He describes spending several hours daily organizing files he has brought home from work; he says he feels he cannot stop until "everything is in order" in his home office. The patient says his wife may notice these behaviors more since he started working from home but "I've always been like this." They have had increasingly frequent arguments about his behavior and his unwillingness to spend money on home improvements that his wife wants. He has not had difficulty sleeping. Medications are simvastatin and a multivitamin. Vital signs cannot be obtained. The patient appears fatigued. Limited physical examination discloses no abnormalities. On mental status examination, the patient describes his mood as "anxious"; affect is congruent. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.stemHtml: A 45-year-old man has a video telemedicine visit with a physician for a routine examination. He has hypercholesterolemia and says he often feels anxious about work and his family's finances. He is employed as a business executive and has been working at home since the outbreak of a novel viral illness 9 months ago that resulted in an emergency declaration and stay-at-home orders. When asked how he is coping with the changes in his life, he says, "My wife thinks something is wrong, but I think I'm OK. I can relax when I need to, and I never enjoyed socializing much anyway." He says he has always worked hard but works "even more now," which he attributes to the ease of working from home and concerns about the economic future of the company. He adds, "I don't trust some of my employees to do things the way they should be done." He describes spending several hours daily organizing files he has brought home from work; he says he feels he cannot stop until "everything is in order" in his home office. The patient says his wife may notice these behaviors more since he started working from home but "I've always been like this." They have had increasingly frequent arguments about his behavior and his unwillingness to spend money on home improvements that his wife wants. He has not had difficulty sleeping. Medications are simvastatin and a multivitamin. Vital signs cannot be obtained. The patient appears fatigued. Limited physical examination discloses no abnormalities. On mental status examination, the patient describes his mood as "anxious"; affect is congruent. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.subject: Psychiatry

explanationPanel.whyCorrect:
Educational Objective: Obsessive-compulsive personality disorder (OCPD) is a

cluster C personality disorder characterized by excessively rigid routines and perfectionism, as seen in this patient.

Evaluation: OCPD is a cluster C personality disorder, the anxious or fearful cluster. It is

characterized by excessively rigid routines and perfectionism. Patients often display an obsession with control and the belief that their approach to a particular problem or situation is the only correct approach. The patient’s family, friends, or coworkers often

note rigid, stubborn thought patterns. This rigidity and obsession with perfection may occur at the expense of a patient’s social relationships or career, as evidenced by this patient’s difficulty in accommodating his wife’s wishes.

Definition: Personality disorders are persistently maladaptive ways of relating to the self

and to society that typically appear by early adulthood.

Prevention: As the precise cause is unknown, there is no universal prevention strategy for

OCPD.

Treatment: OCPD is difficult to treat but may respond to psychotherapy.

Differential: Patients with OCPD do not display intrusive, recurrent thoughts or compulsive

behaviors as seen in obsessive-compulsive disorder. The ego-syntonic nature of the patient’s behaviors, in which the patient does not recognize the problematic nature of their behaviors, distinguishes OCPD from most anxiety disorders.

wrongAnswers.A: Adjustment disorder with anxiety is incorrect. Adjustment disorder with anxiety refers to disproportionate anxiety related to a stressor. This patient does not present with a discrete stressor; the patient instead views the viral outbreak as a benefit for his productivity. Additionally, his rigid behaviors are longstanding and pervasive, which is more consistent with a personality disorder.
wrongAnswers.B: Generalized anxiety disorder is incorrect. Generalized anxiety disorder features excessive and persistent worrying that may be associated with sympathetic hyperactivity. Patients do not typically display excessive orderliness, rigidity, or perfectionism.
wrongAnswers.C: Obsessive-compulsive disorder is incorrect. Patients with OCPD do not display intrusive, recurrent thoughts or compulsive behaviors as seen in obsessive-compulsive disorder. The ego-syntonic nature of the patient’s behaviors, in which the patient does not recognize the problematic nature of their behaviors, distinguishes OCPD from most anxiety disorders.
wrongAnswers.E:
Schizoid personality disorder is incorrect. Schizoid personality disorder, a cluster A personality disorder, manifests as extreme social detachment and a cold, restricted affect. Inflexible orderliness and perfectionism are not typical features of schizoid personality disorder. As well, this married patient does not present with social

detachment.
wrongAnswers.F: Normal response to stress is incorrect. This patient’s rigid perfectionism is excessive and causing problems in his life. This patient does not present with a discrete stressor; the patient instead views the viral outbreak as a benefit for his productivity.

explanationPanel.rule: Longstanding ego-syntonic perfectionism, rigidity, control, and frugality impairing relationships is OCPD.
explanationPanel.trap: OCD has intrusive ego-dystonic obsessions and compulsions rather than personality-level rigidity.

layer4.rule: Longstanding ego-syntonic perfectionism, rigidity, control, and frugality impairing relationships is OCPD.
layer4.trap: OCD has intrusive ego-dystonic obsessions and compulsions rather than personality-level rigidity.

questions.stem: A 5-year-old girl is brought to the physician by her mother because of a 3-day history of an increasingly severe rash on her face. Physical examination shows a 6-cm, honey-colored crusting lesion over the right cheek. A Gram stain of the exudate shows gram-positive cocci in chains. This patient is at increased risk for developing which of the following complications?
questions.stemHtml: A 5-year-old girl is brought to the physician by her mother because of a 3-day history of an increasingly severe rash on her face. Physical examination shows a 6-cm, honey-colored crusting lesion over the right cheek. A Gram stain of the exudate shows gram-positive cocci in chains. This patient is at increased risk for developing which of the following complications?
questions.subject: Infectious Disease

explanationPanel.whyCorrect:
Educational Objective: This patient is at increased risk for developing

glomerulonephritis, which is a possible complication of impetigo. Impetigo is a superficial skin infection commonly caused by streptococcal species.

Evaluation: Impetigo commonly affects children, although occasionally it affects adults.

Clinically, impetigo manifests with superficial erythematous erosions of the face and overlying honey-colored crust. Impetigo can be diagnosed clinically; however, bacterial culture may be performed to identify the specific causal pathogen.

Definition: Impetigo is a common, superficial infection caused by streptococcal or

staphylococcal species. The most severe complication of impetigo is poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis. The glomerulonephritis is caused by deposition of IgG, IgM, and complement in the glomerular basement membrane 2 to 4 weeks after infection. Poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis is a type III (immune complex-mediated) hypersensitivity reaction.

Prevention: Adequate treatment of impetigo may prevent downstream complications,

including poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis.

Treatment: Topical antibiotics such as mupirocin are the mainstay of treatment in localized

cases of impetigo. Systemic antibiotics are reserved for severe cases.

Differential: In children who develop erythematous, eroded plaques with overlying honey-

colored crust, the most likely diagnosis is impetigo, commonly caused by streptococcal species. A known complication of impetigo is poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis.

wrongAnswers.A: Erythema marginatum is incorrect. Erythema marginatum is a reactive, inflammatory, evanescent, nonpruritic, annular or urticarial rash of the trunk and extremities. Erythema marginatum is one of the major criteria for rheumatic fever, associated with group A streptococci infection of the oropharynx.
wrongAnswers.C: Migratory polyarthritis is incorrect. Migratory polyarthritis is associated with multiple inflamed and painful joints. Migratory polyarthritis is a major criterion for rheumatic fever, associated with group A streptococci infection of the oropharynx.
wrongAnswers.D: Myocarditis is incorrect. Myocarditis is associated with the development of inflammation within the heart. Myocarditis, in addition to polyarthritis, Sydenham chorea, erythema marginatum, and subcutaneous nodules, represent the major criteria for rheumatic fever.
wrongAnswers.E: Sydenham chorea is incorrect. Sydenham chorea is associated with abrupt onset of asymmetric, involuntary, jerking movements in the setting of acute rheumatic fever. It is one of the major criteria associated with acute rheumatic fever. This patient most likely has impetigo.

explanationPanel.rule: Streptococcal impetigo can cause poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis 2-4 weeks later.
explanationPanel.trap: Acute rheumatic fever complications follow pharyngitis, not streptococcal skin infection.

layer4.rule: Streptococcal impetigo can cause poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis 2-4 weeks later.
layer4.trap: Acute rheumatic fever complications follow pharyngitis, not streptococcal skin infection.

questions.stem: A 52-year-old woman is evaluated in an ambulatory surgical center because of rectal bleeding. Two hours ago, she underwent screening colonoscopy; a 1.5-cm pedunculated polyp was removed from the descending colon. She felt well after the procedure but then noticed that she had some bright red blood per rectum. She has not had dizziness or shortness of breath. Vital signs are within normal limits. Rectal examination discloses bright red blood. On repeat colonoscopy, blood is noted to be oozing from the site of the polypectomy. Cautery is applied, and the bleeding stops. Repeat complete blood count shows a stable hemoglobin concentration. When communicating information about this event to the patient, which of the following is the most appropriate initial course of action?
questions.stemHtml: A 52-year-old woman is evaluated in an ambulatory surgical center because of rectal bleeding. Two hours ago, she underwent screening colonoscopy; a 1.5-cm pedunculated polyp was removed from the descending colon. She felt well after the procedure but then noticed that she had some bright red blood per rectum. She has not had dizziness or shortness of breath. Vital signs are within normal limits. Rectal examination discloses bright red blood. On repeat colonoscopy, blood is noted to be oozing from the site of the polypectomy. Cautery is applied, and the bleeding stops. Repeat complete blood count shows a stable hemoglobin concentration. When communicating information about this event to the patient, which of the following is the most appropriate initial course of action?
choices: Explain how the bleeding happened and apologize
Reassure the patient that this was a minor complication and that the blood loss was not significant
Remind the patient that she was told that bleeding is a known potential complication of colonoscopy
Review the patient's consent form with her
questions.subject: Ethics/Social Sciences

explanationPanel.correct: B. Explain how the bleeding happened and apologize
explanationPanel.whyCorrect:
Educational Objective: When discussing adverse events with patients, physicians

should tend to patients’ informational and emotional needs, including needs for transparency and acknowledgment. Acknowledgment commonly involves an apology; the physician should explain to this patient how the bleeding happened and apologize.

Key Concept: When an adverse event occurs, physicians should address both the

informational and emotional needs of patients and families. This should include providing pertinent details and empathically acknowledging the negative impact the event had on the patient. Explanation: Specifically, the discussion of the adverse event should include admitting there was an adverse event, describing the details of the adverse event, acknowledging responsibility, expressing sympathy, and discussing strategies for preventing event recurrence. Physicians should also be available to provide ongoing support after the event. This approach of transparency and accountability maintains trust with patients and promotes a culture of safety.

Differential: Though bleeding is a known complication of colonoscopy, reminding the

patient of this neglects the patient’s emotional need of acknowledging their negative experience of having an adverse event.

wrongAnswers.A: Contact the malpractice insurance carrier is inappropriate. The physician’s first responsibility is to the patient’s well-being, including the patient’s emotional and informational needs. Also, this is likely unnecessary if the physician adhered to standards of care.
wrongAnswers.C: Reassure the patient that this was a minor complication and that the blood loss was not significant and remind the patient that she was told that bleeding is a known potential complication of colonoscopy are incorrect. Though both statements are true, they avoid providing details and minimize the event, thereby neglecting the patient’s negative experience. Physicians should instead tend to patients’ emotional need for acknowledgment and validation of their experience.
wrongAnswers.D: Reassure the patient that this was a minor complication and that the blood loss was not significant and remind the patient that she was told that bleeding is a known potential complication of colonoscopy are incorrect. Though both statements are true, they avoid providing details and minimize the event, thereby neglecting the patient’s negative experience. Physicians should instead tend to patients’ emotional need for acknowledgment and validation of their experience.
wrongAnswers.E: Review the patient's consent form with her is inappropriate. This defensive action implies fault of the patient for agreeing to the procedure and its risks. The physician should instead attend to the informational and emotional needs of the patient.

explanationPanel.rule: After an adverse event, first explain what happened, acknowledge harm, and apologize.
explanationPanel.trap: Reviewing consent forms or minimizing the event is defensive and fails the patient’s informational/emotional needs.

layer4.rule: After an adverse event, first explain what happened, acknowledge harm, and apologize.

A 60-year-old man comes to the office for a health maintenance examination. He has a 3-month history of progressive fatigue but otherwise feels well. There is no family history of cancer. The patient has no known occupational exposures and does not smoke cigarettes or drink alcoholic beverages. He is 178 cm (5 ft 10 in) tall and weighs 75 kg (165 lb); BMI is 24 kg/m². Temperature is 37.0°C (98.6°F), pulse is 75/min, and blood pressure is 130/80 mm Hg. Physical examination shows conjunctival pallor. There is no lymphadenopathy. Cardiopulmonary examination discloses no abnormalities. Abdominal examination shows hepatosplenomegaly. Results of blood laboratory studies are shown:
Hematocrit30%
Hemoglobin10 g/dL
WBC40,000/mm³
Neutrophils, segmented27%
Lymphocytes73%
Platelet count150,000/mm³

Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in diagnosis?

Cardiopulmonary examination discloses no abnormalities. Abdominal examination shows hepatosplenomegaly. Results of blood laboratory studies are shown:

Hematocrit30%
Hemoglobin10 g/dL
WBC40,000/mm³
Neutrophils, segmented27%
Lymphocytes73%
Platelet count150,000/mm³

Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in diagnosis?
questions.subject: Hematology/Oncology

explanationPanel.whyCorrect:
Educational Objective: This patient presents with a history of fatigue and is found

to have lymphocytic-predominant leukocytosis, raising concern for chronic lymphocytic leukemia (CLL). The most appropriate next step in diagnosis is flow cytometry analysis of the patient’s blood.

Evaluation: Patients typically present with asymptomatic lymphocytosis, but can also have

symptoms such as lymphadenopathy, B symptoms, or fatigue, as with this patient. The gold standard for diagnosis of CLL is flow cytometry of the circulating B-lymphocyte population.

Definition: CLL is a progressive illness characterized by the accumulation of mature

lymphocytes secondary to pathogenic events that occur to a B lymphocyte, resulting in a monoclonal B-lymphocyte population.

Prevention: There are no well-established ways to prevent CLL.

Treatment: Treatment often includes Bruton tyrosine kinase inhibitors such as ibrutinib.

Differential: The differential for this patient is narrowed by his fatigue and leukocytosis. His

history is not consistent with infection; however, with leukocytosis, infection must be on the differential. Flow cytometry will further aid in confirmation of the diagnosis of CLL.

wrongAnswers.A: Bone marrow biopsy is not the most appropriate next step. CLL can be adequately diagnosed through flow cytometry of circulating B lymphocytes.
wrongAnswers.B: Chromosomal analysis is not the most appropriate next step. While chromosomal analysis can be completed on malignant cells, it is not necessary for the diagnosis of this patient.
wrongAnswers.D: Serum leukocyte alkaline phosphatase activity is incorrect. Serum leukocyte alkaline phosphatase activity is a marker of granulocyte differentiation and can be used to differentiate chronic myelogenous leukemia from other causes of leukocytosis. Serum leukocyte alkaline phosphatase activity is not necessary for a diagnosis of CLL.

explanationPanel.rule: Older adult with lymphocyte-predominant leukocytosis and fatigue is diagnosed by peripheral blood flow cytometry.
explanationPanel.trap: Bone marrow biopsy or cytogenetics may stage/risk-stratify but are not the initial diagnostic test.

layer4.rule: Older adult with lymphocyte-predominant leukocytosis and fatigue is diagnosed by peripheral blood flow cytometry.
layer4.trap: Bone marrow biopsy or cytogenetics may stage/risk-stratify but are not the initial diagnostic test.

A 15-year-old boy is brought to the emergency department because of a 2-day history of moderate chest pain. He also has a cough that began 1 week ago when he was diagnosed with mycoplasma pneumonia. The cough is worse at night and has not improved with azithromycin therapy. He adds that, since he was diagnosed, when he plays basketball, he begins coughing, his chest feels tight, and he feels unable to breathe. His temperature is 37°C (98.6°F), pulse is 74/min, respirations are 18/min, and blood pressure is 110/68 mm Hg. Pulse oximetry on room air shows an oxygen saturation of 98%. Examination shows no abnormalities. Pulmonary function testing shows:
FEV₁78% of predicted
FVC96% of predicted
FEV₁:FVC ratio79%
Forced expiratory flow66% of predicted

The flow volume loop is shown. Which of the following best describes this patient’s airway mechanics?
questions.stemHtml:
A 15-year-old boy is brought to the emergency department because of a 2-day history of moderate chest pain. He also has a cough that began 1 week ago when he was diagnosed with mycoplasma pneumonia. The cough is worse at night and has not improved with azithromycin therapy. He adds that, since he was diagnosed, when he plays basketball, he begins coughing, his chest feels tight, and he feels unable to breathe. His temperature is 37°C (98.6°F), pulse is 74/min, respirations are 18/min, and blood pressure is 110/68 mm Hg. Pulse oximetry on room air shows an oxygen saturation of 98%. Examination shows no abnormalities. Pulmonary function testing shows:

FEV₁78% of predicted
FVC96% of predicted
FEV₁:FVC ratio79%
Forced expiratory flow66% of predicted

The flow volume loop is shown. Which of the following best describes this patient’s airway mechanics?
choices: Incomplete effort resulting in invalid measurements
questions.subject: Pulmonology

explanationPanel.whyCorrect:
Educational Objective: Bronchospasm is the likely cause of this patient’s chest

pain, cough, chest tightness, and dyspnea in the setting of a recent pulmonary illness. Bronchospasm results in airflow obstruction, which is shown by this patient’s decreased FEV₁:FVC ratio and the concave shape of the expiratory portion of his flow volume loop.

Key Concept: Bronchospasm, which is often triggered by exercise, allergens, and illness,

results in airflow obstruction primarily during expiration. Bronchospasm typically presents with dyspnea, cough, wheezing, chest tightness, and increased work of breathing. Explanation: Bronchospasm can occur in the setting of underlying lung disease, such as asthma, or in isolation. The diagnosis is suspected based on clinical history and examination, though it can be confirmed through pulmonary function tests (PFTs) that show an obstructive pattern. This pattern is characterized by a decrease in FEV₁, decreased FEV₁:FVC ratio, and preservation of FVC. Flow volume loops generally show abrupt decreases in the expiratory flow rate compared to those of an unaffected patient, which creates a concave appearance of the expiratory flow loop as initial expiratory flow rates rapidly decrease in the setting of obstruction.

Differential: Typically, restrictive lung disease results in a decreased FEV₁:FVC ratio with

lower lung volumes and flow rates seen on the flow volume loop. An incomplete effort would result in a decrease in both FEV₁ and FVC measurement. This patient has abnormalities on both his PFTs and flow volume loop.

wrongAnswers.B: Incomplete effort resulting in invalid measurements is incorrect. An incomplete effort could be identified by a decreased FEV₁ and FVC. This patient has a decrease in his FEV₁ relative to his FVC, making an obstructive lung pathology more likely.
wrongAnswers.C: Pulmonary restriction and airway obstruction is incorrect. A combination of pulmonary restriction and airway obstruction may be difficult to elucidate on PFTs but could result in decreased values of both FEV₁ and FVC, with larger decreases in FEV₁. This patient has a normal FVC, making restrictive lung disease unlikely.
wrongAnswers.D: Pulmonary restriction only is incorrect. Restrictive lung disease is shown by similar decreases in both FEV₁ and FVC. Flow volume loops will also show lower lung volumes with decreased flow rates. This patient has a decreased FEV₁ with a normal FVC, making obstructive pathology more likely than restrictive lung disease.
wrongAnswers.E: Normal is incorrect. This patient has abnormal PFTs, as evidenced by his decreased FEV₁ and FEV₁:FVC ratio. His flow volume loop is also abnormal, with a concave expiratory limb, suggesting airflow obstruction.

explanationPanel.rule: Bronchospasm/obstruction shows decreased FEV₁:FVC with normal FVC and a concave expiratory limb.
explanationPanel.trap: Restriction lowers FVC and lung volumes; poor effort lowers both FEV₁ and FVC.

layer4.rule: Bronchospasm/obstruction shows decreased FEV₁:FVC with normal FVC and a concave expiratory limb.
layer4.trap: Restriction lowers FVC and lung volumes; poor effort lowers both FEV₁ and FVC.

questions.stem: A previously healthy 5-year-old girl is brought to the physician by her parents because they are concerned about her height. Records show that her growth had proceeded at a normal velocity, along the 50th percentile for age. During the past year, she has grown only 1 cm (0.5 in) but has continued to gain weight. She has a good appetite and eats a variety of foods. She frequently has constipation and says she often feels cold. She has not had fever, vision problems, headache, nausea, diarrhea, or change in urination. She is now at the 3rd percentile for height and 75th percentile for weight. Her temperature is 37°C (98.6°F), pulse is 65/min, respirations are 20/min, and blood pressure is 80/60 mm Hg. The skin is cool and dry. The neck is supple, and there is no lymphadenopathy. The thyroid gland is symmetric and normal in size. Cardiopulmonary examination shows no abnormalities. Patellar and Achilles tendon reflexes are 2+ bilaterally with a slow return phase. The remainder of the examination shows no abnormalities. A complete blood count and urinalysis show no abnormalities. Serum studies show a free thyroxine concentration of 0.2 ng/dL (N=0.8–2.2) and thyroid-stimulating hormone concentration of 150 mIU/L (N=0.7–6.4). Which of the following is the most likely explanation for this patient’s findings?
