Records show that her growth had proceeded at a normal velocity, along the 50th percentile for age. During the past year, she has grown only 1 cm (0.5 in) but has continued to gain weight. She has a good appetite and eats a variety of foods. She frequently has constipation and says she often feels cold. She has not had fever, vision problems, headache, nausea, diarrhea, or change in urination. She is now at the 3rd percentile for height and 75th percentile for weight. Her temperature is 37°C (98.6°F), pulse is 65/min, respirations are 20/min, and blood pressure is 80/60 mm Hg. The skin is cool and dry. The neck is supple, and there is no lymphadenopathy. The thyroid gland is symmetric and normal in size. Cardiopulmonary examination shows no abnormalities. Patellar and Achilles tendon reflexes are 2+ bilaterally with a slow return phase. The remainder of the examination shows no abnormalities. A complete blood count and urinalysis show no abnormalities. Serum studies show a free thyroxine concentration of 0.2 ng/dL (N=0.8–2.2) and thyroid-stimulating hormone concentration of 150 mIU/L (N=0.7–6.4). Which of the following is the most likely explanation for this patient’s findings?
choices: Destructive mass in the sella turcica
questions.subject: Endocrinology

explanationPanel.whyCorrect:
Educational Objective: This patient presents with slowed growth, constipation, and

cold intolerance with a physical examination notable for slow return phase of reflexes. She is found to have a severely increased TSH concentration and a decreased concentration of free thyroxine (FT4), most suggestive of autoimmune-mediated thyroiditis resulting in hypothyroidism.

Evaluation: Autoimmune-mediated thyroiditis, or chronic lymphocytic (Hashimoto)

thyroiditis specifically, is an autoimmune disorder that is characterized by hypothyroidism secondary to destruction of the thyroid gland from the immune system. It typically presents with symptoms of thyroiditis.

Definition: Laboratory studies will show increased TSH concentrations, decreased FT4

concentrations, and presence of thyroid-specific autoantibodies, such as antithyroid peroxidase and antithyroglobulin antibodies.

Prevention: There are no known strategies to prevent the development of autoimmune-

mediated thyroiditis.

Treatment: Thyroid hormone replacement therapy with levothyroxine is the cornerstone of

treatment for this disease, which manages the effects of hypothyroidism.

Differential: This young female patient has symptoms and a physical examination

consistent with manifestations of hypothyroidism. Her laboratory studies confirm these findings. In pediatric patients who are iodine-sufficient, which can be assumed based on this patient’s robust dietary history, the most common cause of acquired hypothyroidism is autoimmune-mediated thyroiditis.

wrongAnswers.B: Destructive mass in the sella turcica is incorrect. This would cause hypopituitarism, which would present with a decreased serum TSH concentration.
wrongAnswers.C: Iodine deficiency is incorrect. While iodine deficiency can lead to hypothyroidism that would present similarly to this patient, one would expect the patient to have a less robust nutrition status. This patient’s history is more consistent with autoimmune-mediated thyroiditis.
wrongAnswers.D: Nonfunctioning thyroid nodule is incorrect. If the patient’s hypothyroidism was caused by a nonfunctioning nodule, one would expect the thyroid gland examination to be notable for a palpable mass. It is less likely at this patient’s young age to develop a nonfunctioning thyroid nodule. Autoimmune-mediated thyroiditis is the more likely diagnosis.
wrongAnswers.E: Thyroid dysgenesis is incorrect. Thyroid dysgenesis would likely be present earlier in life. It would be abnormal for a patient to live for 5 years before developing any symptoms of hypothyroidism. The most likely diagnosis in this patient is autoimmune-mediated thyroiditis.

explanationPanel.rule: Child with growth deceleration, weight gain, constipation, cold intolerance, high TSH, and low free T4 has autoimmune thyroiditis.
explanationPanel.trap: A sellar mass causes central hypothyroidism with low/normal TSH, not markedly elevated TSH.

layer4.rule: Child with growth deceleration, weight gain, constipation, cold intolerance, high TSH, and low free T4 has autoimmune thyroiditis.
layer4.trap: A sellar mass causes central hypothyroidism with low/normal TSH, not markedly elevated TSH.

questions.stem: A 44-year-old woman comes to the clinic because of a 3-day history of "painful sores near my vagina." She has no history of serious illness or similar symptoms and takes no medications. She identifies as heterosexual and reports regular unprotected vaginal intercourse with her husband of 20 years. She is 157 cm (5 ft 2 in) tall and weighs 60 kg (133 lb); BMI is 24 kg/m². Temperature is 37.4°C (99.3°F), pulse is 90/min, respirations are 18/min, and blood pressure is 140/88 mm Hg. She appears moderately uncomfortable. Examination discloses vulvar ulcers. There is one enlarged and tender inguinal lymph node. One of the labial lesions is swabbed and submitted for further testing. Which of the following infectious agents is the most likely cause of this patient’s condition?
questions.stemHtml: A 44-year-old woman comes to the clinic because of a 3-day history of "painful sores near my vagina." She has no history of serious illness or similar symptoms and takes no medications. She identifies as heterosexual and reports regular unprotected vaginal intercourse with her husband of 20 years. She is 157 cm (5 ft 2 in) tall and weighs 60 kg (133 lb); BMI is 24 kg/m². Temperature is 37.4°C (99.3°F), pulse is 90/min, respirations are 18/min, and blood pressure is 140/88 mm Hg. She appears moderately uncomfortable. Examination discloses vulvar ulcers. There is one enlarged and tender inguinal lymph node. One of the labial lesions is swabbed and submitted for further testing. Which of the following infectious agents is the most likely cause of this patient’s condition?
questions.subject: Infectious Disease

explanationPanel.whyCorrect:
Educational Objective: The most likely cause of this patient’s condition is herpes simplex virus (HSV), which causes vesicular lesions on the vulva, vagina, perineum, or rectum. HSV typically presents with the initial formation of vesicles, which lyse and progress to shallow, painful ulcers with an erythematous border.

Evaluation: During the initial presentation of HSV, patients may present with symptoms such as painful genital ulcers, dysuria, fever, as well as localized, tender inguinal lymphadenopathy.

Definition: Most cases of genital herpes are caused by HSV-2; however, HSV-1 has also been associated with genital herpes infection. Transmission of genital HSV is often from sexual relationships and may spread when symptoms are absent due to subclinical viral shedding.

Prevention: Transmission may be prevented by avoidance of sexual activity during active disease and by use of barrier contraception.

Treatment: HSV is treated with acyclovir or valacyclovir, which are guanosine analogs that inhibit viral DNA polymerase. These medications decrease the duration of viral shedding and severity of symptoms.

Differential: This patient presents with vulvar ulcers, and a tender inguinal lymph node is identified. HSV is the most likely infectious agent causing her symptoms.

wrongAnswers.A: Candida albicans is incorrect. C. albicans is a fungus that also forms part of the normal vaginal flora. Overgrowth of Candida species may produce vulvovaginitis, which presents with pruritus and a white vaginal discharge.
wrongAnswers.B: Chlamydia trachomatis is not the most likely infectious agent. Lymphogranuloma venereum is caused by infection with C. trachomatis subtypes L1, L2, and L3. It presents as small, painless genital ulcers with tender inguinal lymphadenopathy.
wrongAnswers.C: Haemophilus ducreyi is incorrect. H. ducreyi is a gram-negative organism that causes the sexually transmitted infection chancroid. While chancroid also presents with painful genital ulceration and inguinal lymphadenopathy, chancroid more commonly causes a single lesion rather than multiple small lesions. HSV is more likely in this case.
wrongAnswers.E: Neisseria gonorrhoeae is not the most likely infectious agent. N. gonorrhoeae can cause vaginitis, cervicitis, and pelvic inflammatory disease. HSV is more likely in this case.
wrongAnswers.F: Treponema pallidum is incorrect. T. pallidum is the causative spirochete bacterium of syphilis. Syphilis presents in multiple stages with varying symptoms, including primary with a painless chancre, secondary with fever, diffuse maculopapular rash, lymphadenopathy, and condylomata lata, and tertiary with tabes dorsalis, aortitis, and gummas.

explanationPanel.rule: Painful grouped genital ulcers with tender nodes = HSV; treat with acyclovir/valacyclovir and counsel on shedding.
explanationPanel.trap: Trap: chancroid also hurts, but HSV classically begins as multiple vesicles that ulcerate.

layer4.rule: Painful grouped genital ulcers with tender nodes = HSV; treat with acyclovir/valacyclovir and counsel on shedding.
layer4.trap: Trap: chancroid also hurts, but HSV classically begins as multiple vesicles that ulcerate.

questions.stem: A 26-year-old woman comes to the office because of a 6-month history of an increase in facial hair and occasional breakouts of acne. She has no history of serious illness. Menses have occurred at irregular 45- to 60-day intervals since menarche at the age of 8 years. Ultrasonography of the ovary 1 month ago showed no abnormalities. She takes no medications. She is 160 cm (5 ft 3 in) tall and weighs 70 kg (155 lb); BMI is 28 kg/m². Vital signs are within normal limits. Physical examination shows increased facial and body hair, increased sebaceous secretions, and moderate clitoral enlargement. Serum studies are most likely to show an increase in which of the following?
questions.stemHtml: A 26-year-old woman comes to the office because of a 6-month history of an increase in facial hair and occasional breakouts of acne. She has no history of serious illness. Menses have occurred at irregular 45- to 60-day intervals since menarche at the age of 8 years. Ultrasonography of the ovary 1 month ago showed no abnormalities. She takes no medications. She is 160 cm (5 ft 3 in) tall and weighs 70 kg (155 lb); BMI is 28 kg/m². Vital signs are within normal limits. Physical examination shows increased facial and body hair, increased sebaceous secretions, and moderate clitoral enlargement. Serum studies are most likely to show an increase in which of the following?
questions.subject: Endocrinology

explanationPanel.whyCorrect:
Educational Objective: This patient presents with hirsutism, acne, and irregular menses most consistent with nonclassic congenital adrenal hyperplasia, which results from a partial 21-hydroxylase deficiency. Laboratory studies would be notable for an increased concentration of 17-hydroxyprogesterone.

Evaluation: In contrast to classic congenital adrenal hyperplasia that presents in infancy with salt-wasting crisis, nonclassic congenital adrenal hyperplasia is a less severe variant that presents later in life with signs of androgen excess, such as hirsutism, acne, and irregular menses in patients assigned female as birth. Because of the partial 21- hydroxylase deficiency, there is an increase in adrenocorticotropic hormone production, which subsequently leads to overproduction of adrenal androgens.

Definition: The decrease in 21-hydroxylase enzyme also drives an increase in 17- hydroxyprogesterone concentration, which is often measured as the gold standard for diagnosis of nonclassic congenital adrenal hyperplasia.

Prevention: There are no established preventive measures as this is a genetic diagnosis. Genetic counseling is recommended for affected families.

Treatment: Treatment includes glucocorticoid therapy to decrease the stimulation of adrenocorticotropic hormone and antiandrogen medications to control hirsutism and menstrual irregularities.

Differential: The differential diagnosis for this patient includes polycystic ovary syndrome and idiopathic hirsutism. Serum studies will be helpful in confirming the most likely diagnosis in this patient.

wrongAnswers.A: Aldosterone is incorrect. Increased concentrations of aldosterone are seen in primary aldosteronism, which typically presents with hypertension, hypokalemia, and metabolic alkalosis.
wrongAnswers.B: Cortisol is incorrect. Increased concentrations of cortisol are seen in Cushing syndrome, which typically presents with central obesity, hypertension, weakness, and hyperglycemia.
wrongAnswers.C: 11-Deoxycorticosterone and 11-deoxycortisol are incorrect. These are increased in congenital adrenal hyperplasia from 11β-hydroxylase deficiency, which is less common than 21-hydroxylase deficiency.
wrongAnswers.D: 11-Deoxycorticosterone and 11-deoxycortisol are incorrect. These are increased in congenital adrenal hyperplasia from 11β-hydroxylase deficiency, which is less common than 21-hydroxylase deficiency.
wrongAnswers.F: Pregnenolone is incorrect. Increased concentrations of pregnenolone are seen in lipoid congenital adrenal hyperplasia, which is one of the rarest and most severe forms of congenital adrenal hyperplasia. This would present early in life with salt wasting and lack of androgenic hormone production. This patient’s presentation is the opposite.

explanationPanel.rule: Female hirsutism/acne/oligomenorrhea with clitoromegaly and normal ovaries = nonclassic 21-hydroxylase deficiency with high 17-hydroxyprogesterone.
explanationPanel.trap: Trap: PCOS causes hyperandrogenism but not virilization/clitoromegaly to this degree and does not raise 17-hydroxyprogesterone.

layer4.rule: Female hirsutism/acne/oligomenorrhea with clitoromegaly and normal ovaries = nonclassic 21-hydroxylase deficiency with high 17-hydroxyprogesterone.
layer4.trap: Trap: PCOS causes hyperandrogenism but not virilization/clitoromegaly to this degree and does not raise 17-hydroxyprogesterone.

questions.stem: A 47-year-old man comes to the office for a follow-up examination 6 weeks after testing positive for hepatitis C during laboratory screening for life insurance. He has a history of osteoarthritis of the knees and takes ibuprofen, one tablet, twice daily. He does not smoke cigarettes and drinks one glass of wine four to five times weekly. He does not use intravenous drugs and has had no blood transfusions. He is sexually active and monogamous with his wife. Vital signs are within normal limits. The patient appears well. Examination shows no abnormalities. Results of liver function tests, complete blood count, and serum studies, including measurement of total cholesterol concentration, are within the reference ranges. In addition to serologic testing for hepatitis A and B, which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
questions.stemHtml: A 47-year-old man comes to the office for a follow-up examination 6 weeks after testing positive for hepatitis C during laboratory screening for life insurance. He has a history of osteoarthritis of the knees and takes ibuprofen, one tablet, twice daily. He does not smoke cigarettes and drinks one glass of wine four to five times weekly. He does not use intravenous drugs and has had no blood transfusions. He is sexually active and monogamous with his wife. Vital signs are within normal limits. The patient appears well. Examination shows no abnormalities. Results of liver function tests, complete blood count, and serum studies, including measurement of total cholesterol concentration, are within the reference ranges. In addition to serologic testing for hepatitis A and B, which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
questions.subject: Infectious Disease

explanationPanel.whyCorrect:
Educational Objective: This patient who drinks four to five glasses of wine weekly is found to have hepatitis C exposure. Alcohol use can exacerbate liver damage and progression to cirrhosis in patients with hepatitis C; thus, the most appropriate next step in management is recommendation for alcohol cessation.

Evaluation: A positive hepatitis C test indicates the presence of hepatitis C antibodies, which suggest either current or past infection. Hepatitis C leads to chronic inflammation and scarring in hepatocytes, which can progress to cirrhosis and/or hepatocellular carcinoma.

Definition: The clinical presentation of hepatitis C is variable; however, nonspecific symptoms such as fatigue, anorexia, or jaundice are classic. Many patients remain asymptomatic, which is why screening guidelines include a test for hepatitis C in all patients aged 18 to 79 years.

Prevention: Prevention of hepatitis C infection includes screening blood products, avoiding intravenous drug use, and mitigating risk for sexually transmitted infections. It is unclear how this patient was exposed.

Treatment: Antiviral therapy is the mainstay of treatment for hepatitis C, with direct-acting antiviral therapy such as glecaprevir-pibrentasvir. The goal of treatment is to eradicate hepatitis C virus infection.

Differential: Patients who have had hepatitis C infection undergo counseling for many lifestyle changes such as weight loss, smoking cessation, and alcohol cessation. Furthermore, patients with hepatitis C infection should undergo vaccination for hepatitis A and B, and if concomitant chronic liver disease is present, the pneumococcal vaccine is indicated.

wrongAnswers.A: Administration of meningococcal vaccine and administration of varicella-zoster vaccine are incorrect. At time of diagnosis, the vaccines indicated are hepatitis A, hepatitis B, and potentially the pneumococcal vaccine.
wrongAnswers.B: Administration of meningococcal vaccine and administration of varicella-zoster vaccine are incorrect. At time of diagnosis, the vaccines indicated are hepatitis A, hepatitis B, and potentially the pneumococcal vaccine.
wrongAnswers.C: Measurement of serum cryoglobulin concentration is incorrect. It is a marker for cryoglobulinemia, which can be associated with hepatitis C-related mixed cryoglobulinemia. In this patient with diagnosis on asymptomatic screening, cryoglobulin concentrations are not indicated.
wrongAnswers.E: Recommendation for ibuprofen cessation is incorrect. While NSAIDs are often avoided in patients with cirrhosis, this patient does not have synthetic dysfunction or physical examination signs consistent with cirrhosis. Recommendation for alcohol cessation is the most appropriate next step.

explanationPanel.rule: Chronic hepatitis C requires alcohol cessation counseling plus HAV/HBV immunization because alcohol accelerates fibrosis/cirrhosis.
explanationPanel.trap: Trap: NSAIDs are avoided in cirrhosis, not asymptomatic HCV with normal synthetic function.

layer4.rule: Chronic hepatitis C requires alcohol cessation counseling plus HAV/HBV immunization because alcohol accelerates fibrosis/cirrhosis.
layer4.trap: Trap: NSAIDs are avoided in cirrhosis, not asymptomatic HCV with normal synthetic function.

questions.stem: A 25-year-old woman comes to the office 1 week after she received an increased blood pressure reading at a health fair. She says that she also has had episodes of cramping of her legs and occasional headaches during the past 9 months. She takes no medications. Pulse is 80/min, and blood pressure is 160/98 mm Hg in the left upper extremity and 162/100 mm Hg in the right upper extremity. A bruit is heard over the left side of the abdomen. Cardiopulmonary examination shows no abnormalities. Ultrasonography of the kidneys with Doppler flow shows decreased blood flow to the left kidney. Which of the following sets of findings is most likely in this patient?
questions.stemHtml: A 25-year-old woman comes to the office 1 week after she received an increased blood pressure reading at a health fair. She says that she also has had episodes of cramping of her legs and occasional headaches during the past 9 months. She takes no medications. Pulse is 80/min, and blood pressure is 160/98 mm Hg in the left upper extremity and 162/100 mm Hg in the right upper extremity. A bruit is heard over the left side of the abdomen. Cardiopulmonary examination shows no abnormalities. Ultrasonography of the kidneys with Doppler flow shows decreased blood flow to the left kidney. Which of the following sets of findings is most likely in this patient?
questions.subject: Nephrology/Urology

explanationPanel.whyCorrect:
Educational Objective: Renal artery stenosis is a cause of secondary hypertension due to abnormal activation of the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system. The patient in this case likely has left renal artery stenosis which would result in decreased right renal vein renin secretion, increased serum aldosterone, and decreased serum potassium.

Evaluation: In younger patients, fibromuscular dysplasia is the most common cause of renal artery stenosis. It may present with hypertension as well as an abdominal bruit as is seen in this case.

Definition: Renal artery stenosis is a cause of secondary hypertension due to the abnormal stimulation of the juxtaglomerular apparatus from low afferent blood flow, leading to excessive production of renin and angiotensin. Due to activation of the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system and high concentrations of angiotensin II, secondary hypertension develops. Angiotensin II also leads to increased sodium reabsorption in the renal tubules, aldosterone release by the adrenal cortex with subsequent increased sodium, fluid retention, and hypokalemia, vasopressin release from the posterior pituitary leading to increased fluid retention, enhanced adrenergic function through inhibition of norepinephrine reuptake in sympathetic nerve endings, and stimulation of hypothalamic thirst centers.

Prevention: This younger patient has likely developed renal artery stenosis due to underlying fibromuscular dysplasia. There is no known way to prevent fibromuscular dysplasia.

Treatment: Treatment of renal artery stenosis involves blood pressure management and possible angioplasty or stenting of the stenosed renal artery to improve renal blood flow.

Differential: The patient in this case is presenting with hypertension and cramping, likely due to electrolyte abnormalities, with decreased blood flow to the left kidney identified on ultrasonography. She most likely has renal artery stenosis, which would result in decreased right renal vein renin secretion, increased serum aldosterone, and decreased serum potassium.

wrongAnswers.A: Each of these answer choices indicates there would be an increased release of renin from the right renal vein. In cases of unilateral renal artery stenosis, an increased release of renin would be identified from the affected kidney with decreased renin release from the unaffected side.
wrongAnswers.B: Each of these answer choices indicates there would be an increased release of renin from the right renal vein. In cases of unilateral renal artery stenosis, an increased release of renin would be identified from the affected kidney with decreased renin release from the unaffected side.
wrongAnswers.C: Each of these answer choices indicates there would be an increased release of renin from the right renal vein. In cases of unilateral renal artery stenosis, an increased release of renin would be identified from the affected kidney with decreased renin release from the unaffected side.
wrongAnswers.D: Each of these answer choices indicates there would be an increased release of renin from the right renal vein. In cases of unilateral renal artery stenosis, an increased release of renin would be identified from the affected kidney with decreased renin release from the unaffected side.
wrongAnswers.E: This choice correctly identifies decreased right renal vein renin release and increased serum aldosterone, but aldosterone excess lowers serum potassium; it should not increase potassium.
wrongAnswers.G: These choices indicate decreased serum aldosterone. In renal artery stenosis, decreased renal blood flow increases renin release from the affected kidney with subsequent increases in serum angiotensin and aldosterone.
wrongAnswers.H: These choices indicate decreased serum aldosterone. In renal artery stenosis, decreased renal blood flow increases renin release from the affected kidney with subsequent increases in serum angiotensin and aldosterone.

explanationPanel.rule: Unilateral renal artery stenosis increases renin from the affected kidney, suppresses contralateral renal-vein renin, increases aldosterone, and lowers potassium.
explanationPanel.trap: Trap: do not mark both kidneys as high-renin; the normal kidney is suppressed by systemic hypertension.

questions.stem: A 10-month-old boy is brought to the office by his parents for a well-child examination. His parents say they are concerned because people have told them his head seems too large for his body. He eats a variety of table foods and is able to feed himself soft foods with his hands. He drinks approximately 16 oz of breast milk by bottle daily and is breast-fed nightly. He crawls and takes steps holding onto his parents' hands. He babbles and laughs. Medical history is unremarkable and he receives no medications. The patient's growth charts are shown. Vital signs are within normal limits. Physical examination discloses no abnormalities. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
questions.stemHtml: A 10-month-old boy is brought to the office by his parents for a well-child examination. His parents say they are concerned because people have told them his head seems too large for his body. He eats a variety of table foods and is able to feed himself soft foods with his hands. He drinks approximately 16 oz of breast milk by bottle daily and is breast-fed nightly. He crawls and takes steps holding onto his parents' hands. He babbles and laughs. Medical history is unremarkable and he receives no medications. The patient's growth charts are shown. Vital signs are within normal limits. Physical examination discloses no abnormalities. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
choices: Obtain lumbar puncture to measure opening pressure
questions.subject: Pediatrics/Neonatology

explanationPanel.correct: A. Measure the parents' head circumferences
explanationPanel.whyCorrect:
Educational Objective: Familial megalencephaly is the most common cause of macrocephaly in an infant with otherwise normal development. The diagnosis can be confirmed by measuring the head circumferences of the parents.

Evaluation: Patients with familial megalencephaly are asymptomatic and often show normal development.

Definition: Macrocephaly refers to an occipitofrontal circumference that is greater than two standard deviations compared with the average for infants of the same age and sex. Once parental head circumferences are measured, a Weaver curve can be used to help determine if there is a genetic contribution to the infant’s head size.

Prevention: There is no known way to prevent familial megalencephaly.

Treatment: Asymptomatic familial megalencephaly does not require treatment. Measurement of the patient’s head circumference at routine visits is recommended.

Differential: This patient presents with signs of normal development and a head circumference persistently near the 95th percentile on growth charts. In the absence of abnormalities, familial megalencephaly should be considered. This may be confirmed with measurement of the parents’ head circumferences.

wrongAnswers.B: Obtain cranial ultrasonography is incorrect. Cranial ultrasonography may be used for evaluation if there is concern for an expanding lesion leading to macrocephaly or concern for hydrocephalus. Imaging with cranial ultrasonography can only be used in patients with an open fontanelle.
wrongAnswers.C: Obtain lumbar puncture to measure opening pressure is not the most appropriate next step in management. Lumbar puncture is not included in the initial management or diagnosis in cases of macrocephaly. A lumbar puncture would be contraindicated in a patient with an intracranial space-occupying lesion, as there may be risk for cerebral herniation.
wrongAnswers.D: Obtain MRI of the brain is incorrect. An MRI of the brain may be an appropriate next step in management if there is concern for underlying pathology leading to the development of macrocephaly. This patient presents with normal development. Measuring the parents’ head circumferences is more appropriate.
wrongAnswers.E: Report to child protective services is not the most appropriate next step in management. No signs of abuse or injury to the patient are shown on physical examination. Measuring the parents’ head circumferences is more appropriate.

explanationPanel.rule: Normally developing infant with stable large head circumference near family range = measure parental head circumferences before imaging.
explanationPanel.trap: Trap: neuroimaging is for rapidly crossing percentiles, neurologic signs, developmental delay, or abuse concern.

layer4.rule: Normally developing infant with stable large head circumference near family range = measure parental head circumferences before imaging.
layer4.trap: Trap: neuroimaging is for rapidly crossing percentiles, neurologic signs, developmental delay, or abuse concern.

questions.stem: A 60-year-old woman comes to the ambulatory surgical center to undergo a cardiac ablation. She has a history of six episodes of paroxysmal atrial fibrillation in the past 4 years. She has had four prior successful electrical cardioversions and spontaneously converted twice. Her only medication is rivaroxaban daily, which was prescribed 1 month ago. She is 160 cm (5 ft 3 in) tall and weighs 46 kg (101 lb); BMI is 18 kg/m². Temperature is 37.0°C (98.6°F), pulse is 72/min and regular, respirations are 14/min, and blood pressure is 110/75 mm Hg. Physical examination shows no abnormalities. It is most appropriate for this patient to undergo a transesophageal echocardiography prior to the ablation procedure for the detection of which of the following?
questions.stemHtml: A 60-year-old woman comes to the ambulatory surgical center to undergo a cardiac ablation. She has a history of six episodes of paroxysmal atrial fibrillation in the past 4 years. She has had four prior successful electrical cardioversions and spontaneously converted twice. Her only medication is rivaroxaban daily, which was prescribed 1 month ago. She is 160 cm (5 ft 3 in) tall and weighs 46 kg (101 lb); BMI is 18 kg/m². Temperature is 37.0°C (98.6°F), pulse is 72/min and regular, respirations are 14/min, and blood pressure is 110/75 mm Hg. Physical examination shows no abnormalities. It is most appropriate for this patient to undergo a transesophageal echocardiography prior to the ablation procedure for the detection of which of the following?
choices: Size of the right and left atria
questions.subject: Cardiology

explanationPanel.whyCorrect:
Educational Objective: Prior to cardiac instrumentation of the left atrium, or prior to cardioversion of stable atrial fibrillation in nonanticoagulated patients, transesophageal echocardiography is necessary to assess for left atrial thrombus. Mechanical disruption of a thrombus with a catheter or conversion to sinus rhythm with restored atrial contraction can result in thromboembolism with resultant distal arterial occlusion.

Key Concept: Atrial fibrillation prevents coordinated contraction of the left atrium, and stagnant blood, especially in the left atrial appendage, is prone to thrombosis. Restoration of sinus rhythm or mechanical disruption of the thrombus can result in thromboembolism with resultant stroke or end-organ ischemia/infarction.

Explanation: Ablation of atrial fibrillation involves the insertion of a catheter into the left atrium at the entry points of the pulmonary veins. Once in the atrium, the catheter can cauterize hyperactive areas of myocardium, which eliminates the ability of the cells to fire an action potential. By consequence, if a thrombus exists within the left atrium, the insertion of the catheter would penetrate or otherwise disrupt the existing thrombus, resulting in fragmentation and embolization. Therefore, prior to atrial instrumentation, echocardiography should be performed to assess for the presence of a thrombus and characterize the procedural risk. Transthoracic echocardiography does not sufficiently image the left atrium, due to the deep positioning of the left atrium at the posterior aspect of the heart. The left atrium is best assessed by transesophageal approach.

Differential: Cardiac ejection fraction, pulmonary embolism, size and structure of chambers, and valvular disease are all assessable by echocardiography; however, prior to instrumentation, an assessment of atrial thrombosis should occur.

wrongAnswers.B: Cardiac ejection fraction is incorrect. Cardiac ejection fraction can be assessed from echocardiography; however, transthoracic echocardiography, as opposed to transesophageal, is adequate for this purpose. Further, while the ejection fraction can predict tolerance of procedures requiring sedation or instrumentation, unless the ejection is extremely reduced, assessment of it is not as vital as assessing for the presence of thrombosis prior to left atrial instrumentation.
wrongAnswers.C: Pulmonary embolism is incorrect. A patient with a large, hemodynamically limiting, acute, or unmanaged pulmonary embolism should not undergo a scheduled, nonemergent transcatheter atrial ablation. However, left atrial ablation occurs via a left-sided, not right-sided, approach; thus, any pulmonary embolism would not likely be disrupted or affected by a transcatheter atrial ablation. Further, pulmonary embolism is not diagnosed by transesophageal echocardiography; rather, pulmonary embolism is best assessed by CT pulmonary angiography or nuclear medicine ventilation-perfusion scanning.
wrongAnswers.D: Size of the right and left atria and valvular disease are incorrect. Size of the right and left atria and valvular disease are assessable by echocardiography, but abnormalities involving these structures are not as pertinent in consideration of the procedural approach and complication risk for transcatheter atrial ablation as is the presence of a left atrial thrombus.
wrongAnswers.E: Size of the right and left atria and valvular disease are incorrect. Size of the right and left atria and valvular disease are assessable by echocardiography, but abnormalities involving these structures are not as pertinent in consideration of the procedural approach and complication risk for transcatheter atrial ablation as is the presence of a left atrial thrombus.

explanationPanel.rule: Before left atrial instrumentation/cardioversion risk, TEE is used to exclude left atrial/appendage thrombus to prevent embolic stroke.
explanationPanel.trap: Trap: transthoracic echo can assess EF/valves but is less reliable for left atrial appendage thrombus.

layer4.rule: Before left atrial instrumentation/cardioversion risk, TEE is used to exclude left atrial/appendage thrombus to prevent embolic stroke.
layer4.trap: Trap: transthoracic echo can assess EF/valves but is less reliable for left atrial appendage thrombus.

questions.stem: A 54-year-old man comes to the office for a routine health maintenance examination. Medical history is remarkable for well-controlled hypertension. Medications are hydrochlorothiazide and lisinopril. The patient's wife died of breast cancer 2 years ago. During the past 9 months, he has had unprotected sexual intercourse with three female partners. Temperature is 37.6°C (99.7°F), pulse is 70/min, respirations are 16/min, and blood pressure is 128/70 mm Hg. Pulse oximetry on room air shows an oxygen saturation of 100%. Physical examination shows no abnormalities. HIV antibody/antigen testing is positive. CD4+ T-lymphocyte count is 800/mm³. Results of testing for hepatitis B, hepatitis C, and syphilis are negative. A PPD skin test shows 7 mm of induration at 48 hours. Chest x-ray shows no abnormalities. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
questions.stemHtml: A 54-year-old man comes to the office for a routine health maintenance examination. Medical history is remarkable for well-controlled hypertension. Medications are hydrochlorothiazide and lisinopril. The patient's wife died of breast cancer 2 years ago. During the past 9 months, he has had unprotected sexual intercourse with three female partners. Temperature is 37.6°C (99.7°F), pulse is 70/min, respirations are 16/min, and blood pressure is 128/70 mm Hg. Pulse oximetry on room air shows an oxygen saturation of 100%. Physical examination shows no abnormalities. HIV antibody/antigen testing is positive. CD4+ T-lymphocyte count is 800/mm³. Results of testing for hepatitis B, hepatitis C, and syphilis are negative. A PPD skin test shows 7 mm of induration at 48 hours. Chest x-ray shows no abnormalities. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
choices: Repeat PPD skin test in 3 months
Repeat PPD skin test in 1 year
questions.subject: Infectious Disease

explanationPanel.whyCorrect:
Educational Objective: Isoniazid therapy is the most appropriate next step in management for this patient. A diagnosis of latent tuberculosis is determined by tuberculin (PPD) skin testing with a measured induration at or above 5 mm at 48 hours in immunocompromised patients. Results of this patient’s PPD skin test shows 7 mm of induration at 48 hours.

Key Concept: Latent tuberculosis is defined as a positive tuberculin skin test or interferon-gamma release assay (IGRA) in the absence of active pulmonary or disseminated infection with Mycobacterium tuberculosis. The treatment of choice is isoniazid, often in combination with a rifamycin-based regimen.

Explanation: The tuberculin skin test is considered positive at varying sizes of induration based on the population in which the test is done. While patients with HIV infection and other conditions that cause immunosuppression are considered to have a positive tuberculin skin test if the induration is measured at or above 5 mm, the general population is considered to have a positive test if the induration is 15 mm or greater. Health care workers or those who work with high-risk populations (eg, residents of prisons or shelters) are often considered to have positive results warranting treatment at 10 mm of induration. Active infection should be excluded with chest x-ray prior to initiating therapy. Additionally, patients with HIV infection and a CD4+ T-lymphocyte count below 200 cells/mm³ may initially have a negative test, so they should be retested when CD4+ T-lymphocyte count is above 200 cells/mm³.

Differential: This patient should have a chest x-ray to rule out active tuberculosis infection, but his positive tuberculin skin test does not necessitate a sputum culture or IGRA for confirmation of latent tuberculosis. His tuberculin skin test is positive based on his immunocompromised status, so deferring treatment with plans for repeat testing in the future is inappropriate.

wrongAnswers.A: Culture of sputum for tuberculosis is incorrect. Sputum culture is used in the diagnosis of suspected pneumonia, either based on symptomatology or changes on chest x-ray. It can be used to diagnose active tuberculosis, which presents with subacute or chronic cough, weight loss, and night sweats. This patient has latent tuberculosis, and a sputum culture would not likely be positive in the absence of symptoms.
wrongAnswers.B: Interferon-gamma release assay is incorrect. An IGRA is a blood test used to diagnose latent or active tuberculosis. IGRA is more specific than the tuberculin skin test and is most commonly used in those who have received the BCG vaccine against tuberculosis, which makes the tuberculin skin test nonspecific.
wrongAnswers.D: Repeat PPD skin test in 3 months or in 1 year are incorrect. This patient is immunocompromised and has evidence of latent tuberculosis. He should receive treatment as soon as possible to prevent associated morbidity and mortality.
wrongAnswers.E: Repeat PPD skin test in 3 months or in 1 year are incorrect. This patient is immunocompromised and has evidence of latent tuberculosis. He should receive treatment as soon as possible to prevent associated morbidity and mortality.

explanationPanel.rule: In HIV/immunocompromised patients, PPD induration >=5 mm with normal chest x-ray = latent TB; treat with isoniazid-based therapy.
explanationPanel.trap: Trap: do not wait for 10-15 mm or repeat testing once the HIV-specific threshold is met.

layer4.rule: In HIV/immunocompromised patients, PPD induration >=5 mm with normal chest x-ray = latent TB; treat with isoniazid-based therapy.
layer4.trap: Trap: do not wait for 10-15 mm or repeat testing once the HIV-specific threshold is met.

questions.stem: A 1-month-old boy is brought to the physician by his 17-year-old mother for a well-child examination. He is at the 30th percentile for length and 25th percentile for weight. During the examination, his mother reports that she is feeling stressed by the demands of motherhood. She and her son are living with her parents, and she does not get along well with them. She also notes that she is becoming increasingly irritable with her son whom she frequently finds difficult to soothe. She is breast-feeding but finds the process difficult and frustrating. She says that she is not depressed but has feelings of sadness and inadequacy. She still takes pleasure in activities she typically enjoys. She has not had suicidal ideation. Her sleep is disrupted by her newborn at night, but she is learning to nap when her baby sleeps. Observation of the mother-newborn dyad shows difficulty with reading the newborn's cues. The mother appears distracted during an attempt to feed her son. Which of the following is the most appropriate recommendation?
questions.stemHtml: A 1-month-old boy is brought to the physician by his 17-year-old mother for a well-child examination. He is at the 30th percentile for length and 25th percentile for weight. During the examination, his mother reports that she is feeling stressed by the demands of motherhood. She and her son are living with her parents, and she does not get along well with them. She also notes that she is becoming increasingly irritable with her son whom she frequently finds difficult to soothe. She is breast-feeding but finds the process difficult and frustrating. She says that she is not depressed but has feelings of sadness and inadequacy. She still takes pleasure in activities she typically enjoys. She has not had suicidal ideation. Her sleep is disrupted by her newborn at night, but she is learning to nap when her baby sleeps. Observation of the mother-newborn dyad shows difficulty with reading the newborn's cues. The mother appears distracted during an attempt to feed her son. Which of the following is the most appropriate recommendation?
choices: Discuss the importance of letting the baby cry at night
Switch the newborn to a cow milk-based formula
Recommend a teen-parent education and support program
Begin individual psychotherapy for the mother
Begin a trial of fluoxetine for the mother
questions.subject: Pediatrics/Neonatology

explanationPanel.correct: C. Recommend a teen-parent education and support program
explanationPanel.whyCorrect:
Educational Objective: Teen-parent education and support programs are available to help teenage parents in all aspects of their lives as parents, students, and family members. This teenage parent, with challenges interacting with and caring for her infant, strained relationships with her own parents, and emotional distress, should be referred to a teen-parent education and support program.

Key Concept: Caring for a newborn during maternal teenage years comes with additional challenges including but not limited to social isolation, difficulty balancing responsibilities (eg, school, work), financial cost, risk for maternal depression and anxiety, and relationship challenges between the mother and child as well as between the mother and her friends and family.

Explanation: Raising a newborn child can be challenging. The time demands, limited sleep, financial cost, relationship strain, and health concerns, among other aspects, can be sufficiently challenging even for adult-age, well-adjusted, well-resourced persons. These challenges are compounded for teenagers who may still be in school, have strained relationships with family and friends, and have limited maturity, financial resources, and family support. Further, many teen pregnancies are unplanned. Teen-parent education and support programs are available to assist teenage parents with navigating the scope of parenting and life challenges as teenagers. Support groups help decrease isolation, provide emotional, educational, financial, and other forms of support, and promote the development of parenting abilities and skills. Studies have shown that participation in teen-parent education and support programs can promote better outcomes for children of teenage parents, decrease the risk for abuse and neglect, improve parent-child relationships, and promote parental and child education.

Differential: This parent presents with challenges adapting to motherhood, with no other signs of medical or psychiatric primary disease. The best course of action at this time is to recommend a teen-parent education and support program.

wrongAnswers.A: Discuss the importance of letting the baby cry at night is not the best answer. In general, comforting crying newborns promotes the development of stable attachment between the parent and child, which strengthens the parental relationship. While appropriate care and behaviors by parents can help promote sleeping, this infant’s developmental stage is not yet at a point where sleeping through the night is feasible, as there will be frequent awakenings for feeding, urinating, and stooling.
wrongAnswers.B: Switch the newborn to a cow milk-based formula is incorrect. Formula-feeding may be appropriate if breast-feeding is unsuccessful or undesired; however, this situation has not yet arisen in this patient’s case.
wrongAnswers.D: Begin individual psychotherapy for the mother is not the best answer. While psychotherapy has many roles and may be helpful, this parent may benefit first from coaching, support, and education, which may decrease or eliminate the challenges she is experiencing.
wrongAnswers.E: Begin a trial of fluoxetine for the mother is incorrect. Fluoxetine, a selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor, is an oral antidepressant indicated in the management of major depressive disorder and generalized anxiety disorder, among other conditions. The mother in this case does not currently have an indication for initiation of fluoxetine.

explanationPanel.rule: Teen parent with caregiving stress, poor infant cue-reading, and social strain but no MDD = refer to teen-parent education/support program.
explanationPanel.trap: Trap: sadness and inadequacy alone do not equal major depression requiring SSRI.

layer4.rule: Teen parent with caregiving stress, poor infant cue-reading, and social strain but no MDD = refer to teen-parent education/support program.
layer4.trap: Trap: sadness and inadequacy alone do not equal major depression requiring SSRI.

questions.stem: A 10-month-old girl is brought to the physician because of a 5-day history of a rash over the cheeks and diaper area that she constantly rubs. Her mother says that for the past 24 hours, her daughter has been unwilling to stand. She is afebrile and otherwise healthy. Her mother and 6-year-old brother have asthma. A photograph of the face is shown; a similar rash is noted over the diaper area. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.stemHtml: A 10-month-old girl is brought to the physician because of a 5-day history of a rash over the cheeks and diaper area that she constantly rubs. Her mother says that for the past 24 hours, her daughter has been unwilling to stand. She is afebrile and otherwise healthy. Her mother and 6-year-old brother have asthma. A photograph of the face is shown; a similar rash is noted over the diaper area. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.subject: Dermatology

explanationPanel.whyCorrect:
Educational Objective: The most likely diagnosis in this 10-month-old patient with history of a pruritic rash involving the cheeks and diaper area is atopic dermatitis.

Evaluation: Atopic dermatitis, the most common type of eczema, presents with an initial itch followed by pruritic rash commonly affecting the extensor surface of newborns and infants. As children age, atopic dermatitis transitions to the flexural surfaces in toddlers, children, and adults. The diagnosis of atopic dermatitis can be made based on a patient’s clinical presentation.

Definition: Atopic dermatitis is characterized by itch preceding development of a rash. Atopic dermatitis is initially characterized by erythematous papules and vesicles with exudates and crusting. Over time, with chronic scratching, the skin becomes dry, scaly, and thickened in a process called lichenification. Atopic dermatitis is often associated with hay fever, asthma, and family history of eczema. Atopic dermatitis is driven by inflammatory mediators including interleukins 4, 13, and 31, and the Janus kinase (JAK) pathway.

Prevention: The symptoms of atopic dermatitis may be mitigated by gentle skin care: minimizing long baths in warm water, which causes drying of the skin, avoiding products with fragrance, and using bland emollients such as petroleum jelly daily. Gentle skin care can allow for restoration of the normal skin barrier.

Treatment: Initial treatments for atopic dermatitis include the use of mild to moderate potency topical corticosteroids (eg, triamcinolone) and avoidance of triggers. In older children and adults, severe cases may benefit from biologic medications that target the interleukin pathway, including dupilumab, or JAK inhibitors, such as upadacitinib.

Differential: This 10-month-old patient presents with an acute, ill-defined, red rash involving the extensor surfaces, associated with pruritus and pain. In addition, this patient’s family history includes asthma, which is commonly associated with atopy. Given these findings, the most likely diagnosis is atopic dermatitis.

wrongAnswers.B: Candidiasis is incorrect. Candidiasis is a superficial skin infection associated with the development of beefy red patches and plaques with overlying white plaques and pustules. Candidiasis is treated with topical or oral antifungal agents.
wrongAnswers.C: Food allergy is incorrect. Food allergies, including shellfish and tree nuts, may be associated with the development of urticaria. While diet may play a role in inflammatory skin conditions, breakdown of the normal skin barrier and downstream inflammation is the main cause of eczema.
wrongAnswers.D: Tinea corporis is incorrect. Tinea corporis is associated with annular, red plaques with peripheral scale and central clearing. It is treated with topical or oral antifungal medications.
wrongAnswers.E: Toxic epidermal necrolysis is incorrect. Toxic epidermal necrolysis is associated with the development of widespread, red to violaceous, atypical targetoid lesions involving the skin and mucosal surfaces that rapidly slough. Toxic epidermal necrolysis is caused by various medication exposures including antibiotics and antiepileptic medications.

explanationPanel.rule: Infant with intensely pruritic eczematous cheeks/diaper-area rash and family atopy = atopic dermatitis.
explanationPanel.trap: Trap: Candida diaper rash is beefy red with satellite pustules, not diffuse itchy eczematous atopy.

layer4.rule: Infant with intensely pruritic eczematous cheeks/diaper-area rash and family atopy = atopic dermatitis.
layer4.trap: Trap: Candida diaper rash is beefy red with satellite pustules, not diffuse itchy eczematous atopy.

questions.stem: A 72-year-old woman calls the clinic because of a 3-day history of frequent urination, urinary urgency, and pain with urination. She is currently visiting her daughter in a different state and has limited access to health care; she requests a prescription for antibiotics for a bladder infection be sent to a local pharmacy. The patient says that the only treatment that has improved her symptoms in the past is nitrofurantoin macrocrystals taken every 6 hours. The clinic nurse enters a prescription in the patient's electronic health record (EHR) for the physician to sign; the prescription includes the correct medication but incorrect dosing instructions. The physician does not notice the error and signs the prescription to be sent to the pharmacy. When the physician is notified of the error by the pharmacist, the physician realizes that the nurse had chosen dosing for a similar antibiotic, nitrofurantoin monohydrate/macrocrystals, which is dosed twice daily. Which of the following interventions is most likely to prevent this error from recurring?
questions.stemHtml: A 72-year-old woman calls the clinic because of a 3-day history of frequent urination, urinary urgency, and pain with urination. She is currently visiting her daughter in a different state and has limited access to health care; she requests a prescription for antibiotics for a bladder infection be sent to a local pharmacy. The patient says that the only treatment that has improved her symptoms in the past is nitrofurantoin macrocrystals taken every 6 hours. The clinic nurse enters a prescription in the patient's electronic health record (EHR) for the physician to sign; the prescription includes the correct medication but incorrect dosing instructions. The physician does not notice the error and signs the prescription to be sent to the pharmacy. When the physician is notified of the error by the pharmacist, the physician realizes that the nurse had chosen dosing for a similar antibiotic, nitrofurantoin monohydrate/macrocrystals, which is dosed twice daily. Which of the following interventions is most likely to prevent this error from recurring?
choices: Asking the nurse to disclose her role in the error at the next clinic meeting for staff training purposes
Autopopulating correct dosing instructions for this medication in the EHR
Creating a policy requiring this medication be phoned into the pharmacy rather than entered into the EHR
Flagging all antibiotics in the EHR with an alert reminding practitioners to pause and review dosing instructions
Requiring the physician to undergo medication safety training
questions.subject: Ethics/Social Sciences

explanationPanel.correct: B. Autopopulating correct dosing instructions for this medication in the EHR
explanationPanel.whyCorrect:
Educational Objective: Autopopulating correct dosing instructions, which can be integrated into electronic health records (EHRs), can decrease medication ordering errors.

Key Concept: Medication ordering errors are relatively common. In the case of medication ordering errors due to medications that look or sound alike, there are several strategies that can be employed. A key strategy involves systems-level changes to the EHR, including computerized physician order entry systems in combination with clinical decision support systems.

Explanation: Computerized physician order entry systems allow for electronic medication orders (rather than paper, phone, or verbal forms), and clinical decision support systems offer automated dosing suggestions and medication alerts (eg, medication interactions). These systems have been shown to improve patient safety. Causes of adverse events, including medication errors, can be identified via root cause analysis. Rather than presuming the cause of an event, root cause analysis involves a multidisciplinary team defining and analyzing the problem to design a set of corrective actions based on the analysis.

Differential: In addition to automated dosing instructions, a targeted medication alert that notifies the physician that the current dose is atypical could also be beneficial.

wrongAnswers.A: Asking the nurse to disclose her role in the error at the next clinic meeting for staff training purposes and requiring the physician to undergo medication safety training are inappropriate. These options assign individual culpability, when systems-level factors were at play instead.
wrongAnswers.C: Creating a policy requiring this medication be phoned into the pharmacy rather than entered into the EHR is incorrect. Medication errors are common when prescriptions are phoned in. EHR tools such as automated dosing suggestions and medication alerts can promote patient safety.
wrongAnswers.D: Flagging all antibiotics in the EHR with an alert reminding practitioners to pause and review dosing instructions is incorrect. This option is likely to increase the frequency of alerts to the point of alert fatigue and decrease effectiveness of alerts.
wrongAnswers.E: Asking the nurse to disclose her role in the error at the next clinic meeting for staff training purposes and requiring the physician to undergo medication safety training are inappropriate. These options assign individual culpability, when systems-level factors were at play instead.

explanationPanel.rule: Medication-ordering errors from look-alike/similar dosing are prevented best by system-level EHR decision support/autopopulated correct dosing.
explanationPanel.trap: Trap: blaming the nurse/physician misses the systems cause and does not reliably prevent recurrence.

layer4.rule: Medication-ordering errors from look-alike/similar dosing are prevented best by system-level EHR decision support/autopopulated correct dosing.
layer4.trap: Trap: blaming the nurse/physician misses the systems cause and does not reliably prevent recurrence.

questions.stem: A 23-year-old man with sickle cell disease is admitted to the hospital because of a 5-day history of shortness of breath and severe pain in his chest and legs. He has not had fever or cough. During the past 3 years, he has been hospitalized for painful sickle cell crises approximately twice yearly. Ten years ago, he underwent cholecystectomy for cholecystitis. His medications are folic acid and acetaminophen with codeine; 3 days ago, he began taking double his usual dose of acetaminophen with codeine to manage his increased pain. He does not smoke cigarettes, drink alcohol, or use illicit drugs. His temperature is 39°C (102.2°F), pulse is 120/min, respirations are 22/min, and blood pressure is 116/70 mm Hg. Pulse oximetry on room air shows an oxygen saturation of 94%. The chest wall is tender to palpation. Bilateral basilar crackles are heard. His hemoglobin concentration is 9 g/dL, hematocrit is 27%, and leukocyte count is 15,000/mm³. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in diagnosis?
questions.stemHtml: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in diagnosis?
questions.subject: Hematology/Oncology

explanationPanel.whyCorrect:
Educational Objective: This patient with a history of sickle cell disease presents with increasing pain, shortness of breath, and bilateral crackles on physical examination, suggestive of acute chest syndrome. The most appropriate next step to evaluate for acute chest syndrome is an x-ray of the chest.

Evaluation: Acute chest syndrome is a complication of sickle cell disease and has a variable presentation. Classically, acute chest syndrome presents with fever, chest pain, and respiratory symptoms. It can be triggered by a variety of predisposing illnesses, such as infection or venous thromboembolism.

Definition: Acute chest syndrome is defined by the presence of new pulmonary infiltrates on chest x-ray in conjunction with a clinical syndrome of fever and/or respiratory symptoms.

Prevention: Preventive strategies include the use of hydroxyurea to decrease vasoocclusion, along with early recognition of vasoocclusive crises and the administration of age-appropriate vaccinations.

Treatment: Treatment involves supportive care, including oxygen therapy, blood transfusions, and antibiotic coverage.

Differential: The differential diagnosis is broad and includes pneumonia and pulmonary embolism. For this patient, it is narrowed by a history consistent with acute chest syndrome in the setting of sickle cell disease.

wrongAnswers.B: CT scan of the chest is not the most appropriate next step in diagnosis. While a CT scan would provide the diagnosis, the most appropriate next step is an x-ray of the chest, which requires less radiation and cost to the patient and is also diagnostically accurate.
wrongAnswers.C: Bone scan is incorrect. A bone scan is used for evaluating joint pain, such as unspecified hip pain. This patient’s pain likely results from sickle cell disease, eliminating the need for a bone scan.
wrongAnswers.D: Bone marrow biopsy is incorrect. This patient has a history of sickle cell disease, which is likely driving the anemia.
wrongAnswers.E: No further testing is indicated is incorrect. This patient likely has acute chest syndrome, which is a life-threatening complication of sickle cell disease.

explanationPanel.rule: Sickle cell patient with new respiratory symptoms/crackles/chest pain = obtain chest x-ray to diagnose acute chest syndrome.
explanationPanel.trap: Trap: CT chest is more radiation/cost; chest x-ray is the first diagnostic test.

layer4.rule: Sickle cell patient with new respiratory symptoms/crackles/chest pain = obtain chest x-ray to diagnose acute chest syndrome.
layer4.trap: Trap: CT chest is more radiation/cost; chest x-ray is the first diagnostic test.

Ten years ago, he underwent cholecystectomy for cholecystitis. His medications are folic acid and acetaminophen with codeine; 3 days ago, he began taking double his usual dose of acetaminophen with codeine to manage his increased pain. He does not smoke cigarettes, drink alcohol, or use illicit drugs. His temperature is 39°C (102.2°F), pulse is 120/min, respirations are 22/min, and blood pressure is 116/70 mm Hg. Three days later, the patient's shortness of breath is more severe. Pulse oximetry on 4 L/min of oxygen via nasal cannula shows an oxygen saturation of 94%. A chest x-ray shows increased infiltrates. questions.stemHtml: A chest x-ray shows small bilateral basilar infiltrates. Treatment with supplemental oxygen, intravenous antibiotics, and intravenous fluids is begun. Three days later, the patient's shortness of breath is more severe. Pulse oximetry on 4 L/min of oxygen via nasal cannula shows an oxygen saturation of 94%. A chest x-ray shows increased infiltrates. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
questions.subject: Hematology/Oncology

explanationPanel.whyCorrect:
Educational Objective: This patient with a history of sickle cell disease presents with increasing pain, shortness of breath, bilateral crackles on physical examination, and small bilateral infiltrates on chest x-ray, consistent with acute chest syndrome. Exchange transfusion is the most appropriate immediate management of acute chest syndrome with severe features.

Evaluation: Acute chest syndrome is a complication of sickle cell disease and has a variable presentation. Classically, acute chest syndrome presents with fever, chest pain, and respiratory symptoms. It can be triggered by a variety of predisposing illnesses, such as infection or venous thromboembolism.

Definition: Acute chest syndrome is defined by the presence of new pulmonary infiltrates on chest x-ray in conjunction with a clinical syndrome of fever and/or respiratory symptoms.

Prevention: Preventive strategies include the use of hydroxyurea to decrease vasoocclusion, along with early recognition of vasoocclusive crises and the administration of age-appropriate vaccinations.

Treatment: Treatment involves supportive care, including oxygen therapy, blood transfusions, and antibiotic coverage. Exchange transfusions are important components of care, especially in those with a severe decline in their respiratory status. Exchange transfusion involves removing blood from the patient’s circulation and replacing it with donor blood. For this patient, this removes cells affected by sickle cell disease and replaces them with normal red blood cells that will not adopt sickled morphology and therefore not aggregate and occlude microvasculature.

Differential: The differential diagnosis is broad and includes pneumonia and pulmonary embolism. For this patient, it is narrowed by chest x-ray results and clinical history consistent with acute chest syndrome in the setting of sickle cell disease.

wrongAnswers.A: Noninvasive positive pressure ventilation is incorrect. This patient does not need positive pressure ventilation; he is on 4 L/min of oxygen via nasal cannula with an oxygen saturation sufficiently above goal.
wrongAnswers.C: Heparin therapy is not the most appropriate next step in management. This patient likely has acute chest syndrome because of sickle cell disease, making exchange transfusion the more appropriate next step in management. However, if the patient’s shortness of breath persists, it would be reasonable to order a CT scan of the chest to evaluate for pulmonary embolism, which is on the differential diagnosis for this patient.
wrongAnswers.D: Hydroxyurea therapy is incorrect. Hydroxyurea therapy can be done in the outpatient setting to mitigate vasoocclusion; however, it is not the most appropriate next step in management of this patient’s ongoing respiratory failure as it does not provide sufficiently prompt relief of respiratory failure from acute chest syndrome.
wrongAnswers.E: Plasmapheresis is not the most appropriate next step in management. Plasmapheresis can be trialed in management of severe cases of acute chest syndrome that have not responded to exchange transfusion.
wrongAnswers.F: Intubation and mechanical ventilation is not necessary for this patient at this time. This patient is oxygenating well on oxygen via nasal cannula and is ventilating well.

explanationPanel.rule: Acute chest syndrome that worsens despite oxygen/antibiotics/fluids or has progressive infiltrates/respiratory decline = exchange transfusion.
explanationPanel.trap: Trap: hydroxyurea is chronic prevention, not rapid treatment for deteriorating acute chest syndrome.

questions.stem: A 17-year-old patient, gravida 1, para 0, aborta 1, is brought to the emergency department because of progressive vaginal bleeding and severe low abdominal pain since pregnancy ended in spontaneous abortion at 14 weeks' gestation at home 2 hours ago. Pregnancy previously had been uncomplicated. She has hypothyroidism and takes levothyroxine and a prenatal vitamin. Temperature is 37.0°C (98.6°F), pulse is 100/min, respirations are 14/min, and blood pressure is 90/50 mm Hg. Pulse oximetry on room air shows an oxygen saturation of 96%. She appears to be in mild distress. Pelvic examination shows a dilated cervix and active bleeding from the cervical os. Intravenous administration of fluids and morphine is begun, and laboratory studies are ordered. In addition to pelvic ultrasonography, which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
questions.stemHtml: A 17-year-old patient, gravida 1, para 0, aborta 1, is brought to the emergency department because of progressive vaginal bleeding and severe low abdominal pain since pregnancy ended in spontaneous abortion at 14 weeks' gestation at home 2 hours ago. Pregnancy previously had been uncomplicated. She has hypothyroidism and takes levothyroxine and a prenatal vitamin. Temperature is 37.0°C (98.6°F), pulse is 100/min, respirations are 14/min, and blood pressure is 90/50 mm Hg. Pulse oximetry on room air shows an oxygen saturation of 96%. She appears to be in mild distress. Pelvic examination shows a dilated cervix and active bleeding from the cervical os. Intravenous administration of fluids and morphine is begun, and laboratory studies are ordered. In addition to pelvic ultrasonography, which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
choices: Bedside manual exploration of the uterus
Transfusion of packed red blood cells
questions.subject: Obstetrics

explanationPanel.whyCorrect:
Educational Objective: This patient with abdominal pain and persistent vaginal bleeding from an open cervical os after a spontaneous abortion likely has retained products of conception. The most appropriate next step in management is dilatation and curettage to remove the remaining products.

Key Concept: Retained products of conception often present with vaginal bleeding, abdominal pain, and occasional fever. The treatment of choice is dilatation and curettage.

Explanation: Retained products of conception can cause significant vaginal bleeding due to the inability of the placental bed to involute. In rare instances, retained products of conception may become secondarily infected, presenting with abdominal pain, fever, and a malodorous discharge. Dilatation and curettage is a procedure involving dilatation of the cervix and curettage of the endometrium to remove any remaining products of conception. The presence of retained products of conception can be confirmed on pelvic ultrasonography.

Differential: This patient has evidence of retained products of conception, with active bleeding from an open cervical os. Misoprostol would be ineffective, and the patient would be unlikely to tolerate manual uterine exploration. While this patient is currently hemodynamically stable and not in need of blood transfusion, observation would also be inappropriate and increase her risk for further complications.

wrongAnswers.A: Bedside manual exploration of the uterus is incorrect. Manual exploration of the uterus for retained products of conception is occasionally used in postpartum patients with postpartum hemorrhage and a fully dilated cervix. It is typically reserved for patients with a functioning neuraxial anesthetic, as it is extremely painful.
wrongAnswers.C: Rectal administration of misoprostol is incorrect. Misoprostol is a synthetic prostaglandin that induces uterine smooth muscle contraction and is used in the treatment of postpartum hemorrhage due to uterine atony. Misoprostol is not used in the treatment of bleeding due to retained products of conception.
wrongAnswers.D: Transfusion of packed red blood cells is incorrect. While this patient may require transfusion of packed red blood cells due to her ongoing blood loss, she currently has relatively normal vital signs that may improve with crystalloid infusion. Priority should be given to proceeding with dilatation and curettage to minimize additional bleeding.
wrongAnswers.E: Observation only is incorrect. This patient has active and ongoing vaginal bleeding, likely due to retained products of conception after spontaneous abortion. Observation would be inappropriate, as her bleeding will likely persist until the retained products are removed.

explanationPanel.rule: Ongoing heavy bleeding/open os after spontaneous abortion = retained products; manage with dilation and curettage.
explanationPanel.trap: Trap: uterotonics treat uterine atony, not bleeding from retained products requiring evacuation.

layer4.rule: Ongoing heavy bleeding/open os after spontaneous abortion = retained products; manage with dilation and curettage.
layer4.trap: Trap: uterotonics treat uterine atony, not bleeding from retained products requiring evacuation.

Question: The physicians responsible for the patient's care discuss the risks of transfusing the patient with packed red blood cells with him and his family. Following consent and administration of two units of packed RBCs, which of the following is the most likely complication of blood transfusion in this patient?
questions.subject: Hematology/Oncology

explanationPanel.whyCorrect:
Educational Objective: This patient is critically ill with hemorrhagic shock secondary to hematemesis, and a blood transfusion is indicated. The most common complication of blood transfusion is a febrile nonhemolytic transfusion reaction.

Evaluation: Febrile nonhemolytic transfusion reactions are adverse events associated with blood transfusions characterized by development of a fever a few hours after blood transfusion. They result from the release of cytokines from donor leukocytes.

Definition: Febrile nonhemolytic transfusion reaction is a clinical diagnosis based on temporal association of fever development with transfusion.

Prevention: Prevention strategies include leukoreduction of blood products.

Treatment: Treatment of febrile nonhemolytic transfusion reaction involves stopping administration of blood products and supporting the patient’s symptoms as needed with acetaminophen.

Differential: The development of febrile nonhemolytic transfusion reaction presents with fever, chills, and rigors. Therefore, the differential initially is broad and includes infectious causes as well as other transfusion reactions. The most common transfusion reaction is febrile nonhemolytic transfusion reaction.

wrongAnswers.B: Graft-versus-host disease is incorrect. Graft-versus-host disease would not occur in a patient receiving a blood transfusion; it occurs in patients who undergo transplant, such as stem cell transplantation.
wrongAnswers.C: Transfusion-associated acute lung injury is incorrect. Transfusion-associated acute lung injury is a complication of receiving a blood transfusion characterized by noncardiogenic pulmonary edema and subsequent acute respiratory distress. It is less common than febrile nonhemolytic transfusion reaction.
wrongAnswers.D: Transfusion-associated circulatory overload is incorrect. Transfusion-associated circulatory overload is a complication of receiving a blood transfusion characterized by volume overload and cardiogenic pulmonary edema. It is less common than febrile nonhemolytic transfusion reaction.
wrongAnswers.E: Transfusion-associated sepsis is incorrect. Transfusion-associated sepsis is a complication of transfusion with bacterial contamination of blood products. This is much less common than development of a febrile nonhemolytic transfusion reaction.

explanationPanel.rule: The most common packed RBC transfusion complication is febrile nonhemolytic transfusion reaction from donor leukocyte cytokines.
explanationPanel.trap: Trap: TRALI/TACO/sepsis are important but less common than febrile nonhemolytic reaction.

layer4.rule: The most common packed RBC transfusion complication is febrile nonhemolytic transfusion reaction from donor leukocyte cytokines.
layer4.trap: Trap: TRALI/TACO/sepsis are important but less common than febrile nonhemolytic reaction.

questions.stem: A 24-year-old nulligravid woman comes to the office because of a 6-month history of urinary urgency and moderate pain with urination and sexual intercourse. She has been avoiding intercourse with her partner during this time because of the pain. She has major depressive disorder and irritable bowel syndrome. Her only medication is bupropion. The patient has had no recent changes to her diet or bowel movements, except for occasional loose stools. She does not smoke cigarettes or drink alcoholic beverages. She is 174 cm (5 ft 7 in) tall and weighs 66 kg (145 lb); BMI is 23 kg/m². Pulse is 82/min, and blood pressure is 127/85 mm Hg. The abdomen is soft and nontender. Bladder palpation reproduces discomfort similar to her pain. There is no cervical motion tenderness or discharge. Urine β-hCG testing, urine culture, and sexually transmitted infection screening are negative. Cystoscopy shows punctate hemorrhages in the bladder mucosa. The patient has temporary pain relief after saline distention of the bladder. Biopsy specimen of the bladder shows granulation across the mucosa, lamina propria, and muscularis layers and prominent mast cells. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
