She has been avoiding intercourse with her partner during this time because of the pain. She has major depressive disorder and irritable bowel syndrome. Her only medication is bupropion. The patient has had no recent changes to her diet or bowel movements, except for occasional loose stools. She does not smoke cigarettes or drink alcoholic beverages. She is 174 cm (5 ft 7 in) tall and weighs 66 kg (145 lb); BMI is 23 kg/m². Pulse is 82/min, and blood pressure is 127/85 mm Hg. The abdomen is soft and nontender. Bladder palpation reproduces discomfort similar to her pain. There is no cervical motion tenderness or discharge. Urine β-hCG testing, urine culture, and sexually transmitted infection screening are negative. Cystoscopy shows punctate hemorrhages in the bladder mucosa. The patient has temporary pain relief after saline distention of the bladder. Biopsy specimen of the bladder shows granulation across the mucosa, lamina propria, and muscularis layers and prominent mast cells. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.subject: Gynecology

explanationPanel.whyCorrect:
Educational Objective: The patient in this case is most likely presenting with interstitial cystitis, an idiopathic, inflammatory disorder of the bladder that presents with urinary frequency, urgency, chronic suprapubic pain, and dyspareunia.

Evaluation: Interstitial cystitis often presents with uncomfortable or painful bladder symptoms that are related to bladder filling and are often improved with voiding.

Definition: The cause and pathophysiology of interstitial cystitis have been debated. Patients will typically have an unremarkable urinalysis and sterile urine culture. If cystoscopy is performed, the patient may be identified to have Hunner lesions with increased numbers of mast cells identified on biopsy analysis. Patients with interstitial cystitis may have other chronic pain conditions such as fibromyalgia, vulvodynia, and irritable bowel syndrome.

Prevention: There is no definitive way to prevent interstitial cystitis.

Treatment: Conservative management may include pelvic floor therapy or treatment with amitriptyline. For those with refractory symptoms, intravesical therapy may be pursued.

Differential: The patient in this case is presenting with chronic urinary symptoms with punctate hemorrhages appreciated on cystoscopy and biopsy showing prominent mast cells. The most likely diagnosis in this case is interstitial cystitis.

wrongAnswers.A: Bladder carcinoma is incorrect. Bladder cancer classically presents with painless hematuria, which may be grossly visible or microscopic, and occasionally presents with dysuria or urinary frequency. Cystoscopy with biopsy is the gold standard for the diagnosis of bladder cancer.
wrongAnswers.B: Bladder diverticulum is not the most likely diagnosis. A bladder diverticulum may develop from defects in the detrusor muscle fibers leading to herniation of the mucosa of the bladder. Bladder diverticula may present with inadequate bladder emptying, lower abdominal fullness, and urinary tract infection. A bladder diverticulum would most likely be identified on cystoscopy.
wrongAnswers.C: Endometriosis is incorrect. Endometriosis is caused by ectopic endometrial tissue outside the uterus and presents with chronic dysmenorrhea, dyspareunia, dyschezia, and possibly infertility. Symptoms are typically cyclical and do not often include dysuria.
wrongAnswers.E: Vestibulodynia is not the most likely diagnosis. Vestibulodynia refers to persistent pain localized to the vulvar region ongoing for at least 3 months without identifiable cause. The patient in this case has punctate hemorrhages identified on cystoscopy with biopsy showing prominent mast cells, which is more consistent with interstitial cystitis.

explanationPanel.rule: Chronic bladder pain/urgency/dysuria with sterile cultures, dyspareunia, Hunner lesions/mast cells = interstitial cystitis.
explanationPanel.trap: Trap: recurrent UTI/STI is unlikely when cultures and STI testing are negative.

layer4.rule: Chronic bladder pain/urgency/dysuria with sterile cultures, dyspareunia, Hunner lesions/mast cells = interstitial cystitis.
layer4.trap: Trap: recurrent UTI/STI is unlikely when cultures and STI testing are negative.

questions.stem: A 76-year-old man is admitted to the hospital for management of severe dehydration. He says he is “fine” and has not felt like drinking much water lately. He was hospitalized 3 months ago following a cerebral infarction, which resulted in left-sided weakness. At that time, he was discharged to the care of his daughter. At discharge, he weighed 84 kg (186 lb). He has hyperlipidemia, hypertension, and benign prostatic hyperplasia. His medications are atorvastatin, enalapril, finasteride, and aspirin. On questioning, he says his daughter is away most of the time and sometimes forgets to buy groceries. He last saw her 3 days ago. He says he would like to live with his son. Today, the patient is 178 cm (5 ft 10 in) tall and weighs 73 kg (162 lb); BMI is 23 kg/m². Pulse is 80/min, and blood pressure is 100/66 mm Hg. Pulse oximetry on room air shows an oxygen saturation of 94%. Examination shows decreased skin turgor. Muscle strength is 3/5 in the left extremities. On mental status examination, he describes his mood as “fine” and has a distant affect. There is no evidence of suicidal ideation. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

Pulse oximetry on room air shows an oxygen saturation of 94%. Examination shows decreased skin turgor. Muscle strength is 3/5 in the left extremities. On mental status examination, he describes his mood as “fine” and has a distant affect. There is no evidence of suicidal ideation. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
choices: Arrange for the patient to live with his son
Discharge the patient to a nursing care facility
Request assistance from a home health agency
Talk with the patient’s daughter about the care of her father
questions.subject: Ethics/Social Sciences

explanationPanel.whyCorrect:
Educational Objective: Physicians are legally mandated to report suspected abuse, neglect, or exploitation of older patients. Adult protective services investigate suspected abuse and coordinate appropriate interventions to ensure older patients’ safety. This physician should contact adult protective services as the next step in management.

Key Concept: Signs of abuse, neglect, and exploitation include multiple bruises, malnutrition and/or weight loss as in this patient, poor personal hygiene, sudden behavioral changes such as becoming less social, unsanitary living conditions, sudden changes in a patient’s assets or living will, and caregivers refusing to let the patient be seen alone. Adult protective services investigate suspected abuse and coordinate appropriate interventions to ensure older patients’ safety. As well, if a patient does not have a safe disposition, they should be admitted to the hospital for alternative disposition planning while adult protective services conduct their investigation.

Explanation: Physicians should ask direct, open-ended questions of the patient alone about physical examination findings indicative of abuse. However, when elder abuse is suspected, the physician is legally mandated to report the suspected abuse to adult protective services regardless of the patient’s response. Neglect and exploitation of older adults are also reportable offenses.

Differential: Though the physician should engage this patient and his family in discussions related to disposition, first the physician should contact adult protective services.

wrongAnswers.A: Arrange for the patient to live with his son and discharge the patient to a nursing care facility would be premature. First, the physician should notify adult protective services. Next, the physician should involve social work, who can assist with psychosocial assessments and assist in developing an appropriate disposition plan.
wrongAnswers.C: Arrange for the patient to live with his son and discharge the patient to a nursing care facility would be premature. First, the physician should notify adult protective services. Next, the physician should involve social work, who can assist with psychosocial assessments and assist in developing an appropriate disposition plan.
wrongAnswers.D: Request assistance from a home health agency is inappropriate. Home health agencies do not provide constant supervision and do not typically assist with grocery shopping, so this patient would still be exposed to the effects of neglect.
wrongAnswers.E: Talk with the patient’s daughter about the care of her father is incorrect. The physician’s first priority should be keeping this older patient safe by reporting elder abuse to adult protective services. Adult protective services will investigate the situation by speaking with involved family members such as the daughter.

explanationPanel.rule: Suspected elder neglect with dehydration, weight loss, absent caregiver, and unsafe disposition must be reported to adult protective services.
explanationPanel.trap: Trap: do not first confront the caregiver or arrange placement before mandatory reporting.

layer4.rule: Suspected elder neglect with dehydration, weight loss, absent caregiver, and unsafe disposition must be reported to adult protective services.
layer4.trap: Trap: do not first confront the caregiver or arrange placement before mandatory reporting.

questions.stem: A 32-year-old woman, gravida 2, para 2, comes to the office for a routine health maintenance examination. She feels well. She has no history of serious illness. Her only medication is a contraceptive ring, which she started 6 weeks ago. Her mother received the diagnosis of breast cancer 1 week ago at the age of 68 years, and her paternal aunt died of breast cancer at the age of 61 years. The patient does not smoke cigarettes. She is 168 cm (5 ft 6 in) tall and weighs 87 kg (191 lb); BMI is 31 kg/m². Blood pressure is 150/90 mm Hg. Examination shows no other abnormalities. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
questions.stemHtml: A 32-year-old woman, gravida 2, para 2, comes to the office for a routine health maintenance examination. She feels well. She has no history of serious illness. Her only medication is a contraceptive ring, which she started 6 weeks ago. Her mother received the diagnosis of breast cancer 1 week ago at the age of 68 years, and her paternal aunt died of breast cancer at the age of 61 years. The patient does not smoke cigarettes. She is 168 cm (5 ft 6 in) tall and weighs 87 kg (191 lb); BMI is 31 kg/m². Blood pressure is 150/90 mm Hg. Examination shows no other abnormalities. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
choices: Genetic testing for BRCA1 and BRCA2 mutations
questions.subject: Gynecology

explanationPanel.whyCorrect:
Educational Objective: Contraceptive medications, especially those containing estrogen, are known to cause hypertension as an adverse effect. Generally, the increase in blood pressure is low, and the risk for hypertension induced by a contraceptive is also low. For this patient with a new diagnosis of hypertension after starting an estrogen-based contraceptive, it is most appropriate to discontinue use of the contraceptive ring.

Key Concept: Contraceptives containing estrogen, in both oral and insertable/implantable form, have been shown to cause hypertension as an adverse effect.

Explanation: The risk for hypertension when using estrogen-based contraceptives is generally low, but it is more pronounced in patients who already experience hypertension or have known cardiovascular disease. The mechanism of hypertension is not fully known but is hypothesized to relate to fluid and water retention. Other cardiovascular risks of note when using hormonal contraceptives (ie, estrogen-based) include cerebral infarction and venous thromboembolic disease. An increase in blood pressure generally occurs within 3 months to as long as 3 years after starting an estrogen-based contraceptive and usually resolves within a few months after discontinuation. Low-dose estrogen components in contraceptives are associated with lower increases in blood pressure, and some estrogen analogs are actually shown to decrease blood pressure (eg, drospirenone, a spironolactone analog). Patients at highest risk for developing hypertension from estrogen-based contraceptives include those with a personal or family history of hypertension, those aged 35 to 44 years, and those with an increased BMI. Patients with unacceptable increases in blood pressure after initiation of an estrogen-based contraceptive should have the contraceptive discontinued or removed.

Differential: In new diagnoses of hypertension, clinicians should search for reversible causes of blood pressure increases along with recommending lifestyle modification. Culprit medications or lifestyle factors should be discontinued or modified if possible. Initiation of medications or further evaluation can follow discontinuation of medications and lifestyle modification.

wrongAnswers.A: β-Adrenergic blocking agent therapy is incorrect. β-Adrenergic blocking agent therapy is only appropriate in the management of gestational hypertension as a first-line drug. It is otherwise not first-line in the management of essential hypertension. Secondary causes of hypertension, such as heart failure, may be treated with β-adrenergic blocking therapy; however, this is due to the β-adrenergic blocker’s indication for use in heart failure, not for hypertension. Even still, initiating pharmacotherapy in this patient is inappropriate, as discontinuation of her contraceptive is the most appropriate next step in management.
wrongAnswers.B: Aspirin therapy is incorrect. Aspirin therapy is recommended to reduce risk for cerebral infarctions in at-risk patients, as well as reducing risks associated with gestational hypertension and preeclampsia. This patient is not pregnant and not at increased risk for a cerebral infarction beyond what could be managed by discontinuing her contraceptive.
wrongAnswers.D: Genetic testing for BRCA1 and BRCA2 mutations, MRI of the breasts, second breast examination in 6 months, and ultrasonography of the breasts are not the best choices. Any of these options may be appropriate in evaluating this patient’s risk for breast cancer given her family history; however, none of these measures address her new diagnosis of hypertension after placement of a contraceptive ring. At age 32 years, her greatest health maintenance need currently is evaluation of new-onset hypertension. Evaluation or screen of potential breast cancer generally begins with a diagnostic or screening mammography, as opposed to genetic testing, MRI, repeating examinations, or ultrasonography.

questions.stem: A 65-year-old woman comes to the office because of a 3-month history of mild abdominal discomfort and bloating. She has not had vaginal bleeding. Medical history is unremarkable, and she does not use any medications or other substances. She is 165 cm (5 ft 4 in) tall and weighs 82 kg (181 lb); BMI is 30 kg/m². Vital signs are within normal limits. Physical examination discloses no abnormalities. Pelvic examination discloses a large right adnexal mass. Ultrasonography confirms the presence of a complex solid and cystic mass. Oophorectomy is done; resection results show a 10-cm cystic ovary with solid papillary excrescences composed of a highly atypical cellular proliferation with fibrovascular cores and epithelial tufting. There are also numerous nodules measuring up to 1 cm in diameter on the omentum. Recurrence of disease in this patient should be monitored periodically with which of the following serum concentration studies?

Ultrasonography confirms the presence of a complex solid and cystic mass. There are also numerous nodules measuring up to 1 cm in diameter on the omentum. Recurrence of disease in this patient should be monitored periodically with which of the following serum concentration studies?
questions.subject: Gynecology

explanationPanel.whyCorrect:
Educational Objective: CA 125 testing is the best test for monitoring of disease recurrence in this patient with a history of ovarian malignancy.

Key Concept: Ovarian cancer often presents insidiously, with vague symptoms of abdominal discomfort, bloating, and nausea. CA 125 is a protein present on ovarian epithelium; increased CA 125 concentrations are associated with recurrence of malignancy.

Explanation: CA 125 is a transmembrane protein found on epithelial cells in the female reproductive tract such as the endometrium, fallopian tube, and ovary. CA 125 is also found in lung, gastrointestinal, and breast tissue. CA 125 concentrations fluctuate with age and menarcheal/menopausal status, pregnancy, in the setting of uterine fibroids, and in cancers of the endometrium, ovary, lung, gastrointestinal tract, and breast. CA 125 is thus not used as a screening test for ovarian cancer as there are many competing benign and malignant causes for its increase; however, it is used to monitor the tumor burden in ovarian cancer over time, with uptrending concentrations suggesting active or recurrent disease.

Differential: CA 125 is used as a tumor marker in cases of ovarian cancer. Carcinoembryonic antigen (CEA), α-fetoprotein, β-hCG, and lactate dehydrogenase are also tumor markers; however, they are not used to trend potential recurrence of ovarian malignancy.

wrongAnswers.B: Carcinoembryonic antigen is incorrect. CEA is a tumor marker in many malignancies, including colorectal and pancreatic. CEA is not a known marker of ovarian cancer.
wrongAnswers.C: α-Fetoprotein is incorrect. α-Fetoprotein is a tumor marker of liver cancer and is not a known marker of ovarian cancer. α-Fetoprotein is also used to assess fetal developmental abnormalities as a part of prenatal testing.
wrongAnswers.D: β-hCG is incorrect. β-hCG is a tumor marker of reproductive germ cell tumors and choriocarcinoma. β-hCG is also used to trend early pregnancy to assess for normal or abnormal progression (eg, potential ectopic location).
wrongAnswers.E: Lactate dehydrogenase is incorrect. Lactate dehydrogenase is increased in several malignant and nonmalignant conditions and is a general marker of cell turnover. Lactate dehydrogenase activity may be abnormal in hematologic and solid organ malignancies, hemolytic disease, and rhabdomyolysis, among other causes.

explanationPanel.rule: CA-125 is used to monitor recurrence/tumor burden in epithelial ovarian cancer, not for population screening.
explanationPanel.trap: Trap: AFP, beta-hCG, and LDH point to germ-cell or other tumors, not serous epithelial ovarian cancer recurrence.

layer4.rule: CA-125 is used to monitor recurrence/tumor burden in epithelial ovarian cancer, not for population screening.
layer4.trap: Trap: AFP, beta-hCG, and LDH point to germ-cell or other tumors, not serous epithelial ovarian cancer recurrence.

questions.stem: A 57-year-old woman comes to the physician because of a 1-week history of decreased vision in her right eye. Four months ago, she began topiramate therapy for seizure disorder. She has no other history of serious illness and takes no other medications. Examination of the right eye shows an injected conjunctiva and a steamy cornea. Dilated funduscopic examination is limited and shows a good red reflex. The left pupil is 4 mm and reactive to light; the right pupil is 4 mm and nonreactive to light. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.stemHtml: A 57-year-old woman comes to the physician because of a 1-week history of decreased vision in her right eye. Four months ago, she began topiramate therapy for seizure disorder. She has no other history of serious illness and takes no other medications. Examination of the right eye shows an injected conjunctiva and a steamy cornea. Dilated funduscopic examination is limited and shows a good red reflex. The left pupil is 4 mm and reactive to light; the right pupil is 4 mm and nonreactive to light. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.subject: Ophthalmology

explanationPanel.whyCorrect:
Educational Objective: This patient most likely has glaucoma. In acute glaucoma, patients typically present with acute unilateral vision loss, eye pain, light halos, headache, nausea, and vomiting. Ocular examination commonly shows a red eye, corneal cloudiness, and a poorly reactive mid-dilated pupil.

Evaluation: Acute glaucoma refers to an increase in intraocular pressure and consequent optic nerve damage. Angle-closure is the most common cause of acute glaucoma (whereas open-angle glaucoma is typically a chronic and progressive optic neuropathy). The closure of the anterior chamber angle leads to the sudden accumulation of aqueous humor in the eyeball (and increased intraocular pressure).

Definition: Some patients' eyes are anatomically predisposed to acute angle-closure. Secondary causes of acute glaucoma include certain medications (eg, anticholinergic agents, adrenergic agents, sulfonamide derivatives such as topiramate) and the accumulation of blood or inflammation in the angle. Patients typically present with acute unilateral vision loss, eye pain, light halos, headache, nausea, and vomiting. Ocular examination commonly shows a red eye, corneal cloudiness, and a poorly reactive mid-dilated pupil.

Prevention: Avoiding offending medications can help prevent acute angle-closure glaucoma.

Treatment: Management involves acute control with β-adrenergic blockers, α-adrenergic agonists, miosis-causing agents, and acetazolamide or mannitol to decrease intraocular pressure. Definitive treatment is laser peripheral iridotomy or cataract surgery.

Differential: Though both retinal detachment and acute glaucoma present with the acute onset of vision changes, acute glaucoma is typically painful, while retinal detachment is painless. Acute glaucoma can be distinguished from infectious eye conditions by the presence of a mid-dilated, nonreactive pupil and the absence of hypopyon (inflammation of the anterior chamber of the eye, appearing as a layer of fluid in the lower part of the eye).

wrongAnswers.A: Chemical conjunctivitis is incorrect. Chemical conjunctivitis presents with conjunctival injection secondary to inflammation of the conjunctiva, resulting from exposure to acids, alkalis, and other irritants such as alcohols. Corneal cloudiness and a poorly reactive pupil would be atypical.
wrongAnswers.B: Endophthalmitis is incorrect. Endophthalmitis is a severe infection of the aqueous humors of the eyes. Patients commonly present with decreased vision, eye pain, and photophobia with examination findings including conjunctival injection, hypopyon, and vitritis (inflammation of the vitreous humor, which has a hazy appearance on fundoscopy). Pupillary changes are less common than in glaucoma, and glaucoma does not typically present with hypopyon or vitritis.
wrongAnswers.D: Retinal detachment is incorrect. Retinal detachment typically presents with the acute onset of painless peripheral vision loss, blurred vision, light flashes, and floaters. Acute angle-closure glaucoma is typically painful. Retinal detachment does not typically present with conjunctival injection, corneal clouding, or a nonreactive pupil.
wrongAnswers.E: Uveitis is incorrect. Uveitis is inflammation of the uveal tract and typically presents with conjunctival injection, blurred vision, floaters, eye pain, and photophobia. Sometimes hypopyon is present. Uveitis typically presents with miosis rather than a mid-dilated pupil.

explanationPanel.rule: Painful/red eye with cloudy cornea and fixed mid-dilated pupil, especially after topiramate, = acute angle-closure glaucoma.
explanationPanel.trap: Trap: retinal detachment causes painless flashes/floaters/curtain without injected eye or cloudy cornea.

layer4.rule: Painful/red eye with cloudy cornea and fixed mid-dilated pupil, especially after topiramate, = acute angle-closure glaucoma.
layer4.trap: Trap: retinal detachment causes painless flashes/floaters/curtain without injected eye or cloudy cornea.

Question: Which of the following is the most likely complication of this patient's current condition?
questions.subject: Musculoskeletal/Orthopedics

explanationPanel.whyCorrect:
Educational Objective: Intertrochanteric femur fractures often require surgical correction and may result in further inpatient rehabilitation in either an acute rehabilitation unit or skilled nursing facility if a decline in functional baseline has been identified by physical and occupational therapy. Patients like this one are at an increased risk for falls after surgical correction of an intertrochanteric femur fracture, especially in the early postoperative period.

Evaluation: Intertrochanteric femur fractures may develop due to falls or direct trauma. Definition: Patients may be at an increased risk for falls in the postoperative period due to altered functional ability to ambulate and transfer. This may occur due to pain, deconditioning, orthostatic hypotension, or adverse effects from medications started during the hospitalization.

Prevention: Falls may be prevented after femur intramedullary nailing with gait training, use of an assistive walking device, and with careful review of the patient’s medication regimen.

Treatment: In this case, a review of the patient’s medications would be important to decrease her risk for falls. Both metoclopramide and promethazine, which may be used to address her nausea, are central nervous system depressants. In addition, monitoring of the patient’s blood pressure and decrease of her antihypertensive therapy may be indicated.

Differential: The patient in this case is presenting with a decreased systolic blood pressure after starting amlodipine 4 days ago as well as nausea with possible administration of metoclopramide and/or promethazine. Her decreased systolic blood pressure, nausea, and subjective generalized weakness with recent intramedullary nailing of her femur fracture places the patient at an increased risk for falls.

wrongAnswers.B: Hypovolemic shock is incorrect. Hypovolemic shock may be a complication immediately following her motor vehicle collision. The patient in this case is at a higher risk for falls.
wrongAnswers.C: Ischemic stroke is not the most likely complication. Ischemic stroke may be a complication of conditions such as atrial fibrillation or deep venous thrombosis if the patient has a patent foramen ovale. Falls are the most likely complication in this patient.
wrongAnswers.D: Progression to dementia is incorrect. Dementia is not likely to develop secondary to an intertrochanteric femur fracture. The patient in this case is at a higher risk for falls.
wrongAnswers.E: Type 2 diabetes mellitus is not the most likely complication of this patient's current condition. This patient already has a diagnosis of type 2 diabetes mellitus with her current hemoglobin A1c measured as 7.2%. Recent operative repair of a femur fracture places this patient at a higher risk for falls.

explanationPanel.rule: Older patient after intertrochanteric fracture repair with weakness, low BP, CNS-active antiemetics = high fall risk.
explanationPanel.trap: Trap: the immediate rehab complication is falls, not dementia progression or stroke.

layer4.trap: Trap: the immediate rehab complication is falls, not dementia progression or stroke.

questions.stem: A 3-year-old boy is brought to the office by his father because of a 2-month history of intermittently bloody stools. The father describes the stools as hard balls and says that there are often streaks of blood on the outside. The patient has a bowel movement every 1 to 2 days. He is fully toilet trained for urine but refuses to use the toilet to stool. During the past week, his appetite has decreased, and he has only been picking at foods. He eats the same meals as his family but does not like most vegetables. The only fruits he eats are bananas and grapes. He drinks 24 to 28 oz of low-fat cow milk daily. His father reports no changes to his urination. Medical history is unremarkable and he receives no medications. Vaccinations are up-to-date. He is 90 cm (2 ft 11 in; 10th percentile) tall and weighs 12.5 kg (27.5 lb; 10th percentile); BMI is 15.4 kg/m² (30th percentile). Temperature is 37.6°C (99.7°F), pulse is 120/min, respirations are 22/min, and blood pressure is 90/64 mm Hg. Pulse oximetry on room air shows an oxygen saturation of 98%. Bowel sounds are normoactive. There is diffuse mild tenderness to palpation of the abdomen with no rebound tenderness or guarding. The remainder of the physical examination discloses no abnormalities. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

The father describes the stools as hard balls and says that there are often streaks of blood on the outside. The patient has a bowel movement every 1 to 2 days. He is fully toilet trained for urine but refuses to use the toilet to stool. During the past week, his appetite has decreased, and he has only been picking at foods. He eats the same meals as his family but does not like most vegetables. The only fruits he eats are bananas and grapes. He drinks 24 to 28 oz of low-fat cow milk daily. His father reports no changes to his urination. Medical history is unremarkable and he receives no medications. Vaccinations are up-to-date. He is 90 cm (2 ft 11 in; 10th percentile) tall and weighs 12.5 kg (27.5 lb; 10th percentile); BMI is 15.4 kg/m² (30th percentile). Temperature is 37.6°C (99.7°F), pulse is 120/min, respirations are 22/min, and blood pressure is 90/64 mm Hg. Pulse oximetry on room air shows an oxygen saturation of 98%. Bowel sounds are normoactive. There is diffuse mild tenderness to palpation of the abdomen with no rebound tenderness or guarding. The remainder of the physical examination discloses no abnormalities. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.subject: Pediatrics/Neonatology

explanationPanel.whyCorrect:
Educational Objective: The most likely diagnosis in this young patient with hard stools, intermittent streaks of blood on the outside of his stools, decreased fiber intake, and stool withholding is functional constipation.

Evaluation: Functional constipation typically presents with infrequent bowel movements, hard stools, abdominal pain, and stool withholding behaviors. Blood streaks on the toilet paper can result from anal fissures caused by hard stools.

Definition: The diagnosis of functional constipation is clinical and is based on the Rome IV criteria, which include, among other things, a history of excessive stool retention, painful bowel movements, hard stools, and large-diameter stools.

Prevention: Prevention of functional constipation in children includes ensuring adequate fiber intake in the diet, ensuring adequate fluid intake, and enforcing regular toilet routines.

Treatment: Treatment includes stool softeners, such as oral polyethylene glycol, behavioral interventions, and, if needed, fecal disimpaction.

Differential: There are a variety of disorders on the differential for constipation including cow’s milk intolerance, anorectal anomalies, and Hirschsprung disease. This patient’s clinical presentation of new onset constipation in the setting of decreased fiber intake is most consistent with functional constipation.

wrongAnswers.A: Congenital megacolon (Hirschsprung disease) is incorrect. Hirschsprung disease is most often diagnosed in the neonatal period. It can present in childhood with chronic constipation; however, this is less likely given this patient’s age.
wrongAnswers.C: Meckel diverticulum is incorrect. Meckel diverticulum is associated with painless rectal bleeding and intussusception, not constipation.
wrongAnswers.D: Milk protein allergy is incorrect. Milk protein allergy can present with constipation; however, this is less likely given the introduction to milk is not new or correlated with the onset of symptoms.
wrongAnswers.E: Ulcerative colitis is incorrect. Ulcerative colitis classically presents with abdominal pain, fecal urgency, and hematochezia. It does not typically present with constipation.

explanationPanel.rule: Toddler with hard ball-like stools, withholding, low-fiber diet, and blood streaks on stool = functional constipation with fissures.
explanationPanel.trap: Trap: Meckel causes painless bleeding; it does not cause hard stools/withholding.

layer4.rule: Toddler with hard ball-like stools, withholding, low-fiber diet, and blood streaks on stool = functional constipation with fissures.
layer4.trap: Trap: Meckel causes painless bleeding; it does not cause hard stools/withholding.

questions.stem: A 47-year-old woman comes to the office because of a 3-day history of fever, fatigue, and loss of appetite. Five weeks ago, she underwent uncomplicated kidney transplant for end-stage kidney disease caused by type 2 diabetes mellitus. Her postoperative course had been uncomplicated and stable with her current immunosuppression therapy. Medical history is also remarkable for hypercholesterolemia and essential hypertension. Medications are insulin, prednisone, cyclosporine, mycophenolate mofetil, atorvastatin, and irbesartan. Temperature is 38.0°C (100.4°F), pulse is 100/min, respirations are 16/min, and blood pressure is 146/90 mm Hg. Abdominal examination shows a well-healing incision and tenderness to palpation over the right lower quadrant at the transplant site. There is 1+ pedal edema. Results of laboratory studies are shown: Leukocyte count 4500/mm³; serum Na⁺ 130 mEq/L, K⁺ 5.5 mEq/L, Cl⁻ 92 mEq/L, HCO₃− 20 mEq/L, urea nitrogen 34 mg/dL, creatinine 3.1 mg/dL, glucose 180 mg/dL. Which of the following is the most likely explanation for these findings?

explanationPanel.whyCorrect:
Educational Objective: This patient who underwent kidney transplant 5 weeks ago presents with acute kidney injury, fever, and tenderness to palpation over the transplant site. The most likely explanation for these findings is transplant rejection.

Evaluation: Acute renal allograft rejection often presents within 6 months after transplantation and can present with graft dysfunction. Definition: Renal biopsy is the gold standard to confirm the suspected diagnosis of acute transplant rejection and further classify the subtype of rejection. Acute rejection can be evidenced by mononuclear infiltrates, vasculitis, and immunopathologic staining evidence of graft destruction.

Prevention: Graft rejection is prevented with pretransplant desensitization and immunosuppression.

Treatment: Treatment of antibody-mediated rejection involves plasmapheresis, intravenous immune globulin, high-dose corticosteroids, and modification of immunosuppressive agents. Treatment of T-cell-mediated rejection involves glucocorticoids, rabbit antithymocyte globulin, and modification of immunosuppressive agents.

Differential: This patient with acute kidney injury 5 weeks after transplant presents with graft dysfunction most consistent with rejection. The differential for acute kidney injury after transplant is broad, but the suspected diagnosis for this patient is acute transplant rejection.

wrongAnswers.A: Compressive lymphocele is incorrect. This refers to a collection of lymphatic fluid that can occur after surgical procedures such as kidney transplant. While it may cause acute kidney injury if it compresses on the urinary system, it would be abnormal to cause systemic signs such as those seen in this patient.
wrongAnswers.B: Cyclosporine toxicity is incorrect. Cyclosporine toxicity can present with acute kidney injury, but it would be abnormal for it to cause fever, tachycardia, or tenderness to palpation over the transplant site.
wrongAnswers.C: Cytomegalovirus infection is incorrect. Cytomegalovirus infection classically presents with fever and absence of end-organ disease. This patient’s acute kidney injury makes this diagnosis less likely.
wrongAnswers.D: Diabetic nephropathy is incorrect. Diabetic nephropathy would not typically present in a transplanted kidney 5 weeks after transplant. Diabetic nephropathy is a chronic disease that develops over years.

explanationPanel.rule: Fever, graft tenderness, and acute kidney injury within months of renal transplant = acute allograft rejection until proven by biopsy.
explanationPanel.trap: Trap: cyclosporine toxicity causes AKI but not fever or focal graft tenderness.

layer4.rule: Fever, graft tenderness, and acute kidney injury within months of renal transplant = acute allograft rejection until proven by biopsy.
layer4.trap: Trap: cyclosporine toxicity causes AKI but not fever or focal graft tenderness.

questions.stem: A 27-year-old man comes to the office because of a 2-day history of moderate chest pain and shortness of breath. He also has a 1-week history of a cough and low-grade fever that have not improved. He has no personal or family history of major medical illness. Temperature is 38.0°C (100.4°F), pulse is 92/min, respirations are 20/min, and blood pressure is 95/65 mm Hg. Pulse oximetry on room air shows an oxygen saturation of 97%. The lungs are clear to auscultation. Distant heart sounds are heard, and an anterior friction rub is heard and palpated. Results of laboratory studies, including complete blood count, and serum concentrations of electrolytes, urea nitrogen, and creatinine, are within the reference ranges. CT scan of the chest is shown. Which of the following is the most likely cause of these findings?

He also has a 1-week history of a cough and low-grade fever that have not improved. He has no personal or family history of major medical illness. Temperature is 38.0°C (100.4°F), pulse is 92/min, respirations are 20/min, and blood pressure is 95/65 mm Hg. Pulse oximetry on room air shows an oxygen saturation of 97%. The lungs are clear to auscultation. Distant heart sounds are heard, and an anterior friction rub is heard and palpated. Results of laboratory studies, including complete blood count, and serum concentrations of electrolytes, urea nitrogen, and creatinine, are within the reference ranges. CT scan of the chest is shown. Which of the following is the most likely cause of these findings?
questions.subject: Cardiology

explanationPanel.whyCorrect:
Educational Objective: This patient, who presents with fever, chest discomfort, preceding viral infectious symptoms, friction rub, and distant heart sounds, likely has virally triggered pericarditis as a result of coxsackievirus. This diagnosis is further supported by pericardial effusion shown on CT scan of the chest. Coxsackievirus infection is a common trigger of carditis.

Evaluation: Pericarditis should be suspected in patients who present with central chest pain, which is often pleuritic and improves with bending forward. Pericarditis can occur idiopathically or in patients with inflammatory, infectious, or malignant conditions, such as viral infection, systemic lupus erythematosus, tuberculosis, and lymphoma. Pericarditis may also follow myocardial infarction. Pericarditis is evaluated with ECG, echocardiography, and laboratory studies that include inflammatory markers and troponin assay.

Definition: Pericarditis describes inflammation of the pericardial space, including the visceral and parietal pericardium. Pericarditis is a relatively common cause of chest discomfort in young patients without cardiac risk factors, especially in the setting of viral infection. Coxsackievirus and other enteroviruses are known triggers of pericarditis and myocarditis. Pericarditis can lead to the development of pericardial effusion, as seen on this patient’s CT scan of the chest, as inflammatory fluid accumulates in the pericardial space. In severe cases, cardiac tamponade leading to hemodynamic instability can result.

Prevention: As there are many underlying triggers of pericarditis, there is no specific preventive measure apart from maintaining general health. Measures to decrease risk for developing coxsackievirus include regular hand washing after bathroom use, handwashing before and after preparing food, and disinfecting common areas.

Treatment: Coxsackievirus-induced pericarditis is treated with anti-inflammatory medications such as indomethacin, colchicine, and glucocorticoids in some cases. If a moderate to severe effusion with associated tamponade is present, pericardiocentesis is indicated.

Differential: Causes of pericarditis are many; this patient’s young age, absence of major comorbidities, and preceding viral infection narrow the cause to viral infection.

wrongAnswers.A: Autoimmune pericarditis is incorrect. While autoimmune pericarditis is a known cause of pericarditis, this patient is young and healthy, with no personal or family history of autoimmune disease. Further, his preceding viral symptoms argue for an infectious, not autoimmune, trigger.
wrongAnswers.B: Chronic uremia is incorrect. Uremia is a known cause of pericarditis; however, increased blood urea nitrogen concentration is required to make the diagnosis, which generally occurs in the setting of renal failure. This patient has normal renal function and electrolytes, ruling out this cause.
wrongAnswers.D: Sarcoidosis is incorrect. Sarcoidosis is most common in biologically female patients aged 20 to 40 years and generally presents with chronic shortness of breath and hilar lymphadenopathy. This patient has had no such preceding symptoms and has no known major medical illnesses.
wrongAnswers.E: Tuberculosis is incorrect. Tuberculosis is a known cause of pericardial effusion and pericarditis in infected patients; however, this patient has no risk factors for or signs of tuberculosis. He does not present with cough, fever, night sweats, weight loss, rash, history of immunocompromise, documented or disclosed recent travel, or living in close quarters.

explanationPanel.trap: Trap: uremic/TB/autoimmune pericarditis needs renal failure, TB risk, or autoimmune features.

questions.stem: A 12-year-old boy is brought to the physician for a routine examination. He has a history of aortic root enlargement, mitral valve prolapse, and lens dislocation that was surgically repaired at 2 years of age. His father and one of his three siblings have similar histories and physical findings. He is at the 95th percentile for height and 25th percentile for weight. Examination shows long fingers and toes, hyperextensible joints, pectus excavatum, and scoliosis. Which of the following best describes the mode of inheritance of this patient's condition?
questions.stemHtml: A 12-year-old boy is brought to the physician for a routine examination. He has a history of aortic root enlargement, mitral valve prolapse, and lens dislocation that was surgically repaired at 2 years of age. His father and one of his three siblings have similar histories and physical findings. He is at the 95th percentile for height and 25th percentile for weight. Examination shows long fingers and toes, hyperextensible joints, pectus excavatum, and scoliosis. Which of the following best describes the mode of inheritance of this patient's condition?
questions.subject: Genetics

explanationPanel.whyCorrect:
Educational Objective: Marfan syndrome is an autosomal dominant connective tissue disorder resulting in an inherited mutation of the FBN1 gene. Features include tall and thin stature, ocular lens dislocation, mitral valve prolapse, and aneurysms.

Key Concept: Marfan syndrome is a genetic disorder affecting connective tissue, in which mutations in the FBN1 gene lead to a wide variety of traits such as tall and thin stature, ocular lens dislocation, mitral valve prolapse, and aneurysms. Marfan syndrome is inherited in an autosomal dominant pattern and follows the principles of mendelian genetics.

Explanation: Expression of an autosomal dominant disorder occurs when the disease phenotype is expressed, whether there is a single copy of the mutated allele (heterozygous) or two copies of the mutated allele (homozygous). Marfan syndrome is an autosomal dominant disorder with complete penetrance, therefore, only an individual who is homozygous for the wild-type (no disease) allele will be unaffected.

Differential: Inheritance of disease is based on autosomal, mitochondrial, and X-linked genetics of the parents, genes distributed into the gametes, de novo mutations acquired during embryonic cell division and differentiation, penetrance and expressivity of the condition, mosaicism, and epigenetic modifications of expression. This patient with classic features of Marfan syndrome and an affected father and siblings most likely has this autosomal-dominant inherited disorder.

wrongAnswers.B: Autosomal recessive inheritance is incorrect. Expression of an autosomal recessive disorder occurs when the disease phenotype is expressed only if two copies of the mutated allele are present. Examples of autosomal recessive disorders include cystic fibrosis, spinal muscular atrophy, and Tay-Sachs disease.
wrongAnswers.C: Multifactorial inheritance is incorrect. Diseases with multifactorial inheritance often develop from contributions of multiple genes and environmental factors. Examples of multifactorial inheritance include autism spectrum disorder, cleft lip and palate, congenital heart defects, and schizophrenia.
wrongAnswers.D: X-linked dominant inheritance is incorrect. X-linked disorders can only be transmitted maternally—this patient has inherited the disease from his father. In X-linked dominant disorders, both male and female patients possessing the mutated allele manifest the disease. X-linked dominant inheritance is observed in fragile X syndrome, incontinentia pigmenti, hypophosphatemic rickets, and Rett syndrome.
wrongAnswers.E: X-linked recessive inheritance is incorrect. X-linked disorders can only be transmitted maternally—this patient has inherited the disease from his father. In X-linked recessive disorders, only male patients with the mutated allele manifest the disease because female patients have a second, wild-type allele on their other X chromosome. X- linked recessive inheritance is observed in hemophilia and red-green color blindness.
wrongAnswers.F: No genetic component is incorrect. This constellation of features and presence in the patient’s father and siblings are suggestive of a genetic disorder.

explanationPanel.rule: Marfan syndrome from FBN1 mutation is autosomal dominant and can be transmitted father-to-son.
explanationPanel.trap: Trap: father-to-son transmission excludes X-linked inheritance.

layer4.rule: Marfan syndrome from FBN1 mutation is autosomal dominant and can be transmitted father-to-son.
layer4.trap: Trap: father-to-son transmission excludes X-linked inheritance.

questions.stem: A 19-year-old man comes to the emergency department because of a 3-hour history of severe chest pain below the sternum. The pain is described as sharp and pleuritic and radiates to his back. He also reports pain with swallowing and shortness of breath. He says he "drank a lot of alcohol" at a party yesterday evening and had several episodes of nonbloody vomiting this morning; his current symptoms began 1 hour later. He has gastroesophageal reflux disease and generalized anxiety disorder. Medications are omeprazole and escitalopram. The patient has no known allergies. He drinks alcoholic beverages "heavily" on weekends; he does not smoke cigarettes or use any other substances. He is 178 cm (5 ft 10 in) tall and weighs 77 kg (170 lb); BMI is 24 kg/m². Temperature is 37.6°C (99.6°F), pulse is 138/min, respirations are 20/min, and blood pressure is 87/40 mm Hg. Pulse oximetry on room air shows an oxygen saturation of 95%. The patient appears confused but is in no respiratory distress. Pulmonary examination discloses tachypnea with shallow inspirations. Cardiac examination discloses tachycardia and normal S₁ and S₂. There is tenderness to palpation of the anterior chest wall. Bowel sounds are normal. Abdomen is diffusely tender to palpation. The remainder of the physical examination discloses no abnormalities. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
questions.subject: Gastroenterology

explanationPanel.whyCorrect:
Educational Objective: This patient presents with severe chest pain after vomiting and is found to have tachycardia, hypotension, and tachypnea. This presentation is consistent with transmural rupture of the esophagus secondary to forceful vomiting, or Boerhaave syndrome. While this patient requires management of the acute condition, mitigating his hypotension with volume resuscitation is critical. The most appropriate next step in management is 0.9% saline therapy.

Evaluation: Boerhaave syndrome is transmural rupture of the esophagus that typically occurs after an increase in intraesophageal pressure, often seen in vomiting. The forceful vomiting increases pressure in the esophagus and causes esophageal rupture. Patients often present with severe retrosternal chest pain, subcutaneous emphysema, and critical illness. 1

Definition: The gold standard for diagnosis of esophageal rupture is contrast esophagography with water-soluble contrast or CT scan with oral contrast to show the site of perforation.

Prevention: Prevention of this condition involves preventing conditions that predispose to severe vomiting, such as alcohol use.

Treatment: The mainstay of treatment is hemodynamic stabilization and early surgical intervention. Patients also receive intravenous antibiotics and remain nil per os with nutritional support until they have recovered.

Differential: The differential diagnosis for a young male patient with severe chest pain is broad and includes myocardial infarction, aortic dissection, and pulmonary embolism. This patient’s history of alcohol use and vomiting increases the suspicion for esophageal rupture.

wrongAnswers.A: Broad-spectrum antibiotic therapy, CT scan of the abdomen, and ECG are not the best answers. These are all indicated in this patient; however, given his hemodynamic instability, the most appropriate next step is volume resuscitation with 0.9% saline therapy.
wrongAnswers.B: Broad-spectrum antibiotic therapy, CT scan of the abdomen, and ECG are not the best answers. These are all indicated in this patient; however, given his hemodynamic instability, the most appropriate next step is volume resuscitation with 0.9% saline therapy.
wrongAnswers.C: Broad-spectrum antibiotic therapy, CT scan of the abdomen, and ECG are not the best answers. These are all indicated in this patient; however, given his hemodynamic instability, the most appropriate next step is volume resuscitation with 0.9% saline therapy.

explanationPanel.rule: Suspected esophageal rupture with shock after forceful vomiting needs immediate hemodynamic resuscitation before diagnostics/antibiotics.
explanationPanel.trap: Trap: CT/esophagram and broad antibiotics are indicated, but hypotension makes IV isotonic saline first.

questions.stem: A 25-year-old woman comes to the office because of a 1-month history of a lump in her neck. The lump has remained unchanged in size during this time. She has not had pain, difficulty swallowing, or difficulty breathing. Medical history is remarkable for generalized anxiety disorder diagnosed 5 years ago. Her only medication is an oral contraceptive. She had been receiving care from a mental health counselor for 3 years but discontinued seeing the counselor 3 months ago because of financial difficulties. Family history is remarkable for papillary thyroid cancer in the patient's mother. The patient is 173 cm (5 ft 8 in) tall and weighs 57 kg (125 lb); BMI is 19 kg/m². Temperature is 37.1°C (98.7°F), pulse is 88/min, respirations are 17/min, and blood pressure is 101/72 mm Hg. Palpation of the neck discloses a firm, 2-cm nodule in the right lobe of the thyroid gland. There is a mild tremor in both hands. Results of laboratory studies show a serum TSH concentration of 3.5 µU/mL and free T concentration of 1.2 ng/dL. Ultrasonography of the thyroid gland shows a 2-cm hypoechoic nodule in the right inferior lobe. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

She has not had pain, difficulty swallowing, or difficulty breathing. Medical history is remarkable for generalized anxiety disorder diagnosed 5 years ago. Her only medication is an oral contraceptive. She had been receiving care from a mental health counselor for 3 years but discontinued seeing the counselor 3 months ago because of financial difficulties. Family history is remarkable for papillary thyroid cancer in the patient's mother. The patient is 173 cm (5 ft 8 in) tall and weighs 57 kg (125 lb); BMI is 19 kg/m². Temperature is 37.1°C (98.7°F), pulse is 88/min, respirations are 17/min, and blood pressure is 101/72 mm Hg. Palpation of the neck discloses a firm, 2-cm nodule in the right lobe of the thyroid gland. There is a mild tremor in both hands. Results of laboratory studies show a serum TSH concentration of 3.5 µU/mL and free T concentration of 1.2 ng/dL. Ultrasonography of the thyroid gland shows a 2-cm hypoechoic nodule in the right inferior lobe. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
choices: Discontinuation of oral contraceptive followed by repeat laboratory studies in 3 months
Prophylactic right lobectomy of the thyroid gland
questions.subject: Endocrinology

explanationPanel.correct: B. Fine-needle aspiration of the nodule
explanationPanel.whyCorrect:
Educational Objective: This patient presents with a lump in her neck and is found to have a 2-cm nodule in the right inferior lobe of her thyroid with normal serum TSH and free thyroxine (FT4) concentrations. The most appropriate next step in management for this patient is a fine-needle aspiration (FNA) of the nodule to ensure it is not malignant.

Evaluation: Thyroid nodules are categorized by hormone production and size. Nonfunctioning thyroid nodules present as asymptomatic, painless masses in the neck. Further classification of size and radiographic features will determine the next steps in management.

Definition: Thyroid nodules that are hypoechoic and greater than 1.5 cm should undergo FNA to rule out malignancy.

Prevention: The cause of thyroid nodules is unclear. Prevention of thyroid malignancy includes close monitoring of thyroid nodules, avoiding radiation exposure to the head and neck, and maintaining a healthy lifestyle.

Treatment: Treatment for this patient will depend on the cytologic findings that result from FNA. Malignant nodules may require surgical intervention.

Differential: The differential for this patient’s nodule is broad. Given the size and hypoechoic radiographic description, there is enough concern for malignancy that FNA is most appropriate to rule out cancer.

wrongAnswers.A: Discontinuation of oral contraceptive followed by repeat laboratory studies in 3 months is incorrect. Oral contraceptive medications do not cause thyroid nodules.
wrongAnswers.C: Prophylactic right lobectomy of the thyroid gland is incorrect. Surgical management may be appropriate depending on the results of FNA; however, it is imperative to biopsy the lesion first to ascertain the diagnosis.
wrongAnswers.D: Radioactive iodine uptake and scan is incorrect. Radioactive iodine uptake and scan is a test that is used in the evaluation of a thyroid nodule when serum TSH is decreased.
wrongAnswers.E: Serum free triiodothyronine (free T3) concentration is incorrect. Monitoring serum free T3 concentrations is indicated when there are abnormal TSH or FT4 concentrations, or if the patient has established thyroid disease and is receiving treatment.

explanationPanel.rule: Normal TSH with hypoechoic thyroid nodule >1.5 cm = fine-needle aspiration.
explanationPanel.trap: Trap: radioactive iodine uptake scan is for low TSH/hyperfunctioning nodules.

layer4.rule: Normal TSH with hypoechoic thyroid nodule >1.5 cm = fine-needle aspiration.
layer4.trap: Trap: radioactive iodine uptake scan is for low TSH/hyperfunctioning nodules.

questions.stem: A 5-minute-old boy is admitted to the neonatal intensive care unit because of absent breath sounds on the left, significant respiratory distress with increased work of breathing, and profound hypoxia that developed 5 minutes after birth. The patient was born at 36 weeks' gestation to a 21-year-old primigravid woman via normal spontaneous vaginal delivery. The pregnancy was uncomplicated despite no prenatal care. The newborn's temperature is 37.2°C (99.0°F), pulse is 170/min, and respirations are 40/min. Pulse oximetry on room air shows an oxygen saturation of 82%. The patient is intubated. Physical examination discloses fair breath sounds on the right and absent breath sounds on the left. Bowel sounds are auscultated in the left hemithorax. The remainder of the physical examination, including abdominal examination, discloses no abnormalities. Chest x-ray is shown. Which of the following anatomic abnormalities is most likely to be found in this patient?
questions.stemHtml: A 5-minute-old boy is admitted to the neonatal intensive care unit because of absent breath sounds on the left, significant respiratory distress with increased work of breathing, and profound hypoxia that developed 5 minutes after birth. The patient was born at 36 weeks' gestation to a 21-year-old primigravid woman via normal spontaneous vaginal delivery. The pregnancy was uncomplicated despite no prenatal care. The newborn's temperature is 37.2°C (99.0°F), pulse is 170/min, and respirations are 40/min. Pulse oximetry on room air shows an oxygen saturation of 82%. The patient is intubated. Physical examination discloses fair breath sounds on the right and absent breath sounds on the left. Bowel sounds are auscultated in the left hemithorax. The remainder of the physical examination, including abdominal examination, discloses no abnormalities. Chest x-ray is shown. Which of the following anatomic abnormalities is most likely to be found in this patient?
questions.subject: Pediatrics/Neonatology

explanationPanel.whyCorrect:
Educational Objective: Congenital diaphragmatic hernia (CDH) is the most likely diagnosis in this newborn with respiratory distress, hypoxia, bowel sounds on auscultation of the chest, and evidence of bowel loops in the thoracic cavity on chest x-ray. Pulmonary hypoplasia is a common consequence of CDH.

Evaluation: CDH typically presents immediately after birth with respiratory distress, absent breath sounds unilaterally (most commonly on the left), and a scaphoid abdomen. Bowel sounds may be heard on auscultation of the chest, as with this patient.

Definition: CDH allows herniation of the abdominal organs into the thorax, which compress the lungs while they are developing in utero. Pulmonary hypoplasia results through a complex mechanism that involves direct compression of the developing lungs, which affects bronchial and vascular architecture with reduced branching, blood supply, and increased thickness of alveolar septa. Newborns with pulmonary hypoplasia commonly develop persistent pulmonary hypertension due to increased pulmonary vascular resistance, resulting in potentially severe heart failure. This collection of respiratory and circulatory difficulties may be life-threatening to the newborn.

Prevention: There is no specific prevention for CDH and its consequent pulmonary hypoplasia.

Treatment: Treatment involves surgical repair of the hernia, although the management of CDH must also consider the multitude of secondary pulmonary and cardiovascular problems that result from the herniation of the abdominal viscera into the developing thorax.

Differential: This patient has evident bowel loops in the left thorax on chest x-ray, confirming the diagnosis of CDH. Pulmonary hypoplasia is a direct result of CDH.

wrongAnswers.A: Bronchogenic cyst is incorrect. A bronchogenic cyst is caused by an abnormal outpouching of the foregut during embryonic development and typically presents in childhood with chronic cough, wheezing, and recurrent infections. Although a bronchogenic cyst may cause respiratory distress in the newborn if large or rapidly expanding, it would not explain the bowel loops in the thoracic cavity on this patient’s chest x-ray.
wrongAnswers.B: Congenital pulmonary airway malformation (CPAM) is incorrect. CPAM refers to a cystic structure that results from the abnormal branching of the lungs during development. CPAM may be asymptomatic or result in severe respiratory distress in the newborn depending on size. While the bowel loops in the thoracic cavity could be mistaken for a cystic mass, a CPAM would not cause bowel sounds to be auscultated in the chest.
wrongAnswers.C: Duodenal atresia is incorrect. Duodenal atresia presents with vomiting and abdominal distension, as well as distension of the stomach and proximal duodenum on abdominal x-ray. This patient does not have any of these signs or symptoms.
wrongAnswers.D: Intestinal malrotation is incorrect. Malrotation is a congenital anomaly in which the midgut incompletely rotates during development, leaving it attached to a thin stalk of mesentery at the base of the superior mesenteric artery instead of the normal broad-based mesenteric stalk. Malrotation increases the risk for volvulus of the small bowel and consequent small bowel obstruction. It is not associated with severe respiratory distress.

explanationPanel.rule: Newborn respiratory distress with bowel sounds/loops in hemithorax = congenital diaphragmatic hernia causing pulmonary hypoplasia.
explanationPanel.trap: Trap: CPAM can look cystic but does not place bowel in the chest or cause bowel sounds there.

layer4.rule: Newborn respiratory distress with bowel sounds/loops in hemithorax = congenital diaphragmatic hernia causing pulmonary hypoplasia.
layer4.trap: Trap: CPAM can look cystic but does not place bowel in the chest or cause bowel sounds there.

questions.stem: An 80-year-old man comes to the office for a routine examination. He says he fell in the grocery store last week but feels well overall. He did not have light-headedness, palpitations, or chest pain before the fall, and he did not hit his head or have loss of consciousness. He has no history of other falls during the past year. He sustained a pulmonary embolism 2 months ago. He has hypertension, stage 2 chronic kidney disease, and osteoarthritis. Medications are amlodipine, lisinopril, dabigatran, and acetaminophen. Temperature is 37.6°C (99.7°F), pulse is 70/min, respirations are 16/min, and blood pressure is 140/80 mm Hg while sitting. Within 2 minutes after standing, pulse is 70/min, and blood pressure is 135/80 mm Hg. He appears well. Examination shows a large ecchymosis on the right upper extremity. Cardiopulmonary examination discloses no abnormalities. He performs a Timed Up and Go test in 30 seconds, indicating he is at increased fall risk. Which of the following is the most appropriate recommendation at this time?
questions.stemHtml: An 80-year-old man comes to the office for a routine examination. He says he fell in the grocery store last week but feels well overall. He did not have light-headedness, palpitations, or chest pain before the fall, and he did not hit his head or have loss of consciousness. He has no history of other falls during the past year. He sustained a pulmonary embolism 2 months ago. He has hypertension, stage 2 chronic kidney disease, and osteoarthritis. Medications are amlodipine, lisinopril, dabigatran, and acetaminophen. Temperature is 37.6°C (99.7°F), pulse is 70/min, respirations are 16/min, and blood pressure is 140/80 mm Hg while sitting. Within 2 minutes after standing, pulse is 70/min, and blood pressure is 135/80 mm Hg. He appears well. Examination shows a large ecchymosis on the right upper extremity. Cardiopulmonary examination discloses no abnormalities. He performs a Timed Up and Go test in 30 seconds, indicating he is at increased fall risk. Which of the following is the most appropriate recommendation at this time?
choices: Participation in a strength and balance exercise program
Use of a walker for ambulation
questions.subject: Preventive Medicine

explanationPanel.correct: D. Participation in a strength and balance exercise program
explanationPanel.whyCorrect:
Educational Objective: This patient is at an increased risk for falls. The most appropriate recommendation for him at this time is participation in a strength and balance exercise program.

Evaluation: The Timed Up and Go test evaluates the time it takes for a patient to rise from the sitting position and ambulate 10 feet. A time of greater than 12 seconds indicates the patient is at an increased risk for falls.

Definition: Falls are a common cause of morbidity and mortality in the older population. Falls may result in fractures, traumatic brain injuries, and death. Prompt identification of those at risk for falling is important so timely intervention may be provided.

Prevention: In the older patient population, it is important to evaluate for secondary causes that may contribute to an increased risk for falls, such as polypharmacy or orthostatic hypotension.

Treatment: Fall risk may be decreased with participation in a strength and balance exercise program. In addition, gait aids such as a walker or cane may be indicated depending on the patient’s gait and frequency of falls.

Differential: This patient is identified to be at increased fall risk on the Timed Up and Go test. The most appropriate recommendation for him is to participate in a strength and balance exercise program.

wrongAnswers.A: Avoiding leaving home unaccompanied is incorrect. This recommendation may be too restrictive for this patient and may promote further deconditioning by limiting the frequency of ambulation. Participation in a strength and balance exercise program is more appropriate.
wrongAnswers.B: Discontinuation of amlodipine is not the most appropriate recommendation at this time. Discontinuation of amlodipine may be appropriate if the patient had been found to have hypotension or orthostatic hypotension, both of which may increase his risk for falling. A strength and balance exercise program is more appropriate.
wrongAnswers.C: Discontinuation of dabigatran is incorrect. This patient is currently being treated for a pulmonary embolism and has only had one recent fall. A risk and benefit conversation may be needed in the future if he continues to have frequent falls, as anticoagulation increases the risk for intracranial bleeding during a head injury.
wrongAnswers.E: Use of a walker for ambulation is not the most appropriate recommendation at this time. A walker may be indicated in the future if this patient continues to have falls. However, the least restrictive assistive device that provides appropriate support for patients is best.

explanationPanel.rule: Older adult with Timed Up and Go >12 seconds = prescribe strength and balance exercise program.
explanationPanel.trap: Trap: do not stop needed anticoagulation for a single fall when treating recent PE.

layer4.rule: Older adult with Timed Up and Go >12 seconds = prescribe strength and balance exercise program.
layer4.trap: Trap: do not stop needed anticoagulation for a single fall when treating recent PE.

questions.stem: A 15-year-old girl is brought to the emergency department 1 hour after she fell onto her outstretched right arm while playing soccer. She experienced immediate pain. She says she did not think the injury was serious and was able to finish the game. She has not had weakness, numbness, or any other symptoms in her right hand and wrist. On arrival, she is in no distress. Her pulse is 60/min, respirations are 12/min, and blood pressure is 110/60 mm Hg. Examination of the right upper extremity shows moderate tenderness over the distal radius. There is no swelling, erythema, or deformity. Capillary refill time in the fingers of the right hand is 2 seconds. An x-ray of the right wrist is shown. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
questions.stemHtml: A 15-year-old girl is brought to the emergency department 1 hour after she fell onto her outstretched right arm while playing soccer. She experienced immediate pain. She says she did not think the injury was serious and was able to finish the game. She has not had weakness, numbness, or any other symptoms in her right hand and wrist. On arrival, she is in no distress. Her pulse is 60/min, respirations are 12/min, and blood pressure is 110/60 mm Hg. Examination of the right upper extremity shows moderate tenderness over the distal radius. There is no swelling, erythema, or deformity. Capillary refill time in the fingers of the right hand is 2 seconds. An x-ray of the right wrist is shown. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
choices: Application of a bandage with a sling
questions.subject: Musculoskeletal/Orthopedics

explanationPanel.whyCorrect:
Educational Objective: Buckle, or torus, fractures may occur in the pediatric population, frequently involving the distal metaphysis of the radius, as in this patient. Treatment of buckle fractures includes cast immobilization.

Evaluation: Falling onto an outstretched hand can lead to traumatic injuries such as distal radius fractures, elbow dislocations, or fractures of the carpal bones of the wrist. Presenting symptoms often include pain and swelling at the site of fracture.

Definition: Fractures to the radius may occur in multiple locations in the pediatric patient. Buckle fractures are more likely to develop in the pediatric population due to the increased elasticity of their bones. Buckle fractures may occur in regions such as the distal radius or ribs. X-rays do not typically show distinct fracture lines and instead show subtle deformity of the cortex.

Prevention: A radius fracture may be prevented by the avoidance of falls or trauma.

Treatment: Buckle fractures are managed with immobilization. Surgery is rarely indicated.

Differential: This patient presents with moderate tenderness over the right radius after a fall onto an outstretched hand, with an x-ray showing cortical irregularities in the distal metaphysis indicating a radius fracture. The most appropriate next step in management for this patient is cast immobilization.

wrongAnswers.A: Reassurance is incorrect. This patient has a distal radius fracture. Cast immobilization is more appropriate.
wrongAnswers.B: Application of a sling only is not the most appropriate next step in management. A sling would not adequately immobilize this patient who has a distal radius fracture. The most appropriate next step is cast immobilization.
wrongAnswers.C: Application of a bandage with a sling is incorrect. A sling with a bandage would not adequately immobilize this patient who has a distal radius fracture. Cast immobilization is the most appropriate next step in management.
wrongAnswers.E: Open reduction is not the most appropriate next step in management. Open reduction may be indicated in cases of displaced radius fractures. Cast immobilization is the most appropriate next step in management for this patient.

explanationPanel.rule: Pediatric FOOSH with distal radius cortical buckling/torus fracture = immobilization with cast/splint.
explanationPanel.trap: Trap: minimal swelling/deformity does not mean reassurance when x-ray shows buckle fracture.

layer4.rule: Pediatric FOOSH with distal radius cortical buckling/torus fracture = immobilization with cast/splint.
layer4.trap: Trap: minimal swelling/deformity does not mean reassurance when x-ray shows buckle fracture.

questions.stem: A 35-year-old woman comes to the clinic because of a 4-month history of progressive fatigue when running or walking long distances. She also has had occasional episodes of mild shortness of breath and light-headedness that resolve with rest. Medical history is remarkable for hypertension and type 2 diabetes mellitus that both resolved 3 years ago after she underwent Roux-en-Y gastric bypass. Since the procedure, she has lost 45 kg (100 lb). Her only medication is a multivitamin with iron, calcium, and vitamin D. She drinks three to four glasses of wine weekly; she does not smoke cigarettes or use other substances. She exercises by walking, running, or doing yoga five times weekly. She is 165 cm (5 ft 5 in) tall and weighs 70 kg (155 lb); BMI is 26 kg/m². Temperature is 36.5°C (97.7°F), pulse is 98/min, respirations are 14/min, and blood pressure is 110/60 mm Hg. Examination shows no abnormalities except for pale conjunctivae. Results of laboratory studies are shown: Hematocrit 24%, hemoglobin 8.0 g/dL, MCV 105 µm³, WBC 4500/mm³, platelet count 155,000/mm³. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

questions.subject: Hematology/Oncology
questions.topic: Vitamin B12 deficiency after gastric bypass

explanationPanel.whyCorrect:
Educational Objective: The most appropriate next step in management of this patient’s condition is intramuscular vitamin B12 (cyanocobalamin) therapy. Vitamin B12 deficiency presents with megaloblastic anemia, fatigue, pallor, and light-headedness; neurologic manifestations such as subacute combined degeneration may also be present. Deficiency can occur in patients who follow a vegetarian or vegan diet, as well as in patients with pernicious anemia, malabsorption, or gastrointestinal infections.

Evaluation: Megaloblastic anemia occurs in the setting of impaired DNA synthesis, often related to folate or vitamin B12 deficiency. Megaloblastic anemia is characterized by anemia with erythrocyte macrocytosis (as seen in this patient with increased mean corpuscular volume) and hypersegmented neutrophils, with associated generalized symptoms of fatigue, pallor, and light-headedness.

Definition: Vitamin B12 deficiency may be distinguished from vitamin B9 (folate) deficiency by the presence of neuropsychiatric symptoms, specifically subacute combined degeneration, which presents with ataxic gait, muscle weakness, paresthesia, abnormal deep tendon reflexes, and loss of proprioception and vibration sense. However, vitamin B12 also acts as a cofactor for the conversion of methylmalonyl CoA to succinyl CoA, and its deficiency is associated with increased methylmalonic acid concentrations, which can help to distinguish between these two deficiencies.

Prevention: Vitamin B12 deficiency may occur in patients who follow a vegetarian or vegan diet, as well as in patients with pernicious anemia (intrinsic factor deficiency), malabsorption, or gastrointestinal infections. Vitamin B9 deficiency is often seen in patients with malnutrition, alcohol use disorder, and patients taking antifolate medications (eg, phenytoin, methotrexate). Patients with these risk factors should take supplements and be monitored for these deficiencies.

Treatment: Treatment is accomplished with supplementation of the deficient vitamin.

Differential: Resection of the gastric fundus in Roux-en-Y gastric bypass decreases secretion of intrinsic factor, limiting absorption of vitamin B12. While folate deficiency can also occur in this population, vitamin B12 deficiency is more common post gastric bypass.

wrongAnswers.B: Intravenous iron therapy is incorrect. While bariatric surgery patients are at risk for iron deficiency, iron deficiency anemia is associated with microcytosis (decreased mean corpuscular volume). This patient’s macrocytic anemia is more consistent with vitamin B12 deficiency.
wrongAnswers.C: Oral folic acid therapy is incorrect. In bariatric surgery patients who develop small bowel bacterial overgrowth, an excess of folate can be found. Vitamin B12 deficiency is more likely after bariatric surgery.
wrongAnswers.D: Transfusion of packed red blood cells is incorrect. The underlying cause of the patient’s anemia should be diagnosed and treated. Temporary symptomatic treatment with blood transfusion can be indicated in patients with a hemoglobin concentration of less than 7.0 g/dL.

explanationPanel.rule: Macrocytic anemia after Roux-en-Y gastric bypass = vitamin B12 deficiency from reduced intrinsic factor; treat with IM cyanocobalamin.
explanationPanel.trap: Trap: iron deficiency after bariatric surgery is microcytic, not macrocytic.

layer4.rule: Macrocytic anemia after Roux-en-Y gastric bypass = vitamin B12 deficiency from reduced intrinsic factor; treat with IM cyanocobalamin.
layer4.trap: Trap: iron deficiency after bariatric surgery is microcytic, not macrocytic.
