questions.subject: Infectious Disease

explanationPanel.whyCorrect:
Educational Objective: Infection with Neisseria gonorrhoeae is the most likely cause of this patient’s condition. N. gonorrhoeae is a cause of septic arthritis that may present with purulent arthritis of one or more joints. Synovial fluid analysis in cases of gonococcal arthritis often shows a leukocyte count between 20,000 and 50,000/mm³.

Evaluation: Septic arthritis caused by gonococcal infection may present with fever and malaise with polyarthritis or oligoarthritis. However, patients may also present solely with purulent arthritis of one or more joints (eg, knees, elbows, ankles). Physical examination often shows a swollen, erythematous joint with decreased range of motion. Arthrocentesis with synovial fluid analysis as well as collection of blood cultures should be performed prior to administration of antibiotics.

Definition: N. gonorrhoeae is a sexually transmitted gram-negative diplococcus that can cause pharyngitis, urethritis, epididymitis, vaginitis, cervicitis, pelvic inflammatory disease, and septic arthritis.

Prevention: Infection with N. gonorrhoeae may be prevented with barrier contraception, as it is a sexually transmitted infection.

Treatment: Treatment of gonococcal arthritis requires antibiotics. Ceftriaxone is the antibiotic of choice.

Differential: This sexually active patient who does not consistently use condoms presents with symptoms of septic arthritis, with synovial fluid analysis showing a leukocyte count of 20,000/mm³. Infection with N. gonorrhoeae is the most likely cause of her condition.

wrongAnswers.A: Borrelia burgdorferi is not the most likely cause of this patient’s condition. B. burgdorferi is the organism responsible for Lyme disease. Lyme disease is only endemic to certain parts of the United States and is transmitted by bites from the deer tick Ixodes scapularis. Patients usually present with a characteristic rash known as erythema migrans.
wrongAnswers.C: Staphylococcus aureus is incorrect. Synovial fluid analysis in cases of septic arthritis caused by S. aureus characteristically shows purulent fluid with a leukocyte count of greater than 50,000/mm³ as well as gram-positive cocci. S. aureus is the most common cause of septic arthritis in adults; however, this patient’s history and synovial fluid leukocyte count make infection with N. gonorrhoeae more likely.
wrongAnswers.D: Streptococcus pneumoniae is not the most likely cause of this patient’s condition. S. pneumoniae is a gram-positive diplococcus that causes a wide array of infections, including pneumonia, meningitis, otitis media, and skin and soft tissue infections. Infection with N. gonorrhoeae is the most likely cause of this patient’s condition.

explanationPanel.rule: Sexually active young adult with acute purulent monoarthritis and synovial WBC often 20,000-50,000 = disseminated gonococcal arthritis.
explanationPanel.trap: Trap: Staph aureus is most common overall, but usually has more purulent fluid with WBC >50,000 and different risk profile.

layer4.rule: Sexually active young adult with acute purulent monoarthritis and synovial WBC often 20,000-50,000 = disseminated gonococcal arthritis.
layer4.trap: Trap: Staph aureus is most common overall, but usually has more purulent fluid with WBC >50,000 and different risk profile.

questions.stem: A 62-year-old woman comes to the office because of a 5-month history of persistent painful marks on the right side of her abdomen. She also says her appetite has been decreased since her last office visit 2 years ago. At that visit, the patient was evaluated for painful forehead lesions and was diagnosed with herpes zoster. Acyclovir therapy was prescribed, but the patient was lost to follow-up. Today, she says she took "most" of the acyclovir and that her forehead lesions resolved. Prior to that visit, she had not been evaluated by a physician for more than 15 years. Medical history also is remarkable for cocaine use for 5 years when she was in her 30s. She takes no routine medications. Vaccinations are not up-to-date. She does not smoke cigarettes, drink alcoholic beverages, or use any other substances. She has had multiple sexual partners since her last visit; she uses condoms inconsistently. She is unemployed and has not traveled outside of the United States recently. She is 165 cm (5 ft 5 in) tall and weighs 86 kg (190 lb); BMI is 32 kg/m². Temperature is 37.1°C (98.7°F), pulse is 89/min, respirations are 18/min, and blood pressure is 130/80 mm Hg. Examination of the skin discloses the findings shown in the photograph. The rash is extremely tender to light touch. The remainder of the physical examination discloses no abnormalities. Which of the following is most likely to have prevented this patient's condition?

Which of the following is most likely to have prevented this patient's condition?
questions.subject: Neurology

explanationPanel.whyCorrect:
Educational Objective: Postherpetic neuralgia may develop after an episode of herpes zoster, which presents as a unilateral vesicular eruption in a dermatomal distribution. Herpes zoster vaccination decreases the risk for developing herpes zoster and subsequent postherpetic neuralgia, and is most likely to have prevented this patient's condition.

Evaluation: Herpes zoster presents as a unilateral vesicular eruption in a dermatomal pattern and may result in subsequent postherpetic neuralgia. Postherpetic neuralgia often presents with neuropathic pain that is worsened by mechanical or thermal stimuli.

Definition: Acute herpes zoster develops from reactivation of latent varicella zoster virus, which can lie dormant in the dorsal root ganglia after a primary varicella zoster virus infection. The pathogenesis of subsequent postherpetic neuralgia is uncertain but may result from postinflammatory nerve degeneration. Risk factors for developing postherpetic neuralgia include older age, female sex, and an immunocompromised state.

Prevention: The risk for developing herpes zoster and postherpetic neuralgia may be decreased with herpes zoster vaccination.

Treatment: Treatment includes neuropathic pain medication such as tricyclic antidepressants and gabapentinoids. Refractory pain may be treated with interventions such as epidurals, nerve blocks, or neuromodulation.

Differential: The patient in this case with a history of herpes zoster is presenting with a 5- month history of painful marks on her abdomen in a dermatomal distribution. The most likely cause of her pain is postherpetic neuralgia. Herpes zoster vaccination would have most likely prevented this patient’s condition.

wrongAnswers.A: Adherence to acyclovir therapy is incorrect. Treatment with acyclovir has not been found to decrease the incidence of postherpetic neuralgia. Herpes zoster vaccination is associated with a decreased risk for herpes zoster and postherpetic neuralgia.
wrongAnswers.B: Amitriptyline therapy is not likely to have prevented this patient’s condition. Amitriptyline is a treatment option to decrease pain in cases of postherpetic neuralgia, but it is not a preventive measure.
wrongAnswers.D: Use of condoms is incorrect. Herpes zoster may develop after a primary varicella zoster virus infection. Herpes zoster is not considered a sexually transmitted infection.

explanationPanel.rule: Herpes zoster vaccination reduces risk of zoster and subsequent postherpetic neuralgia.
explanationPanel.trap: Trap: acyclovir treats acute zoster but does not reliably prevent postherpetic neuralgia.

layer4.rule: Herpes zoster vaccination reduces risk of zoster and subsequent postherpetic neuralgia.
layer4.trap: Trap: acyclovir treats acute zoster but does not reliably prevent postherpetic neuralgia.

questions.stem: A previously healthy 27-year-old woman comes to the physician because of a 2-week history of intermittent, severe headaches. She has not had dizziness, vertigo, light sensitivity, nausea, or vomiting. She takes no medications. Her temperature is 37°C (98.6°F), pulse is 70/min, respirations are 18/min, and blood pressure is 190/100 mm Hg. Examination shows no jugular venous distention. No murmurs or gallops are heard on cardiac examination. A bruit is heard in the epigastrium. Serum studies show: Na⁺ 147 mEq/L, K⁺ 3.0 mEq/L, Cl⁻ 110 mEq/L, HCO₃− 28 mEq/L, creatinine 1.1 mg/dL. A CT scan of the head shows no abnormalities. An increase in which of the following is the most likely cause of this patient's increased blood pressure?

questions.subject: Nephrology/Urology

explanationPanel.whyCorrect:
Educational Objective: This young patient, presenting with headaches, hypertension, hypernatremia, hypokalemia, and metabolic alkalosis, most likely has increased plasma renin as a result of renovascular hypertension, a secondary cause of severe increases in blood pressure. This patient’s abdominal bruit suggests fibromuscular dysplasia, which decreases blood flow to the kidneys, resulting in stimulated renin production.

Evaluation: Fibromuscular dysplasia, a thickening of the tunica media of the artery, results in renovascular hypertension when present in the renal arteries, causing stenosis. The condition should be suspected if hypertension is accompanied by hypernatremia, hypokalemia, and metabolic alkalosis. Fibromuscular dysplasia causing renal artery stenosis is diagnosed by renal arteriography, generally CT scan or MR angiography, in addition to renal Doppler ultrasonography. Definition: Renal artery stenosis is a cause of secondary hypertension related to activation of the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system. Low afferent blood flow to the affected kidney leads to abnormal stimulation of the juxtaglomerular apparatus and excessive production of renin. Renin converts angiotensinogen to angiotensin I, which is then converted to angiotensin II by angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) in the pulmonary vasculature. Angiotensin II is a potent vasoconstrictor that directly mediates systemic hypertension. Angiotensin II also leads to increased Na⁺ reabsorption in the renal tubules, aldosterone release by the adrenal cortex with subsequent increased Na⁺ and fluid retention and hypokalemia, vasopressin release from the posterior pituitary leading to increased fluid retention, enhanced adrenergic function through inhibition of norepinephrine reuptake in sympathetic nerve endings, and stimulation of hypothalamic thirst centers. In younger patients, fibromuscular dysplasia is the most common cause of renal artery stenosis, while in older patients it is typically due to atherosclerosis. An abdominal bruit may be disclosed in the region of the stenosis.

Prevention: There is no known method of preventing fibromuscular dysplasia. Renal artery stenosis caused by atherosclerotic disease can be prevented by managing hypertension, diabetes mellitus, hyperlipidemia, and smoking cessation, in other words, limiting atherosclerotic disease risk factors.

Treatment: Treatment involves angioplasty or stenting of the stenosed renal artery to improve flow. ACE inhibitors can be considered for unilateral stenosis but can lead to acute kidney injury in the setting of bilateral renal artery stenosis.

Differential: The constellation of hypernatremia, hypokalemia, metabolic alkalosis, headaches, and markedly increased blood pressure in a young, otherwise healthy patient suggests renal artery stenosis as a cause, likely from fibromuscular dysplasia. While there may be associated increases in many neuroendocrine mediators in fibromuscular dysplasia, increased plasma renin is the underlying derangement of significance.

wrongAnswers.A: Plasma catecholamines is incorrect. While activation of the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system enhances responsiveness to catecholamines, the increased renin is the underlying problem. Additionally, sympathetic nervous system mediators should be inhibited by negative feedback in cases of severe secondary hypertension. Catecholamine increases causing hypertension would be the underlying cause in pheochromocytoma, not fibromuscular dysplasia with renal artery stenosis.
wrongAnswers.B: Plasma cortisol is incorrect. Plasma cortisol concentrations may be increased in Cushing disease as a cause of secondary hypertension. Cushing disease presents with fat redistribution and weight gain, striae, abnormal hair growth, and irregular menses, among other features, all of which this patient lacks.
wrongAnswers.D: Serum angiotensin I and serum angiotensinogen are not the best choices. While angiotensin and its precursors may be increased in renal artery stenosis, the driving hormonal signal behind these increases is increased plasma renin.
wrongAnswers.E: Serum angiotensin I and serum angiotensinogen are not the best choices. While angiotensin and its precursors may be increased in renal artery stenosis, the driving hormonal signal behind these increases is increased plasma renin.

explanationPanel.rule: Young woman with severe hypertension, abdominal bruit, hypokalemic metabolic alkalosis = renal artery stenosis with increased plasma renin.
explanationPanel.trap: Trap: angiotensin levels rise downstream, but renin is the primary driving hormone from renal hypoperfusion.

layer4.rule: Young woman with severe hypertension, abdominal bruit, hypokalemic metabolic alkalosis = renal artery stenosis with increased plasma renin.
layer4.trap: Trap: angiotensin levels rise downstream, but renin is the primary driving hormone from renal hypoperfusion.

questions.stem: A 30-year-old primigravid woman at 8 weeks' gestation comes to the office because of a 3-week history of excessive sweating, difficulty sleeping, and unintentional 2-kg (4-lb) weight loss. She receives routine prenatal care. She has no history of serious illness, and her only medication is a prenatal vitamin; she does not use any other substances. Temperature is 37.0°C (98.6°F), pulse is 85/min, respirations are 18/min, and blood pressure is 128/74 mm Hg. Physical examination shows a blank stare and lid lag. Neurologic examination shows brisk deep tendon reflexes in the upper and lower extremities and proximal weakness. There is a fine resting tremor in both hands. Laboratory studies show a TSH concentration of less than 0.05 µU/mL and a free thyroxine (FT4) concentration of 6.0 ng/dL. It is most appropriate for the patient to begin taking which of the following medications at this time?

She receives routine prenatal care. She has no history of serious illness, and her only medication is a prenatal vitamin; she does not use any other substances. Temperature is 37.0°C (98.6°F), pulse is 85/min, respirations are 18/min, and blood pressure is 128/74 mm Hg. Physical examination shows a blank stare and lid lag. Neurologic examination shows brisk deep tendon reflexes in the upper and lower extremities and proximal weakness. There is a fine resting tremor in both hands. Laboratory studies show a TSH concentration of less than 0.05 µU/mL and a free thyroxine (FT4) concentration of 6.0 ng/dL. It is most appropriate for the patient to begin taking which of the following medications at this time?
questions.subject: Endocrinology

explanationPanel.whyCorrect: Correct Answer: C. Educational Objective: This patient has signs and symptoms of hyperthyroidism, such as heat intolerance, insomnia, weight loss, lid lag, brisk deep tendon reflexes, and a resting tremor. This is further confirmed by her decreased TSH concentration and increased free thyroxine (FT4) concentration. The most appropriate treatment of symptomatic hyperthyroidism during the first trimester of pregnancy is propylthiouracil. Key Concept: Thionamides, such as methimazole, are the first-line antithyroid treatment in pregnant and nonpregnant patients. While methimazole is generally preferred, propylthiouracil should be used in the first trimester of pregnancy given an association between methimazole and fetal aplasia cutis. Explanation: Hyperthyroidism in pregnancy is often caused by human chorionic gonadotropin-mediated hyperthyroidism or Graves disease. Though some patients may present with subtle symptoms, overt hyperthyroidism typically presents with anxiety, emotional lability, heat intolerance, weight loss, tachycardia, palpitations, diaphoresis, diarrhea, and tremor. β-Adrenergic blocker therapy may be used for symptomatic treatment, but antithyroid medications should be initiated in pregnant and nonpregnant patients to obtain euthyroidism. Differential: While all of these medications are options for treating hyperthyroidism, radioactive iodine is not safe in pregnancy. Methimazole can be teratogenic when used in the first trimester. β-Adrenergic blockers, such as propranolol, may treat symptoms associated with hyperthyroidism but do not help a patient reach a euthyroid state.

wrongAnswers.A: Methimazole is incorrect. Methimazole is an appropriate choice in some pregnant patients for the treatment of hyperthyroidism. However, this patient is in the first trimester at 8 weeks’ gestation. Because of potential fetal aplasia cutis associated with methimazole use during the first trimester, propylthiouracil is the preferred treatment.
wrongAnswers.B: Propranolol is incorrect. Propranolol can be used to treat the tachycardia and tremor associated with hyperthyroidism. While it may be used to treat this patient’s symptoms, propranolol does not return her to a euthyroid state, so the more appropriate next step in management is an antithyroid medication.
wrongAnswers.D: Radioactive iodine is incorrect. Radioactive iodine is contraindicated in pregnancy. While it would cure this patient’s hyperthyroidism, it would result in loss of thyroid function for the fetus and lifelong hypothyroidism.

explanationPanel.rule: First-trimester symptomatic hyperthyroidism in pregnancy is treated with propylthiouracil to achieve euthyroidism.
explanationPanel.trap: Methimazole is generally preferred outside the first trimester but is avoided early because of fetal aplasia cutis/embryopathy; propranolol only treats symptoms.

layer4.rule: First-trimester symptomatic hyperthyroidism in pregnancy is treated with propylthiouracil to achieve euthyroidism.
layer4.trap: Methimazole is generally preferred outside the first trimester but is avoided early because of fetal aplasia cutis/embryopathy; propranolol only treats symptoms.

questions.stem: A 35-year-old woman comes to the emergency department because she has not had a menstrual period for 3 months. Results of two home pregnancy tests during this time have been negative. She has bipolar disorder accompanied by anxiety and was prescribed a new medication by her psychiatrist for her bipolar disorder 5 months ago. She is unable to recall the name of the new medication. Vital signs are within normal limits. Physical examination shows no abnormalities. She appears agitated but is cooperative and cordial. Laboratory studies show a serum prolactin concentration of 70 ng/mL (N<25). This patient was most likely prescribed which of the following drugs?
questions.stemHtml: A 35-year-old woman comes to the emergency department because she has not had a menstrual period for 3 months. Results of two home pregnancy tests during this time have been negative. She has bipolar disorder accompanied by anxiety and was prescribed a new medication by her psychiatrist for her bipolar disorder 5 months ago. She is unable to recall the name of the new medication. Vital signs are within normal limits. Physical examination shows no abnormalities. She appears agitated but is cooperative and cordial. Laboratory studies show a serum prolactin concentration of 70 ng/mL (N<25). This patient was most likely prescribed which of the following drugs?
questions.subject: Psychiatry

explanationPanel.whyCorrect: Correct Answer: E. Educational Objective: This patient presents with amenorrhea and an increased prolactin concentration most consistent with hyperprolactinemia from risperidone use. Evaluation: Hyperprolactinemia from risperidone use is a side effect that arises due to risperidone’s antagonizing effects on dopamine receptors in the anterior pituitary gland. This inhibits dopamine’s ability to inhibit prolactin secretion, resulting in increased prolactin concentrations, which can present with galactorrhea, amenorrhea, and gynecomastia. Definition: The measurement of serum prolactin concentrations with a compelling clinical history is the standard for diagnosis. Prevention: Prevention includes using the lowest effective dose of risperidone and routine monitoring of prolactin concentrations. Treatment: Treatment includes decreasing the risperidone dose or switching to a different class of antipsychotic medication. Differential: The differential includes prolactin-secreting tumors such as pituitary adenoma. However, this patient is experiencing new symptoms soon after beginning a new medication, making it more likely that this is an adverse effect of the newly prescribed antipsychotic. It would be appropriate to further evaluate this patient to rule out alternative causes of her hyperprolactinemia.

wrongAnswers.A: Carbamazepine, lamotrigine, and valproic acid are incorrect. These medications function by inhibiting voltage-gated sodium channels and do not affect prolactin concentrations.
wrongAnswers.B: Carbamazepine, lamotrigine, and valproic acid are incorrect. These medications function by inhibiting voltage-gated sodium channels and do not affect prolactin concentrations.
wrongAnswers.C: Lithium carbonate is incorrect. Lithium carbonate is a mood stabilizer that does not increase prolactin concentrations.
wrongAnswers.D: Olanzapine is incorrect. Olanzapine is an antipsychotic that can cause increased prolactin concentrations through its effects on dopamine D2 receptor antagonism. However, it has a lower receptor binding capacity compared to risperidone, which has potent antagonism of the dopamine receptors. Therefore, risperidone is associated with a higher incidence of hyperprolactinemia and is the most likely prescribed drug.
wrongAnswers.F: Carbamazepine, lamotrigine, and valproic acid are incorrect. These medications function by inhibiting voltage-gated sodium channels and do not affect prolactin concentrations.

explanationPanel.rule: Risperidone is the antipsychotic most associated with hyperprolactinemia from dopamine D2 blockade in the tuberoinfundibular pathway.
explanationPanel.trap: Mood stabilizers do not raise prolactin, and olanzapine can do so but has lower D2-related prolactin effect than risperidone.

layer4.rule: Risperidone is the antipsychotic most associated with hyperprolactinemia from dopamine D2 blockade in the tuberoinfundibular pathway.
layer4.trap: Mood stabilizers do not raise prolactin, and olanzapine can do so but has lower D2-related prolactin effect than risperidone.

questions.stem: A 20-year-old man is brought to the emergency department immediately after being ejected from a motor vehicle during a high-speed collision. He was awake and responsive to questions at the scene. He became obtunded en route to the hospital and was intubated. On arrival, he responds only to painful stimuli. Temperature is 37.0°C (98.6°F), pulse is 100/min, respirations are 30/min and shallow, and palpable systolic blood pressure is 80 mm Hg. Pupils are equal in size. Examination shows an abrasion on the right side of the chest. There are no other external signs of trauma. Breath sounds are absent on the right. Intravenous fluid therapy is begun. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
questions.stemHtml: A 20-year-old man is brought to the emergency department immediately after being ejected from a motor vehicle during a high-speed collision. He was awake and responsive to questions at the scene. He became obtunded en route to the hospital and was intubated. On arrival, he responds only to painful stimuli. Temperature is 37.0°C (98.6°F), pulse is 100/min, respirations are 30/min and shallow, and palpable systolic blood pressure is 80 mm Hg. Pupils are equal in size. Examination shows an abrasion on the right side of the chest. There are no other external signs of trauma. Breath sounds are absent on the right. Intravenous fluid therapy is begun. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
choices: Focused assessment with sonography for trauma (FAST)
Placement of a chest tube on the right
X-rays of the chest and pelvis
questions.subject: Emergency/Critical Care

explanationPanel.correct: C. Placement of a chest tube on the right
explanationPanel.whyCorrect: Correct Answer: C. Educational Objective: The most appropriate next step in management of this patient is placement of an emergent chest tube on the right because of concern for tension pneumothorax. Placement of a chest tube allows evacuation of air from the pleural space, which allows expansion of the lung and an improvement in blood return to the heart. Evaluation: Tension pneumothorax commonly presents with dyspnea, hypoxia, tachycardia, hypotension, jugular venous distension, tracheal deviation, and unilaterally absent breath sounds. Tension pneumothorax can rapidly lead to cardiac arrest and death if not identified. Definition: A pneumothorax results from air entering the intrapleural space from either an external (eg, stab wound) or internal (eg, bronchopleural fistula) source. As the air accumulates within the space, the lung parenchyma becomes compressed, resulting in reduced breath sounds and respiratory distress. In tension pneumothorax, the collected air causes mediastinal structures to be stretched or compressed, compromising venous return and resulting in obstructive shock. Pneumothorax will appear on chest x-ray as radiolucent air and the absence of interstitial lung marking in the pleural space adjacent to the lung parenchyma. However, tension pneumothorax is often a clinical diagnosis made without imaging, as a delay in treatment may lead to patient death. Prevention: There is no specific prevention of tension pneumothorax in trauma patients. Treatment: Treatment includes rapid evacuation of the pneumothorax with needle decompression or placement of a chest tube. Differential: Priority should always be given to treating life-threatening injuries, in this case a tension pneumothorax, as quickly as possible. A CT angiography of the chest is not the diagnostic test of choice and would further delay treatment of this patient’s pneumothorax.

wrongAnswers.A: CT angiography of the chest is incorrect. A CT angiography of the chest could be used to identify a pulmonary embolism, which would present with tachycardia, respiratory distress, and if large, hypotension. However, this is less likely than pneumothorax in the setting of an acute trauma and would not explain this patient’s absent unilateral breath sounds.
wrongAnswers.B: Focused assessment with sonography for trauma (FAST) is incorrect. A FAST is an important step in the evaluation of a hemodynamically unstable trauma patient, as it allows for the diagnosis of intra-abdominal hemorrhage and pericardial effusion or tamponade. This patient’s pneumothorax, which is acutely life-threatening, should first be evacuated prior to completing the FAST, in line with the standard Airway-Breathing- Circulation protocol.
wrongAnswers.D: Placement of a nasogastric tube is incorrect. While a nasogastric or orogastric tube is inserted after intubation in trauma patients, it is low in priority in the acute resuscitation of these patients. This patient needs an emergent placement of a chest tube before his tension pneumothorax leads to cardiovascular collapse.
wrongAnswers.E: X-rays of the chest and pelvis is incorrect. While these imaging studies are likely to be obtained in the evaluation of a trauma patient to assess for such injuries as hemothorax, nontension pneumothorax, and pelvic fracture, this patient has signs and symptoms of a tension pneumothorax, which warrants emergent evacuation without relying on chest imaging to confirm the diagnosis.

explanationPanel.rule: Unstable trauma patient with unilateral absent breath sounds = presumed tension pneumothorax; decompress/place chest tube before diagnostic imaging.
explanationPanel.trap: FAST, CT, or x-ray may be part of trauma evaluation but delays treatment of an immediate airway/breathing threat.

layer4.rule: Unstable trauma patient with unilateral absent breath sounds = presumed tension pneumothorax; decompress/place chest tube before diagnostic imaging.
layer4.trap: FAST, CT, or x-ray may be part of trauma evaluation but delays treatment of an immediate airway/breathing threat.

questions.stem: A 55-year-old man comes to the emergency department 1 hour after the sudden onset of severe left abdominal and flank pain; he also has had blood in his urine during this period. He has not had fever, chills, or difficulty with urination. His family history is unknown because he was adopted. He appears to be in pain. Temperature is 37.2°C (99.0°F), pulse is 110/min, and blood pressure is 140/100 mm Hg. Pulmonary and cardiac examinations disclose no abnormalities. Abdominal examination discloses a palpable, tender mass in the left upper quadrant and a mass in the right upper quadrant. Serum studies show a creatinine concentration of 2.4 mg/dL. CT scans of the abdomen are shown. This patient is at greatest risk for which of the following?
questions.stemHtml: A 55-year-old man comes to the emergency department 1 hour after the sudden onset of severe left abdominal and flank pain; he also has had blood in his urine during this period. He has not had fever, chills, or difficulty with urination. His family history is unknown because he was adopted. He appears to be in pain. Temperature is 37.2°C (99.0°F), pulse is 110/min, and blood pressure is 140/100 mm Hg. Pulmonary and cardiac examinations disclose no abnormalities. Abdominal examination discloses a palpable, tender mass in the left upper quadrant and a mass in the right upper quadrant. Serum studies show a creatinine concentration of 2.4 mg/dL. CT scans of the abdomen are shown. This patient is at greatest risk for which of the following?
questions.subject: Nephrology/Urology

explanationPanel.whyCorrect: Correct Answer: E. Educational Objective: This patient likely has polycystic kidney disease (PKD) and is at greatest risk for subarachnoid hemorrhage. PKD is caused by genetic mutations in polycystin (PKD1 or PKD2) that result in the development of multiple cysts in the kidney because of structural abnormalities of the renal tubules. The disease is associated with aneurysmal vascular disease such as berry aneurysms, mitral valve prolapse, and hepatic cysts. Evaluation: PKD may present with flank pain, hematuria, hypertension, and progressive chronic kidney disease. Definition: Autosomal dominant PKD is caused by genetic mutations in polycystin (PKD1 or PKD2) that result in the development of multiple cysts in the kidney because of structural abnormalities of the renal tubules. These large cysts generally form in adulthood in the autosomal dominant variant, and eventually compress adjacent normal renal parenchyma. Prevention: There is no known way to prevent PKD as it is caused by a genetic mutation. Treatment: Management includes treatment of hypertension and dietary sodium restriction. Kidney transplantation and dialysis may be required in end-stage renal disease. Differential: The patient in this case is presenting with flank pain, increased creatinine concentration, and multiple large kidney cysts on CT scan of the abdomen, which is consistent with PKD. Patients with PKD have been found to have an increased prevalence of cerebral aneurysms, increasing their risk for subarachnoid hemorrhage.

wrongAnswers.A: Adrenal insufficiency is incorrect. Adrenal insufficiency may occur from insufficient production of or responsiveness to adrenal hormones. Intracerebral aneurysm and subsequent subarachnoid hemorrhage is a greater risk in patients with PKD.
wrongAnswers.B: Gastrointestinal bleeding is not the greatest risk for this patient. Patients with PKD have been found to have an increased risk for developing colonic diverticula. The patient in this case is at the greatest risk for developing a subarachnoid hemorrhage.
wrongAnswers.C: Liver cancer is incorrect. Patients with PKD are at an increased risk for developing liver cysts and possibly liver cancer. The prevalence of intracerebral aneurysms is about four times higher in patients with PKD compared to the general population.
wrongAnswers.D: Pheochromocytoma is incorrect. Pheochromocytoma is a rare catecholamine-secreting tumor that typically presents with episodic headaches, diaphoresis, tachycardia, and hypertension. Patients with von Hippel-Lindau disease, neurofibromatosis 1, and multiple endocrine neoplasia type 2 are at increased risk for developing pheochromocytoma. This patient is at greatest risk for subarachnoid hemorrhage.

explanationPanel.rule: Autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease increases risk for berry aneurysms and subarachnoid hemorrhage.
explanationPanel.trap: Pheochromocytoma points to MEN2/VHL/NF1, not ADPKD; hepatic cysts are common but the tested life-threatening risk is SAH.

layer4.rule: Autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease increases risk for berry aneurysms and subarachnoid hemorrhage.
layer4.trap: Pheochromocytoma points to MEN2/VHL/NF1, not ADPKD; hepatic cysts are common but the tested life-threatening risk is SAH.

questions.stem: A 47-year-old woman comes to the physician because of a 3-month history of shortness of breath on exertion and swelling of her ankles. She has a 22-year history of hypertension and a 2-year history of iron deficiency anemia due to menorrhagia. Current medications are hydrochlorothiazide, atenolol, lisinopril, and ferrous sulfate. Her temperature is 36.9°C (98.4°F), pulse is 88/min, respirations are 16/min, and blood pressure is 148/88 mm Hg. Jugular venous pressure is 10 cm H2O. Crackles are heard at both lung bases. There is pitting edema of the lower extremities to the knees. Her hemoglobin concentration is 10.2 g/dL, and serum creatinine concentration is 1.2 mg/dL. Echocardiography shows a thickened left ventricular wall and a decrease in early diastolic mitral flow velocity. Which of the following is the most likely cause of this patient's edema?

She has a 22-year history of hypertension and a 2-year history of iron deficiency anemia due to menorrhagia. Current medications are hydrochlorothiazide, atenolol, lisinopril, and ferrous sulfate. Her temperature is 36.9°C (98.4°F), pulse is 88/min, respirations are 16/min, and blood pressure is 148/88 mm Hg. Jugular venous pressure is 10 cm H2O. Crackles are heard at both lung bases. There is pitting edema of the lower extremities to the knees. Her hemoglobin concentration is 10.2 g/dL, and serum creatinine concentration is 1.2 mg/dL. Echocardiography shows a thickened left ventricular wall and a decrease in early diastolic mitral flow velocity. Which of the following is the most likely cause of this patient's edema?
questions.subject: Cardiology

explanationPanel.whyCorrect: Correct Answer: D. Educational Objective: Peripheral edema is a sign of right-sided heart failure, marked by increased pressure within the pulmonary circuit. Increased capillary hydrostatic (hydraulic) pressure results in transudation of fluid out of capillaries, manifesting as edema in this patient’s case. Key Concept: Right-sided heart failure describes aberrancy in circulatory function of the right side of the heart. This may be due to impaired systolic contraction or valvulopathy leading to impaired forward blood flow, or due to increased pressure within the blood pumped by the heart, among other causes. Explanation: This patient with chronic hypertension, progressive dyspnea, edema, increased jugular venous pressure, crackles on lung examination, and echocardiography showing left ventricular hypertrophy and decreased diastolic mitral flow velocity has a presentation consistent with heart failure. Left ventricular hypertrophy and decreased mitral flow velocity are consistent with diastolic dysfunction from thickened myocardium with impaired relaxation. In turn, increased pressure within the blood flowing to the left side of the heart is reflected in pulmonary capillary beds, leading to pulmonary edema. The right side of the heart in turn pumps at higher pressure to overcome pulmonary capillary resistance, leading to increased hydrostatic pressure translation to the venous and capillary peripheral beds. In patients with longstanding uncontrolled hypertension, the cardiac myocytes undergo hypertrophy in response to the chronic increase in afterload. This ventricular hypertrophy and increased muscle mass lead to increased stiffness and decreased compliance of the left ventricle, making it more difficult to fill. Patients with decompensated heart failure can present with multiple symptoms. In left-sided heart failure, patients may present with dyspnea and orthopnea and often have crackles on lung auscultation due to pulmonary edema from increased left-sided heart pressure. In right-sided heart failure, patients may present with peripheral edema, jugular venous distension, and hepatic congestion, all due to increased hydrostatic pressure. Differential: The pathophysiology of edema in heart failure is increased hydrostatic pressure, leading to transudation of fluid across the capillary walls. Capillary permeability changes in infectious and inflammatory states, among others, and oncotic pressure changes in response to changes in concentrations of osmotically active substances like albumin.

wrongAnswers.A: Decreased capillary hydraulic pressure is incorrect. In heart failure, due to increased pressures of blood flowing through the heart, capillary bed pressure increases as well. This increased pressure results in transudation of fluid across the capillary wall, leading to edema.
wrongAnswers.B: Decreased capillary permeability and increased capillary permeability are incorrect. Capillary permeability changes in response to cytokines, classically in the setting of infection, necrosis, trauma, or inflammation.
wrongAnswers.C: Decreased plasma oncotic pressure and increased interstitial oncotic pressure are incorrect. Decreased plasma oncotic pressure results in edema due to the loss of proteins in the bloodstream that maintain an osmolar gradient. This is not the pathophysiology of edema in heart failure. Increased interstitial oncotic pressure results when there is an increase in proteins in the interstitial space, which results in edema. Such a situation may arise from lymphatic obstruction or myxedema, among other causes. Changes in plasma and interstitial protein concentrations are not the pathophysiology of edema in heart failure.
wrongAnswers.E: Decreased capillary permeability and increased capillary permeability are incorrect. Capillary permeability changes in response to cytokines, classically in the setting of infection, necrosis, trauma, or inflammation.
wrongAnswers.F: Decreased plasma oncotic pressure and increased interstitial oncotic pressure are incorrect. Decreased plasma oncotic pressure results in edema due to the loss of proteins in the bloodstream that maintain an osmolar gradient. This is not the pathophysiology of edema in heart failure. Increased interstitial oncotic pressure results when there is an increase in proteins in the interstitial space, which results in edema. Such a situation may arise from lymphatic obstruction or myxedema, among other causes. Changes in plasma and interstitial protein concentrations are not the pathophysiology of edema in heart failure.

explanationPanel.rule: Heart-failure edema is caused by increased venous/capillary hydrostatic pressure driving transudation into tissues.
explanationPanel.trap: Do not choose oncotic or permeability mechanisms unless the stem suggests nephrotic/liver disease or inflammation/capillary leak.

layer4.trap: Do not choose oncotic or permeability mechanisms unless the stem suggests nephrotic/liver disease or inflammation/capillary leak.

questions.subject: Pulmonology

explanationPanel.whyCorrect: Correct Answer: A. Educational Objective: Aspiration pneumonia is the most likely diagnosis of this patient with fever, productive cough that worsens with eating and drinking, and crackles in the right lower lung base in the setting of a neurodegenerative disorder. The most appropriate study to confirm diagnosis at this time is a chest x-ray. Evaluation: Aspiration pneumonia typically presents as shortness of breath, a cough productive of sputum, and fever, with a focal consolidation on chest x-ray, often in the superior segment of the inferior right lobe of the lung. Definition: Aspiration pneumonia occurs secondary to the aspiration of foreign materials into the lungs, including food, beverages, emesis or gastric contents, and oral secretions. Typically, this occurs in patients with altered mental status, decreased consciousness, or an impaired swallowing mechanism. Aspiration can result in an isolated inflammatory response, termed aspiration pneumonitis, but aspiration pneumonia refers to the aspiration of bacteria-containing substances that cause a subsequent infection in the lungs. Prevention: In hospitalized patients, recognition of decreased consciousness or a risk for aspiration should prompt endotracheal intubation to protect the airway, which can prevent aspiration. In patients with an isolated impaired swallowing mechanism, alternatives to oral feeding, such as a nasogastric feeding tube or gastrostomy, can decrease (but not prevent) aspiration. Treatment: Treatment of aspiration pneumonia consists of antibiotic therapy with regimens based on patient location (eg, community or healthcare facilities), severity of illness, and risk factors for antibiotic-resistant organisms. Anaerobic coverage may be included. Differential: A chest x-ray is the most appropriate initial diagnostic study for aspiration pneumonia because of its rapid availability, lower cost, and reduced radiation exposure as compared to alternatives. It also provides quick visual confirmation of the condition, unlike functional studies or cultures, which are either indirect or delayed in yielding diagnostic information.

wrongAnswers.B: CT scan of the chest is incorrect. A CT scan of the chest would show consolidation in the setting of aspiration pneumonia. However, it is associated with higher cost and increased radiation exposure when compared to chest x-ray.
wrongAnswers.C: Esophagogastroduodenoscopy is incorrect. Esophagogastroduodenoscopy is used to investigate abnormalities of the esophagus, stomach, and initial portion of the small intestine, such as esophageal atresia, gastric varices, or duodenal ulcer. While it may show pathologies that would put this patient at increased risk for aspiration, it would not directly confirm the diagnosis of aspiration pneumonia.
wrongAnswers.D: Modified barium swallow is incorrect. A modified barium swallow is a test that uses x-rays while a patient swallows barium to identify abnormalities in the swallowing process. This test can be used in patients with oropharyngeal tumors or with a history of stroke to identify an increased risk for aspiration but not to directly diagnose aspiration pneumonia.
wrongAnswers.E: Sputum culture is incorrect. A sputum culture can be useful in the management of aspiration pneumonia, as it can allow a more specific antibiotic regimen based on the isolated bacteria. However, it is not required for the diagnosis of aspiration pneumonia.

explanationPanel.rule: Aspiration pneumonia with fever, productive cough after swallowing, and focal crackles is initially confirmed with chest x-ray.
explanationPanel.trap: Modified barium swallow assesses aspiration risk/dysphagia mechanism but does not diagnose the pneumonia itself.

layer4.rule: Aspiration pneumonia with fever, productive cough after swallowing, and focal crackles is initially confirmed with chest x-ray.
layer4.trap: Modified barium swallow assesses aspiration risk/dysphagia mechanism but does not diagnose the pneumonia itself.

questions.stem: A 72-year-old woman comes to the clinic because of a 6-month history of “feeling down.” During this time, she has had no appetite, resulting in a 19-kg (42-lb) weight loss. She also has had low energy and has not been motivated to begin tasks that she should complete around her home. She says she used to enjoy going to bars with friends but she now prefers to stay home. She has also noted that her alcohol consumption has increased. During the past few years, she had been drinking one glass of wine each evening; now, she drinks two or three glasses. The patient does not use nicotine products or other substances. She has an 8-month history of low back pain, for which she takes over-the-counter pain medications, usually buying “whatever is on sale.” She takes no other medications. She is 168 cm (5 ft 6 in) tall and weighs 66 kg (146 lb); BMI is 24 kg/m². Vital signs are within normal limits. Physical examination discloses back tenderness when she bends at the waist. On mental status examination, she reports a “sad” mood and has a congruent affect. The physician prescribes appropriate medication for the patient's depression and related symptoms. It is most appropriate to counsel this patient about her alcohol use as well as which of the following?

The patient does not use nicotine products or other substances. She has an 8-month history of low back pain, for which she takes over-the-counter pain medications, usually buying “whatever is on sale.” She takes no other medications. She is 168 cm (5 ft 6 in) tall and weighs 66 kg (146 lb); BMI is 24 kg/m². Vital signs are within normal limits. Physical examination discloses back tenderness when she bends at the waist. On mental status examination, she reports a “sad” mood and has a congruent affect. The physician prescribes appropriate medication for the patient's depression and related symptoms. It is most appropriate to counsel this patient about her alcohol use as well as which of the following?
questions.subject: Psychiatry

explanationPanel.whyCorrect: Correct Answer: B. Educational Objective: This patient should be counseled about the combination of alcohol and NSAIDs, which can lead to an overall increased risk for gastrointestinal bleeding and renal damage due to a combination of deleterious effects. Key Concept: Alcohol and NSAIDs can be dangerous if used together. Explanation: Alcohol amplifies gastric mucosal damage by NSAIDs and leads to gastrointestinal bleeding. Binge drinking alcohol can also lead to renal hypoperfusion, increasing the risk for acute kidney injury by itself and especially in combination with NSAIDs, which are nephrotoxic. Patients who use alcohol in excess should be counseled about this risk and monitored for complications. Differential: Alcohol and acetaminophen use together is also dangerous, as chronic alcohol consumption can increase the risk for acetaminophen-induced hepatotoxicity. Patients with alcohol use and depressive symptoms should be counseled on alcohol’s depressant effect. Alcohol cessation is most likely to improve these patients’ depressive symptoms.

wrongAnswers.A: Increasing her social contacts is incorrect. Though increasing social connection can help with depressive symptoms, decreasing alcohol use is more likely to be beneficial, and the more pressing concern for this patient is the dangerous combination of alcohol and NSAIDs.
wrongAnswers.C: Vitamin D supplementation is incorrect. Though vitamin D supplementation may enhance neurologic function, its relationship with depression is unclear. The more pressing concern for this patient is the dangerous combination of alcohol and NSAIDs.
wrongAnswers.D: Weight loss is incorrect. This patient is a normal weight.

explanationPanel.rule: Older patient with increased alcohol intake plus OTC pain-medication use should be warned about NSAID-alcohol GI bleeding and renal injury.
explanationPanel.trap: Social support and vitamin D may matter, but the immediate safety issue is alcohol combined with likely NSAID use.

layer4.rule: Older patient with increased alcohol intake plus OTC pain-medication use should be warned about NSAID-alcohol GI bleeding and renal injury.
layer4.trap: Social support and vitamin D may matter, but the immediate safety issue is alcohol combined with likely NSAID use.

questions.stem: A 54-year-old woman comes to the office because of a 2-year history of gradually enlarging patches of discoloration on her hands. There is no itching or pain. She says she has not been using new soaps or lotions. Physical examination shows the findings in the photograph. It is most appropriate for the physician to evaluate this patient for the presence of which of the following additional conditions?
questions.stemHtml: A 54-year-old woman comes to the office because of a 2-year history of gradually enlarging patches of discoloration on her hands. There is no itching or pain. She says she has not been using new soaps or lotions. Physical examination shows the findings in the photograph. It is most appropriate for the physician to evaluate this patient for the presence of which of the following additional conditions?
questions.subject: Dermatology

explanationPanel.whyCorrect: Correct Answer: E. Educational Objective: It is most appropriate for the physician to evaluate this patient with vitiligo for the presence of thyroiditis. Thyroiditis is an autoimmune condition associated with inflammation of the thyroid gland. Vitiligo, which is caused by the autoimmune destruction of melanocytes, is commonly associated with autoimmune diseases such as thyroiditis. Evaluation: Vitiligo presents with the development of circumscribed, hypopigmented macules and patches on the skin. New lesions may occur over time, and lesions may grow as well. Vitiligo commonly involves the acral surfaces. Definition: Vitiligo is associated with the autoimmune destruction of melanocytes, which are present throughout the epidermis, including the hair follicles. In patients who develop vitiligo there is an increased risk for other autoimmune diseases including thyroiditis, Addison disease, type 1 diabetes mellitus, systemic lupus erythematosus, and rheumatoid arthritis. Prevention: There are no effective methods to prevent development of vitiligo. Treatment: Vitiligo is treated commonly with multiple modalities including topical corticosteroids or topical calcineurin inhibitors, such as tacrolimus. UV light therapy, which suppresses the T lymphocyte response, may be used to promote repigmentation of affected areas. Additionally, a novel topical Janus kinase inhibitor, ruxolitinib, may be used for treatment of vitiligo. Differential: In this patient with the development of asymptomatic macules progressing into patches on the acral surfaces, the most likely diagnosis is vitiligo. Vitiligo is associated with several autoimmune diseases, including thyroiditis.

wrongAnswers.A: Colon cancer is incorrect. Leser-Trélat sign is associated with the rapid development of hundreds to thousands of seborrheic keratoses and itching that may suggest gastrointestinal malignancy. Seborrheic keratoses are brown, stuck-on papules involving the face, trunk, or extremities. This patient’s asymptomatic patches of discoloration on her hands is consistent with vitiligo.
wrongAnswers.B: Diabetes insipidus is incorrect. Diabetes insipidus is associated with insufficient antidiuretic hormone, central diabetes insipidus, or inability to respond to antidiuretic hormone at the level of the kidneys, nephrogenic diabetes insipidus. Diabetes insipidus is not associated with vitiligo.
wrongAnswers.C: Hypercortisolism is incorrect. Hypercortisolism is associated with excess production of cortisol, or in iatrogenic cases, associated systemic corticosteroids. Hypercortisolism is associated with the development of a cushingoid appearance in which patients develop moon facies, central obesity, thin skin, easy bruising, and muscular wasting. This patient has vitiligo.
wrongAnswers.D: Melanoma is incorrect. Melanoma presents with evolving, asymmetrically shaped, pigmented growths with irregular borders. While patients with vitiligo may have an increased risk for the development of skin cancers, vitiligo is more commonly associated with the development of thyroiditis.

explanationPanel.rule: Vitiligo is autoimmune melanocyte destruction and is associated with autoimmune thyroiditis.
explanationPanel.trap: Melanoma is an evolving pigmented lesion; vitiligo is depigmented patches and prompts autoimmune screening.

layer4.rule: Vitiligo is autoimmune melanocyte destruction and is associated with autoimmune thyroiditis.
layer4.trap: Melanoma is an evolving pigmented lesion; vitiligo is depigmented patches and prompts autoimmune screening.

questions.stem: A 32-year-old woman, gravida 1, para 1, comes to the office because of a 2-day history of foul-smelling vaginal discharge. One week ago, she underwent forceps-assisted vaginal delivery of a newborn at 38 weeks' gestation. Delivery was complicated by a deep vaginal sulcus laceration that was repaired in the delivery room. Vital signs are within normal limits. Examination shows a retained surgical sponge, which is removed. The physician alerts the patient to the finding and irrigates the laceration, which appears intact. No surrounding infection is noted. Delivery was performed by one of the physician's partners. In addition to apologizing to the patient, which of the following is the most appropriate next step by the physician?
questions.stemHtml: A 32-year-old woman, gravida 1, para 1, comes to the office because of a 2-day history of foul-smelling vaginal discharge. One week ago, she underwent forceps-assisted vaginal delivery of a newborn at 38 weeks' gestation. Delivery was complicated by a deep vaginal sulcus laceration that was repaired in the delivery room. Vital signs are within normal limits. Examination shows a retained surgical sponge, which is removed. The physician alerts the patient to the finding and irrigates the laceration, which appears intact. No surrounding infection is noted. Delivery was performed by one of the physician's partners. In addition to apologizing to the patient, which of the following is the most appropriate next step by the physician?
choices: Discuss the event with the partner who performed the delivery but do not report it
Implement a new sponge counting procedure
Initiate a root cause analysis with the hospital's patient safety team
Re-educate staff on the existing sponge counting policy
Report the delivery provider and delivery nurse to the department chair
questions.subject: Ethics/Social Sciences

explanationPanel.correct: C. Initiate a root cause analysis with the hospital's patient safety team
explanationPanel.whyCorrect: Correct Answer: C. Educational Objective: This physician should initiate a root cause analysis (RCA) with the hospital's patient safety team. RCA involves determining the core systems-level issue that leads to an adverse event. Rather than presuming the cause of an adverse event, RCA involves a multidisciplinary team defining and analyzing the problem to design a set of corrective actions based on the analysis. Key Concept: When the underlying cause of an adverse event such as a retained surgical sponge is unclear, physicians should conduct an RCA of the event to determine the factors contributing to the event. Explanation: RCA involves determining the core systems-level issue(s) that leads to the chain reaction of events that culminate in the adverse event. There are several RCA strategies, including creating a timeline, surveying the controls in place that may have failed, and completing a risk tree analysis where the impact of each event is considered. Regardless of strategy, a typical RCA involves assembling a multidisciplinary team and meeting with this team regularly for a period of time. This team works to define and analyze the problem to design a set of corrective actions based on the analysis. Differential: This patient presents with a retained surgical sponge, but the underlying cause of this adverse event is unclear. To determine the factors contributing to the adverse event, the physician should conduct an RCA of the event.

wrongAnswers.A: Discuss the event with the partner who performed the delivery but do not report it is incorrect. This option avoids examining the systems-level factors that contributed and prevents all caregivers from learning from the event.
wrongAnswers.B: Implement a new sponge counting procedure and re-educate staff on the existing sponge counting policy are premature. Interventions should be deferred until the cause of error is determined through RCA.
wrongAnswers.D: Implement a new sponge counting procedure and re-educate staff on the existing sponge counting policy are premature. Interventions should be deferred until the cause of error is determined through RCA.
wrongAnswers.E: Report the delivery provider and delivery nurse to the department chair is incorrect. Most adverse events are driven by systems-level factors rather than the culpability of individual caregivers.

explanationPanel.rule: A retained surgical sponge is a sentinel adverse event requiring root cause analysis by the patient-safety team.
explanationPanel.trap: Do not jump to re-education/new policy or individual blame before the systems cause is identified.

layer4.rule: A retained surgical sponge is a sentinel adverse event requiring root cause analysis by the patient-safety team.
layer4.trap: Do not jump to re-education/new policy or individual blame before the systems cause is identified.

Question: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in evaluation?
choices: CT scan of the abdomen and pelvis
questions.subject: Hematology/Oncology

explanationPanel.whyCorrect: Correct Answer: D. Educational Objective: This patient who presents with fatigue and difficulty concentrating is found to have a low erythropoietin concentration and erythrocytosis, most consistent with polycythemia vera (PV). The most appropriate next step in evaluation is a JAK2 mutation test. Evaluation: PV is a myeloproliferative neoplasm that arises from a mutation in the JAK2 gene (JAK2 V617F), leading to constitutive activation of the JAK-STAT pathway. PV classically presents with symptoms related to increased concentrations of red blood cells, such as headaches, erythromelalgia, and splenomegaly. Definition: The diagnosis of PV occurs when a patient has increased hemoglobin concentrations, a bone marrow biopsy showing trilineage growth, and a JAK2 mutation. While some patients present with thrombocytosis and leukocytosis as well, an increased hemoglobin concentration with increased red cell mass is the classic and definitive presentation of this disease. Prevention: There are no established methods to prevent PV. Treatment: First-line treatment includes phlebotomy or cytoreductive therapy to control red cell mass, and aspirin to prevent microvascular symptoms and decrease cardiovascular risk. Differential: The differential diagnosis for erythrocytosis includes causes such as chronic hypoxia or an erythropoietin-secreting tumor. This patient’s low erythropoietin concentration narrows the differential diagnosis, making PV the most likely diagnosis.

wrongAnswers.A: Bone marrow biopsy with fluorescence and peripheral blood smear are not appropriate next steps. This patient has a clear history, increased hemoglobin concentration above the defined threshold for polycythemia, and low erythropoietin concentration. Further hematologic studies such as bone marrow biopsy and peripheral blood smear are unnecessary.
wrongAnswers.B: Chest x-ray is incorrect. A chest x-ray may be used to evaluate a patient with shortness of breath or dyspnea. This patient has no evidence of respiratory symptoms.
wrongAnswers.C: CT scan of the abdomen and pelvis is incorrect. This patient has no abdominal symptoms or concerning findings on physical examination that warrant evaluation with a CT scan of the abdomen and pelvis.
wrongAnswers.E: Bone marrow biopsy with fluorescence and peripheral blood smear are not appropriate next steps. This patient has a clear history, increased hemoglobin concentration above the defined threshold for polycythemia, and low erythropoietin concentration. Further hematologic studies such as bone marrow biopsy and peripheral blood smear are unnecessary.

explanationPanel.rule: Erythrocytosis with low erythropoietin suggests polycythemia vera; the next test is JAK2 mutation testing.
explanationPanel.trap: High EPO would push toward hypoxia or EPO-secreting tumors; low EPO points to a primary marrow process.

layer4.rule: Erythrocytosis with low erythropoietin suggests polycythemia vera; the next test is JAK2 mutation testing.
layer4.trap: High EPO would push toward hypoxia or EPO-secreting tumors; low EPO points to a primary marrow process.

questions.stem: A 40-year-old woman comes to the office because of a 5-month history of a lump on the midportion of her neck. She has no history of serious illness and takes no medications. She is 168 cm (5 ft 6 in) tall and weighs 54 kg (120 lb); BMI is 19 kg/m². Vital signs are within normal limits. A photograph of the patient is shown. Serum TSH and thyroxine (T4) concentrations are within the reference ranges; no thyroid autoantibodies are detected. A photomicrograph of an ultrasonography-guided fine-needle aspiration of the nodule also is shown. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.stemHtml: A 40-year-old woman comes to the office because of a 5-month history of a lump on the midportion of her neck. She has no history of serious illness and takes no medications. She is 168 cm (5 ft 6 in) tall and weighs 54 kg (120 lb); BMI is 19 kg/m². Vital signs are within normal limits. A photograph of the patient is shown. Serum TSH and thyroxine (T4) concentrations are within the reference ranges; no thyroid autoantibodies are detected. A photomicrograph of an ultrasonography-guided fine-needle aspiration of the nodule also is shown. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.subject: Endocrinology

explanationPanel.whyCorrect: Correct Answer: D. Educational Objective: This patient presents with a neck mass and undergoes fine-needle aspiration. The resulting photomicrograph is notable for papillary fronds with fibrovascular cores, most suggestive of papillary carcinoma. Evaluation: Papillary carcinoma is the most common type of thyroid malignancy that typically presents with an asymptomatic thyroid nodule, as seen in this patient. Laboratory study of hormone concentrations is often normal in these patients. Definition: The gold standard for diagnosis of papillary thyroid carcinoma is fine-needle aspiration, which is notable for typical pathologic findings such as arborizing papilla. Prevention: Minimizing exposure to head and neck ionizing radiation can decrease the risk for developing papillary carcinoma of the thyroid. Treatment: Treatment is surgical resection, which can then be followed by radioactive iodine therapy to treat potential metastatic disease. Differential: The differential diagnosis is broad for this patient who presents with a neck mass. Further evaluation shows a photomicrograph that is most consistent with papillary carcinoma of the thyroid.

wrongAnswers.A: Anaplastic carcinoma is incorrect. While anaplastic carcinoma may also present with a neck mass, the photomicrograph would likely show marked nuclear pleomorphism and high mitotic activity.
wrongAnswers.B: Follicular carcinoma is incorrect. While follicular carcinoma may also present with a neck mass, the photomicrograph would likely show a microfollicular pattern with coarse, granular chromatin.
wrongAnswers.C: Medullary carcinoma is incorrect. While medullary carcinoma may also present with a neck mass, the photomicrograph would likely show psammoma bodies, intranuclear cytoplasmic inclusions, and nuclear grooves.

explanationPanel.rule: Papillary thyroid carcinoma presents as an asymptomatic thyroid nodule with FNA papillary fronds/fibrovascular cores.
explanationPanel.trap: Medullary carcinoma is C-cell/calcitonin with amyloid; follicular carcinoma requires capsular/vascular invasion.

layer4.rule: Papillary thyroid carcinoma presents as an asymptomatic thyroid nodule with FNA papillary fronds/fibrovascular cores.
layer4.trap: Medullary carcinoma is C-cell/calcitonin with amyloid; follicular carcinoma requires capsular/vascular invasion.

questions.stem: A 68-year-old woman comes to the office for a routine follow-up examination 6 months after completing treatment for colorectal cancer. Her treatment consisted of surgical excision of the colon followed by a 6-month course of chemotherapy with leucovorin, fluorouracil, oxaliplatin, and radiation therapy. The procedure was complicated by a prolonged recovery, and she has been mostly sedentary during this time. The patient now reports a 4-week history of decreased sensation in her fingertips, as well as numbness and tingling in both feet. Medical history otherwise is unremarkable. She currently takes no medications. She is 163 cm (5 ft 4 in) tall and weighs 84 kg (185 lb); BMI is 32 kg/m². Vital signs are within normal limits. Examination shows decreased sensation to pinprick over all fingers and toes. Which of the following is the most likely cause of this patient's symptoms?
questions.stemHtml: A 68-year-old woman comes to the office for a routine follow-up examination 6 months after completing treatment for colorectal cancer. Her treatment consisted of surgical excision of the colon followed by a 6-month course of chemotherapy with leucovorin, fluorouracil, oxaliplatin, and radiation therapy. The procedure was complicated by a prolonged recovery, and she has been mostly sedentary during this time. The patient now reports a 4-week history of decreased sensation in her fingertips, as well as numbness and tingling in both feet. Medical history otherwise is unremarkable. She currently takes no medications. She is 163 cm (5 ft 4 in) tall and weighs 84 kg (185 lb); BMI is 32 kg/m². Vital signs are within normal limits. Examination shows decreased sensation to pinprick over all fingers and toes. Which of the following is the most likely cause of this patient's symptoms?
choices: Deconditioning from prolonged inactivity during treatment
Metabolic imbalance related to her cancer
Nutritional deficiency following surgical excision of the colon
questions.subject: Hematology/Oncology

explanationPanel.whyCorrect: Correct Answer: A. Educational Objective: This patient presents with peripheral neuropathy after treatment for colorectal cancer, which is most likely an adverse effect of chemotherapy with oxaliplatin. Evaluation: Oxaliplatin is a platinum-based chemotherapy used for treatment of colorectal cancer. The dose-limiting toxicity of oxaliplatin is a progressive peripheral neuropathy, as seen in this patient, which presents with decreased sensation in distal extremities. Definition: Chronic peripheral neuropathy from oxaliplatin typically manifests with sensory symptoms. It develops weeks to months after treatment and can persist. Prevention: Prevention of oxaliplatin-induced peripheral neuropathy includes many approaches such as dose reduction if able, supplemental magnesium and calcium infusions, and interspersing a different chemotherapy agent between oxaliplatin doses. Treatment: Treatment of symptoms can be achieved through use of medications for neuropathic pain, such as duloxetine and gabapentin. Differential: The differential diagnosis for peripheral neuropathy includes causes such as vitamin deficiencies, alcohol use, diabetic neuropathy, and medication effects. In this patient who has recently finished a course of platinum-based chemotherapy, peripheral neuropathy secondary to exposure to oxaliplatin is most likely.

wrongAnswers.B: Deconditioning from prolonged inactivity during treatment is incorrect. Deconditioning would cause weakness but would be rare to cause sensory deficits in all extremities.
wrongAnswers.C: Metabolic imbalance related to her cancer is incorrect. Metabolic imbalance would present with weight loss and cachexia, but would not cause neuropathy.
wrongAnswers.D: Nutritional deficiency following surgical excision of the colon is incorrect. Neuropathy may result from vitamin deficiencies, especially if there was resection of the small bowel such as the terminal ileum in the surgery. However, given the recent exposure to oxaliplatin and the time course of vitamin deficiency development, this is a less likely cause.
wrongAnswers.E: Radiation therapy is incorrect. While radiation therapy in a region with many nerves, such as the brachial plexus, may cause a more localized neuropathic pain, radiation therapy of the abdomen is unlikely to cause peripheral neuropathy.

explanationPanel.rule: Oxaliplatin causes delayed, dose-limiting distal sensory peripheral neuropathy after colorectal cancer chemotherapy.
explanationPanel.trap: Deconditioning causes weakness, not symmetric pinprick sensory loss in fingers and toes.

layer4.rule: Oxaliplatin causes delayed, dose-limiting distal sensory peripheral neuropathy after colorectal cancer chemotherapy.
layer4.trap: Deconditioning causes weakness, not symmetric pinprick sensory loss in fingers and toes.

He first noticed the lump while he was lifting weights and it continues to bother him daily. He has not sustained recent trauma to the area. He has no history of serious illness and takes no medications. Vital signs are within normal limits. Examination shows a reducible, nontender mass in the inguinal region when the patient is standing and coughing. The remainder of the examination shows no abnormalities. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

He first noticed the lump while he was lifting weights and it continues to bother him daily. He has not sustained recent trauma to the area. He has no history of serious illness and takes no medications. Vital signs are within normal limits. Examination shows a reducible, nontender mass in the inguinal region when the patient is standing and coughing. The remainder of the examination shows no abnormalities. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

Recommendation for use of a truss
questions.subject: General Surgery/Trauma

explanationPanel.whyCorrect: Correct Answer: C. Educational Objective: This patient presents with an intermittently painful mass in the inguinal region most suggestive of an inguinal hernia. The most appropriate next step in management in this otherwise healthy patient is surgical repair. Evaluation: Inguinal hernias occur when there is protrusion of abdominal contents through a defect in the inguinal canal. Inguinal hernia classically presents with a mass in the groin area during activities that increase intra-abdominal pressure, such as coughing and standing. Definition: Physical examination can diagnose an inguinal hernia. Imaging may be used if the diagnosis is uncertain. Prevention: Prevention of inguinal hernias includes maintaining a healthy weight, avoiding heavy lifting, and avoiding constipation. However, some patients are predisposed to hernia formation because of anatomic variations. Treatment: Treatment of inguinal hernia is surgical repair. Differential: The differential for a mass in the groin includes hydrocele, malignancy, and lymphadenopathy. This patient’s examination is notable for a reducible, nontender mass in the inguinal region, consistent with a hernia.

wrongAnswers.A: CT scan of the abdomen and pelvis and ultrasonography of the groin are not indicated in this patient. This patient has a hernia diagnosis on the basis of his medical history and physical examination. CT scan and ultrasonography are unnecessary.
wrongAnswers.B: Recommendation for use of a truss is incorrect. A truss is a nonsurgical therapy for a groin hernia that can be offered to male patients with asymptomatic inguinal hernia. There is insufficient evidence to prove the efficacy of a truss, and it can further complicate the course of disease if it causes damage to the bowel within the hernia.
wrongAnswers.D: CT scan of the abdomen and pelvis and ultrasonography of the groin are not indicated in this patient. This patient has a hernia diagnosis on the basis of his medical history and physical examination. CT scan and ultrasonography are unnecessary.
wrongAnswers.E: Reassurance only is incorrect. This patient requires surgical repair of his inguinal hernia given the presenting symptoms of intermittent pain.

explanationPanel.rule: Symptomatic reducible inguinal hernia in a healthy adult should undergo surgical repair.
explanationPanel.trap: Imaging is unnecessary when the diagnosis is clear on exam; truss/watchful waiting is for selected asymptomatic patients.

questions.stem: A 28-year-old woman, gravida 3, para 2, at 22 weeks’ gestation comes to the office for a routine prenatal visit. Pregnancy has been complicated by major depressive disorder, diagnosed 1 year ago. Current medications are citalopram and a prenatal vitamin. Her two previous pregnancies ended in uncomplicated vaginal deliveries at term 2 and 5 years ago. She feels well and has no other history of serious illness. Her husband is currently deployed with the military, and her family lives in a different state. She is the primary caregiver for her two young children. The patient has smoked one-half pack of cigarettes daily for 5 years and has continued to smoke during pregnancy. She does not drink alcoholic beverages or use other substances. Examination shows a uterus consistent in size with a 22-week gestation. Pelvic ultrasonography shows a bilateral fetal diaphragmatic defect with abdominal contents in the fetal chest with minimal lung tissue. The patient is offered pregnancy termination and she declines. It is most appropriate for the physician to consider which of the following factors in determining newborn treatment at delivery?

Pregnancy has been complicated by major depressive disorder, diagnosed 1 year ago. Current medications are citalopram and a prenatal vitamin.
