questions.subject: Pulmonology

explanationPanel.whyCorrect: Correct Answer: B. Educational Objective: A pulmonary embolism (PE) is the most likely diagnosis in this postoperative patient with dyspnea, chest pain, hypoxia, tachycardia, and a filling defect on chest x-ray. The treatment of choice for pulmonary emboli without hemodynamic compromise in a patient at low-risk for bleeding is anticoagulation. Heparin therapy, which can be titrated while the patient is observed for signs of bleeding after her recent surgical procedure, is the most appropriate next step in management. Evaluation: Pulmonary emboli presents with dyspnea, pleuritic chest pain, hemoptysis, and occasionally, light-headedness or syncope. Hemodynamic collapse can also occur. Definition: Pulmonary emboli are often caused by thromboemboli due to deep venous thrombosis (DVT). The formation of DVT is facilitated by the features of Virchow triad: venous stasis (eg, immobility, venous occlusion), endothelial injury (eg, infection, trauma, inflammation), and hypercoagulability (eg, malignancy, pregnancy). Symptoms of DVT include unilateral swelling, erythema, and pain to the affected limb. When clots embolize to the pulmonary vasculature, the profile of their symptomatology is a function of the size and location of the embolism. Clinical signs include tachycardia, tachypnea, hypoxia, and if massive, hypotension and cardiovascular collapse. Prevention: Modifiable actions to reduce the incidence of DVT and consequent pulmonary emboli include minimizing immobility, especially in the prothrombotic postoperative state, avoiding hormonal birth control, smoking cessation, weight loss, and if immobilized, using a prophylactic anticoagulant, such as low-dose subcutaneous heparin. Treatment: In hemodynamically stable patients, anticoagulation is first-line therapy if it is not contraindicated by increased bleeding risk. If it is contraindicated, an inferior vena cava filter may be placed. For hemodynamically unstable patients, thrombolysis or thrombectomy are indicated. Differential: This patient has a confirmed pulmonary embolism on CT scan of her chest so additional diagnostic studies are not necessary. This patient is hemodynamically stable and can safely receive titrated anticoagulation, making thrombolysis and placement of an inferior vena cava filter inappropriate treatment choices.

wrongAnswers.A: Angiography of the pulmonary vessels is incorrect. Angiography of the pulmonary vessels is an invasive technique in which dye is injected into the pulmonary vasculature to identify filling defects or vascular abnormalities. This patient has a pulmonary emboli confirmed by CT scan of the chest, so additional diagnostic techniques, such as angiography, are not warranted.
wrongAnswers.C: Placement of an inferior vena cava filter is incorrect. An inferior vena cava filter is often placed in patients with DVT or PE in whom anticoagulation would be unsafe, such as those with a recent intracranial bleed or stroke. While this patient recently had intra-abdominal surgery, it was uncomplicated, and anticoagulation with heparin can be carefully initiated while monitoring for signs of bleeding.
wrongAnswers.D: Radiolabeled ventilation-perfusion lung scans is incorrect. Ventilation-perfusion lung scans are an additional technique that can be used to confirm the diagnosis of PE if the presentation is uncertain. CT scan of this patient’s chest has already confirmed a pulmonary emboli.
wrongAnswers.E: Streptokinase therapy is incorrect. Streptokinase is a thrombolytic and may be used in the treatment of hemodynamically unstable pulmonary emboli if mechanical thrombectomy is not readily available. This patient is hemodynamically stable and had a recent surgery, making the administration of streptokinase inappropriate.
wrongAnswers.F: Ultrasonography of the lower extremities is incorrect. Ultrasonography of the lower extremities could be used to diagnose a concurrent DVT of the lower extremities. However, this patient has confirmed PE, which should be treated with anticoagulation. Identification of DVT, which would be treated with the anticoagulation if it was present, is not necessary.
wrongAnswers.G: Use of compression stockings is incorrect. The use of compression stockings may reduce the formation of DVT in the lower extremities. However, they would not treat this patient’s symptomatic PE.

explanationPanel.rule: Hemodynamically stable pulmonary embolism confirmed on CT is treated with anticoagulation, often titratable heparin postoperatively.
explanationPanel.trap: Thrombolysis is for unstable massive PE; IVC filter is for patients who cannot receive anticoagulation.

layer4.rule: Hemodynamically stable pulmonary embolism confirmed on CT is treated with anticoagulation, often titratable heparin postoperatively.
layer4.trap: Thrombolysis is for unstable massive PE; IVC filter is for patients who cannot receive anticoagulation.

questions.stem: An 18-month-old boy is brought to the emergency department because of a 2-day history of temperatures to 38.9°C (102.0°F). During the past 6 months, he has had four episodes of otitis media that resolved with amoxicillin therapy. He currently receives no medications. Immunizations are up-to-date. The patient is at the 10th percentile for length, weight, and head circumference. Temperature is 39.4°C (103.0°F), pulse is 130/min, and respirations are 36/min. Examination of the left knee shows swelling, erythema, and tenderness to palpation. Leukocyte count is 10,000/mm³ (N=6000–14,000), and absolute neutrophil count is 480/mm³ (N>500). Serum immunoglobulin concentrations are decreased, and B lymphocytes are absent. Culture of fluid aspirated from the knee grows Streptococcus pneumoniae, and the patient's symptoms improve with intravenous ceftriaxone therapy. The patient’s mother reports that her maternal great uncle died of sepsis as a child. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
questions.stemHtml: An 18-month-old boy is brought to the emergency department because of a 2-day history of temperatures to 38.9°C (102.0°F). During the past 6 months, he has had four episodes of otitis media that resolved with amoxicillin therapy. He currently receives no medications. Immunizations are up-to-date. The patient is at the 10th percentile for length, weight, and head circumference. Temperature is 39.4°C (103.0°F), pulse is 130/min, and respirations are 36/min. Examination of the left knee shows swelling, erythema, and tenderness to palpation. Leukocyte count is 10,000/mm³ (N=6000–14,000), and absolute neutrophil count is 480/mm³ (N>500). Serum immunoglobulin concentrations are decreased, and B lymphocytes are absent. Culture of fluid aspirated from the knee grows Streptococcus pneumoniae, and the patient's symptoms improve with intravenous ceftriaxone therapy. The patient’s mother reports that her maternal great uncle died of sepsis as a child. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
choices: Intravenous antibiotic therapy with infections only
Intravenous immune globulin therapy every 4 weeks
questions.subject: Pediatrics/Neonatology

explanationPanel.correct: C. Intravenous immune globulin therapy every 4 weeks
explanationPanel.whyCorrect: Correct Answer: C. Educational Objective: This young male patient with a family history of sepsis presents with a history of recurrent otitis media, fever, failure to thrive, and left knee infected with Streptococcus pneumoniae. Laboratory study results are notable for decreased immunoglobulin concentrations and absent B lymphocytes. This clinical presentation is most consistent with X-linked agammaglobulinemia. The most appropriate next step in management is intravenous immune globulin therapy every 4 weeks. Evaluation: X-linked agammaglobulinemia is an immunodeficiency syndrome that results in decreased or no gamma globulin due to a mutation that affects B lymphocyte development. It is caused by mutations in Bruton tyrosine kinase, which leads to a deficiency of B lymphocytes and immunoglobulins. It typically presents in males within the first 2 years of life as recurrent bacterial infections. Otitis media, pneumonia, and septic arthritis are common. Definition: The gold standard for diagnosis of X-linked agammaglobulinemia is genetic testing for mutations, with flow cytometry showing markedly decreased B lymphocytes in the peripheral blood. Prevention: Genetic counseling and carrier detection are the mainstay of prevention in families with a known history of X-linked agammaglobulinemia. Treatment: The mainstay of treatment is lifelong immune globulin replacement therapy with intravenous immune globulin. Differential: The differential diagnosis for this patient includes other immunodeficiency syndromes such as hyper-IgM syndrome. However, the low concentrations of all types of immunoglobulins and the absent B lymphocytes are most consistent with X-linked agammaglobulinemia.

wrongAnswers.A: Bone marrow transplant is incorrect. Bone marrow transplant can be used to treat immunodeficiencies such as severe combined immunodeficiency, but it is not a typical treatment for X-linked agammaglobulinemia.
wrongAnswers.B: Intravenous antibiotic therapy with infections only is incorrect. This patient will need intravenous antibiotic therapy with infections, but he will also need intravenous immune globulin repletion.
wrongAnswers.D: Weekly intravenous antibiotic therapy is incorrect. While patients with X-linked agammaglobulinemia may receive prophylactic antibiotics such as azithromycin, this is an oral medication and is not dosed weekly.
wrongAnswers.E: No additional management is indicated is incorrect. This patient requires lifelong immune globulin repletion with intravenous immune globulin.

explanationPanel.rule: X-linked agammaglobulinemia with absent B cells and low immunoglobulins requires lifelong IVIG replacement.
explanationPanel.trap: Treating infections only with antibiotics does not correct the absent humoral immunity.

layer4.rule: X-linked agammaglobulinemia with absent B cells and low immunoglobulins requires lifelong IVIG replacement.
layer4.trap: Treating infections only with antibiotics does not correct the absent humoral immunity.

questions.stem: A 1-week-old girl is brought to the office by her father for a well-child examination. She has no history of serious illness and receives no medications. Vaccinations are up-to-date. She was born at 39 weeks' gestation to a 29-year-old woman, gravida 1, para 1, following uncomplicated spontaneous vaginal delivery. Growth and development have been normal. She is 50 cm (20 in; 50th percentile) long and weighs 3400 g (7 lb 8 oz; 50th percentile); head circumference is 34.2 cm (13.5 in; 50th percentile). Vital signs are within normal limits. Examination discloses instability of the right hip on flexion when posterior pressure is applied to the femur. No other abnormalities are noted. Ultrasonography of the hips confirms the diagnosis. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
questions.stemHtml: A 1-week-old girl is brought to the office by her father for a well-child examination. She has no history of serious illness and receives no medications. Vaccinations are up-to-date. She was born at 39 weeks' gestation to a 29-year-old woman, gravida 1, para 1, following uncomplicated spontaneous vaginal delivery. Growth and development have been normal. She is 50 cm (20 in; 50th percentile) long and weighs 3400 g (7 lb 8 oz; 50th percentile); head circumference is 34.2 cm (13.5 in; 50th percentile). Vital signs are within normal limits. Examination discloses instability of the right hip on flexion when posterior pressure is applied to the femur. No other abnormalities are noted. Ultrasonography of the hips confirms the diagnosis. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
questions.subject: Musculoskeletal/Orthopedics

explanationPanel.correct: E. Use of a Pavlik harness
explanationPanel.whyCorrect: Correct Answer: E. Educational Objective: Developmental dysplasia of the hip (DDH) may present with palpable hip instability on physical examination. Management often involves the use of a Pavlik harness, the most appropriate next step for this patient, which helps to facilitate the normal development of a dysplastic hip joint. Evaluation: DDH can present with limited hip range of motion, palpable hip instability, unequal leg lengths, and asymmetric thigh skinfolds. Definition: DDH may present in either the unilateral or bilateral hips. The Barlow maneuver and Ortolani test can be performed on physical examination to evaluate for DDH. In patients with high clinical suspicion of DDH, ultrasonography is used to visualize the anatomy of the femoral head and acetabulum. Prevention: Risk factors for DDH include family history of DDH, breech positioning, female sex, and intrauterine spatial abnormalities such as oligohydramnios. Treatment: Treatment of DDH is initially conservative with the use of a hip abduction device or Pavlik harness. Surgery is often reserved for patients for whom conservative management was unsuccessful or for those who present at an age older than 6 months. Differential: This newborn patient presents with a positive Barlow maneuver, or instability of the right hip on flexion with posterior pressure, with ultrasonography confirming DDH. Use of a Pavlik harness is the most appropriate next step in management.

wrongAnswers.A: Application of a spica cast is not the most appropriate next step in management. Application of a spica cast may be a reasonable treatment option for patients who are older than 6 months. Use of a Pavlik harness is the most appropriate next step in management for this patient.
wrongAnswers.B: Double-diapering technique is incorrect. Double-diapering technique has not been shown to demonstrate clinical benefit. The use of a Pavlik harness is more appropriate.
wrongAnswers.C: Intravenous cefazolin therapy is not the most appropriate next step in management. Cefazolin may be used for various types of infections. The use of a Pavlik harness is more appropriate, as this patient presents with signs of DDH.
wrongAnswers.D: Operative repair is incorrect. Operative repair may be indicated for patients older than 6 months or patients for whom conservative management was unsuccessful. The more appropriate next step in management for this patient is use of a Pavlik harness.

explanationPanel.rule: Developmental dysplasia of the hip in a young infant is treated first with a Pavlik harness.
explanationPanel.trap: Spica casting or operative repair is reserved for older infants or failed conservative therapy.

layer4.rule: Developmental dysplasia of the hip in a young infant is treated first with a Pavlik harness.
layer4.trap: Spica casting or operative repair is reserved for older infants or failed conservative therapy.

questions.stem: A 3-year-old girl is brought to the urgent treatment center by her father because of a 3- week history of rash on her face and buttocks; the rash is not itchy or painful. The father says they have not recently changed bath soaps or laundry detergents and have not begun eating any new foods recently. The patient is otherwise asymptomatic. She has no history of serious illness and receives no medications. The father says his daughter is a "very picky eater." Vital signs and oxygen saturation are within normal limits. Examination shows a perioral rash with mild edema and erythema. The rash on the buttocks is more erythematous, but there are no satellite lesions or other signs of infection. The remainder of the examination discloses no abnormalities. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.stemHtml: A 3-year-old girl is brought to the urgent treatment center by her father because of a 3- week history of rash on her face and buttocks; the rash is not itchy or painful. The father says they have not recently changed bath soaps or laundry detergents and have not begun eating any new foods recently. The patient is otherwise asymptomatic. She has no history of serious illness and receives no medications. The father says his daughter is a "very picky eater." Vital signs and oxygen saturation are within normal limits. Examination shows a perioral rash with mild edema and erythema. The rash on the buttocks is more erythematous, but there are no satellite lesions or other signs of infection. The remainder of the examination discloses no abnormalities. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.subject: Pediatrics/Neonatology

explanationPanel.whyCorrect: Correct Answer: E. Educational Objective: This patient most likely has a zinc deficiency. Zinc deficiency presents with disturbances of taste and smell, neuropsychiatric disturbances, dermatitis (perioral and anogenital), brittle hair, alopecia, paronychia, delayed wound healing, and immune dysfunction. Zinc deficiency may occur in the setting of malnutrition or malabsorption. The diagnosis is confirmed with serum laboratory study of zinc concentration. Treatment is with oral zinc supplementation. Evaluation: Zinc deficiency typically presents with signs and symptoms including disturbances of taste and smell (hyposmia or hypogeusia), neuropsychiatric disturbances, dermatitis, brittle hair, alopecia, paronychia, delayed wound healing, and immune dysfunction. The dermatitis is often scaly and erythematous and may present with angular cheilitis or anogenital lesions. Definition: Zinc deficiency can be seen in patients with inadequate dietary intake, general malnutrition (including in patients with alcohol use disorder or anorexia nervosa), chronic liver disease, chronic kidney disease, or malabsorption. The diagnosis is confirmed with serum laboratory study of zinc concentration. Prevention: Prevention of deficiency is accomplished with daily multivitamins; extra supplementation may be indicated in patients with the above risk factors. Treatment: Treatment is with oral zinc supplementation. Differential: A perioral and buttocks rash in a “very picky eater” (likely consuming an inadequate diet) is most consistent with zinc deficiency.

wrongAnswers.A: Allergic reaction is incorrect. Patients with contact dermatitis present with well-demarcated, eczematous patches with focal vesiculation and overlying/surrounding crust. A nonitchy, multifocal, poorly demarcated rash is more consistent with a systemic cause.
wrongAnswers.B: Atopic dermatitis is incorrect. Atopic dermatitis, or eczema, is characterized by pruritus and recurrent episodes of dermatitis on the flexural surfaces of children, which may persist into adulthood. Atopic dermatitis is commonly associated with asthma and allergies (food or seasonal). This patient does not have any comorbidities, and a nonitchy perioral and anogenital rash is not consistent with eczema.
wrongAnswers.C: Candidiasis is incorrect. Cutaneous candidiasis commonly presents with red, macerated, thin plaques with satellite papules, which helps to differentiate it from other causes of dermatitis. While candidiasis can cause the rash distribution seen in this patient (diaper dermatitis and oral candidiasis), the lack of satellite lesions and pruritus makes this diagnosis unlikely.
wrongAnswers.D: Seborrheic dermatitis is incorrect. Seborrheic dermatitis is also caused by an overgrowth of the yeast Malassezia but typically presents as erythematous, greasy patches with yellow scale along the sides of the nose, in the eyebrows, along the ears and beard area, and in the scalp (dandruff), unlike the rash seen in this patient.

explanationPanel.rule: Perioral/anogenital dermatitis in a malnourished picky eater suggests zinc deficiency.
explanationPanel.trap: Candidiasis usually has pruritic erythema with satellite lesions; atopic dermatitis is pruritic and flexural.

layer4.rule: Perioral/anogenital dermatitis in a malnourished picky eater suggests zinc deficiency.
layer4.trap: Candidiasis usually has pruritic erythema with satellite lesions; atopic dermatitis is pruritic and flexural.

questions.stem: A 16-year-old boy is brought to the clinic because of a 3-month history of a 9.1-kg (20-lb) weight gain that he attributes to increased eating. His mother died in a motor vehicle collision 6 months ago. Since then, he says it takes him an hour to fall asleep, he wakes up at 4 AM every morning, and he lies in bed not wanting to get out. He spends most of the day in his bedroom. He has missed 4 weeks of school and is failing some classes. He was an avid wrestler but is not participating this year. He says, “I just don’t care about anything. Eating is the only thing that seems to help.” He snacks throughout the day and has been eating double his normal portions at meals. He feels guilty about his increased eating and has been inducing vomiting four times weekly “so I don’t get fat.” He has been attending individual and family therapy during the past 4 months. He has no history of serious illness and takes no medications. He does not use nicotine products, drink alcohol, or use other substances. He is at the 25th percentile for height, 70th percentile for weight, and 84th percentile for BMI. Vital signs are within normal limits. He makes poor eye contact during the visit. Physical examination discloses no abnormalities. On mental status examination, he has a blunted and dysphoric affect and describes his mood as "whatever." He has no suicidal ideation or thoughts of self harm. Which of the following is the most appropriate pharmacotherapy at this time?

His mother died in a motor vehicle collision 6 months ago. Since then, he says it takes him an hour to fall asleep, he wakes up at 4 AM every morning, and he lies in bed not wanting to get out. He spends most of the day in his bedroom. He has missed 4 weeks of school and is failing some classes. He was an avid wrestler but is not participating this year. He says, “I just don’t care about anything. Eating is the only thing that seems to help.” He snacks throughout the day and has been eating double his normal portions at meals. He feels guilty about his increased eating and has been inducing vomiting four times weekly “so I don’t get fat.” He has been attending individual and family therapy during the past 4 months. He has no history of serious illness and takes no medications. He does not use nicotine products, drink alcohol, or use other substances. He is at the 25th percentile for height, 70th percentile for weight, and 84th percentile for BMI. Vital signs are within normal limits. He makes poor eye contact during the visit. Physical examination discloses no abnormalities. On mental status examination, he has a blunted and dysphoric affect and describes his mood as "whatever." He has no suicidal ideation or thoughts of self harm. Which of the following is the most appropriate pharmacotherapy at this time?
choices: No pharmacotherapy is indicated at this time
questions.subject: Psychiatry

explanationPanel.whyCorrect: Correct Answer: B. Educational Objective: Physicians should select medications that address multiple problems when practical. Patients who meet criteria for both major depressive disorder (MDD) and bulimia nervosa, like this patient, should be offered fluoxetine, which is FDA approved for both of these disorders. Key Concept: When selecting a psychiatric medication, physicians should consider whether the medication can treat multiple problems. Using one medication for multiple problems decreases the total number of medications a patient needs, which decreases the risk for adverse medication effects. Explanation: Patients who meet criteria for both MDD and bulimia nervosa should be offered fluoxetine, which is FDA approved for both of these disorders. Symptoms of MDD include 2 or more weeks of depressed mood, anhedonia, guilt or worthlessness, difficulty concentrating, suicidal thoughts, and/or neurovegetative symptoms (eg, decreased energy, sleep disturbance, appetite disturbance). Bulimia nervosa (purging type) involves cycles of uncontrollable eating and compensatory behaviors such as vomiting and laxative or diuretic misuse that occur at least once weekly over 3 months or longer. Differential: Other antidepressant medications can be considered, but only fluoxetine is approved for bulimia nervosa so should be trialed first.

wrongAnswers.A: Bupropion is incorrect. Bupropion use should be avoided in patients with eating disorders when possible, as the combination of bupropion and electrolyte disturbances from eating disorder behaviors, such as purging, can decrease the seizure threshold.
wrongAnswers.C: Lisdexamfetamine is incorrect. Lisdexamfetamine is approved for binge eating disorder, not bulimia nervosa. As well, lisdexamfetamine is not a first-line medication for MDD.
wrongAnswers.D: Mirtazapine is incorrect. Mirtazapine is not approved for bulimia nervosa and is associated with weight gain, which may worsen this patient’s weight gain.
wrongAnswers.E: No pharmacotherapy is indicated at this time is incorrect. This patient meets the criteria for MDD and bulimia nervosa, and medication is recommended for both conditions.

explanationPanel.rule: Fluoxetine treats both major depressive disorder and bulimia nervosa and is preferred when both are present.
explanationPanel.trap: Bupropion is avoided in eating disorders because purging-related electrolyte shifts increase seizure risk.

layer4.rule: Fluoxetine treats both major depressive disorder and bulimia nervosa and is preferred when both are present.
layer4.trap: Bupropion is avoided in eating disorders because purging-related electrolyte shifts increase seizure risk.

questions.stem: A hospitalized 46-year-old woman undergoes uncomplicated vaginal hysterectomy and bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy for leiomyoma uteri and heavy menstrual bleeding. Estimated blood loss is 100 mL. Immediately following the operation, cystoscopy shows an intact bladder, a brisk urine jet from the left ureteral orifice, and no urine jet from the right ureteral orifice. Which of the following operative steps is the most likely cause of the cystoscopy findings?
questions.stemHtml: A hospitalized 46-year-old woman undergoes uncomplicated vaginal hysterectomy and bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy for leiomyoma uteri and heavy menstrual bleeding. Estimated blood loss is 100 mL. Immediately following the operation, cystoscopy shows an intact bladder, a brisk urine jet from the left ureteral orifice, and no urine jet from the right ureteral orifice. Which of the following operative steps is the most likely cause of the cystoscopy findings?
choices: Anterior entry into the peritoneal cavity
Posterior entry into the pouch of Douglas
questions.subject: Gynecology

explanationPanel.correct: B. Ligation of the uterine vessels
explanationPanel.whyCorrect: Correct Answer: B. Educational Objective: The most likely cause of this patient’s cystoscopy findings is ligation of the uterine vessels. Ureteral injury is a known complication of gynecologic surgery both due to underlying causes and complications leading to surgery in the first place (eg, pelvic inflammation and fibrosis that may have already involved the ureters) and due to iatrogenic injury during operative intervention involving adjacent anatomic structures. Key Concept: The ureter travels near the uterine/gonadal artery and vein in the retroperitoneal space. Even with caution and attention to the location of the ureter, injury can occur during surgery. Explanation: The ureter originates at the renal pelvis, then travels inferiorly along the anterior aspect of the psoas major muscle. The ureter enters the pelvic inlet and courses inferiorly and anteriorly near the common and internal iliac vessels. The ureter then passes posterior to the ovary and ovarian artery and vein prior continuing beneath the uterine artery and vein along the path to insertion on the posterolateral bladder. During salpingo-oophorectomy, ligation of the uterine artery and vein can inadvertently injure the ureter if the ureter becomes entrapped in suture or lacerated by a suture needle. Additionally, if inflammation and/or fibrosis exists surrounding the ovary, fallopian tube, broad ligament, uterus, or uterine/adnexal vessels, such inflammation and/or fibrosis may also extend to or entrap adjacent structures including the ureter and other pelvic anatomical structures, which can transmit traction forces leading to shearing or laceration. In this patient’s case, the absence of a ureteral jet from the right side on cystoscopy suggests a discontinuity in or obstruction of the right ureter, likely from iatrogenic injury. Differential: The absence of a right ureteral jet indicates that urine cannot flow from the right kidney to the bladder, and in the setting of recent pelvic surgery, indicates an injury to the right ureter. The ureter is anatomically adjacent to the uterine artery and vein, and ligation of these structures carries a known risk to the ureter.

wrongAnswers.A: Anterior entry into the peritoneal cavity is incorrect. The ureter is a retroperitoneal structure, and courses along the posterior aspect of the peritoneal cavity. The ureter is not an anterior structure, and anterior entry would not result in ureteral injury.
wrongAnswers.C: Posterior entry into the pouch of Douglas is incorrect. The pouch of Douglas is the space separating the rectum and the uterus and is the most dependent portion of the peritoneal cavity, making it a site of gravity-mediated fluid accumulation. The pouch of Douglas is a midline space and is not entered from a posterior approach during a laparotomy for hysterectomy and bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy, as such an approach would violate the rectum and result in peritoneal contamination with fecal matter. The ureter does not traverse the pouch of Douglas.
wrongAnswers.D: Suturing of the adnexal vessels is not the most likely cause of the cystoscopy findings. While suturing of the adnexal vessels could in concept injure the ureter, the proximity of the uterine vessels to the ureter results in higher likelihood of injury during the surgical manipulation of the uterine vessels.

explanationPanel.rule: The ureter passes under the uterine artery, so uterine-vessel ligation is the classic hysterectomy step causing ureteral obstruction/injury.
explanationPanel.trap: Adnexal vessel suturing can be near the ureter but uterine vessels are the highest-yield “water under the bridge” site.

layer4.rule: The ureter passes under the uterine artery, so uterine-vessel ligation is the classic hysterectomy step causing ureteral obstruction/injury.
layer4.trap: Adnexal vessel suturing can be near the ureter but uterine vessels are the highest-yield “water under the bridge” site.

questions.stem: Physicians at an outpatient clinic would like to increase the percentage of patients with type 2 diabetes mellitus treated in the clinic who undergo recommended annual diabetic foot examination. The baseline percentage of patients with type 2 diabetes mellitus in this patient population who underwent diabetic foot examination during the past year was 30%. The clinic would like to improve this number to greater than 70% during the next 6 months. Which of the following measurement tools is most appropriate for the physicians to track their progress?
questions.stemHtml: Physicians at an outpatient clinic would like to increase the percentage of patients with type 2 diabetes mellitus treated in the clinic who undergo recommended annual diabetic foot examination. The baseline percentage of patients with type 2 diabetes mellitus in this patient population who underwent diabetic foot examination during the past year was 30%. The clinic would like to improve this number to greater than 70% during the next 6 months. Which of the following measurement tools is most appropriate for the physicians to track their progress?
questions.subject: Ethics/Social Sciences

explanationPanel.whyCorrect: Correct Answer: D. Educational Objective: These physicians should track their progress using run charts, which display data points in order of time and can therefore measure whether a quality improvement intervention is helping. Key Concept: Run charts are simple charts that display data points in order of time, which assists in identifying data trends. They can therefore measure whether a quality improvement intervention is succeeding. Explanation: Charts are commonly used to measure process or outcome measures of quality improvement interventions. Process-related graphics, such as run charts, may more directly assess the quality of care, while outcome-related graphics have increased applicability but can be confounded by external factors. Differential: Another process-related graphic is a statistical process control chart, which is a line graph that includes statistically calculated lines including a central line (the mean) and upper control limit and lower control limit lines.

wrongAnswers.A: Bar chart and Pareto chart are incorrect. Both are types of bar charts that display categorical data using bars with heights proportionate to the value of the data. Pareto charts also include a line graph that reflects the cumulative percentage of the values. Both are used in quality improvement but are more commonly used to display outcome measures rather than process measures, as they lack a time element.
wrongAnswers.B: Bar chart and Pareto chart are incorrect. Both are types of bar charts that display categorical data using bars with heights proportionate to the value of the data. Pareto charts also include a line graph that reflects the cumulative percentage of the values. Both are used in quality improvement but are more commonly used to display outcome measures rather than process measures, as they lack a time element.
wrongAnswers.C: Pie chart is incorrect. A pie chart is a circular graphic with slices proportionate to the value of the data. Pie charts are used in quality improvement but are more commonly used to display outcome measures rather than process measures, as they lack a time element.

explanationPanel.rule: Run charts track a process measure over time and are used to follow quality-improvement progress.
explanationPanel.trap: Bar, pie, and Pareto charts summarize categories but do not show time-sequenced improvement.

layer4.rule: Run charts track a process measure over time and are used to follow quality-improvement progress.
layer4.trap: Bar, pie, and Pareto charts summarize categories but do not show time-sequenced improvement.

questions.stem: A 45-year-old woman comes to the clinic to discuss the results of fiberoptic bronchoscopy performed 2 days ago for evaluation of a 6-month history of a progressively worsening cough. She was initially seen in the clinic 10 days ago after she had three episodes of blood-streaked sputum in 3 days. Chest x-ray and CT scan of the chest obtained at the initial visit showed a 2.5-cm centrally located opacity in the right upper lobe. Today, the patient says she feels well. Medical history is remarkable for hypertension; she underwent a hysterectomy 3 years ago for leiomyomata uteri. Her only medication is hydrochlorothiazide. The patient does not smoke cigarettes, drink alcoholic beverages, or use other substances. She is 170 cm (5 ft 7 in) tall and weighs 68 kg (150 lb); BMI is 24 kg/m². Temperature is 37.0°C (98.6°F), pulse is 75/min, respirations are 12/min, and blood pressure is 120/80 mm Hg. Physical examination discloses no abnormalities. Results of fiberoptic bronchoscopy show an endobronchial mass. Biopsy of the mass confirms the diagnosis. The mass is well differentiated. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

She was initially seen in the clinic 10 days ago after she had three episodes of blood-streaked sputum in 3 days. Chest x-ray and CT scan of the chest obtained at the initial visit showed a 2.5-cm centrally located opacity in the right upper lobe. Today, the patient says she feels well. Medical history is remarkable for hypertension; she underwent a hysterectomy 3 years ago for leiomyomata uteri. Her only medication is hydrochlorothiazide. The patient does not smoke cigarettes, drink alcoholic beverages, or use other substances. She is 170 cm (5 ft 7 in) tall and weighs 68 kg (150 lb); BMI is 24 kg/m². Temperature is 37.0°C (98.6°F), pulse is 75/min, respirations are 12/min, and blood pressure is 120/80 mm Hg. Physical examination discloses no abnormalities. Results of fiberoptic bronchoscopy show an endobronchial mass. Biopsy of the mass confirms the diagnosis. The mass is well differentiated. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
questions.subject: Pulmonology

explanationPanel.whyCorrect: Correct Answer: C. Educational Objective: It is most likely that this patient with an endobronchial mass, limited symptoms, and no prior tobacco exposure has a low-grade neuroendocrine tumor, specifically a bronchial carcinoid. The most appropriate next step in the management of this otherwise healthy patient is surgical resection. Evaluation: Neuroendocrine tumors of the lungs often present with symptoms, such as cough, hemoptysis, or recurrent pneumonia, often due to airway obstruction. In rare cases, these tumors may be hormonally active, producing serotonin, vasoactive substances, and ectopic adrenocorticotropic hormone or growth hormone-releasing hormone, resulting in additional symptoms. Definition: Neuroendocrine tumors of the lung result from hyperplasia and malignant transformation of normal neuroendocrine cells. They include large and small cell tumors, as well as carcinoid tumors. Large and small cell carcinomas are more aggressive and linked to tobacco use, whereas carcinoid tumors tend to grow more slowly and be unrelated to smoking history. Large cell tumors typically present in the periphery, whereas small cell carcinoma and carcinoid masses occur in the central airways. Well-differentiated neuroendocrine tumors, such as the bronchial carcinoid suspected in this patient, often cause obstructing mass lesions of the proximal bronchi, which leads to their presentation. Typical carcinoid tumors rarely metastasize. Prevention: There is no known prevention for carcinoid tumors of the lung. Treatment: First-line treatment includes surgical resection and lymph node dissection, in addition to management of any present paraneoplastic or carcinoid syndrome. Adjuvant therapy with chemoradiation may be indicated in patients with aggressive or advanced disease but is often ineffective. Differential: Surgical resection is the treatment of choice for any isolated lung mass if the patient has the cardiopulmonary reserve to tolerate resection. While additional testing may be warranted for further evaluation of this patient, prioritization should be given to resection.

wrongAnswers.A: Radiation therapy is incorrect. Radiation therapy may be used in patients with aggressive or advanced disease based on the histopathology of the resected tumor. Radiation has not been consistently shown to improve outcomes in patients with neuroendocrine tumors of the lung, and thus should not be used as a first-line treatment in a patient who can tolerate surgical resection.
wrongAnswers.B: Somatostatin receptor scintigraphy is incorrect. Most neuroendocrine tumors, though less so in lung-based ones, express somatostatin receptors allowing somatostatin receptor scintigraphy to be used to localize these tumors. While imaging may be done to assess for residual disease or to determine the effectiveness of somatostatin analogues in advanced disease, it is less important in this patient with localized, low-grade disease than surgical resection.
wrongAnswers.D: Urine 5-hydroxyindoleacetic acid concentration is incorrect. 5- Hydroxyindoleacetic acid is the primary metabolite of serotonin, and increased urine concentrations suggest an increased concentration of serotonin in the blood, confirming the diagnosis of carcinoid syndrome. This patient does not have any of the classic signs of carcinoid syndrome, such as flushing or diarrhea, making this test unnecessary.
wrongAnswers.E: Whole body PET scan is incorrect. Whole body PET scan may be used to evaluate for distant or small metastases that may not otherwise be evident on imaging. Low-grade neuroendocrine tumors rarely metastasize, and surgical resection with assessment for local metastasis to the lymph nodes should be completed first.

explanationPanel.rule: Localized well-differentiated bronchial carcinoid is treated with surgical resection.
explanationPanel.trap: 5-HIAA or somatostatin imaging is for carcinoid syndrome/metastatic evaluation, not the first step for a localized resectable mass.

questions.stem: A 62-year-old man comes to the office because of increasing difficulty achieving an erection during the past 2 years; for 2 months, he has been unable to achieve an erection. Two years ago, he noted that he had no semen discharge with orgasm. He has a 13-year history of hypertension treated with lisinopril and a 20-year history of type 2 diabetes mellitus treated with metformin. He also takes atorvastatin. Pulse is 90/min, respirations are 16/min, and blood pressure is 155/92 mm Hg while sitting and 130/80 mm Hg while standing. Lungs are clear to auscultation. An S gallop is heard; there are no murmurs. Pedal pulses are intact. Prostate is symmetrically enlarged; there is no tenderness or nodules. Proprioception and sensation to vibration and light touch are decreased to the knees bilaterally. Ankle reflexes are absent bilaterally. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.stemHtml: A 62-year-old man comes to the office because of increasing difficulty achieving an erection during the past 2 years; for 2 months, he has been unable to achieve an erection. Two years ago, he noted that he had no semen discharge with orgasm. He has a 13-year history of hypertension treated with lisinopril and a 20-year history of type 2 diabetes mellitus treated with metformin. He also takes atorvastatin. Pulse is 90/min, respirations are 16/min, and blood pressure is 155/92 mm Hg while sitting and 130/80 mm Hg while standing. Lungs are clear to auscultation. An S gallop is heard; there are no murmurs. Pedal pulses are intact. Prostate is symmetrically enlarged; there is no tenderness or nodules. Proprioception and sensation to vibration and light touch are decreased to the knees bilaterally. Ankle reflexes are absent bilaterally. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.subject: Endocrinology

explanationPanel.whyCorrect: Correct Answer: B. Educational Objective: This patient with a history of diabetes mellitus presents with sexual dysfunction, decreased peripheral sensation, and absent ankle reflexes most consistent with diabetic neuropathy. Diabetic neuropathy can present with a variety of nervous system effects, such as distal symmetric neuropathy, mononeuropathy, and/or autonomic neuropathy. Evaluation: The pathophysiology of diabetic autonomic neuropathy is complicated but involves hyperglycemia-induced metabolic and vascular changes that lead to oxidative stress, inflammation, and damage to peripheral nerves. Definition: The diagnosis of diabetic autonomic neuropathy is made through clinical examination and nerve conduction studies. Patients with diabetes mellitus should undergo annual screening for diabetic autonomic neuropathy. Prevention: The mainstay of prevention is optimizing glycemic control and managing comorbidities that contribute to metabolic syndrome. Treatment: Beyond glycemic control, treatment is primarily symptom driven and includes gabapentin and duloxetine. Differential: There is initially a broad differential diagnosis for this older patient with hypertension and diabetes mellitus presenting with sexual dysfunction. His physical examination is notable and narrows the differential to most likely neurologic causes, with diabetic autonomic neuropathy as the leading diagnosis.

wrongAnswers.A: Aortoiliac insufficiency is incorrect. This patient has intact pedal pulses on examination, but the abnormalities noted on examination are primarily neurologic and consistent with peripheral neuropathy secondary to diabetes mellitus.
wrongAnswers.C: Medication adverse effect is incorrect. This patient’s medication profile of lisinopril, metformin, and atorvastatin should not cause sexual dysfunction and should not cause peripheral neuropathy with bilateral areflexia.
wrongAnswers.D: Midthoracic spinal cord injury is incorrect. A midthoracic spinal cord may cause bilateral sensation changes; however, it would be very abnormal to present in the chronic setting with bilateral ankle areflexia. Spinal cord injuries are central nervous system injuries, and when chronic, present with hyperreflexia.
wrongAnswers.E: Zinc deficiency is incorrect. Zinc deficiency typically presents with nonspecific symptoms, such as dermatitis, alopecia, and weight loss.

explanationPanel.rule: Longstanding diabetes can cause autonomic neuropathy with erectile dysfunction, retrograde ejaculation, and orthostatic blood pressure changes.
explanationPanel.trap: Aortoiliac insufficiency would cause vascular findings such as diminished pulses or claudication, not distal neuropathy/areflexia.

layer4.rule: Longstanding diabetes can cause autonomic neuropathy with erectile dysfunction, retrograde ejaculation, and orthostatic blood pressure changes.
layer4.trap: Aortoiliac insufficiency would cause vascular findings such as diminished pulses or claudication, not distal neuropathy/areflexia.

questions.stem: A 7-year-old girl is brought to the office by her parents because of a 7-week history of intermittent fever, joint pain, malaise, and an unintentional 2-kg (5-lb) weight loss, despite no change in appetite. She also has had progressive difficulty rising from a chair and walking up stairs during this time. Medical history is unremarkable. She takes no medications and has never been hospitalized. She is at the 50th percentile for height and 25th percentile for weight. Vital signs are normal except for a temperature of 38.0°C (100.4°F). Physical examination discloses the findings shown in the photographs. Muscle strength is 3/5 in the proximal aspects of the upper and lower extremities. When asked to walk across the examination room, the patient appears to walk on her toes. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in diagnosis?
questions.stemHtml: A 7-year-old girl is brought to the office by her parents because of a 7-week history of intermittent fever, joint pain, malaise, and an unintentional 2-kg (5-lb) weight loss, despite no change in appetite. She also has had progressive difficulty rising from a chair and walking up stairs during this time. Medical history is unremarkable. She takes no medications and has never been hospitalized. She is at the 50th percentile for height and 25th percentile for weight. Vital signs are normal except for a temperature of 38.0°C (100.4°F). Physical examination discloses the findings shown in the photographs. Muscle strength is 3/5 in the proximal aspects of the upper and lower extremities. When asked to walk across the examination room, the patient appears to walk on her toes. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in diagnosis?
choices: Measurement of serum muscle enzyme activity
questions.subject: Rheumatology

explanationPanel.correct: C. Measurement of serum muscle enzyme activity
explanationPanel.whyCorrect: Correct Answer: C. Educational Objective: This patient’s physical examination findings are suggestive of dermatomyositis, an autoimmune condition affecting the skin and primarily the proximal muscles. Initial laboratory studies include measurement of serum muscle enzyme activity to evaluate for underlying muscle damage. Evaluation: Dermatomyositis classically presents with cutaneous findings and primarily proximal muscle weakness. Cutaneous findings include Gottron papules, heliotrope rash on the eyelids, and a light pink rash with telangiectasias on the upper back and chest. Definition: Dermatomyositis is an autoimmune disease affecting the skin and muscles that shows positive antinuclear antibodies (ANA), as well as anti-Jo-1, anti-SRP, and anti-Mi-2 antibodies. Initial laboratory studies include measurement of serum muscle enzyme activity, including creatinine kinase, lactate dehydrogenase, aldolase, alanine aminotransferase, and aspartate aminotransferase. An increase in these enzymes may indicate underlying muscle damage. A muscle biopsy specimen would most likely show muscle inflammation with findings of perifascicular myocyte atrophy. Prevention: There is no known way to prevent dermatomyositis, as it is an autoimmune disease. Dermatomyositis is associated with occult malignancy, and patients with a new diagnosis of dermatomyositis should undergo age-appropriate screening for malignancy. Treatment: Treatment of dermatomyositis involves systemic corticosteroids and immunosuppressive therapy. Differential: This patient presents with joint pain and proximal weakness as well as a heliotrope rash on the eyelids and rash on the knuckles consistent with Gottron papules. Measurement of serum muscle enzyme activity to evaluate for underlying muscle damage is the most appropriate next step in diagnosis.

wrongAnswers.A: Electromyography and nerve conduction studies is incorrect. Electromyography and nerve conduction studies may be used to differentiate a myopathic process from a neuropathic process such as radiculopathy, neuropathy, or polyneuropathy. Measurement of serum muscle enzyme activity is less invasive and is the most appropriate next step in diagnosis.
wrongAnswers.B: Exercise stress test is not the most appropriate next step in diagnosis. This patient presents with intermittent fever, proximal muscle weakness, and characteristic heliotrope rash, as well as hand findings consistent with Gottron papules. Measurement of serum muscle enzyme activity is the most appropriate next step in diagnosis.
wrongAnswers.D: Muscle biopsy is incorrect. While muscle biopsy may be performed as part of the workup for suspected dermatomyositis, initial laboratory evaluation of serum muscle enzyme activity is less invasive and is the most appropriate next step.
wrongAnswers.E: Skin biopsy is not the most appropriate next step in diagnosis. Skin biopsy may be used for the evaluation of various dermatologic conditions. Although this patient presents with dermatologic findings, she also presents with intermittent fever, joint pain, and proximal muscle weakness, which makes dermatomyositis the most likely diagnosis. Measurement of serum muscle enzyme activity is the most appropriate next step in diagnosis.

explanationPanel.rule: Suspected dermatomyositis is initially evaluated with serum muscle enzymes such as CK, aldolase, AST, ALT, and LDH.
explanationPanel.trap: Muscle biopsy and EMG can support diagnosis but come after less invasive enzyme testing.

layer4.rule: Suspected dermatomyositis is initially evaluated with serum muscle enzymes such as CK, aldolase, AST, ALT, and LDH.
layer4.trap: Muscle biopsy and EMG can support diagnosis but come after less invasive enzyme testing.

In addition to treating the patient's hemorrhoids, which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
choices: No additional treatment; schedule follow up in 1 month
questions.subject: Gastroenterology

explanationPanel.whyCorrect: Correct Answer: C. Educational Objective: This patient presents with a history of constipation and rectal bleeding and is found to have microcytic anemia most consistent with iron deficiency anemia. The most appropriate next step in management is scheduling a colonoscopy to evaluate the cause of this patient’s iron deficiency anemia and gastrointestinal bleeding. Evaluation: Colonoscopy is indicated in patients with lower gastrointestinal bleeding and unexplained iron deficiency anemia. There is a high prevalence of gastrointestinal malignancy in patients with iron deficiency anemia, especially those with blood in their stool, such as this patient. Definition: Colonic malignancy causes bleeding, which can be occult, and can result in iron deficiency anemia. Furthermore, African American individuals epidemiologically have a higher risk for colonic malignancy. Prevention: Prevention of colonic malignancy involves mitigating risk factors such as smoking cessation and dietary changes. Treatment: If this patient is diagnosed with colon cancer, treatment would likely include chemotherapy and, potentially, surgical resection if the stage of cancer is amenable. Differential: The differential diagnosis for this patient with microcytic anemia and gastrointestinal bleeding includes peptic ulcer disease, esophagitis, and inflammatory bowel disease. Colonoscopy will further aid in diagnosis.

wrongAnswers.A: Oral iron supplementation is incorrect. While the patient likely has iron deficiency, and would benefit from supplementation, it is most critical to work up the cause of the anemia via colonoscopy.
wrongAnswers.B: Proton pump inhibitor therapy is incorrect. This patient’s symptoms are most consistent with a lower gastrointestinal bleed due to the stool symptoms and less suggestive of peptic ulcer disease.
wrongAnswers.D: Sigmoidoscopy is not the most appropriate next step. Colonic malignancy must be ruled out given this patient’s symptoms. A colonoscopy examines the entire colon, while a sigmoidoscopy only examines the distal part of the colon. Limited evaluation of the distal colon increases the risk for missing lesions in the proximal colon.
wrongAnswers.E: No additional treatment; schedule follow up in 1 month is incorrect. This patient needs evaluation and diagnosis of his underlying condition.

explanationPanel.rule: Rectal bleeding with microcytic anemia requires colonoscopy to evaluate for colorectal cancer, even if hemorrhoids are seen.
explanationPanel.trap: Do not attribute iron-deficiency anemia to hemorrhoids without evaluating the colon.

layer4.rule: Rectal bleeding with microcytic anemia requires colonoscopy to evaluate for colorectal cancer, even if hemorrhoids are seen.
layer4.trap: Do not attribute iron-deficiency anemia to hemorrhoids without evaluating the colon.

questions.stem: Twenty-four hours after undergoing laparotomy for appendicitis, a 2-year-old girl receives morphine for pain management. Fifteen minutes later, she is somnolent. Her pulse is 80/min, respirations are 15/min, and blood pressure is 80/50 mm Hg. Pulse oximetry on room air shows an oxygen saturation of 60%. The patient is administered naloxone and immediately awakens; pulse oximetry on room air now shows an oxygen saturation of 100%, and all vital signs are within normal limits. A root cause analysis of this adverse event should be designed to examine which of the following?
questions.stemHtml: Twenty-four hours after undergoing laparotomy for appendicitis, a 2-year-old girl receives morphine for pain management. Fifteen minutes later, she is somnolent. Her pulse is 80/min, respirations are 15/min, and blood pressure is 80/50 mm Hg. Pulse oximetry on room air shows an oxygen saturation of 60%. The patient is administered naloxone and immediately awakens; pulse oximetry on room air now shows an oxygen saturation of 100%, and all vital signs are within normal limits. A root cause analysis of this adverse event should be designed to examine which of the following?
choices: Hiring policies and procedures at this hospital
System-based issues that led to the event
questions.subject: Ethics/Social Sciences

explanationPanel.correct: E. System-based issues that led to the event
explanationPanel.whyCorrect: Correct Answer: E. Educational Objective: Root cause analysis (RCA) of this adverse event should examine the system-based issues that led to the event. Rather than presuming the cause of an adverse event, RCA involves a multidisciplinary team defining and analyzing the problem to design a set of corrective actions based on the analysis. Key Concept: This patient appears to have received too much opioid medication, but the underlying cause of this adverse event is unclear. To determine the factors contributing to the adverse event, an RCA of the event should be conducted. Explanation: RCA involves determining the core systems-level issue(s) that leads to the chain reaction of events that culminate in the adverse event. There are several RCA strategies, including creating a timeline, surveying the controls in place that may have failed, and completing a risk tree analysis where the impact of each event is considered. Regardless of strategy, a typical RCA involves assembling a multidisciplinary team and meeting with this team regularly for a period of time. This team works to define and analyze the problem to design a set of corrective actions based on the analysis. Differential: Though it may seem more convenient to identify an individual responsible for an adverse event, most adverse events are driven by systems-level factors rather than the culpability of individual caregivers.

wrongAnswers.A: Culpability for the event and hiring policies and procedures at this hospital are incorrect. Most adverse events are driven by systems-level factors rather than the culpability of individual caregivers.
wrongAnswers.B: Ethics of pain management is incorrect. Managing postoperative pain is ethical, as adverse events are relatively uncommon and are outweighed by the benefit of allaying suffering.
wrongAnswers.C: Culpability for the event and hiring policies and procedures at this hospital are incorrect. Most adverse events are driven by systems-level factors rather than the culpability of individual caregivers.
wrongAnswers.D: Indications for laparotomy is incorrect. This patient’s somnolence is related to the administration of opioid pain medication, not the laparotomy itself.

explanationPanel.rule: Root cause analysis is designed to find system-based factors that led to an adverse event.
explanationPanel.trap: RCA is not primarily for assigning blame, judging pain management ethics, or evaluating hiring policies.

layer4.rule: Root cause analysis is designed to find system-based factors that led to an adverse event.
layer4.trap: RCA is not primarily for assigning blame, judging pain management ethics, or evaluating hiring policies.

questions.stem: A 58-year-old woman comes to the office because of a 1-day history of pain and redness of her right great toe. She says the pain woke her from sleep last night. She rates the pain as a 7 on a 10-point scale. She has not had fever and there is no discharge from the toe. The patient has never had a similar episode in the past. She has not recently changed her diet. Medical history is remarkable for hypertension, hyperlipidemia, and osteoarthritis. Medications are losartan, hydrochlorothiazide, simvastatin, ezetimibe, and acetaminophen. She does not smoke cigarettes, drink alcoholic beverages, or use other substances. She is 160 cm (5 ft 3 in) tall and weighs 61 kg (135 lb); BMI is 24 kg/m². Vital signs are within normal limits. Physical examination shows erythema, warmth, and tenderness to palpation at the metatarsophalangeal joint of the right great toe. Analysis of fluid aspirated from the right great toe is most likely to show which of the following?
questions.stemHtml: A 58-year-old woman comes to the office because of a 1-day history of pain and redness of her right great toe. She says the pain woke her from sleep last night. She rates the pain as a 7 on a 10-point scale. She has not had fever and there is no discharge from the toe. The patient has never had a similar episode in the past. She has not recently changed her diet. Medical history is remarkable for hypertension, hyperlipidemia, and osteoarthritis. Medications are losartan, hydrochlorothiazide, simvastatin, ezetimibe, and acetaminophen. She does not smoke cigarettes, drink alcoholic beverages, or use other substances. She is 160 cm (5 ft 3 in) tall and weighs 61 kg (135 lb); BMI is 24 kg/m². Vital signs are within normal limits. Physical examination shows erythema, warmth, and tenderness to palpation at the metatarsophalangeal joint of the right great toe. Analysis of fluid aspirated from the right great toe is most likely to show which of the following?
choices: Xanthochromic fluid with red blood cells
questions.subject: Rheumatology

explanationPanel.whyCorrect: Correct Answer: B. Educational Objective: This patient is most likely experiencing an episode of gout, an acute, monoarticular arthropathy resulting from an intra-articular inflammatory reaction to the precipitation of monosodium urate crystals within the joint space. Negatively birefringent, needle-shaped crystals are most likely to be shown on synovial fluid analysis in cases of gout. Evaluation: Gout may present with a warm, tender joint often with a palpable effusion or overlying edema. Definition: Gout classically presents following consumption of a purine-rich meal, especially red meat or seafood, often in men aged between 30 and 60 years, though it also affects women, as in this patient. Other risk factors for gout flares include trauma, surgery, dehydration, and use of diuretics. As uric acid accumulates, it crystallizes and precipitates in synovial fluid, which is identified as negatively birefringent, needle-shaped crystals on microscopy. The crystals trigger an inflammatory reaction in the joint characterized by the infiltration of leukocytes with resultant production of inflammatory cytokines and chemokines. Prevention: Gout flares may be avoided with dietary modifications and avoidance of thiazide or loop diuretics. Treatment: Treatment of acute gout consists of NSAIDs, colchicine, and/or corticosteroids. Chronic urate-lowering therapy with medications such as allopurinol, febuxostat, or probenecid may be considered in cases of frequent or disabling gout flares or those with tophi and structural joint damage. Differential: This patient presents with 1 day of pain and redness at the metatarsophalangeal joint of the right great toe, a common joint involved in cases of acute gout. Analysis of fluid aspirated from this joint is most likely to show negatively birefringent, needle-shaped crystals.

wrongAnswers.A: Increased uric acid concentration is not the most likely finding to be shown on analysis of aspirated joint fluid. Serum studies of this patient may show an increased uric acid concentration. Uric acid crystalizes and precipitates in the joint fluid in the form of monosodium urate.
wrongAnswers.C: Positively birefringent, rhomboid-shaped crystals is incorrect. Patients with calcium pyrophosphate crystal deposition disease may have positively birefringent crystals shown on synovial fluid analysis. Gout is characterized by negatively birefringent, needle-shaped crystals on joint fluid analysis.
wrongAnswers.D: Purulent fluid with gram-positive cocci is not the most likely finding to be shown on joint fluid analysis. Septic arthritis secondary to Staphylococcus aureus may have synovial fluid analysis that shows gram-positive cocci. S. aureus is the most common cause of septic arthritis in adults.
wrongAnswers.E: Xanthochromic fluid with gram-negative rods is incorrect. Septic arthritis secondary to a gram-negative rod, such as Pseudomonas aeruginosa, may have synovial fluid analysis with these findings. An acute gout flare is more likely in this patient.
wrongAnswers.F: Xanthochromic fluid with red blood cells is incorrect. Hemarthrosis may result in these synovial fluid findings. Hemarthrosis may develop from several different conditions including trauma, bleeding disorders, vascular disorders, and malignancy. Gout is the more likely cause of this patient’s symptoms.

explanationPanel.rule: Acute podagra from gout shows negatively birefringent needle-shaped monosodium urate crystals in synovial fluid.
explanationPanel.trap: Serum uric acid can be misleading during a flare and is not the diagnostic synovial-fluid finding.

layer4.rule: Acute podagra from gout shows negatively birefringent needle-shaped monosodium urate crystals in synovial fluid.
layer4.trap: Serum uric acid can be misleading during a flare and is not the diagnostic synovial-fluid finding.

Question: In addition to recommending smoking cessation, which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
questions.subject: Preventive Medicine

explanationPanel.whyCorrect: Correct Answer: B. Educational Objective: This patient has increased total cholesterol and LDL fraction. In determining whether lipid-decreasing therapy is appropriate, a patient’s atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease (ASCVD) risk should be calculated. Key Concept: For adults aged 40 to 75 years without known ASCVD or diabetes mellitus, 3– it is recommended to begin pharmacotherapy with a moderate to high intensity statin if the 10-year ASCVD risk is 7.5% or greater. Explanation: ASCVD risk is calculated by considering multiple modifiable and nonmodifiable factors. These include the presence of known ASCVD, age, the presence or absence of diabetes mellitus, biological sex, cholesterol concentrations (total, HDL, LDL), blood pressure and/or treatment for it, and smoking status. These variables estimate the 10-year risk for ASCVD including myocardial infarction, stroke, or death due to coronary artery disease or stroke. Differential: This patient’s generally good health status, apart from smoking history and increased cholesterol, suggests that her ASCVD risk should first be formally calculated to determine the appropriate next steps. She may not yet have sufficient benefit from statin therapy to merit initiation. Calculation is required before determining appropriate therapy.

questions.stem: A 32-year-old man comes to the clinic because of a 2-year history of fear that he is making inappropriate comments at work and an inability to stop worrying about them. The patient "constantly" worries that he is saying the "wrong thing," and he routinely asks coworkers and friends if his comments at work are appropriate. He says they frequently assure him that he did not say anything inappropriate, but they describe his constant checking as "obnoxious." The patient states that he wishes he could stop asking about his behavior, but he says "self-assurance" isn't enough; he "needs to be sure what others are thinking" about him. He has no history of serious illness and takes no medications. Both of his parents have generalized anxiety disorder. Physical examination of the patient discloses no abnormalities. On mental status examination, the patient has good insight and repeatedly asks questions during the interview such as, "Was that offensive?," "Did I over-share?," and "Am I saying that right?" Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

He has no history of serious illness and takes no medications. Both of his parents have generalized anxiety disorder. Physical examination of the patient discloses no abnormalities. On mental status examination, the patient has good insight and repeatedly asks questions during the interview such as, "Was that offensive?," "Did I over-share?," and "Am I saying that right?" Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.subject: Psychiatry

explanationPanel.whyCorrect: Correct Answer: C. Educational Objective: The most likely diagnosis for this patient is obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD), which manifests with recurrent, intrusive urges or thoughts (obsessions) that the patient tries to relieve or neutralize by repetitive rituals (compulsions). Some patients experience obsessions around social appropriateness. Evaluation: OCD manifests as recurrent, intrusive urges or thoughts (obsessions) that the patient tries to relieve or neutralize by repetitive rituals (compulsions). These symptoms are time-consuming and cause significant anxiety to and markedly impair the functioning of the patient. Definition: Compulsive checking can occur in response to fears about saying or doing the “wrong thing,” as in this patient. Other common obsession-compulsion symptoms are related to cleaning, symmetry, harm to self or others, completeness, and taboo thoughts or ideas. Prevention: As the precise cause is unknown, there is no universal prevention strategy for OCD. Treatment: OCD is commonly treated with selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors, clomipramine, or venlafaxine, in addition to cognitive behavioral therapy. Differential: Though this patient’s obsessions and compulsions focus on social appropriateness, his reassurance seeking is ego-dystonic rather than ego-syntonic, making OCD more likely than social anxiety disorder. Additionally, the underlying, deep fear in social anxiety disorder is typically social rejection, whereas this patient’s preoccupations are, more superficially, about social appropriateness. OCD and generalized anxiety disorder can also present similarly with obsessive worries. The worries are more varied in generalized anxiety disorder. Moreover, the patient’s response to the worries is more excessive and ego-dystonic in OCD but more logical and ego-syntonic in generalized anxiety disorder.

wrongAnswers.A: Dependent personality disorder is incorrect. Dependent personality disorder is a cluster C personality disorder in which the patient is excessively submissive. Personality disorders are chronic pervasive patterns of interpersonal dysfunction. This patient does not demonstrate a chronic pattern of submissiveness; instead, he demonstrates obsessive worries and compulsions.
wrongAnswers.B: Generalized anxiety disorder is incorrect. In generalized anxiety disorder, a patient’s worries are varied, more logical, and ego-syntonic. This patient’s worries are specifically focused on social appropriateness, and his response to the worries is more excessive and ego-dystonic.
wrongAnswers.D: Paranoid personality disorder is incorrect. Paranoid personality disorder is a cluster A personality disorder, the odd or eccentric cluster, characterized by a pervasive mistrust of others and viewing others as possessing malicious intent. Though this patient worries that others will judge what he says as socially inappropriate, he does not assume malicious intent.
wrongAnswers.E: Social anxiety disorder (social phobia) is incorrect. Though this patient’s obsessions and compulsions focus on social appropriateness, his reassurance seeking is ego-dystonic rather than ego-syntonic, making OCD more likely than social anxiety disorder. Furthermore, the underlying, deep fear in social anxiety disorder is typically social rejection, whereas this patient’s preoccupations are, more superficially, about social appropriateness.

explanationPanel.rule: OCD can present as ego-dystonic intrusive fears relieved by compulsive reassurance seeking/checking.
explanationPanel.trap: Social anxiety centers on fear of rejection/embarrassment, not ritualized checking to neutralize an obsession.

layer4.rule: OCD can present as ego-dystonic intrusive fears relieved by compulsive reassurance seeking/checking.

questions.stem: A 25-year-old man who is a veteran of the US Army comes to the office because of frequent nightmares and difficulty sleeping since he was sexually assaulted by two soldiers in his unit 3 years ago while on deployment. He says that in his nightmares, he re-experiences the assault and wakes up "sweating, with my heart beating really fast, and feeling like I was back in our old barracks." He has not had hypervigilance or avoidance of any specific situations. He says he enjoys his current job as a music promoter and has been promoted twice during the past year. He notes he has been happily married to a supportive spouse for the past 5 years, and they hope to have children soon. He has no history of serious illness and takes no medications. He appears well, appears his stated age, and is socially engaged. Vital signs are within normal limits. Physical examination discloses no abnormalities. Mental status examination discloses a euthymic affect. Which of the following is the most appropriate pharmacotherapy at this time?
