Family history is remarkable for postmenopausal breast cancer in her maternal aunt, heart disease in her paternal grandfather, and stroke in her maternal grandmother. The patient's mother has hypertension, and her father was recently diagnosed with coronary artery disease. The patient drinks two glasses of wine once monthly. She does not smoke cigarettes or use other substances. She is sexually active with a new male partner. She exercises regularly. Vital signs are within normal limits. Physical examination discloses no abnormalities; specimen for cervical cancer screening is collected today. After providing her with information about how to obtain the cervical cancer screening results, which of the following is the most appropriate screening recommendation for this patient?
questions.subject: Preventive Medicine

explanationPanel.whyCorrect:
Educational Objective: It is recommended that all patients be screened for HIV infection at least once in their lifetime. The most appropriate screening recommendation for this patient who is sexually active with a new partner is testing for HIV infection. Evaluation: HIV is a sexually transmitted infection that may be transmitted by sexual intercourse or contact exposure to body fluids such as breast milk or blood that has a detectable viral load. Definition: HIV is an enveloped, single-stranded RNA retrovirus that causes AIDS. The acute viral syndrome resembles an influenza-like illness that transitions into a prolonged dormant period, followed by the onset of immunodeficiency and opportunistic infections. Prevention: Infection with HIV may be prevented with use of barrier contraception and avoidance of body fluids with a detectable viral load.

Treatment: Treatment of HIV includes antiretroviral therapy. Antiretroviral therapy medications include nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitors, integrase strand transfer inhibitors, non-nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitors, and protease inhibitors. Differential: This patient is sexually active with a new male partner. The most appropriate screening recommendation for her is testing for HIV infection.

wrongAnswers.A: Breast cancer screening is incorrect. It is generally recommended to begin breast cancer screening at age 40 years. Screening for HIV infection is more appropriate for this patient.
wrongAnswers.B: Carotid artery stenosis screening is not the most appropriate recommendation. Screening for carotid artery stenosis in the asymptomatic patient is not recommended. The more appropriate recommendation is screening for HIV infection.
wrongAnswers.C: Colorectal cancer screening is incorrect. The general recommendation is to begin screening for colorectal cancer between ages 45 and 50 years. This patient is 35 years old.
wrongAnswers.E: Ovarian cancer screening is not the most appropriate recommendation. The general recommendation is to not screen for ovarian cancer in the asymptomatic patient. The more appropriate screening recommendation for this patient is testing for HIV infection.

explanationPanel.rule: All adults should have at least one HIV screen; new sexual partner makes HIV screening the best added screen here.
explanationPanel.trap: Breast/colon/ovarian/carotid screening is age- or risk-inappropriate in this 35-year-old.

layer4.rule: All adults should have at least one HIV screen; new sexual partner makes HIV screening the best added screen here.
layer4.trap: Breast/colon/ovarian/carotid screening is age- or risk-inappropriate in this 35-year-old.

questions.stem: A 25-year-old man comes to the office because of a 1-month history of shortness of breath; he has had a 6.8-kg (15-lb) weight loss during this period. Respirations are 22/min. A 1-cm, raised, irregular lesion is noted on the upper back. The lesion is black with gray areas. The remainder of the examination discloses no abnormalities. The physician suspects metastatic disease. A chest x-ray is most likely to show which of the following bilaterally in this patient?
questions.stemHtml: A 25-year-old man comes to the office because of a 1-month history of shortness of breath; he has had a 6.8-kg (15-lb) weight loss during this period. Respirations are 22/min. A 1-cm, raised, irregular lesion is noted on the upper back. The lesion is black with gray areas. The remainder of the examination discloses no abnormalities. The physician suspects metastatic disease. A chest x-ray is most likely to show which of the following bilaterally in this patient?
questions.subject: Dermatology

explanationPanel.whyCorrect:
Educational Objective: This patient presents with dyspnea and weight loss in the setting of a large, discolored, irregular skin lesion. Melanoma metastatic to the lungs is the most likely diagnosis. Most commonly, metastases to the lungs appear as multiple lung nodules. Evaluation: Malignant melanoma presents with a lesion that shows asymmetry, irregular-appearing borders, variable coloration, a diameter greater than 6 mm, and rapid evolution in characteristics. Definition: Malignant melanoma is a neoplasm of melanocytes and is highly associated with cumulative sun exposure. Subtypes include superficial spreading, nodular, lentigo maligna, and acral lentiginous. Melanoma can rapidly invade and metastasize, which carries a poor prognosis when diagnosed late. Common areas of metastasis include the liver, lungs, and brain. Prevention: Melanoma can be prevented with UV light protection. Treatment: For early melanoma, surgical treatment is curative. With increasing depth, risk for systemic metastasis and mortality increases, and additional therapies, such as sentinel lymph node biopsy, chemotherapy, or immunotherapy, must be considered.

Differential: As melanoma and many other malignancies metastasize to the lung, multiple lung nodules due to widespread deposition of tumor cells are most common. While infiltrative disease, pleural effusions, and pleural plaques can be seen in malignancy, they are less specifically associated with metastatic melanoma to the lungs.

wrongAnswers.A: Alveolar infiltrates is incorrect. Alveolar infiltrates are most common in pneumonia, acute respiratory distress syndrome, and pulmonary edema. They would be unexpected in malignant metastasis.
wrongAnswers.B: Interstitial infiltrates is incorrect. Interstitial infiltrates commonly occur as a result of inflammation or fibrosis of the interstitial tissues, such as that seen in interstitial lung disease, though they can also occur in pulmonary edema.
wrongAnswers.D: Pleural effusions is incorrect. Pleural effusions can occur in response to volume overload, pneumonia, or malignancy. Measurement of Light criteria and cytology can help differentiate the causes. Malignant pleural effusions are a less common result of melanoma metastasis.
wrongAnswers.E: Pleural plaques is incorrect. Pleural plaques are typically seen in pulmonary asbestosis, which presents with chronic cough, dyspnea, and progressive pulmonary fibrosis. They would be unexpected in metastatic melanoma.

explanationPanel.rule: Melanoma metastasis to lung classically appears as multiple bilateral pulmonary nodules.
explanationPanel.trap: Do not choose infiltrates or plaques; metastatic hematogenous disease forms nodules.

layer4.rule: Melanoma metastasis to lung classically appears as multiple bilateral pulmonary nodules.
layer4.trap: Do not choose infiltrates or plaques; metastatic hematogenous disease forms nodules.

questions.stem: A 14-year-old boy is brought to the ambulatory surgical center by his parents for elective surgical repair of an anterior cruciate ligament injury. Medical history is remarkable for reactive airway disease. His only medication is albuterol as needed. After his parents leave the examination room, the patient informs the physician that he uses electronic cigarettes containing nicotine and marijuana daily. The patient is at the 50th percentile for height and weight; BMI is at the 48th percentile. Vital signs are within normal limits. Physical examination discloses no unexpected abnormalities. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
questions.stemHtml: A 14-year-old boy is brought to the ambulatory surgical center by his parents for elective surgical repair of an anterior cruciate ligament injury. Medical history is remarkable for reactive airway disease. His only medication is albuterol as needed. After his parents leave the examination room, the patient informs the physician that he uses electronic cigarettes containing nicotine and marijuana daily. The patient is at the 50th percentile for height and weight; BMI is at the 48th percentile. Vital signs are within normal limits. Physical examination discloses no unexpected abnormalities. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
choices: Cancel the procedure and reschedule once the patient quits his substance use
Counsel the patient regarding preoperative risks of marijuana and nicotine use
Notify the patient's parents of his substance use
Schedule pulmonary function tests and reschedule the procedure after the results are obtained
questions.subject: Ethics/Social Sciences

explanationPanel.correct: B. Counsel the patient regarding preoperative risks of marijuana and nicotine use
explanationPanel.whyCorrect:
Educational Objective: This patient should be counseled regarding the preoperative risks of marijuana and nicotine use. Cannabis and nicotine use can increase perioperative risks. Key Concept: When patients possess surgical risk factors such as cannabis and nicotine use, they should be counseled about these risks. It is recommended that patients stop using cannabis at least 3 days, but ideally 2 weeks, prior to an elective procedure. Cessation of electronic cigarette use should also be advised. Explanation: Acute cannabis use can lead to several perioperative risks, including sympathetic hyperarousal, risk for coronary vasospasm, airway irritability, medication interactions with anesthetic agents, and body temperature dysregulation. Chronic cannabis use is associated with slight increases in myocardial ischemia, venous thromboembolism, cerebral infarction, respiratory failure, acute kidney injury, hospital-acquired infection, and procedure-related complications. Nicotine use is also associated with perioperative risks including infections, prolonged wound healing, myocardial infarction, respiratory complications, prolonged hospital stays, and mortality. Differential: For patients with multiple severe perioperative risk factors, physicians may consider withholding a procedure per the ethical principle of nonmaleficence. Though

cannabis and nicotine use increase perioperative risks, neither are strict contraindications for most procedures, particularly in patients who are otherwise healthy.

wrongAnswers.A: Cancel the procedure and reschedule once the patient quits his substance use is incorrect. Though cannabis and nicotine use increase perioperative risks, neither are strict contraindications for most procedures.
wrongAnswers.C: Notify the patient's parents of his substance use is incorrect. In most states, physicians are permitted and encouraged to maintain confidentiality concerning substance use, reproductive health services, and mental health services.
wrongAnswers.D: Schedule pulmonary function tests and reschedule the procedure after the results are obtained is unnecessary. This patient is young and has normal vital signs and no abnormalities on physical examination, so there is minimal evidence he may have respiratory dysfunction.

explanationPanel.rule: Adolescents using cannabis/nicotine before elective surgery should be counseled on perioperative risk while maintaining confidentiality.
explanationPanel.trap: Do not notify parents for confidential substance-use disclosure unless there is imminent serious harm.

layer4.rule: Adolescents using cannabis/nicotine before elective surgery should be counseled on perioperative risk while maintaining confidentiality.

questions.stem: A 6-week-old male infant is brought to the office by his mother 5 days after she noticed a spot on his cheek that is increasing in size. The spot was not present at the patient’s last well-child examination 2 weeks ago. He was born at term following an uncomplicated pregnancy and spontaneous vaginal delivery. Apgar scores were 9 and 10 at 1 and 5 minutes, respectively. Growth and development are appropriate for age. He is exclusively breast-fed. A photograph of the lesion is shown. The lesion is easily compressed and is not ulcerated. No other abnormalities are noted. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.stemHtml: A 6-week-old male infant is brought to the office by his mother 5 days after she noticed a spot on his cheek that is increasing in size. The spot was not present at the patient’s last well-child examination 2 weeks ago. He was born at term following an uncomplicated pregnancy and spontaneous vaginal delivery. Apgar scores were 9 and 10 at 1 and 5 minutes, respectively. Growth and development are appropriate for age. He is exclusively breast-fed. A photograph of the lesion is shown. The lesion is easily compressed and is not ulcerated. No other abnormalities are noted. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.subject: Dermatology

explanationPanel.whyCorrect:
Educational Objective: Infantile hemangiomas are benign vascular tumors that are often absent at birth, appear during the first weeks of life, and enlarge during early infancy before gradual involution. They are classically bright red, well-demarcated, and compressible.

Evaluation: This 6-week-old infant has a new, enlarging, easily compressible red lesion on the cheek without ulceration or systemic findings, which is most consistent with an uncomplicated infantile hemangioma.

Definition: Infantile hemangiomas are proliferations of endothelial cells. Most require observation only unless they obstruct vision/airway, ulcerate, bleed, or cause functional/cosmetic complications.

Differential: Capillary malformations are typically flat, noncompressible, and present at birth. Erythema toxicum and pustular melanosis are transient newborn rashes. Pyogenic granulomas are friable, rapidly bleeding vascular papules. Shagreen patches are connective-tissue nevi associated with tuberous sclerosis.

wrongAnswers.A: Capillary malformation is incorrect. Capillary malformations, such as port-wine stains, are usually present at birth, flat, and noncompressible rather than newly appearing and enlarging after birth.
wrongAnswers.B: Erythema toxicum is incorrect. Erythema toxicum is a transient neonatal rash with erythematous macules/papules and pustules, not a solitary compressible vascular papule.
wrongAnswers.D: Pustular melanosis is incorrect. Transient neonatal pustular melanosis presents at birth with pustules that leave hyperpigmented macules, not an enlarging red compressible lesion.
wrongAnswers.E: Pyogenic granuloma is incorrect. Pyogenic granulomas are friable vascular papules that bleed easily, unlike this uncomplicated infantile hemangioma.
wrongAnswers.F: Shagreen patch is incorrect. Shagreen patches are thickened connective-tissue plaques associated with tuberous sclerosis, not compressible vascular lesions.

explanationPanel.rule: Infantile hemangioma appears after birth, enlarges in early infancy, and is bright red/compressible.
explanationPanel.trap: Capillary malformations are usually flat, noncompressible, and present at birth.

layer4.rule: Infantile hemangioma appears after birth, enlarges in early infancy, and is bright red/compressible.
layer4.trap: Capillary malformations are usually flat, noncompressible, and present at birth.

questions.stem: The physician in charge at a skilled nursing care facility instructs a nurse to administer intramuscular influenza vaccine to specific older residents. The vaccine comes in multiple-dose vials that are capped with a rubber stopper. In describing the protocol, the physician tells the nurse to obtain consent, check for allergies, and swab the rubber stopper of the vial and each skin injection site with alcohol before administering the vaccine. Which of the following additional aseptic procedures is most appropriate in this situation?
questions.stemHtml: The physician in charge at a skilled nursing care facility instructs a nurse to administer intramuscular influenza vaccine to specific older residents. The vaccine comes in multiple-dose vials that are capped with a rubber stopper. In describing the protocol, the physician tells the nurse to obtain consent, check for allergies, and swab the rubber stopper of the vial and each skin injection site with alcohol before administering the vaccine. Which of the following additional aseptic procedures is most appropriate in this situation?
choices: Reuse the vial and syringe, but change the needle for each patient
Reuse the vial, but use a new syringe and needle for each patient
Reuse the vial, syringe, and needle for each patient, but do not allow the needle to touch an unsterile surface
Reuse the vial, syringe, and needle for each patient, but wipe the skin and needle with alcohol between injections
Use a new vial, syringe, and needle for each patient
questions.subject: Preventive Medicine

explanationPanel.correct: B. Reuse the vial, but use a new syringe and needle for each patient
explanationPanel.whyCorrect: Educational Objective: It is important that caregivers follow infection control protocols when administering vaccines. Though needles and syringes should be discarded after a single use, noncontaminated multiple-dose vaccine vials can be reused. This nurse can reuse the vial, but use a new syringe and needle for each patient. Key Concept: CDC provides clear guidelines for infection control during vaccinations. Explanation: New syringes and needles should be used for each patient to decrease disease transmission risk. For multiple-dose vials, caregivers should follow proper technique to avoid contamination. If vials are not clearly contaminated, residual doses can be administered until the expiration date. Differential: Some vials are single-dose vials, which should be discarded after the vaccine has been withdrawn.

wrongAnswers.A: Reuse the vial and syringe, but change the needle for each patient; reuse the vial, syringe, and needle for each patient, but do not allow the needle to touch an unsterile surface; reuse the vial, syringe, and needle for each patient, but wipe the skin and needle with alcohol between injections; and use a new vial, syringe, and needle for each patient are incorrect. It is not necessary to discard uncontaminated multiple-dose vials. It is necessary to use new needles and syringes.
wrongAnswers.C: Reuse the vial and syringe, but change the needle for each patient; reuse the vial, syringe, and needle for each patient, but do not allow the needle to touch an unsterile surface; reuse the vial, syringe, and needle for each patient, but wipe the skin and needle with alcohol between injections; and use a new vial, syringe, and needle for each patient are incorrect. It is not necessary to discard uncontaminated multiple-dose vials. It is necessary to use new needles and syringes.
wrongAnswers.D: Reuse the vial and syringe, but change the needle for each patient; reuse the vial, syringe, and needle for each patient, but do not allow the needle to touch an unsterile surface; reuse the vial, syringe, and needle for each patient, but wipe the skin and needle with alcohol between injections; and use a new vial, syringe, and needle for each patient are incorrect. It is not necessary to discard uncontaminated multiple-dose vials. It is necessary to use new needles and syringes.
wrongAnswers.E: Reuse the vial and syringe, but change the needle for each patient; reuse the vial, syringe, and needle for each patient, but do not allow the needle to touch an unsterile surface; reuse the vial, syringe, and needle for each patient, but wipe the skin and needle with alcohol between injections; and use a new vial, syringe, and needle for each patient are incorrect. It is not necessary to discard uncontaminated multiple-dose vials. It is necessary to use new needles and syringes.

explanationPanel.rule: For multidose vaccine vials, reuse the uncontaminated vial but use a new sterile syringe and needle for every patient.
explanationPanel.trap: Changing only the needle still reuses a contaminated syringe and risks transmission.

questions.subject: Hematology/Oncology

explanationPanel.whyCorrect: Educational Objective: This patient presents with acute pain and discoloration in the right great toe after heparin exposure and is found to have arterial thrombosis and severe thrombocytopenia. This patient’s presentation is consistent with heparin-induced thrombocytopenia (HIT), and heparin should be discontinued. The patient should be started on argatroban for anticoagulation. Evaluation: HIT is an immune-mediated reaction to heparin that results in a decrease in platelet count and a hypercoagulable state. The pathophysiology involves the formation of IgG antibodies against platelet factor IV (calcium) and heparin complexes. This creates a consumptive process, drastically decreasing platelet count, and generates thrombin, which results in thrombosis. Definition: HIT classically presents with a platelet count drop of more than 50% 5 to 10 days after initiation of heparin. Thrombosis is a common complication and can be seen in both arteries and veins. Prevention: Prevention of HIT involves minimizing exposure to unfractionated heparin. Treatment: Treatment of HIT involves immediate cessation of heparin products and initiation of a nonheparin anticoagulant. Argatroban is a direct thrombin inhibitor that is often used for treatment of HIT. Differential: The differential diagnosis for HIT includes disseminated intravascular coagulation and thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura. However, in this patient with recent heparin exposure, a significant decrease in platelet count, and arterial thrombosis, HIT is high on the differential diagnosis and should be empirically treated.

wrongAnswers.B: Discontinue heparin and initiate enoxaparin and discontinue heparin and initiate warfarin are incorrect. While discontinuing heparin is correct, enoxaparin is a low-molecular-weight heparin product that should not be used in a suspected case of HIT. Warfarin initiation creates a hypercoagulable state, which would worsen the hypercoagulability caused by HIT.
wrongAnswers.C: Discontinue heparin and initiate enoxaparin and discontinue heparin and initiate warfarin are incorrect. While discontinuing heparin is correct, enoxaparin is a low-molecular-weight heparin product that should not be used in a suspected case of HIT. Warfarin initiation creates a hypercoagulable state, which would worsen the hypercoagulability caused by HIT.
wrongAnswers.D: Discontinue oxycodone and initiate allopurinol, discontinue oxycodone and initiate gabapentin, and discontinue oxycodone and initiate morphine are incorrect as this patient likely has HIT, and heparin must be discontinued immediately.
wrongAnswers.E: Discontinue oxycodone and initiate allopurinol, discontinue oxycodone and initiate gabapentin, and discontinue oxycodone and initiate morphine are incorrect as this patient likely has HIT, and heparin must be discontinued immediately.
wrongAnswers.F: Discontinue oxycodone and initiate allopurinol, discontinue oxycodone and initiate gabapentin, and discontinue oxycodone and initiate morphine are incorrect as this patient likely has HIT, and heparin must be discontinued immediately.

explanationPanel.rule: HIT = platelet fall after heparin plus thrombosis; stop all heparin and start a nonheparin anticoagulant such as argatroban.
explanationPanel.trap: Do not switch to enoxaparin or start warfarin acutely; both are unsafe in active HIT.

questions.stem: A 9-month-old boy is brought to the physician for a well-child examination. His mother reports that he has had a slightly decreased appetite and activity level during the past month but has been otherwise well. His temperature is 37.5°C (99.5°F), pulse is 155/min, and blood pressure is 109/60 mm Hg. Examination shows a firm, irregular, nontender mass in the right side of the abdomen. An abdominal CT scan shows an 8-cm retroperitoneal mass displacing the right kidney inferiorly. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.stemHtml: A 9-month-old boy is brought to the physician for a well-child examination. His mother reports that he has had a slightly decreased appetite and activity level during the past month but has been otherwise well. His temperature is 37.5°C (99.5°F), pulse is 155/min, and blood pressure is 109/60 mm Hg. Examination shows a firm, irregular, nontender mass in the right side of the abdomen. An abdominal CT scan shows an 8-cm retroperitoneal mass displacing the right kidney inferiorly. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.subject: Pediatrics/Neonatology

explanationPanel.whyCorrect:
Educational Objective: This patient presents with a firm, irregular, mass and is found to have an 8-cm retroperitoneal mass displacing the right kidney inferiorly. This is most suggestive of neuroblastoma, a malignant tumor arising from neural crest cells. Evaluation: Neuroblastoma is the third most common childhood cancer and is the most common extracranial solid malignancy in children. It is a malignancy derived from neural crest cells that form the peripheral sympathetic nervous system. It typically presents with a large abdominal mass; however, given that it can affect any neural cells, it can present elsewhere, such as the thorax and vertebrae. Definition: Diagnosis of neuroblastoma begins clinically with a thorough physical examination and is further corroborated by imaging studies such as a CT scan and laboratory studies that will show increased urine catecholamines. Prevention: There are no known methods to prevent neuroblastoma. Treatment: Treatment depends on the case and the patient. Some patients have disease that is amenable to surgical resection, while others have more severe disease and must undergo chemotherapy, radiation, or even myeloablative therapy with stem cell transplant.

Differential: The differential for this young patient with decreased activity level is initially very broad. Once the physical examination is performed, this narrows the differential to causes of a large abdominal mass in a child. Furthermore, the CT scan of the abdomen shows that this mass is retroperitoneal, likely coming from the adrenal gland.

wrongAnswers.B: Non-Hodgkin lymphoma is incorrect. Non-Hodgkin lymphoma can present with a mass; however, it is typically a lymph node, and it would be abnormal to be 8 cm in size and seated just superior to the kidney. This patient is most likely presenting with a neuroblastoma of the right adrenal gland.
wrongAnswers.C: Pheochromocytoma is incorrect. While pheochromocytoma can present with an adrenal mass, it would be atypical to be 8 cm in size. Furthermore, pheochromocytomas typically present with systemic symptoms, such as tachycardia and hypertension.
wrongAnswers.D: Rhabdomyosarcoma is incorrect. Rhabdomyosarcoma can present with a large mass. It is typically a skeletomuscular soft tissue lesion and would not appear in the adrenal gland.
wrongAnswers.E: Teratoma is incorrect. A teratoma is a germ cell tumor that is most often mature and cystic, composed of differentiated elements that would be seen on CT scan of the abdomen. It is more likely that this patient has a neuroblastoma.

explanationPanel.rule: Infant abdominal retroperitoneal/adrenal mass displacing kidney = neuroblastoma.
explanationPanel.trap: Wilms tumor arises from kidney; neuroblastoma displaces the kidney.

layer4.rule: Infant abdominal retroperitoneal/adrenal mass displacing kidney = neuroblastoma.
layer4.trap: Wilms tumor arises from kidney; neuroblastoma displaces the kidney.

questions.stem: A 41-year-old man comes to the office for a follow-up examination. He has schizophrenia, and his symptoms have been well managed since he began taking haloperidol 2 years ago. Recently, auditory hallucinations have been mild; he hears "an occasional whisper," but it does not cause distress. He "self-medicated" with cocaine in the past but has not used it during the past 2 years. He recently married. He plans to complete a masters program in computer science this year. Vital signs are within normal limits. Physical examination discloses no abnormalities. On mental status examination, he has a euthymic mood and congruent affect. Thoughts are linear and well organized. Which of the following studies is most appropriate to obtain periodically to monitor this patient’s long-term care?
questions.stemHtml: A 41-year-old man comes to the office for a follow-up examination. He has schizophrenia, and his symptoms have been well managed since he began taking haloperidol 2 years ago. Recently, auditory hallucinations have been mild; he hears "an occasional whisper," but it does not cause distress. He "self-medicated" with cocaine in the past but has not used it during the past 2 years. He recently married. He plans to complete a masters program in computer science this year. Vital signs are within normal limits. Physical examination discloses no abnormalities. On mental status examination, he has a euthymic mood and congruent affect. Thoughts are linear and well organized. Which of the following studies is most appropriate to obtain periodically to monitor this patient’s long-term care?
questions.subject: Psychiatry

explanationPanel.whyCorrect:
Educational Objective: The chronic use of dopamine-2 (D2) antagonists (particularly high-potency D2 antagonists such as haloperidol) can lead to tardive dyskinesia. Physicians should periodically obtain involuntary movement assessments to monitor for this adverse effect, which is the most appropriate study to monitor this patient’s long-term care. Key Concept: Patients on antipsychotic medications should be periodically monitored for the development of tardive dyskinesia. The most commonly used involuntary movement assessment is the Abnormal Involuntary Movement Scale. Explanation: The chronic use of D2 antagonists (particularly high-potency D2 antagonists such as haloperidol) may upregulate D2 receptors in the basal ganglia, leading to dopamine receptor hypersensitivity and consequent tardive dyskinesia. Tardive dyskinesia is a syndrome of involuntary movements (eg, lip smacking, choreoathetoid movements of the tongue).

Differential: Though antipsychotics have been increasingly associated with cognitive impairment, cognitive assessments are not yet considered routine for patients who chronically use antipsychotics. Antipsychotics are also associated with cytopenias, though adverse hematological effects secondary to antipsychotics other than clozapine are not common enough to warrant routine complete blood count monitoring. In addition to involuntary movement assessments, patients on atypical antipsychotics (eg, olanzapine) should also undergo regular monitoring of BMI, waist circumference, hemoglobin A1c, fasting plasma glucose, and fasting lipid panels.

wrongAnswers.A: Cognitive assessment is incorrect. Though antipsychotics have been increasingly associated with cognitive impairment, cognitive assessments are not yet considered routine for patients who chronically use antipsychotics.
wrongAnswers.B: Complete blood count is incorrect. Antipsychotics are also associated with cytopenias, though adverse hematological effects secondary to antipsychotics other than clozapine are not common enough to warrant routine complete blood count monitoring.
wrongAnswers.D: MRI of the brain is incorrect. Though antipsychotics have been increasingly associated with structural brain changes, routine neuroimaging is not indicated. Neuroimaging is costly and may not influence clinical management.
wrongAnswers.E: Serum TSH concentration is incorrect. Antipsychotics may occasionally affect thyroid function, but routine TSH monitoring is not indicated.
wrongAnswers.F: Urine toxicology screening is incorrect. In patients with a remote history of substance use disorder, periodic assessment of the patient’s self-report of substance use is sufficient.

explanationPanel.rule: Chronic high-potency antipsychotic therapy requires periodic involuntary-movement screening for tardive dyskinesia.
explanationPanel.trap: CBC monitoring is routine for clozapine, not haloperidol.

layer4.rule: Chronic high-potency antipsychotic therapy requires periodic involuntary-movement screening for tardive dyskinesia.
layer4.trap: CBC monitoring is routine for clozapine, not haloperidol.

questions.subject: Nephrology/Urology

explanationPanel.correct: E. Type I renal tubular acidosis
explanationPanel.whyCorrect: Educational Objective: There are three main types of renal tubular acidosis, all of which prevent the kidneys from either absorbing bicarbonate or excreting titratable acid in the form of NH4+. This patient has type I (distal) renal tubular acidosis, which involves impaired secretion of protons by the α-intercalated cells of the collecting tubule. Evaluation: Type I renal tubular acidosis often presents with a normal anion gap metabolic acidosis and is commonly associated with hypokalemia. Definition: Renal tubular acidosis results in a hyperchloremic, non-anion gap metabolic acidosis from the dysregulation of the renal tubules causing the loss of bicarbonate or inability to excrete hydrogen ions. The metabolic acidosis may present with a compensatory respiratory alkalosis, manifesting as tachypnea and shortness of breath. Type I renal tubular acidosis results in a progressive hydrogen ion retention due to impaired hydrogen ion secretion in the distal nephron which often results with a urine pH of 5.5 or greater. Prevention: There is no definitive way to prevent type I renal tubular acidosis. The most common cause in children is due to genetic factors. Treatment: Treatment of type I renal tubular acidosis includes alkali therapy. Administration of bicarbonate or citrate often will result in correction of hypokalemia if present. Differential: The patient in this case is presenting with a non-anion gap metabolic acidosis with hypokalemia and a urine pH of 7.2. These findings make type I renal tubular acidosis the most likely diagnosis.

wrongAnswers.A: Alport syndrome is incorrect. Collagen, type IV is defective in Alport syndrome, causing dysfunction of the glomerular basement membrane. Alport syndrome may result in nephritic syndrome.
wrongAnswers.B: Gitelman syndrome is not the most likely diagnosis. Defects in the sodium-chloride cotransporter results in Gitelman syndrome, a renal tubular defect characterized by hypokalemia, hypomagnesemia, metabolic alkalosis, and hypocalciuria. The patient in this case is presenting with a non-anion gap metabolic acidosis more consistent with type I renal tubular acidosis.
wrongAnswers.C: Juxtaglomerular cell hyperplasia is incorrect. Juxtaglomerular cell hyperplasia occurs in Bartter syndrome. Bartter syndrome is characterized by defects in the sodium-potassium-2 chloride transporter causing abnormal reabsorption in the thick ascending limb of the loop of Henle. The syndrome results in decreased serum potassium concentration, metabolic alkalosis, and hypercalciuria.
wrongAnswers.D: Liddle syndrome is not the most likely diagnosis. Decreased renin and decreased aldosterone concentrations are typically identified in patients with Liddle syndrome, a rare congenital disorder associated with defects in collecting tubule sodium channels. Patients with Liddle syndrome typically present in childhood with hypertension, hypokalemia, and metabolic alkalosis.

explanationPanel.rule: Normal anion gap metabolic acidosis + hypokalemia + urine pH >5.5 = type I distal RTA.
explanationPanel.trap: Gitelman/Bartter/Liddle cause metabolic alkalosis, not acidosis.

layer4.rule: Normal anion gap metabolic acidosis + hypokalemia + urine pH >5.5 = type I distal RTA.
layer4.trap: Gitelman/Bartter/Liddle cause metabolic alkalosis, not acidosis.

questions.stem: A 32-year-old woman is admitted to the intensive care unit after she was involved in a motor vehicle collision. She was intubated and mechanically ventilated at the scene by emergency services personnel when they determined that she was not breathing. CT scan of the head shows a large subdural hematoma and two areas of intracerebral bleeding. The subdural hematoma is evacuated. On postoperative day 2, the patient remains comatose and ventilator dependent. Blood pressure is 110/60 mm Hg. There are no spontaneous respirations. The surgical site is clean and intact. On neurologic examination, the pupils are fixed at the midposition and not reactive to light; there are no corneal reflexes. Doll's eye (oculocephalic) reflex is absent. There is no gag reflex with suctioning. The patient does not respond to painful stimuli. The remainder of the examination discloses no abnormalities. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step when considering whether to withdraw life support from this patient?

CT scan of the head shows a large subdural hematoma and two areas of intracerebral bleeding. The subdural hematoma is evacuated. On postoperative day 2, the patient remains comatose and ventilator dependent. Blood pressure is 110/60 mm Hg. There are no spontaneous respirations. The surgical site is clean and intact. On neurologic examination, the pupils are fixed at the midposition and not reactive to light; there are no corneal reflexes. Doll's eye (oculocephalic) reflex is absent. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step when considering whether to withdraw life support from this patient?
choices: Agreement by the hospital ethics committee that life support should be discontinued
Exclusion of medical conditions that may confound clinical assessment of brain death
Legal documentation of the patient's wish to not receive life support measures
Presence of a surrogate decision-maker who agrees with discontinuing life support
questions.subject: Ethics/Social Sciences

explanationPanel.correct: B. Exclusion of medical conditions that may confound clinical assessment of brain death
explanationPanel.whyCorrect:
Educational Objective: Brain death, or the permanent loss of all brainstem functions, is diagnosed by neurologic examination and apnea test. Confounding medical conditions should be excluded prior to diagnosing brain death, and this is the most appropriate next step for this patient. Key Concept: According to the American Academy of Neurology, brain death is defined as the permanent loss of all brain stem functions. Brain death commonly occurs after an acute catastrophic brain injury secondary to intracranial trauma, intracranial hemorrhage, or cardiovascular collapse. Brain death can be diagnosed by a neurologic examination (showing absent cranial nerve reflexes and a lack of response to central pain) and an apnea test (showing an absence of respiratory drive). Explanation: Several conditions can confound the diagnosis of brain death, including severe electrolyte disturbances, central nervous system depressant intoxication, sedating or neuromuscular blocking agents, high cervical spinal cord injuries, Guillain-Barré

syndrome, and botulism. These conditions should be excluded prior to diagnosing brain death. A patient with brain death is clinically and legally dead. As such, mechanical ventilation may be withdrawn without family permission. Hospital policies may vary to some extent on the exact timing of a brain death examination, and physicians should be familiar with the standard of care in their individual settings. Differential: Several medical conditions can confound brain death diagnosis. Ancillary tests such as EEG and angiography can be used when the diagnosis is uncertain.

wrongAnswers.A: Agreement by the hospital ethics committee that life support should be discontinued, legal documentation of the patient's wish to not receive life support measures, and presence of a surrogate decision-maker who agrees with discontinuing life support are inappropriate. After brain death is verified, the patient is considered legally and clinically dead, and it is ethically supportable to withdraw life support without consulting with surrogate decision-makers, advance directives, or ethics committees.
wrongAnswers.C: Agreement by the hospital ethics committee that life support should be discontinued, legal documentation of the patient's wish to not receive life support measures, and presence of a surrogate decision-maker who agrees with discontinuing life support are inappropriate. After brain death is verified, the patient is considered legally and clinically dead, and it is ethically supportable to withdraw life support without consulting with surrogate decision-makers, advance directives, or ethics committees.
wrongAnswers.D: Agreement by the hospital ethics committee that life support should be discontinued, legal documentation of the patient's wish to not receive life support measures, and presence of a surrogate decision-maker who agrees with discontinuing life support are inappropriate. After brain death is verified, the patient is considered legally and clinically dead, and it is ethically supportable to withdraw life support without consulting with surrogate decision-makers, advance directives, or ethics committees.

explanationPanel.rule: Before declaring brain death, exclude confounders such as sedatives, paralysis, electrolyte derangements, and hypothermia.
explanationPanel.trap: Family consent or ethics approval is not the next step before confirming brain death.

layer4.rule: Before declaring brain death, exclude confounders such as sedatives, paralysis, electrolyte derangements, and hypothermia.
layer4.trap: Family consent or ethics approval is not the next step before confirming brain death.

questions.stem: A 2-month-old boy is brought to the emergency department by his parents 30 minutes after he stopped breathing and turned blue while the parents were laying him down for a nap. They say he resumed breathing after 25 seconds when they rubbed his chest. He has a 1-day history of cough, nasal congestion, and decreased feeding and activity. He has not had fever. He has no history of serious illness and receives no medications. Vaccinations are up-to-date. Temperature is 37.9°C (100.3°F), pulse is 140/min, respirations are 65/min, and blood pressure is 100/70 mm Hg. Pulse oximetry on room air shows an oxygen saturation of 90%. Examination shows nasal congestion and rhinorrhea. Diffuse wheezes are heard bilaterally, and there are subcostal retractions. The remainder of the examination discloses no abnormalities. Chest x-ray is shown. Which of the following is most likely to confirm the etiology of this patient's episode?

They say he resumed breathing after 25 seconds when they rubbed his chest. He has a 1-day history of cough, nasal congestion, and decreased feeding and activity. He has not had fever. He has no history of serious illness and receives no medications. Vaccinations are up-to-date. Temperature is 37.9°C (100.3°F), pulse is 140/min, respirations are 65/min, and blood pressure is 100/70 mm Hg. Pulse oximetry on room air shows an oxygen saturation of 90%. Examination shows nasal congestion and rhinorrhea. Diffuse wheezes are heard bilaterally, and there are subcostal retractions. The remainder of the examination discloses no abnormalities. Chest x-ray is shown. Which of the following is most likely to confirm the etiology of this patient's episode?
choices: Complete blood count with differential and blood culture
questions.subject: Pulmonology

explanationPanel.correct: E. Nasopharyngeal polymerase chain reaction test
explanationPanel.whyCorrect:
Educational Objective: Respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) is the likely diagnosis of this patient with nasal congestion, rhinorrhea, respiratory distress, wheezing, hypoxia, and apneic episodes. The diagnosis of RSV is confirmed with a nasopharyngeal polymerase chain reaction test. Evaluation: RSV commonly present in infants with fever, tachypnea, rhinorrhea, and wheezing, with severe cases resulting in respiratory distress and apneic episodes.

Definition: RSV may result in a mild, self-limited cold. However, RSV often causes bronchiolitis, a lower respiratory tract infection, in children younger than 2 years. Commonly, RSV bronchiolitis starts with a viral prodrome of fever, nasal congestion, and rhinorrhea followed by cough, dyspnea, and lethargy as inflammation progresses to the lower airway. Severe disease is marked by the presence of increased respiratory effort (eg, tachypnea, accessory muscle use, intercostal retractions, nasal flaring, grunting), hypoxemia, and apnea. Prevention: Prevention of RSV includes the use of good hand hygiene, avoiding sick contacts, disinfecting surfaces, and remaining up-to-date on vaccinations. Treatment: For mild cases, treatment is supportive. Hospitalization and respiratory support is warranted for severe cases with respiratory distress, hypoxia, and apneic episodes. Differential: An EEG could be used to determine whether this patient’s apneic episode was related to seizure activity, but it would not explain his rhinorrhea and respiratory distress. A diagnosis of RSV best explains his complete presentation, and nasopharyngeal polymerase chain reaction test is most likely to confirm this diagnosis.

wrongAnswers.A: Complete blood count with differential and blood culture is incorrect. A complete blood count with differential may show leukocytosis in the setting of an RSV infection, but this would be a nonspecific finding. Blood cultures are used in sepsis to rule out bacteremia, which often presents with fever, altered mental status, and hypotension. They are not useful in the diagnosis of a viral infection.
wrongAnswers.B: ECG is incorrect. An ECG could be used to identify cardiac causes of hypoxia, such as myocardial ischemia or congenital heart disease, although ECG would be nonspecific in the latter. A cardiac cause would not explain this patient’s rhinorrhea, nasal congestion, low-grade fever, and period of apnea.
wrongAnswers.C: EEG is incorrect. EEG is often used in the setting of epileptiform activity to determine whether the activity is caused by a seizure. In this case, an EEG could be used to determine if the patient’s apneic episode was related to seizure activity. However, RSV is a much more likely cause of apnea in this patient with rhinorrhea, nasal congestion, and respiratory distress.
wrongAnswers.D: Esophageal pH probe study is incorrect. Esophageal pH probe studies are used to determine the severity of gastroesophageal reflux. Severe gastroesophageal reflux may be associated with aspiration, which can result in fever, cough, and respiratory distress. However, it would most commonly be associated with a consolidation in the right lower lobe on chest x-ray, which is not seen in this patient.
wrongAnswers.F: Stool culture for Clostridium botulinum is incorrect. C. botulinum is the bacteria that causes botulism, an acute disease of the neuromuscular junction that results in rapidly progressive, symmetric hypotonia and hyporeflexia, often in a descending manner. This patient does not have signs and symptoms suggestive of botulism as an underlying diagnosis.

explanationPanel.rule: Infant bronchiolitis with wheeze, hypoxia, and apnea is confirmed by nasopharyngeal PCR for RSV.
explanationPanel.trap: Do not treat it as BRUE/seizure/GERD when respiratory viral symptoms and distress are present.

layer4.rule: Infant bronchiolitis with wheeze, hypoxia, and apnea is confirmed by nasopharyngeal PCR for RSV.
layer4.trap: Do not treat it as BRUE/seizure/GERD when respiratory viral symptoms and distress are present.

questions.stem: A 46-year-old woman comes to the clinic because of a 6-month history of poor sleep and night sweats. Previously her sleep pattern was normal. She falls asleep easily but frequently wakes perspiring and feeling overheated. The night sweats typically occur several times nightly, and happen most frequently after drinking two glasses of red wine before bed, which she does 3 to 4 nights weekly. The patient reports no changes in appetite or mood. She has no history of serious illness, and her only medication is a multivitamin. Menses occur at regular 30- to 32-day intervals. She does not smoke cigarettes or use any other substances. She is sexually active with one female partner and has no pain with intercourse. The patient drinks three cups of coffee daily and exercises for 30 minutes daily. She is 162 cm (5 ft 4 in) tall and weighs 61 kg (134 lb); BMI is 23 kg/m². Vital signs are within normal limits. She appears fatigued. Physical examination discloses no abnormalities. Results of complete blood count and serum TSH concentration are within the reference ranges. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

She appears fatigued. Physical examination discloses no abnormalities. Results of complete blood count and serum TSH concentration are within the reference ranges. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
questions.subject: Gynecology

explanationPanel.whyCorrect:
Educational Objective: This 46-year-old patient’s poor sleep, hot flashes, night sweats, and vasomotor sensitivity to alcoholic beverages suggest perimenopause. Lifestyle counseling regarding management of the symptoms and changes in her body is most appropriate. Evaluation: Perimenopausal symptoms generally occur in patients aged 40 years or older, and include, but are not limited to, hot flashes and sleep disturbances, along with sensitivity to alcoholic beverages. Irregular menses may occur as well in the perimenopausal period. Definition: As hormone concentrations of estrogen and progesterone fluctuate in the perimenopausal and menopausal period, patients may experience many symptoms including mood disturbances, changes in libido, hot flashes, sleep disturbances, night sweats, fat redistribution, changes in skin tone and character, and vaginal atrophy, among 2

others. Symptoms generally begin insidiously in the 5 to 10 years preceding menopause, which occurs in most women who are nonsmokers around age 50 years. Early symptoms include hot flashes, mood changes, and sleep disturbances. Prevention: There is no known method of preventing menopause, as it is a normal sequela of age. Treatment: Symptoms of perimenopause may be managed with lifestyle counseling. Some women may prefer hormone replacement therapy, though any pharmacotherapy would begin after nonpharmacologic measures. Differential: Lifestyle counseling is appropriate for any patient experiencing symptoms of perimenopause. Pharmacotherapy or additional diagnostic measures are not needed in this patient at this time, though may be indicated at a later point if symptoms are not otherwise manageable or if the diagnosis becomes uncertain.

wrongAnswers.A: Hormone therapy is not the most appropriate next step. Hormone replacement therapy may help manage many symptoms of menopause, especially genitourinary syndrome of menopause, which includes vaginal atrophy, dryness, and dyspareunia. Hormone replacement therapy would be premature in this patient who shows no signs of genitourinary syndrome of menopause, is regularly menstruating, and is experiencing mild hot flashes.
wrongAnswers.C: Pelvic ultrasonography is incorrect. Pelvic ultrasonography can be used to assess for multiple infectious, inflammatory, malignant, and pregnancy-related pelvic conditions, among other structural pelvic abnormalities. Pelvic ultrasonography has no role in assessing perimenopausal symptoms.
wrongAnswers.D: Serotonin norepinephrine reuptake inhibitor therapy is incorrect. Serotonin norepinephrine reuptake inhibitor therapy is indicated in cases of depression or anxiety; however, this patient does not report significant mood symptoms.
wrongAnswers.E: Serum follicle-stimulating hormone concentration is incorrect. The serum follicle-stimulating hormone concentration can be used to assess premature ovarian failure or infertility. Menopause and perimenopause are clinical diagnoses; there is no specific laboratory or imaging study required.

explanationPanel.trap: FSH testing is unnecessary because perimenopause is a clinical diagnosis.

Question: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.subject: Otolaryngology

explanationPanel.whyCorrect:
Educational Objective: Otitis externa results from infection and/or inflammation of the external acoustic meatus, and presents with discharge from the ear canal, decreased hearing, erythema of the external acoustic meatus, and pain with palpation and manipulation of the area, all of which are present in this patient’s case. Evaluation: Otitis externa, infection and/or inflammation of the external acoustic meatus, presents with pain, tenderness to palpation, erythema, edema, and discharge from the external acoustic meatus. Patients often report diminished hearing because of impaired sound conduction. The diagnosis is clinical. Definition: Otitis externa results from bacterial infection, though can be fungal or inflammatory in origin. Otitis externa begins when defenses against infection such as maintaining a dry, atraumatic, mildly acidic environment are compromised. Such compromise can occur from excess use of cotton swabs, digital trauma from fingernails, or prolonged exposure to moisture (eg, swimming). Once cutaneous defenses against infection fail, bacteria can invade the dermis, leading to infection/inflammation. Skin and soft tissue flora, along with Pseudomonas, are the most common causative pathogens. In general, infection remains local and does not spread to the middle ear or surrounding deep tissues/bones. If immunocompromise is present, and especially in patients with poorly controlled diabetes mellitus, the infection can become more severe (known as malignant otitis externa) and present with tissue necrosis, abscess, or osteomyelitis, though such severity is rare. This patient presents with a mild infection, localized to the external canal, without any sign of systemic toxicity or severe features. Prevention: Maintaining external ear hygiene can minimize the risk for otitis externa. This includes avoiding insertion of cotton swabs or other foreign bodies into the ear canal, minimizing digital trauma, and avoiding contaminated water sources or prolonged exposure of the ear to moisture.

Treatment: First-line treatment for mild to moderate cases of otitis externa includes topical antibiotics, antifungals, and anti-inflammatories. Examples include but are not limited to ciprofloxacin-dexamethasone drops and acetic acid solution. Severe or complicated cases may require intravenous antibiotics or debridement; however, such situations are rare outside of cases of immunocompromise or uncontrolled diabetes mellitus. Supportive care to minimize pain is also indicated. Differential: Acute symptoms, localized on examination to the external ear canal, without bony tenderness or middle ear involvement, narrows the differential to acute, uncomplicated otitis externa. Fluid or inflammation posterior to the tympanic membrane would suggest otitis media; however, this is absent on examination. Bony tenderness is necessary to diagnose mastoiditis.

wrongAnswers.A: Acute otitis media is incorrect. Acute otitis media presents with pain, fever, diminished hearing, and evidence of involvement of the middle ear on examination, such as an erythematous tympanic membrane, fluid or pus posterior to the tympanic membrane, and/or decreased tympanic membrane mobility on pneumatic otoscopy. The patient does not present with these features. Further, acute otitis media generally follows a preceding upper respiratory infection.
wrongAnswers.B: Chronic suppurative otitis media is incorrect. Chronic suppurative otitis media describes an ear infection lasting more than 2 to 6 weeks, generally associated with tympanic membrane perforation following persistent or recurrent acute otitis media. Symptoms include pain, discharge from the ear canal, and hearing loss, occurring over weeks to months.
wrongAnswers.C: Mastoiditis is incorrect. Mastoiditis is a complication of untreated acute otitis media in which bacterial infection spreads to the adjacent mastoid, causing osteomyelitis. Mastoiditis presents with fever, posterior ear pain, ear proptosis, and tenderness and erythema over the mastoid process. This patient does not present with these features.
wrongAnswers.E: Otomycosis is incorrect. Otomycosis describes a fungal infection of the ear canal and is less common than bacterial otitis externa. Otomycosis is most common in warm, moist climates, and presents with acute to subacute itching, discharge, and scaling of the external ear. Otomycosis is usually less painful than bacterial otitis externa.

explanationPanel.rule: Otitis externa = ear canal erythema/discharge plus pain with pinna traction and mobile tympanic membrane.
explanationPanel.trap: Otitis media has middle-ear effusion or decreased tympanic membrane mobility.

layer4.rule: Otitis externa = ear canal erythema/discharge plus pain with pinna traction and mobile tympanic membrane.
layer4.trap: Otitis media has middle-ear effusion or decreased tympanic membrane mobility.

questions.stem: A 76-year-old man comes to the emergency department because of a 1-day history of severe right-sided facial pain and swelling, fever, and difficulty swallowing. Two weeks ago, he underwent uncomplicated laparoscopic cholecystectomy. He has hypertension treated with hydrochlorothiazide. He does not smoke cigarettes or use illicit drugs. He drinks two glasses of wine daily. He has been in a monogamous relationship with his male partner for 40 years. The patient’s temperature is 39.3°C (102.7°F), pulse is 92/min, respirations are 20/min, and blood pressure is 110/54 mm Hg. Pulse oximetry on room air shows an oxygen saturation of 99%. Examination shows erythema and severe tenderness to palpation of the right pre-and postauricular areas extending to the mandible. Purulent material is expressed from the parotid duct. The lymph nodes in the submandibular region are small and tender to palpation. The abdominal incision is clean and dry. The remainder of the examination shows no abnormalities. Which of the following is the most likely causal agent?

He drinks two glasses of wine daily. He has been in a monogamous relationship with his male partner for 40 years. The patient’s temperature is 39.3°C (102.7°F), pulse is 92/min, respirations are 20/min, and blood pressure is 110/54 mm Hg. Pulse oximetry on room air shows an oxygen saturation of 99%. Examination shows erythema and severe tenderness to palpation of the right pre-and postauricular areas extending to the mandible. Purulent material is expressed from the parotid duct. The lymph nodes in the submandibular region are small and tender to palpation. The abdominal incision is clean and dry. The remainder of the examination shows no abnormalities. Which of the following is the most likely causal agent?
questions.subject: Infectious Disease

explanationPanel.whyCorrect:
Educational Objective: This patient who underwent cholecystectomy 2 weeks ago presents with facial pain, fever, and purulent drainage from the parotid duct. He most likely has suppurative parotitis, a bacterial infection of the parotid gland most commonly caused by Staphylococcus aureus. Evaluation: Suppurative parotitis is an acute bacterial infection of the parotid gland that is most often caused by S. aureus. It presents with rapid-onset pain, swelling, and tenderness over the parotid gland. Purulent discharge and fever are also common. Definition: Suppurative parotitis is a clinical diagnosis of swelling and inflammation of the parotid gland with associated purulent drainage. Gold standard for diagnosis is culture of the drainage showing infection. Prevention: Prevention strategies for suppurative parotitis include remaining hydrated and consistent oral hygiene practices.

Treatment: Treatment includes sialogogues, antibiotics, and hydration. Often empiric antimicrobial coverage will focus on Staphylococcus species and anaerobic species. Differential: The differential for diagnosis includes sialolithiasis and viral parotitis. Once diagnosed as bacterial infection, the bacteria that are most often causal are Staphylococcus species and anaerobes.

wrongAnswers.A: HIV is incorrect. HIV is a potential cause of increased risk for developing parotitis, but this does not present with purulent drainage from an infected gland.
wrongAnswers.B: Klebsiella pneumoniae is incorrect. Along with other Klebsiella species, it can cause suppurative parotitis, but this is less common than Staphylococcus species.
wrongAnswers.C: Neisseria gonorrhoeae is incorrect. Infection with N. gonorrhoeae typically presents with urethritis and pelvic pain. Extragenital manifestations include pharyngeal infections, arthritis, and dermatitis. It does not classically present with parotitis.
wrongAnswers.D: Paramyxovirus is incorrect. Paramyxovirus infections can present in a variety of clinical manifestations, including rhinosinusitis. They do not, however, cause purulent infections and would be unlikely to cause suppurative parotitis.

explanationPanel.rule: Postoperative/dehydrated older patient with painful parotid swelling and purulent duct drainage = S aureus suppurative parotitis.
explanationPanel.trap: Mumps/paramyxovirus causes viral parotitis, not purulent duct drainage.

questions.stem: A 6-year-old girl is brought to the office because of a 2-week history of diffuse aches in her arms, legs, and back and decreased energy. She has not had changes in appetite during this period. She has no history of serious illness. She is at the 10th percentile for height and weight. Vital signs are within normal limits. The patient appears pale but is not in acute distress. Examination shows no rash or petechiae. Shotty lymph nodes are palpated over the cervical and axillary areas. Cardiopulmonary examination shows no abnormalities. The abdomen is soft; there is no organomegaly. There is diffuse, nonspecific tenderness to palpation over the bones of the upper and lower extremities and back. Examination of the joints shows no swelling, erythema, or warmth. Hemoglobin concentration is 9.4 g/dL (N=11.5–14.5), leukocyte count is 5600/mm³, and platelet count is 106,000/mm2. X-rays of the long bones show osteolytic lesions. Blood smear is shown. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

She has not had changes in appetite during this period. She has no history of serious illness. She is at the 10th percentile for height and weight. Vital signs are within normal limits. The patient appears pale but is not in acute distress. Examination shows no rash or petechiae. Shotty lymph nodes are palpated over the cervical and axillary areas. Cardiopulmonary examination shows no abnormalities. The abdomen is soft; there is no organomegaly. There is diffuse, nonspecific tenderness to palpation over the bones of the upper and lower extremities and back. Examination of the joints shows no swelling, erythema, or warmth. Hemoglobin concentration is 9.4 g/dL (N=11.5–14.5), leukocyte count is 5600/mm³, and platelet count is 106,000/mm2. X-rays of the long bones show osteolytic lesions. Blood smear is shown. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.subject: Hematology/Oncology

explanationPanel.whyCorrect: Educational Objective: This young patient presents with fatigue, lymphadenopathy, pancytopenia, osteolytic lesions, and a peripheral blood smear notable for blasts. Her presentation is consistent with acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL). Evaluation: ALL is a hematologic malignancy resulting from proliferation of lymphoblasts. Classic presentation includes fever, fatigue, weight loss, and pancytopenia. Definition: The gold standard for diagnosis of ALL is a bone marrow biopsy notable for lymphoblasts. While this patient’s peripheral blood has blasts, further studies must be done to make a final diagnosis of the type of acute leukemia and the genetic profile of the malignancy. Prevention: There is no known prevention for ALL. Risk factors include genetic predisposition and environmental exposures. Treatment: Treatment involves chemotherapy and, for some patients, hematopoietic stem cell transplantation. Differential: The differential diagnosis for this young patient with lymphadenopathy, weight loss, and fatigue is broad. It is narrowed by the results of blood work notable for pancytopenia and even further narrowed by a peripheral blood smear notable for blasts. These results rule in ALL as the most likely diagnosis.

wrongAnswers.B: Aplastic anemia is incorrect. While aplastic anemia causes pancytopenia and bone marrow failure, aplastic anemia would not have blasts seen on peripheral blood smear.
wrongAnswers.C: Gaucher disease is incorrect. Gaucher disease is a lysosomal storage disease secondary to deficiency in glucocerebrosidase. Gaucher disease can present with cytopenias, hepatosplenomegaly, and osteolytic lesions; however, it does not have blasts on peripheral blood smear.
wrongAnswers.D: Lead poisoning is incorrect. Lead poisoning can present with sideroblastic anemia, which is a microcytic, hypochromic anemia that occurs secondary to lead inhibition of heme synthesis. Blasts are not present on peripheral blood smear, and it would be abnormal to have pancytopenia from lead poisoning.
wrongAnswers.E: Physiologic anemia is incorrect. This patient has pancytopenia, and, furthermore, physiologic anemia would not present with lymphadenopathy, osteolytic lesions, or blasts on peripheral blood smear.

explanationPanel.rule: Child with bone pain, cytopenias, osteolytic lesions, and blasts on smear = acute lymphoblastic leukemia.
explanationPanel.trap: Gaucher can cause bone lesions/cytopenias but does not show circulating blasts.

layer4.rule: Child with bone pain, cytopenias, osteolytic lesions, and blasts on smear = acute lymphoblastic leukemia.

Question: Which of the following is the most likely underlying cause of this patient's condition?
questions.subject: Endocrinology

explanationPanel.correct: D. Decline in autonomic system regulation
explanationPanel.whyCorrect: Educational Objective: This patient presents with brief, self-resolving episodes of chronic dizziness with positional change, consistent with orthostatic hypotension. Given his risk factors (eg, diabetes mellitus), this likely results from a decline in autonomic system regulation. Evaluation: Symptoms of orthostatic hypotension include light-headedness (often described as dizziness), blurring of the visual fields, and occasionally syncope. This patient has orthostatic hypotension, and he should be evaluated for likely causes by considering volume status, autonomic function, contributory medications, or contributory cardiovascular or neurologic disease. Definition: Orthostatic hypotension is defined as a decrease of 20 mm Hg or more in systolic pressure or a decrease of 10 mm Hg or more in diastolic pressure when moving from a supine to a standing position. Typically, the decreased preload that occurs when a patient moves to a standing position is compensated for by increased sympathetic drive, raising heart rate and increasing vascular tone, to prevent hypotension. However, this mechanism can fail to provide adequate compensation in the setting of hypovolemia, autonomic dysfunction, and neurodegenerative disorders. Diabetes mellitus is a known cause of autonomic neuropathy, which may be a causative feature in this patient’s case. Prevention: Maintaining volume status, controlling blood glucose, modifying contributing medications, and managing any concomitant cardiovascular or neurologic disease can prevent or manage orthostatic hypotension. Treatment: Treatment is based on the underlying cause of the condition and is on a case-by-case basis. In cases of hypovolemia, for example, volume should be repleted. If medications are contributing, the clinician should search for alternate regimens if safe. In cases of autonomic instability or decreased vasomotor tone, midodrine may be a reasonable choice. Differential: This patient’s clinical features of brief, resolving hypotension with position change in the setting of suboptimally controlled diabetes mellitus suggests autonomic instability as the cause.

wrongAnswers.A: Adrenal insufficiency is incorrect. Adrenal insufficiency presents with hemodynamic instability along with hyponatremia, hyperkalemia, and acid-base disturbances. This patient does not have notable abnormalities on serum chemistry apart from hyperglycemia, which is explained by type 2 diabetes mellitus.
wrongAnswers.B: Adverse effect of medication is not the most likely cause. This patient is only on one medication that might contribute to orthostatic symptoms, hydrochlorothiazide, which is a weaker diuretic. His clinical volume status is also within normal limits, making this choice less likely. Medications more likely to cause orthostatic hypotension include but are not limited to β-adrenergic blockers, calcium channel blockers, and loop diuretics.
wrongAnswers.C: Cardiac conduction abnormality is incorrect. This patient does have risk factors for cardiovascular disease; however, he has had an appropriate increase in heart rate with standing and has a normal cardiac examination, arguing against a cardiac cause.
wrongAnswers.E: Decrease in baroreceptor sensitivity is not the most likely cause. Specific testing would be required to assess the patient’s baroreceptor function; however, his heart rate has risen appropriately with standing, suggesting an intact baroreceptor mechanism.
wrongAnswers.F: Dehydration is incorrect. This patient is clinically euvolemic and has no historical features to argue for hypovolemia (eg, recent gastrointestinal illness, recent changes in oral intake), nor does he have any laboratory abnormalities that would be consistent with dehydration (eg, increased creatinine, hemoconcentration, electrolyte derangements).

explanationPanel.rule: Orthostatic hypotension in long-standing poorly controlled diabetes is due to autonomic neuropathy/dysregulation.
explanationPanel.trap: Do not blame mild thiazide use when volume status is normal and neuropathy is present.

questions.stem: A prospective study is conducted to assess the effectiveness of tamoxifen as an adjuvant therapy for premenopausal patients with stage I breast cancer who have undergone lumpectomy. A total of 1000 patients from hospitals around the USA are enrolled. The results of this study are compared with those of a previous study of 400 patients with stage I breast cancer treated with lumpectomy who did not receive tamoxifen. Results of the current study show reduced local recurrence of breast cancer in patients treated with tamoxifen. Which of the following raises the most concern about this study?
questions.stemHtml: A prospective study is conducted to assess the effectiveness of tamoxifen as an adjuvant therapy for premenopausal patients with stage I breast cancer who have undergone lumpectomy. A total of 1000 patients from hospitals around the USA are enrolled. The results of this study are compared with those of a previous study of 400 patients with stage I breast cancer treated with lumpectomy who did not receive tamoxifen. Results of the current study show reduced local recurrence of breast cancer in patients treated with tamoxifen. Which of the following raises the most concern about this study?
choices: Adjuvant therapy (tamoxifen) is not used in controlled trials
Lumpectomy is a poor choice for surgical control
The comparison is with noncontemporaneous controls
The size of the control group is inadequate
The size of the study group provides inadequate power
questions.subject: Biostatistics/Epidemiology

explanationPanel.correct: C. The comparison is with noncontemporaneous controls
explanationPanel.whyCorrect:
Educational Objective: The comparison with noncontemporaneous controls used in this trial is the most concerning factor about this study. Noncontemporaneous controls, or historic cohorts, may be used in cases of rare diseases where it is a challenge to evaluate clinical outcomes, but should not be used in lieu of a clinical trial. Key Concept: Cohort studies are completed to determine the clinical outcomes of patients who undergo a specific treatment or have an exposure. In these studies, a treatment or exposure group may be compared with a control group. In most cases, matched control participants are chosen to evaluate a clinical variable or outcome. Noncontemporaneous controls, or historic cohorts, may be used as a comparison group for clinical outcomes for rare diseases. Explanation: In this study, a cohort is provided adjuvant tamoxifen treatment following lumpectomy. The investigators compare this group with a noncontemporaneous cohort from a previous study, who did not receive tamoxifen following lumpectomy. Based on the scenario, groups cannot be matched for age or other risk factors, which limits the interpretation of the investigator’s findings. Differential: In cohort studies, a clinical variable or treatment may be isolated and compared with a similar comparator arm. When studies do not include a

contemporaneous control group or match patients based on age and other risk factors, it limits interpretation of the findings.

wrongAnswers.A: Adjuvant therapy (tamoxifen) is not used in controlled trials is incorrect. The vignette describes a cohort of patients treated with tamoxifen following lumpectomy, compared with a previous cohort of patients treated with lumpectomy alone. In this vignette, the study does not represent a clinical trial and adjuvant cancer treatment may be evaluated in a controlled clinical trial.
wrongAnswers.B: Lumpectomy is a poor choice for surgical control is incorrect. Lumpectomy is a breast-conserving excision, which has shown effectiveness in breast cancer treatment. The concerning factor about the study is lack of an adequate, contemporaneous control group.
wrongAnswers.D: The size of the control group is inadequate and the size of the study group provides inadequate power are both incorrect. Prior to the initiation of clinical trials, a sample size calculation is completed to determine an adequate number of participants for the study to achieve a desired power. In this vignette, the study population is larger than historic control population. While the size of these groups is different, interpretation of the study findings remains limited as the control population represents a noncontemporaneous, unmatched comparator group.
wrongAnswers.E: The size of the control group is inadequate and the size of the study group provides inadequate power are both incorrect. Prior to the initiation of clinical trials, a sample size calculation is completed to determine an adequate number of participants for the study to achieve a desired power. In this vignette, the study population is larger than historic control population. While the size of these groups is different, interpretation of the study findings remains limited as the control population represents a noncontemporaneous, unmatched comparator group.

explanationPanel.rule: Using an old unmatched cohort as the control group creates major bias from noncontemporaneous controls.
explanationPanel.trap: Sample-size imbalance matters less than comparing different eras of care.

Pulse is 82/min and irregular, respirations are 12/min, and blood pressure is 142/84 mm Hg. Pulse oximetry on room air shows an oxygen saturation of 96%.
