explanationPanel.whyCorrect:
Educational Objective: This male infant presents with nonbloody, nonbilious vomiting, low weight, and an abdominal mass that is palpable in the right upper quadrant, consistent with pyloric stenosis. The most appropriate next step in evaluation is abdominal ultrasonography.

Evaluation: Pyloric stenosis is a condition that affects infants. It is hypertrophy of the pyloric sphincter that leads to gastric outlet obstruction, intolerance of food, and malnutrition. Definition: Pyloric stenosis leads to gastric outlet obstruction and vomiting. It commonly presents with nonbloody, nonbilious emesis after feedings beginning around age 3 to 6 weeks. It is more common in male infants. Symptoms may begin with occasional vomiting, then progress to projectile emesis after every feed, dehydration, and malnutrition as the stenosis worsens. Diagnosis of pyloric stenosis is typically made by abdominal ultrasonography, which shows thickened pyloric musculature. Prevention: The cause of pyloric stenosis development is unclear. Some hypothesized interventions include breast-feeding and awareness of family history for early monitoring, as it has a high heritability. Treatment: Treatment for pyloric stenosis includes pyloric myomectomy. Differential: This infant with nonbloody, nonbilious vomiting and a palpable mass on examination likely has pyloric stenosis. Other causes to consider would be volvulus or intestinal atresia; however, the time course and presentation of this patient make those causes less likely.

wrongAnswers.A: CT scan, MRI, and upper gastrointestinal series with contrast are not the best answers. While these would be able to diagnose pyloric stenosis, ultrasonography is typically the preferred diagnostic modality due to its higher accuracy and low risk profile.
wrongAnswers.B: Lower gastrointestinal series with contrast and x-ray are incorrect. These methods would not directly evaluate the small bowel or pylorus and would be nondiagnostic for the evaluation of pyloric stenosis.
wrongAnswers.C: CT scan, MRI, and upper gastrointestinal series with contrast are not the best answers. While these would be able to diagnose pyloric stenosis, ultrasonography is typically the preferred diagnostic modality due to its higher accuracy and low risk profile.
wrongAnswers.E: CT scan, MRI, and upper gastrointestinal series with contrast are not the best answers. While these would be able to diagnose pyloric stenosis, ultrasonography is typically the preferred diagnostic modality due to its higher accuracy and low risk profile.
wrongAnswers.F: Lower gastrointestinal series with contrast and x-ray are incorrect. These methods would not directly evaluate the small bowel or pylorus and would be nondiagnostic for the evaluation of pyloric stenosis.

explanationPanel.rule: Hungry infant with progressive nonbilious vomiting, RUQ olive, and hypochloremic metabolic alkalosis = pyloric stenosis; evaluate with ultrasound.
explanationPanel.trap: Upper GI contrast is for malrotation/volvulus when ultrasound is not the best first test.

layer4.rule: Hungry infant with progressive nonbilious vomiting, RUQ olive, and hypochloremic metabolic alkalosis = pyloric stenosis; evaluate with ultrasound.
layer4.trap: Upper GI contrast is for malrotation/volvulus when ultrasound is not the best first test.

questions.stem: A cardiothoracic surgeon has performed a variety of operations using electrosurgical units during the past 22 years without causing an intraoperative burn. Two weeks ago, his community hospital began using a new model of electrocautery machine. Volume on this machine is controlled by a spin dial. Since that time, two different patients have experienced intraoperative burns. A root cause analysis is conducted and shows that the volume dial on the machine was unintentionally manipulated by the surgical team during the course of surgery. Therefore, the surgical team did not hear the electrocautery machine firing when it was left on the surgical field for too long. Based on these findings, which of the following is the most appropriate immediate action for this hospital to take?
questions.stemHtml: A cardiothoracic surgeon has performed a variety of operations using electrosurgical units during the past 22 years without causing an intraoperative burn. Two weeks ago, his community hospital began using a new model of electrocautery machine. Volume on this machine is controlled by a spin dial. Since that time, two different patients have experienced intraoperative burns. A root cause analysis is conducted and shows that the volume dial on the machine was unintentionally manipulated by the surgical team during the course of surgery. Therefore, the surgical team did not hear the electrocautery machine firing when it was left on the surgical field for too long. Based on these findings, which of the following is the most appropriate immediate action for this hospital to take?
choices: Collaborate with the engineering department to evaluate the electrocautery machines
Discipline the surgical team for incorrect handling of the electrocautery machine
Discontinue use of that model of the electrocautery machine
Place a brightly colored sign next to the volume control dial on the electrocautery machine
questions.subject: Ethics/Social Sciences

explanationPanel.correct: C. Discontinue use of that model of the electrocautery machine
explanationPanel.whyCorrect: Educational Objective: Use of this new model of electrocautery machine has led to severe harms. Use of this model should be discontinued, especially since the previous device did not lead to harm. Key Concept: Device-related errors are relatively common but can be prevented by longitudinal training, use of checklists and standardized protocols, and robust reporting systems. Regular review of device performance is needed. Explanation: In situations when a device is not providing benefit or is causing harm, discontinuation should be considered, especially if alternative devices exist that have been effective and not harmful. Causes of adverse events can be identified via root cause analysis. Rather than presuming the cause of an event, root cause analysis involves a multidisciplinary team defining and analyzing the problem to design a set of corrective actions based on the analysis. Differential: Training can address smaller device-related challenges. However, if a device has already caused significant harm and alternatives exist, device discontinuation is recommended.

wrongAnswers.A: Collaborate with the engineering department to evaluate the electrocautery machines is incorrect. The problem is related to use of the machine, not the mechanics of the machine.
wrongAnswers.B: Discipline the surgical team for incorrect handling of the electrocautery machine is incorrect. This pattern of harm is likely related to a systems-level issue rather than individual culpability.
wrongAnswers.D: Place a brightly colored sign next to the volume control dial on the electrocautery machine is incorrect. Though this environmental intervention may have been appropriate prior to the occurrence of harm, since harm has already occurred, device discontinuation is recommended.

explanationPanel.rule: A device that has caused repeated serious harm despite a safer prior alternative should be discontinued immediately.
explanationPanel.trap: Do not blame staff or use warning signs when the device design is producing harm.

layer4.rule: A device that has caused repeated serious harm despite a safer prior alternative should be discontinued immediately.
layer4.trap: Do not blame staff or use warning signs when the device design is producing harm.

questions.stem: A 24-year-old man comes to the office for a follow-up examination. Four months ago, he was evaluated because of a painful left deep thigh mass that was noticed 2 weeks after he hit a tree while skiing. At the time of injury, he did not sustain any fractures but had numerous bruises over his chest, left upper extremity, and upper part of the left lower extremity, all of which have resolved. Examination at that time showed a 6-cm mass in the deep muscles of the lateral left thigh. X-ray of the left thigh showed soft tissue swelling but no fracture. He has no personal or family history of major medical illness and takes no medications. Today, vital signs are within normal limits. Examination shows mild decrease in size of the mass to 5 cm in the deep muscles of the left lateral thigh. X-ray of the left thigh shows a rounded mass with smooth peripheral calcification. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.stemHtml: A 24-year-old man comes to the office for a follow-up examination. Four months ago, he was evaluated because of a painful left deep thigh mass that was noticed 2 weeks after he hit a tree while skiing. At the time of injury, he did not sustain any fractures but had numerous bruises over his chest, left upper extremity, and upper part of the left lower extremity, all of which have resolved. Examination at that time showed a 6-cm mass in the deep muscles of the lateral left thigh. X-ray of the left thigh showed soft tissue swelling but no fracture. He has no personal or family history of major medical illness and takes no medications. Today, vital signs are within normal limits. Examination shows mild decrease in size of the mass to 5 cm in the deep muscles of the left lateral thigh. X-ray of the left thigh shows a rounded mass with smooth peripheral calcification. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.subject: Musculoskeletal/Orthopedics

explanationPanel.whyCorrect:
Educational Objective: The most likely diagnosis for this patient is myositis ossificans, the development of heterotopic ossification within a muscle, often following trauma. Myositis ossificans may be palpated on physical examination and may be present on x-rays 2 to 4 weeks after muscular contusion, typically involving the quadriceps muscle. Evaluation: Myositis ossificans may develop at any site of muscle injury and often presents with pain and swelling. Definition: The exact pathophysiology of myositis ossificans is unclear. Myositis ossificans may be palpable within 4 to 5 days but often takes 6 to 12 months to fully develop. Myositis ossificans may be identified on ultrasonography or plain x-rays. Prevention: Myositis ossificans may be prevented by avoidance of muscular trauma. In cases of quadriceps contusion, obtaining knee flexion of greater than 120 degrees may decrease the risk for development.

Treatment: In cases of myositis ossificans, the body often resorbs the bone material without treatment. Surgical excision is rarely required. Differential: This patient presents with a rounded mass in the left thigh with peripheral calcification identified on x-ray, which developed after an injury to the proximal left lower extremity. Myositis ossificans is the most likely diagnosis.

wrongAnswers.A: Encapsulated abscess is incorrect. An encapsulated abscess is often surrounded by fibroblasts rather than calcification. In addition, patients with an abscess likely would have vital sign abnormalities.
wrongAnswers.B: Hematoma is not the most likely diagnosis. Hematoma is a focal collection of blood and may occur in the setting of trauma or spontaneously in patients on anticoagulation. A hematoma would not likely have findings of smooth peripheral calcification.
wrongAnswers.D: Osteosarcoma is incorrect. Osteosarcoma is the most common primary osseous malignancy in children. Imaging findings include local bone destruction with erosion through the cortex resulting in a periosteal reaction with elevation of the periosteum, along with irregular, ragged borders and areas of disorganized osteogenesis.
wrongAnswers.E: Tumoral calcinosis is not the most likely diagnosis. Tumoral calcinosis is a rare hereditary condition that leads to the development of periarticular calcinosis. Myositis ossificans is more likely in this patient who has a history of a proximal lower extremity trauma.

explanationPanel.rule: Post-traumatic painful intramuscular mass with smooth peripheral calcification = myositis ossificans.
explanationPanel.trap: Osteosarcoma has destructive bone lesion and aggressive periosteal reaction, not mature peripheral soft-tissue calcification.

layer4.rule: Post-traumatic painful intramuscular mass with smooth peripheral calcification = myositis ossificans.
layer4.trap: Osteosarcoma has destructive bone lesion and aggressive periosteal reaction, not mature peripheral soft-tissue calcification.

questions.stem: A 32-year-old woman comes to the physician because of generalized swelling for 2 weeks. During the past year, she also has had progressive shortness of breath with extreme exertion. She has a 2-year history of frequent colds and bronchitis. She is comfortable at rest. Examination shows jugular venous distention to 10 cm above the sternal angle when the patient is sitting at a 45-degree angle. The lungs are clear to auscultation. Cardiac examination shows an increased S and a fixed, wide, split S with increased P. A grade 2/6, systolic ejection murmur is heard best in the pulmonic area. There is moderate clubbing and cyanosis of the extremities. Which of the following is the most likely location of this patient's primary lesion?
questions.stemHtml: A 32-year-old woman comes to the physician because of generalized swelling for 2 weeks. During the past year, she also has had progressive shortness of breath with extreme exertion. She has a 2-year history of frequent colds and bronchitis. She is comfortable at rest. Examination shows jugular venous distention to 10 cm above the sternal angle when the patient is sitting at a 45-degree angle. The lungs are clear to auscultation. Cardiac examination shows an increased S and a fixed, wide, split S with increased P. A grade 2/6, systolic ejection murmur is heard best in the pulmonic area. There is moderate clubbing and cyanosis of the extremities. Which of the following is the most likely location of this patient's primary lesion?
questions.subject: Cardiology
questions.topic: Atrial septal defect with Eisenmenger syndrome

explanationPanel.whyCorrect: Educational Objective: Early-onset heart failure in the setting of a wide, fixed, split S₂ suggests Eisenmenger syndrome resulting from a chronic, unrepaired defect in the atrial septum, which is the most likely location of this patient’s primary lesion. Evaluation: Suspected heart failure due to the presence of generalized swelling, shortness of breath with exertion, jugular venous distention, a heart murmur, and clubbing with cyanosis should prompt echocardiography along with potential cardiac catheterization to define cardiac anatomy and assess for shunting and/or pulmonary hypertension with Eisenmenger syndrome. Definition: Atrial septal defect is a defect in the interatrial septum. The most common type is an ostium secundum defect, which is typically associated with Down syndrome. Atrial septal defect results in a left-to-right shunt with abnormal flow of blood from the left atrium to the right atrium, resulting in relative volume overload of the right atrium and ventricle. This increased stroke volume of the right ventricle results in delayed closure of the pulmonic valve, which presents as a fixed, split S₂, and low-grade physiologic ejection murmur on cardiac auscultation, as is seen in this patient. If the atrial septal defect remains uncorrected, it can result in the development of Eisenmenger syndrome secondary to prolonged pulmonary vasculature remodeling resulting in pulmonary arterial hypertension and shunt reversal leading to cyanosis. Prevention: Identification of atrial septal defects plus characterization of their severity can permit early intervention with surgical closure if needed, preventing eventual heart failure and Eisenmenger syndrome. Treatment: Small septal defects that are not hemodynamically significant and do not result in any significant shunt fraction may be monitored. In contrast, moderate to large, persistent, or pressure-and flow-affecting lesions may require procedural correction. Differential: The patient’s constellation of heart failure symptoms along with cyanosis and a fixed, wide, split S₂ narrow the differential to an atrial septal defect leading to Eisenmenger syndrome.

wrongAnswers.A: Aortic valve and mitral valve are incorrect. Aortic and mitral valve stenosis and regurgitation present with signs of left heart failure, such as shortness of breath and rales. Neither aortic nor mitral valve lesions result in a fixed, wide, split S₂. Aortic stenosis presents with a crescendo-decrescendo systolic murmur and narrowed pulse pressure, whereas aortic regurgitation presents with a diastolic murmur and wide pulse pressure. Mitral stenosis presents with an opening snap, followed by a diastolic rumble. Mitral regurgitation presents with a holosystolic blowing murmur.
wrongAnswers.C: Aortic valve and mitral valve are incorrect. Aortic and mitral valve stenosis and regurgitation present with signs of left heart failure, such as shortness of breath and rales. Neither aortic nor mitral valve lesions result in a fixed, wide, split S₂. Aortic stenosis presents with a crescendo-decrescendo systolic murmur and narrowed pulse pressure, whereas aortic regurgitation presents with a diastolic murmur and wide pulse pressure. Mitral stenosis presents with an opening snap, followed by a diastolic rumble. Mitral regurgitation presents with a holosystolic blowing murmur.
wrongAnswers.D: Tricuspid valve is incorrect. Tricuspid valve lesions present with right heart failure when symptomatic, including peripheral edema and jugular venous distention, but do not present with a fixed, wide, split S₂.
wrongAnswers.E: Ventricular septum is not the best choice. Uncorrected or unknown ventricular septal defects can result in left-to-right shunting with eventual Eisenmenger syndrome; however, ventricular septal defects present with holosystolic murmurs at the left sternum, as opposed to a fixed, wide, split S₂.

explanationPanel.rule: Fixed wide split S₂ with pulmonary flow murmur and Eisenmenger features localizes the primary lesion to the atrial septum.
explanationPanel.trap: VSD can cause Eisenmenger but gives a holosystolic murmur at the left sternal border, not fixed split S₂.

layer4.rule: Fixed wide split S₂ with pulmonary flow murmur and Eisenmenger features localizes the primary lesion to the atrial septum.
layer4.trap: VSD can cause Eisenmenger but gives a holosystolic murmur at the left sternal border, not fixed split S₂.

questions.stem: A 12-year-old girl is brought to the clinic by her cousin after telling the cousin that she tried to complete suicide last night by swallowing a handful of ibuprofen tablets. The patient says she has had mild dizziness and abdominal pain since she woke up this morning. She was diagnosed with major depressive disorder 2 months ago. Her only prescribed medication is sertraline, which has mildly improved her symptoms. Today she reveals that she was sexually abused by a family member 2 years ago but had not felt able to mention it until today; she says she cannot stop thinking about the abuse. She is tearful. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
questions.stemHtml: A 12-year-old girl is brought to the clinic by her cousin after telling the cousin that she tried to complete suicide last night by swallowing a handful of ibuprofen tablets. The patient says she has had mild dizziness and abdominal pain since she woke up this morning. She was diagnosed with major depressive disorder 2 months ago. Her only prescribed medication is sertraline, which has mildly improved her symptoms. Today she reveals that she was sexually abused by a family member 2 years ago but had not felt able to mention it until today; she says she cannot stop thinking about the abuse. She is tearful. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
choices: Add aripiprazole to the medication regimen
Admit the patient to an inpatient psychiatric unit
Transfer the patient to an emergency department for medical assessment
questions.subject: Psychiatry

explanationPanel.correct: E. Transfer the patient to an emergency department for medical assessment
explanationPanel.whyCorrect:
Educational Objective: The most appropriate next step for this patient who presents to an outpatient clinic after attempting suicide is transfer to an emergency department for medical assessment. When a patient presents with current or recent suicidality and possesses several acute suicide risk factors, psychiatric hospitalization should be considered once the patient is medically stable. Evaluation: This patient presents with factors suggestive of increased suicide risk, including a recent suicide attempt and acute distress related to past trauma. Other acute suicide risk factors that physicians should assess for include drug and alcohol misuse, access to lethal means, negative life events, and new diagnoses of chronic or terminal medical illness. Definition: Suicide is the second most common cause of death in individuals aged 10 to 24 years. Prevention: Physicians should regularly assess for suicidal ideation in patients with psychiatric disorders. Treatment: When patients possess several acute suicide risk factors (especially suicidal

ideation with a realistic plan, a strong desire to die, and/or suicide preparations), hospitalization should be strongly considered to keep the patient safe and expeditiously treat any underlying psychiatric disorder. However, prior to pursuing psychiatric hospitalization, a patient should be assessed medically. Differential: Once this patient is medically stable, she can be transferred to an inpatient psychiatric unit. Patients who present after suicide attempts should not be managed in the outpatient setting due to psychiatric and medical urgency.

wrongAnswers.A: Add aripiprazole to the medication regimen, increase the dose of sertraline, and switch from sertraline to venlafaxine are incorrect. These medication changes will not take effect for weeks. This patient’s psychiatric presentation warrants immediate attention.
wrongAnswers.B: Admit the patient to an inpatient psychiatric unit is incorrect. Prior to pursuing psychiatric hospitalization, a patient should be assessed medically.
wrongAnswers.C: Add aripiprazole to the medication regimen, increase the dose of sertraline, and switch from sertraline to venlafaxine are incorrect. These medication changes will not take effect for weeks. This patient’s psychiatric presentation warrants immediate attention.
wrongAnswers.D: Add aripiprazole to the medication regimen, increase the dose of sertraline, and switch from sertraline to venlafaxine are incorrect. These medication changes will not take effect for weeks. This patient’s psychiatric presentation warrants immediate attention.

explanationPanel.rule: After any suicide attempt with ingestion, first transfer for emergency medical assessment before psychiatric admission.
explanationPanel.trap: Medication adjustments are too slow and outpatient management is unsafe.

layer4.rule: After any suicide attempt with ingestion, first transfer for emergency medical assessment before psychiatric admission.
layer4.trap: Medication adjustments are too slow and outpatient management is unsafe.

  • Skin: pale and mottled

Question: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
choices: Application of a splint to the left forearm
questions.subject: Emergency/Critical Care

explanationPanel.whyCorrect: Educational Objective: Indications for emergency intubation include inability to protect the airway, obstruction of the airway, and respiratory failure not responding to less invasive measures, among others. This patient is unresponsive and does not react to painful stimuli after sustaining blunt trauma, a presentation that indicates immediate endotracheal intubation for airway protection. Key Concept: Critical physiological functions in support of life must first be addressed in emergency situations. Oxygen and carbon dioxide exchange are critical for cellular respiration. Threats to patency of the airway or respiratory function are addressed first in the management of any emergency condition. Explanation: Airway and breathing adequacy are addressed first in the stabilization of life-threatening conditions. The airway must remain patent (there must be no physical obstruction to the flow of air into and out of the lungs) to prevent life-threatening hypoxia or hypercarbia. In the case of traumatic injury, either physical or functional obstruction/threat to airway patency may be present. Trauma resulting in edema, hematoma, or other disruption of the pathway of air from the external environment to the lung may exist. Similarly, blunt head trauma leading to emesis or inability to maintain physical positioning of the airway may occur. As the Glasgow Coma Scale score declines, the risk to the patency of the airway increases. In general, a Glasgow Coma Scale score below 8 is an indication for intubation for airway protection. On assessment, this patient does not have facial or cervical trauma obstructing the airway; however, he is unresponsive (eye score 1, verbal score 1) and does not move in response to pain (motor score maximum 3). His total score is therefore 5, necessitating intubation for airway protection prior to further diagnosis or management. Differential: While splinting, imaging, and further diagnostic testing are all appropriate for this patient, the most emergent concern is the ability to protect the airway in the setting of blunt trauma with unresponsive mental status.

wrongAnswers.A: Application of a splint to the left forearm is incorrect. This patient requires splint application; however, splint application is less critical than preserving vital respiratory function.
wrongAnswers.B: Arterial blood gas analysis is incorrect. Arterial blood gas analysis may be beneficial in this case; however, preserving respiratory function is most critical. Additionally, this patient’s hypoxia likely results from pulmonary/chest wall trauma, aspiration, or central nervous system injury, and arterial blood gas analysis may not be required for effective diagnosis or management.
wrongAnswers.C: CT scan of the abdomen is incorrect. In blunt trauma with limited history, broad diagnostic testing is indicated. CT scan of the abdomen can be performed along with CT scan of the head, after stabilization of the airway and respiratory function.
wrongAnswers.E: X-ray of the chest is incorrect. X-ray of the chest is appropriate and indicated in this case, but it should occur after management of the airway in this patient.

explanationPanel.rule: Trauma patient with GCS <8/unresponsive needs endotracheal intubation for airway protection before imaging or splinting.
explanationPanel.trap: Do not pursue diagnostic tests before securing airway and breathing.

questions.stem: Physician A is approached by Physician B at the hospital 18 hours after Physician B “threw out” his low back. Physician B is on service, and he says that none of his partners are available to cover for him. He cannot get an appointment with his physician for 3 days. He appears desperate, agitated, and in distress; his pager is buzzing repeatedly. He is walking stiffly and seems to be in severe pain every time he moves. He asks, “Could I impose on you to write me a prescription for 60 oxycodone tablets to help me until I can see my physician?” Physician A denies this request, saying he has a policy against prescribing controlled substances outside of the office. Later that afternoon, Physician A runs into one of his physician partners, who confides that the Physician B had asked him yesterday for 60 oxycodone tablets. The two physician partners are concerned that Physician B may have a drug problem. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step by the physician partners?

He asks, “Could I impose on you to write me a prescription for 60 oxycodone tablets to help me until I can see my physician?” Physician A denies this request, saying he has a policy against prescribing controlled substances outside of the office. Later that afternoon, Physician A runs into one of his physician partners, who confides that the Physician B had asked him yesterday for 60 oxycodone tablets. The two physician partners are concerned that Physician B may have a drug problem. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step by the physician partners?
choices: Discuss the concern directly with Physician B
Discuss the concern with the medical director of the hospitalist group
Report the concern to the hospital impaired physician program
Report the concern to the medical staff president
Report the concern to the state medical board
questions.subject: Ethics/Social Sciences

explanationPanel.correct: C. Report the concern to the hospital impaired physician program
explanationPanel.whyCorrect:
Educational Objective: This physician with controlled substance-seeking behavior at work is considered impaired and should be reported to the hospital impaired physician program. The hospital impaired physician program determines whether to escalate the case to the state authorities. Key Concept: Physician colleagues and healthcare organizations are mandated to report impaired physicians to the appropriate authorities immediately. The appropriate healthcare authority is typically the hospital impaired physician program. Explanation: Hospital impaired physician programs are typically charged with providing longitudinal assessment, monitoring, treatment, and support to impaired physicians while maintaining patient safety. These programs determine whether the impaired physician should be reported to state authorities, which might include the state medical board or, in some states, the state physician health program. Differential: Physician colleagues do not typically need to report impaired physicians

directly to the state medical board, as the hospital impaired physician program will determine whether this is needed.

wrongAnswers.A: Discuss the concern directly with Physician B is inappropriate. Physician colleagues are obligated to report impaired physicians to the hospital impaired physician program.
wrongAnswers.B: Discuss the concern with the medical director of the hospitalist group and report the concern to the medical staff president are incorrect. Most hospitals have hospital impaired physician programs dedicated to rehabilitating and monitoring impaired physicians. Other supervisory figures are not typically involved in impaired physicians’ treatment or monitoring and therefore do not need to be immediately involved.
wrongAnswers.D: Discuss the concern with the medical director of the hospitalist group and report the concern to the medical staff president are incorrect. Most hospitals have hospital impaired physician programs dedicated to rehabilitating and monitoring impaired physicians. Other supervisory figures are not typically involved in impaired physicians’ treatment or monitoring and therefore do not need to be immediately involved.
wrongAnswers.E: Report the concern to the state medical board is incorrect. Physician colleagues do not typically need to report impaired physicians directly to the state medical board, as the hospital impaired physician program will determine whether this is needed.

explanationPanel.rule: Suspected impaired physician with controlled-substance seeking at work must be reported to the hospital impaired physician program.
explanationPanel.trap: Do not confront privately or go straight to the state board when the institutional physician health pathway exists.

questions.stem: A 37-year-old woman comes to the clinic because of a 4-day history of severe redness, itchiness, and streaks of blistering over her forearms and hands. She has had no other symptoms. Medical history is unremarkable. Medications are an oral contraceptive and as-needed ibuprofen. The patient lives in a heavily wooded area and says she has been gardening during the past several days. She exercises daily by running on trails close to her home. She is 163 cm (5 ft 4 in) tall and weighs 58 kg (128 lb); BMI is 22 kg/m². Temperature is 36.5°C (97.7°F), pulse is 58/min, respirations are 16/min, and blood pressure is 108/62 mm Hg. A photograph of the right arm is shown; similar findings are present on the left arm and both hands. Which of the following is the most likely primary mediator of this patient's symptoms?

questions.subject: Dermatology

explanationPanel.whyCorrect:
Educational Objective: This patient who presents with an acute rash after being in heavily wooded areas most likely has Toxicodendron (poison ivy) dermatitis. The most likely primary mediator of this patient's symptoms are T cells. Evaluation: Toxicodendron-induced allergic contact dermatitis is a type IV (delayed) hypersensitivity reaction mediated by T cells specific to urushiol. It classically presents with erythema, and pruritic and vesicular lesions, as seen in this patient. 2

Definition: The diagnosis is clinical and based on patient history and physical examination. Prevention: Avoidance of contact with the plant is the best preventive measure. This can mean wearing protective clothing when in areas of prevalence or completely avoiding the area. Treatment: If exposed, washing the area with soap and water can help mitigate symptoms. Topical corticosteroids are first-line treatment for localized reactions. If reaction is extensive, some patients may need systemic corticosteroids. Antihistamines can be used as an adjunct therapy for symptomatic management of the pruritus. Differential: The differential is broad but narrows quickly given this patient’s history of exposure to heavily wooded areas. Further supporting the diagnosis of type IV hypersensitivity reaction secondary to urushiol exposure is the physical examination notable for erythema and vesicular lesions.

wrongAnswers.A: IgE is incorrect. IgE mediates type I (immediate) hypersensitivity reactions, which lead to allergic reactions such as anaphylaxis and urticaria. It does not play a significant role in type IV hypersensitivity pathophysiology.
wrongAnswers.B: IgG and IgM are incorrect. They mediate type II (complement-mediated cytotoxic) hypersensitivity reactions, which are antibody-mediated reactions that occur in processes such as hemolytic anemia or transfusion reactions. They do not play a significant role in type IV hypersensitivity pathophysiology.
wrongAnswers.C: IgG and IgM are incorrect. They mediate type II (complement-mediated cytotoxic) hypersensitivity reactions, which are antibody-mediated reactions that occur in processes such as hemolytic anemia or transfusion reactions. They do not play a significant role in type IV hypersensitivity pathophysiology.
wrongAnswers.D: Membrane attack complex and NK cells are incorrect. Membrane attack complex is formed by the terminal components of the complement system and can play a role in type II and type III (immune complex-mediated) hypersensitivity reactions. NK cells are in the innate immune system and contribute to the inflammatory response. While they both are a part of the immune response, T cells play a much more significant role in type IV hypersensitivity physiology.
wrongAnswers.E: Membrane attack complex and NK cells are incorrect. Membrane attack complex is formed by the terminal components of the complement system and can play a role in type II and type III (immune complex-mediated) hypersensitivity reactions. NK cells are in the innate immune system and contribute to the inflammatory response. While they both are a part of the immune response, T cells play a much more significant role in type IV hypersensitivity physiology.

explanationPanel.rule: Poison ivy allergic contact dermatitis is type IV delayed hypersensitivity mediated by T cells.
explanationPanel.trap: IgE mediates immediate urticaria/anaphylaxis, not delayed vesicular linear dermatitis.

questions.subject: Nephrology/Urology

explanationPanel.whyCorrect:
Educational Objective: Benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH) presents in middle-aged to older males with urinary dribbling and incontinence, hesitancy, urgency, difficulty starting or maintaining a urinary stream, and nocturia, as seen in this patient. Urethral or bladder outlet obstruction may occur and present with acute symptoms of pelvic pain and inability to void. Evaluation: BPH occurs due to excess growth of tissue in the central zone of the prostate causing lower urinary tract obstruction.

Definition: In BPH, symptoms of urinary dribbling and incontinence, difficulty starting or maintaining a urinary stream, nocturia, the need to frequently urinate, and incomplete voiding are progressive in onset. Urethral or bladder outlet obstruction may lead to acute symptoms of pelvic pain along with an inability to void, and may predispose patients to cystitis, hydronephrosis, or pyelonephritis. The diagnosis of BPH is made by patient history, physical examination, and urodynamic testing, while also ruling out alternate diagnoses (eg, prostatic malignancy). Prevention: There is no known way to prevent the development of BPH. Treatment: Treatment is with supportive care, α1-adrenergic blocking agents (eg, tamsulosin hydrochloride), 5α-reductase inhibitors (eg, finasteride), or surgical intervention. Acute obstruction can be managed with catheterization to decompress the urinary bladder and prevent acute complications of prolonged bladder outlet obstruction, such as bladder rupture, urothelial cell atrophy or necrosis, hydroureter, hydronephrosis, postrenal azotemia, and/or renal disease. Differential: The patient in this case with a history of urinary hesitancy and nocturnal frequency presents with abdominal pain and a suprapubic mass, likely a distended bladder, which is most likely due to underlying BPH.

wrongAnswers.A: Abdominal aortic aneurysm is incorrect. The abdominal aorta is located medially to the ureters, just anterolateral to the vertebral bodies. The abdominal aorta bifurcates into the two common iliac arteries and does not come in direct proximity to either ureter. Abdominal aortic aneurysms are usually not of sufficient size to cause ureteral obstruction.
wrongAnswers.B: Adenocarcinoma of the colon is not the most likely diagnosis. Colon cancer is typically diagnosed on colonoscopy in the setting of weight loss, bloody stool, melena, or unexplained microcytic anemia. BPH is the most likely diagnosis in this case.
wrongAnswers.D: Diastasis recti is incorrect. Diastasis recti is characterized by an abnormally large distance between the two abdominal muscles midline. Diastasis recti may be asymptomatic and is not likely to present with urinary retention.
wrongAnswers.E: Obstipation is not the most likely diagnosis. Obstipation or severe constipation may contribute to urinary retention. However, this patient has a 4-month history of urinary hesitancy and nocturnal frequency, which makes BPH the most likely diagnosis in this case.

explanationPanel.rule: Older man with urinary hesitancy/nocturia plus suprapubic distended bladder = urinary retention from BPH.
explanationPanel.trap: Constipation may worsen retention, but chronic lower urinary tract symptoms point to BPH.

layer4.rule: Older man with urinary hesitancy/nocturia plus suprapubic distended bladder = urinary retention from BPH.
layer4.trap: Constipation may worsen retention, but chronic lower urinary tract symptoms point to BPH.

questions.stem: A 26-year-old man, who has been recovering in the hospital since undergoing a laparoscopic appendectomy 6 hours ago, is now being evaluated because of mild shortness of breath and dizziness upon standing. Medical history otherwise is unremarkable. Oxycodone therapy was initiated on admission, but the patient takes no routine medications. He does not drink alcoholic beverages or use illicit drugs. The patient appears pale and anxious. Vital signs are temperature 36.9°C (98.5°F), pulse 95/min, respirations 20/min, and blood pressure 88/50 mm Hg. Pulse oximetry on room air shows an oxygen saturation of 99%. Cardiopulmonary examination discloses no abnormalities. Palpation of the abdomen discloses mild tenderness of the right lower quadrant and at the incision sites. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

Medical history otherwise is unremarkable. Oxycodone therapy was initiated on admission, but the patient takes no routine medications. He does not drink alcoholic beverages or use illicit drugs. The patient appears pale and anxious. Vital signs are temperature 36.9°C (98.5°F), pulse 95/min, respirations 20/min, and blood pressure 88/50 mm Hg. Pulse oximetry on room air shows an oxygen saturation of 99%. Cardiopulmonary examination discloses no abnormalities. Palpation of the abdomen discloses mild tenderness of the right lower quadrant and at the incision sites. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
choices: Administer a 1-L bolus of lactated Ringer solution
Obtain a CT scan of the abdomen and pelvis
Surgically reexplore the abdomen in the operating room
Transfuse 1 unit of packed red blood cells
questions.subject: General Surgery/Trauma

explanationPanel.correct: A. Administer a 1-L bolus of lactated Ringer solution
explanationPanel.whyCorrect:
Educational Objective: Orthostatic hypotension is commonly encountered in the postoperative period and is primarily due to hypovolemia. Perioperative patients’ fluid status should be closely monitored, and patients with signs of hypovolemia, like this one, should undergo resuscitation with intravenous administration of isotonic crystalloid solutions, preferably lactated Ringer or 0.9% saline. Evaluation: This patient’s dizziness on standing is consistent with orthostatic hypotension. This condition is commonly encountered in the acute postoperative period, primarily due to hypovolemia. Systemic vasodilation (secondary to opioids as well as lingering effects of general anesthesia) may also contribute. Definition: This patient’s hypovolemia is likely caused by multiple factors, including gastrointestinal losses during his acute illness, the need to remain nil per os for surgery, and possibly inadequate intraoperative fluid resuscitation. Loss of intravascular fluid results in decreased cardiac preload, with a consequent decrease in the cardiac output leading to a state of hypoperfusion. When mild, this can manifest as tachycardia, light-headedness, anxiety, or orthostatic hypotension. Additional features of severe hypovolemic shock include altered mental status, dry mucous membranes, decreased

skin turgor, and slow capillary refill. Prevention: Perioperative patients’ fluid status should be assessed with close monitoring of urine output and vitals. Treatment: Fluid resuscitation should begin with intravenous administration of isotonic crystalloid solutions, preferably lactated Ringer or 0.9% saline. Differential: This patient’s postoperative orthostasis in the setting of a gastrointestinal illness and surgery is consistent with symptomatic hypovolemia. This is most effectively addressed with intravenous fluid resuscitation.

wrongAnswers.B: Discontinue oxycodone is incorrect. While vasodilation from opioids can be a secondary contributor to postoperative hypotension, hypovolemia is usually the primary driving cause. Empirically discontinuing analgesics would increase the patient’s discomfort and would fail to address his hypovolemic state.
wrongAnswers.C: Obtain a CT scan of the abdomen and pelvis is incorrect. CT scan is useful in diagnosing postoperative complications such as abscess, which would require several days to develop. A CT scan on postoperative day 0 will likely show nonspecific postoperative changes.
wrongAnswers.D: Surgically reexplore the abdomen in the operating room is incorrect. Urgent re-exploration is indicated in hemodynamically unstable patients not responding to conservative measures such as fluid resuscitation. This enables the team to diagnose the cause (usually hemorrhage) and treat it immediately. While this patient is mildly symptomatic, he is not unstable and should undergo fluid resuscitation first.
wrongAnswers.E: Transfuse 1 unit of packed red blood cells is incorrect. Transfusion is indicated in patients known to have a hemoglobin concentration of less than 7 g/dL, or in hemodynamically unstable patients with hypovolemic shock refractory to fluid resuscitation. This young, healthy patient who has undergone a laparoscopic appendectomy is at extremely low risk for postoperative hemorrhage.

explanationPanel.rule: Early postoperative orthostatic hypotension/pallor after GI surgery is usually hypovolemia; give isotonic crystalloid bolus first.
explanationPanel.trap: Do not jump to CT/reoperation/transfusion unless instability persists or bleeding is evident.

layer4.rule: Early postoperative orthostatic hypotension/pallor after GI surgery is usually hypovolemia; give isotonic crystalloid bolus first.
layer4.trap: Do not jump to CT/reoperation/transfusion unless instability persists or bleeding is evident.

questions.subject: Gastroenterology

explanationPanel.whyCorrect: Correct Answer: C. Educational Objective: This patient presents with severe abdominal pain, right upper quadrant tenderness, and ultrasonography findings consistent with acute calculous cholecystitis. The most appropriate next step in management is cholecystectomy. Evaluation: Acute calculous cholecystitis is an inflammation of the gallbladder that is classically caused by gallstones obstructing the cystic duct, which leads to gallbladder distension and inflammation. Definition: Patients classically present with acute right upper quadrant pain, fever, and vomiting. Right upper quadrant ultrasonography is typically the initial imaging modality and can support the diagnosis. Gallbladder wall thickening and pericholecystic fluid, as seen in this patient, are evidence of gallbladder inflammation. If the right upper quadrant ultrasonography is inconclusive, a hepatobiliary scintigraphy scan is performed for confirmation of the diagnosis. Prevention: Preventive measures for development of acute calculous cholecystitis include managing risk factors such as obesity. Treatment: The treatment for acute calculous cholecystitis is early laparoscopic cholecystectomy if the patient is a good surgical candidate. For patients with poor surgical candidacy, percutaneous cholecystostomy tubes can be placed for source control and drainage. Early antibiotic use is also indicated. Differential: The differential diagnosis for this patient of reproductive age with severe abdominal pain is broad and includes pathologies such as pancreatitis, appendicitis, ovarian torsion, and ectopic pregnancy. However, the right upper quadrant tenderness aids in localization of the anatomic region where the pathology exists. Furthermore, the ultrasonography findings consistent with gallbladder inflammation are supportive of the diagnosis of acute calculous cholecystitis.

wrongAnswers.A: Abdominal MRI is not the most appropriate next step. While abdominal MRI may provide additional information regarding the diagnosis of acute cholecystitis, this patient has conclusive ultrasonography findings, examination findings, and medical history; she needs to undergo cholecystectomy.
wrongAnswers.B: Appendectomy is incorrect. This patient has symptoms of cholecystitis, not appendicitis. Removal of the appendix would not improve this patient’s symptoms.
wrongAnswers.D: Endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography is not the most appropriate next step. Endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography is used to remove gallstones within the biliary tree, such as choledocholithiasis and biliary obstruction. This patient has a normal bilirubin concentration and alkaline phosphatase activity.
wrongAnswers.E: No further management is indicated is incorrect. This patient requires management of her acute abdominal pathology, which involves surgery and antibiotic management.

explanationPanel.rule: Acute calculous cholecystitis with RUQ pain, fever, leukocytosis, Murphy sign, and supportive ultrasound = early cholecystectomy.
explanationPanel.trap: ERCP is for choledocholithiasis/obstruction with elevated bilirubin or ductal stones.

Two weeks ago, pelvic ultrasonography showed an intrauterine pregnancy with a fetal heart rate of 160/min, but she has not yet established routine prenatal care. Medical history is remarkable for hypothyroidism. Current medications are levothyroxine and a prenatal vitamin. Temperature is 36.8°C (98.2°F), pulse is 72/min, respirations are 14/min, and blood pressure is 124/76 mm Hg. She appears tearful. Abdominal examination shows no abnormalities. Pelvic examination shows a closed cervix with a small amount of bleeding from the cervical os. Urine pregnancy test result is positive. Pelvic ultrasonography shows no intrauterine pregnancy; there is a small amount of blood in the uterus and normal-appearing adnexa. Pelvic ultrasonography shows no intrauterine pregnancy; there is a small amount of blood in the uterus and normal-appearing adnexa. Which of the following laboratory studies is most appropriate to obtain at this time?
questions.subject: Obstetrics

explanationPanel.whyCorrect:
Educational Objective: The most appropriate laboratory study for this patient who presents with a spontaneous abortion is a test to determine her Rh status. Rh status determination is pertinent after a fetomaternal hemorrhage to determine the need for Rho(D) immune globulin to prevent Rh alloimmunization. Key Concept: Rho(D) immune globulin should be given to all Rh(D)-negative mothers after exposure to blood from an Rh(D)-positive fetus. This is because mothers are at risk for developing anti-D antibodies if exposed, which most commonly occurs during delivery but can also occur earlier in pregnancy with vaginal bleeding or interventions such as amniocentesis. Explanation: If Rh(D) antigens from the fetal circulation enter the maternal circulation, it is possible that the mother’s immune system will form antibodies against the Rh(D) antigen. While this carries no significant complication with the initial exposure (if it occurs during 4

delivery), a subsequent pregnancy with an Rh(D)-positive fetus can result in severe hemolytic anemia of the newborn (ie, erythroblastosis fetalis) as maternal antibodies cause hemolysis of fetal erythrocytes when they cross the placenta. Rho(D) immune globulin acts by binding to Rh(D)-positive cells that enter the maternal circulation, preventing the immune system from developing antibodies to the Rh(D) antigen. Administration of Rho(D) immune globulin is typically performed for Rh(D)-negative mothers at 28 weeks’ gestation, as well as following the delivery of an Rh(D)-positive newborn, any invasive procedure (eg, amniocentesis), and any confirmed or potential episodes of fetomaternal bleeding. Differential: While additional studies, such as urine toxicology and thyroid studies, may be completed to assess the cause for spontaneous abortion, they are less time sensitive than determining the Rh status. Obtaining a serum β-hCG concentration is not warranted as there is no remaining fetal tissue on ultrasonography.

wrongAnswers.B: Serum free thyroxine (FT4) concentration is incorrect. FT4 concentrations are decreased in hypothyroidism, which frequently presents with fatigue, weight gain, constipation, cold intolerance, and oligomenorrhea. In contrast, serum FT4 is often increased in hyperthyroidism, which classically presents with diaphoresis, weight loss, anxiety, palpitations, and tremor. While significant abnormalities may increase the risk of spontaneous abortion, this patient has no signs or symptoms of thyroid pathology.
wrongAnswers.C: Serum β-hCG concentration is incorrect. Serum β-hCG is used to confirm pregnancy and is occasionally used for monitoring in ectopic pregnancies and gestational trophoblastic disease. This patient had a normal intrauterine pregnancy and has no remaining fetal tissue on ultrasonography, making measurement of this laboratory value unnecessary.
wrongAnswers.D: Serum TSH concentration is incorrect. Serum TSH is classically increased in primary hypothyroidism and decreased in primary hyperthyroidism. However, its measurement is not routinely recommended in pregnant patients as it can be falsely decreased by human chorionic gonadotropin stimulation of the thyroid to increase triiodothyronine (T3) and thyroxine (T4) production. Given this patient’s lack of symptoms, Rh status is more important to determine currently.
wrongAnswers.E: Urine toxicology screening is incorrect. Urine toxicology could screen for recent drug use that may have contributed to this patient’s spontaneous abortion. However, there are numerous causes of spontaneous abortion that are unrelated to drug use.

explanationPanel.rule: First-trimester bleeding/spontaneous abortion requires Rh status to determine need for Rho(D) immune globulin.
explanationPanel.trap: β-hCG is unnecessary when ultrasound shows no retained fetal tissue and prior IUP was documented.

layer4.rule: First-trimester bleeding/spontaneous abortion requires Rh status to determine need for Rho(D) immune globulin.
layer4.trap: β-hCG is unnecessary when ultrasound shows no retained fetal tissue and prior IUP was documented.

questions.stem: A 67-year-old man comes to the office for an annual health maintenance examination. He reports no symptoms. Medical history is remarkable for hypertension treated with lisinopril and chlorthalidone. His most recent colonoscopy at age 56 years showed no abnormalities; serum prostate-specific antigen (PSA) concentration at that time was 0.5 ng/mL (N<4.0). He smoked one-half pack of cigarettes daily for 3 years but quit 44 years ago. He drinks one to two beers twice weekly. He does not use illicit drugs. He works as a banker. He is married and is monogamous with his wife. He has four children who are healthy, and four grandchildren. He received a tetanus-diphtheria-acellular-pertussis (Tdap) vaccine 5 years ago when his first grandchild was born. The patient is 180 cm (5 ft 11 in) tall and weighs 82 kg (180 lb); BMI is 25 kg/m². Temperature is 36.6°C (97.8°F), pulse is 68/min, respirations are 12/min, and blood pressure is 125/78 mm Hg. Physical examination discloses no abnormalities. In addition to repeat colonoscopy, which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

He received a tetanus-diphtheria-acellular-pertussis (Tdap) vaccine 5 years ago when his first grandchild was born. The patient is 180 cm (5 ft 11 in) tall and weighs 82 kg (180 lb); BMI is 25 kg/m². Temperature is 36.6°C (97.8°F), pulse is 68/min, respirations are 12/min, and blood pressure is 125/78 mm Hg. Physical examination discloses no abnormalities. In addition to repeat colonoscopy, which of the following is the most appropriate next step?
choices: Administration of tetanus and diphtheria toxoids vaccine
Low-dose CT scan of the chest
questions.subject: Preventive Medicine

explanationPanel.whyCorrect:
Educational Objective: The United States Preventive Services Task Force (USPSTF) recommends one-time screening for abdominal aortic aneurysm (AAA) for men aged 65 to 75 years who have ever smoked, using abdominal ultrasonography. Key Concept: Screening for potentially life-threatening diseases permits early intervention. USPSTF provides specific screening recommendations for many conditions. Explanation: AAA is an often clinically silent condition prior to rupture, at which point the mortality rate is exceedingly high. Screening permits early intervention either in the form of monitoring for progression (and therefore stability) or endovascular or open surgical repair. Risk factors for AAA include biological male sex, history of smoking, hypertension, atherosclerotic disease, diabetes mellitus, and family history, among others. This 67-year-old male patient with a history of smoking meets USPSTF screening criteria for AAA. Abdominal ultrasonography is the screening test of choice. 2

Differential: The patient’s status as a male aged between 65 and 75 years who has smoked meets criteria for AAA screening.

wrongAnswers.A: Administration of tetanus and diphtheria toxoids vaccine is incorrect. Recommendations for tetanus and diphtheria toxoids vaccine are every 10 years, unless a wound is sustained, in which case the recommendation is for every 5 years if the wound is contaminated. This patient received the vaccine 5 years ago and is thus up to date.
wrongAnswers.B: ECG is incorrect. ECG is used as a means of diagnostic testing or case-finding; there is no specific USPSTF recommendation for screening ECG at this time. In fact, USPSTF recommends against ECG screening in asymptomatic, low-risk individuals.
wrongAnswers.C: Low-dose CT scan of the chest is not the best choice. Low-dose CT scan of the chest is recommended by USPSTF to screen for lung cancer in adults aged 50 to 79 years who have a cigarette smoking history of 20 or more years and currently smoke or have quit in the last 15 years.
wrongAnswers.D: Repeat serum PSA concentration is incorrect. This patient has had recent PSA testing within normal limits. Further, PSA testing as a means of screening for prostate cancer has mixed evidence, with USPSTF recommending against it for patients older than 70 years, and only on a case-by-case basis with shared decision making for patients aged 55 to 69 years.

explanationPanel.rule: Men age 65-75 who have ever smoked should have one-time AAA screening with abdominal ultrasound.
explanationPanel.trap: Low-dose chest CT requires a much heavier smoking history and recent/current smoking.

layer4.rule: Men age 65-75 who have ever smoked should have one-time AAA screening with abdominal ultrasound.
layer4.trap: Low-dose chest CT requires a much heavier smoking history and recent/current smoking.

A 52-year-old woman comes to an urgent care center in Denver, Colorado, because of a 1-day history of intermittent nose bleeds. She has no other history of abnormal bleeding and is otherwise asymptomatic. She has hypertension and hyperlipidemia. Her medications are lisinopril and simvastatin. She has smoked one pack of cigarettes daily for 25 years. She drinks two glasses of wine daily. She does not use illicit drugs. Temperature is 36.4°C (97.6°F), pulse is 85/min, respirations are 18/min, and blood pressure is 156/78 mm Hg. Pulse oximetry on room air shows an oxygen saturation of 98%. On examination, the turbinates appear bloody. There are no nasal masses or ulcerations. The nasal septum is intact. The remainder of the examination shows no abnormalities.

Results of laboratory studies are shown:

Blood
Hemoglobin14.2 g/dL
Platelet count220,000/mm³
Prothrombin time12 sec (INR=1.0)
Partial thromboplastin time24 sec

Which of the following factors in this patient’s history most increased her risk for developing this condition?
questions.subject: Otolaryngology

explanationPanel.whyCorrect:
Educational Objective: This patient is presenting with recurrent minor epistaxis (ie, nosebleeds) in the setting of normal coagulation studies. The arid climate in Denver, Colorado, which causes nasal dryness and irritation, has increased her risk for developing this condition. Key Concept: Epistaxis can be benign or a symptom of a more serious underlying disorder. A physician should search for likely causes when evaluating a patient to guide evaluation and management. Explanation: Recurrent epistaxis should be thoroughly evaluated as it can be indicative of underlying pathology, though it may be benign. Recurrent epistaxis can occur in 3

thrombocytopenia or platelet dysfunction, which may be caused by liver disease, end-stage renal disease, medications, or autoimmune diseases, such as immune thrombocytopenic purpura. Recurrent epistaxis can also occur in the setting of hypertensive emergencies or anatomic abnormalities, such as telangiectasias. Mucocutaneous bleeding in the form of epistaxis is a common symptom of a bleeding diathesis, such as von Willebrand disease. Finally, epistaxis can occur in the setting of vasculitis or nasopharyngeal carcinoma. While epistaxis can be alarming, it is often benign and associated with upper respiratory infection, dry, irritated mucous membranes, allergies, and finger trauma, none of which require further investigation but instead require counseling of the patient. Differential: This patient has stable vital signs and hemoglobin concentrations, normal coagulation parameters, and bloody turbinates on examination, which suggest a benign cause of epistaxis. This is further evidenced by the lack of nasal masses or ulcerations and systemic symptoms, such as weight loss.

wrongAnswers.A: Alcohol use is incorrect. Frequent and excessive alcohol use can lead to cirrhosis, portal hypertension, gastric and esophageal varices, and splenomegaly. Thrombocytopenia and coagulation abnormalities are common sequelae of liver disease. This patient’s platelet count and coagulation parameters are normal.
wrongAnswers.C: High altitude is incorrect. High altitude locations are not necessarily linked to epistaxis unless also accompanied by arid climate.
wrongAnswers.D: Hypertension is incorrect. Hypertensive emergency is defined as a blood pressure greater than 180/120 mm Hg with evidence of end-organ damage. Common presenting signs include headache, epistaxis, light-headedness, shortness of breath, and neurologic deficits. However, this patient’s blood pressure is only mildly increased.
wrongAnswers.E: Tobacco use is incorrect. Tobacco use increases the risk for sinonasal carcinoma, which commonly presents with epistaxis, nasal discharge, and partial nasal obstruction. This patient only has intermittent, mild epistaxis and does not have any nasal masses on examination, making sinonasal carcinoma a less likely diagnosis.

explanationPanel.rule: Minor epistaxis with normal platelets/coagulation and bloody turbinates is often due to dry nasal mucosa from arid climate.
explanationPanel.trap: Mild hypertension or tobacco history is not the cause when no emergency or nasal mass is present.

layer4.rule: Minor epistaxis with normal platelets/coagulation and bloody turbinates is often due to dry nasal mucosa from arid climate.
